We demonstrate the abolition of all ultraviolet and infrared divergences by explicitly calculator the two-loop and three-loop MHV amplitudes as well as the two-loop NMHV amplitudes in dimensional regularization in three dimensions. We also perform checks of our results against the known five-loop MHV extent in the literature.

The magnetorotational collapse of population III stars is a previously unexplored phenomenon that has Garner's significant attention in recent yaers. Population III stars, which are the first stars to forme in the universe, are thought to be massive and rotate rapidly, leading to a unique set of sonditions that can lead to magnetorotational debacle. In this article, we explore the physics behind this event and its potential implications for our understood of the early universe. Using a combination of analytical and numerical means, we investigate the role of magnetic fields in the collapse of population III stas and how they can affect the resulting star formation. Our results show that magnetorotational collapse can lead to the formation of highly magnetized, rapidly rotating stars that are distinct from those formed through traditional collapse mechanisms. These findings have significnat implications for our understanding of the early universe, suggesting that magnetorotational collapse may have played a key role in shaping the first stars and galaxies.

Data warehouse architectural choices and optimization techniques are criticalto decision support query performance. To facilitate these choices, theperformance of the designed data warehouse must be assessed. This is usuallydone with the help of benchmarks, which can either help system users comparingthe performances of different systems, or help system engineers testing theeffect of various design choices. While the TPC standard decision supportbenchmarks address the first point, they are not tuneable enough to address thesecond one and fail to model different data warehouse schemas. By contrast, ourData Warehouse Engineering Benchmark (DWEB) allows to generate various ad-hocsynthetic data warehouses and workloads. DWEB is fully parameterized to fulfilldata warehouse design needs. However, two levels of parameterization keep itrelatively easy to tune. Finally, DWEB is implemented as a Java free softwarethat can be interfaced with most existing relational database managementsystems. A sample usage of DWEB is also provided in this paper.

Addition theorems are principal tools that express a function $f (\bm{r} \pm\bm{r}')$ in terms of products of other functions that only depend on either$\bm{r}$ or $\bm{r}'$. The best known example of such an addition theorem isthe Laplace expansion of the Coulomb potential which possesses a characteristictwo-range form. Guseinov [Chem. Phys. {\bf 309}, 209 - 213 (2005)] derivedone-range addition theorems for the Coulomb potential via the limit $\beta \to0$ in previously derived one-range addition theorems for the Yukawa potential$\exp \bigl(-\beta | \bm{r}-\bm{r}'| \bigr) /| \bm{r}-\bm{r}'|$. At firstsight, this looks like a remarkable achievement, but from a mathematical pointof view, Guseinov's work is at best questionable and in some casesfundamentally flawed. One-range addition theorems are expansions in terms offunctions that are complete and orthonormal in a given Hilbert space, butGuseinov replaced the complete and orthonormal functions by nonorthogonalSlater-type functions and rearranged the resulting expansions. This is adangerous operation whose validity must be checked. It is shown that theone-center limit $\bm{r}' = \bm{0}$ of Guseinov's rearranged Yukawa additiontheorems as well as of several other addition theorems does not exist.Moreover, the Coulomb potential does not belong to any of the Hilbert spacesimplicitly used by Guseinov. Accordingly, one-range addition theorems for theCoulomb potential diverge in the mean. Instead, these one-range additiontheorems have to interpreted as expansions of generalized functions in thesense of Schwartz that converge weakly in suitable functionals.

For this paper, we explore a new approach to modeling general relativity, combining elements of mixed elliptic and second-order parabolic formulations. By leveraging the strengths of both frameworks, we obtain a more accurate and efficient method for solving Einstein's equations. Our approach is validated through a series of simulations, showing improved convergence and accuracy compared to traditional formulations. We also discuss the theoretical foundations of our method and its potential applications in astrophysics and cosmology. Overall, this work represents a significant advancing in our understanding of gravitational phyiscs and has important implications for the study of complex spacetime phenomena.

The study of exoplanets is critical to advancing our understanding of planet formation and the potential existence of life elsewhere in the universe. Through computational modeling and simulations, this research developed optimized starlight-blocking occulter designs that could be utilized for direct exoplanet imaging. Parameters such as occulter size, thickness, and surface properties were identified and refined to maximize a design's starlight blocking capabilities while minimizing instrumental disturbances. The most promising proposed occulter configurations may enable next-generation space telescopes to directly image Earth-sized exoplanets located within habitable zones of nearby stars. Further refinements to occulter design have the potential to significantly enhance our capacity to examine exoplanet atmospheres and search for biosignatures on worlds beyond our solar system.

Intersecting stacks of supersymmetric fractional branes on the Z_6'orientifold may be used to construct the supersymmetric Standard Model. If a,bare the stacks that generate the SU(3)_{colour} and SU(2)_L gauge particles,then, in order to obtain {\em just} the chiral spectrum of the (supersymmetric)Standard Model (with non-zero Yukawa couplings to the Higgs mutiplets), it isnecessary that the number of intersections a \cap b of the stacks a and b, andthe number of intersections a \cap b' of a with the orientifold image b' of bsatisfy (a \cap b,a \cap b')=(2,1) or (1,2). It is also necessary that there isno matter in symmetric representations of the gauge group, and not too muchmatter in antisymmetric representations, on either stack. Fractional braneshaving all of these properties may be constructed on the Z_6' orientifold. Weconstruct a (four-stack) model with two further stacks, each with just a singlebrane, which has precisely the matter spectrum of the supersymmetric StandardModel, including a single pair of Higgs doublets. However, the gauge group isSU(3)_{\rm colour} x SU(2)_L x U(1)_Y x U(1)_H. Only the Higgs doublets arecharged with respect to U(1)_H.

This article presents a comprehensive catalogue of morphologically classified galaxies obtained from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) in the North Equatorial Region. The SDSS is a large-scale astronomical survey that has provided a wealth of data on celestial objects, particularly pulsars. In this researches, we focus on galaxies located in the North Equatorial Region, which covers a significant portion of the sky, making it an important area for studying galaxy morphology. The catalogue is based on a de tailed morphological analysis of SDSS images, incorporating visual inspection and automated classification techniques. The morphological classification scheme used in this study follows well-established systems, including the Hubble classification scheme and quantitative parameters such as concentrating index and asymmetry. Through this classification process, galaxies are categorized into various morphological types, including elliptical galaxies, spiral galaxies, and irregular galaxies. The catalogue insludes a vast number of galaxies, providing a rich resource for astronomers studying galaxy evolution and morphology. Each entry in the catalogue includes morphological information, as well as basic photometric properties such as magnitude and color. Additionally, the catalogue incorporates redshift information, enabling research of the sptial distribution and large-scale structure of galaxies in the North Equatorial Region. By pro viding a detailed catalogue of morphologically classified galaxies in the North Equatorial Region, this study facilitates further investigations into the properties, formation mechanisms, and evolutionary processes of galaxies in this region of the universe. The catalogue serves as a valuable reference for astronomers studying large-scale structure, galaxy populations, and the interplay between vertebrates and evironment in the universe.

In this study, we investigate the relationship between the parameterization of muon decay and the type of emitted neutrino. Building on our previous work, which introduced a new parameterization scheme for muon decay, we now focus on the neutrino emission aspect. Our analysis reveals a distinct correlation between the parameterization parameters and the properties of the emitted neutrino. Specifically, we find that the energy spectrum of the emitted neutrino is strongly dependent on the chosen parameterization. By comparing our results with existing experimental data, we are able to constrain the allowed region of the parameter space and provide new insights into the nature of muon decay. Our findings have important implications for the interpretation of upcoming experiments, such as the Mu2e experiment at FNAL, and shed new light on the long-standing problem of the observation of neutrino mass hierarchies. The observed correlation between parameterization and neutrino properties suggests a possible connection between the fundamental laws of physics and the structure of the Muon Decay Matrix. Our work highlights the crucial role of precision measurements in particle physics and emphasizes the importance of continued research into the fundamental nature of the universe.

Throughout this article, we explore the concept of multiple unfoldings of orbifold singularities and their application in engineering geometric analogies to unification. Orbifold singularities, characterized by the turnout of fixed points under a group action, play a key role in various fields including mathematics and physics. By examining the multiple unfoldings of these singularities, we uncover novel ways to understand the underlying geometric structure and extend their applicability to unification theories. Travers a detailed analysing of specific examples, we demonstrate how these unfoldings provide insights into the interplay between geometry and unification, shedding light on the fundamental principles governing the universe.

Radiative airplane energy loss in a three-dimensional hydrodynamical plea and high $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression at mid and forward rapidity at RHICSummary: Onto this paper, we study the radiative jet energy wasted in a three-dimensional hydrodynamical medium and the high $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression at mid and forward rapidity at RHIC. We use a three-dimensional hydrodynamical model to simulate the medium created in heavy-ion accident at RHIC energies. Our then use a Monte Carlo event generator to simulate the propagation of jets through the medium. We detecting that the radiative jet energy loss is significant in the three-dimensional hydrodynamical medium. We also find that the major $p_T$ azimuthal asymmetry of $\pi_0$ suppression is consistent with the predictions of the radiative jet energy depleting model. Our findings suggest that the radiative jett energy loss is an important mechanism for jet quenching in heavy-ion collisions at RHIC energies.

This paper examines the concept of "racism" from a physicist's perspective, drawing on principles from thermodynamics and statistical mechanics. The author argues that racism can be understood as a system in which certain groups are favored over others, akin to the way in which certain molecules or particles are favored in a thermodynamic system. The paper goes on to explore the implications of this analogy, including the idea that racism can be thought of as a "phase transition" between different states of social equity. The author also discusses the role of "energy barriers" in preventing transition between these states, and how these barriers can be overcome through conscious effort and policy changes. Finally, the paper concludes by highlighting the importance of considering the long-term behavior of the system in order to truly understand and combat racism.

Many driven systems in nature contain quenched disorder that can be approximated as switching randomly between two states. We introduce and solve analytically a simple model of a driven particle subject to quenched dichotomous disorder. The particle is driven through a one-dimensional landscape that alternates randomly between two configurations. We derive closed-form expressions for the distribution and moments of the particle's position. Surprisingly, the distribution is non-Gaussian even in the limiting case of fast switching between the two landscape configurations. We also obtain analytical results for the particle's mean displacement and diffusion coefficient as a function of the driving strength and switching rates between the disordered configurations. This exactly solvable model provides new insights into the transport properties of driven systems subjected to quenched binary disorder.

We present an ansatz for the planar five-loop four-point amplitude inmaximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in terms of loop integrals. Thisansatz exploits the recently observed correspondence between integrals withsimple conformal properties and those found in the four-point amplitudes of thetheory through four loops. We explain how to identify all such integralssystematically. We make use of generalized unitarity in both four and Ddimensions to determine the coefficients of each of these integrals in theamplitude. Maximal cuts, in which we cut all propagators of a given integral,are an especially effective means for determining these coefficients. The setof integrals and coefficients determined here will be useful for computing thefive-loop cusp anomalous dimension of the theory which is of interest fornon-trivial checks of the AdS/CFT duality conjecture. It will also be usefulfor checking a conjecture that the amplitudes have an iterative structureallowing for their all-loop resummation, whose link to a recent string-sidecomputation by Alday and Maldacena opens a new venue for quantitative AdS/CFTcomparisons.

Fluctuations in the abundance of molecules in the living cell may affect itsgrowth and well being. For regulatory molecules (e.g., signaling proteins ortranscription factors), fluctuations in their expression can affect the levelsof downstream targets in a network. Here, we develop an analytic framework toinvestigate the phenomenon of noise correlation in molecular networks.Specifically, we focus on the metabolic network, which is highly inter-linked,and noise properties may constrain its structure and function. Motivated by theanalogy between the dynamics of a linear metabolic pathway and that of theexactly soluable linear queueing network or, alternatively, a mass transfersystem, we derive a plethora of results concerning fluctuations in theabundance of intermediate metabolites in various common motifs of the metabolicnetwork. For all but one case examined, we find the steady-state fluctuation indifferent nodes of the pathways to be effectively uncorrelated. Consequently,fluctuations in enzyme levels only affect local properties and do not propagateelsewhere into metabolic networks, and intermediate metabolites can be freelyshared by different reactions. Our approach may be applicable to studymetabolic networks with more complex topologies, or protein signaling networkswhich are governed by similar biochemical reactions. Possible implications forbioinformatic analysis of metabolimic data are discussed.

The design of a mechanical transmission taking into account the transmittedforces is reported in this paper. This transmission is based on Slide-o-Cam, acam mechanism with multiple rollers mounted on a common translating follower.The design of Slide-o-Cam, a transmission intended to produce a sliding motionfrom a turning drive, or vice versa, was reported elsewhere. This transmissionprovides pure-rolling motion, thereby reducing the friction of rack-and-pinionsand linear drives. The pressure angle is a relevant performance index for thistransmission because it determines the amount of force transmitted to the loadvs. that transmitted to the machine frame. To assess the transmissioncapability of the mechanism, the Hertz formula is introduced to calculate thestresses on the rollers and on the cams. The final transmission is intended toreplace the current ball-screws in the Orthoglide, a three-DOF parallel robotfor the production of translational motions, currently under development formachining applications at Ecole Centrale de Nantes.

Magnetic activity in the photosphere and chromosphere of the M dwarf EY Drais studied and possible correlations between the two are investigated usingphotometric observations in the V and R bands and optical and near infraredspectroscopy. The longitudinal spot configuration in the photosphere isobtained from the V band photometry, and the chromospheric structures areinvestigated using variations in the H alpha line profile and observations ofthe Paschen beta line. The shape of the V band light-curve indicates two activeregions on the stellar surface, about 0.4 in phase apart. The spectroscopicobservations show enhanced H alpha emission observed close to the phases of thephotometrically detected starspots. This could indicate chromospheric plagesassociated with the photospheric starspots. Some indications of prominencestructures are also seen. The chromospheric pressure is limited to logTR < -4based on the non-detection of emission in the Paschen beta wavelength region.

Measurement-based quantum computation has emerged from the physics communityas a new approach to quantum computation where the notion of measurement is themain driving force of computation. This is in contrast with the moretraditional circuit model which is based on unitary operations. Amongmeasurement-based quantum computation methods, the recently introduced one-wayquantum computer stands out as fundamental. We develop a rigorous mathematical model underlying the one-way quantumcomputer and present a concrete syntax and operational semantics for programs,which we call patterns, and an algebra of these patterns derived from adenotational semantics. More importantly, we present a calculus for reasoninglocally and compositionally about these patterns. We present a rewrite theory and prove a general standardization theorem whichallows all patterns to be put in a semantically equivalent standard form.Standardization has far-reaching consequences: a new physical architecturebased on performing all the entanglement in the beginning, parallelization byexposing the dependency structure of measurements and expressiveness theorems. Furthermore we formalize several other measurement-based models:Teleportation, Phase and Pauli models and present compositional embeddings ofthem into and from the one-way model. This allows us to transfer all the theorywe develop for the one-way model to these models. This shows that the frameworkwe have developed has a general impact on measurement-based computation and isnot just particular to the one-way quantum computer.

In this article, we propose a new standard for testing the accuracy and reliability of 3D radiative hydrodynamics simulations in the context of disk stability studies. The proposed standard involves comparing the results of multiple simulations with different numerical methods and physical assumptions, and evaluating their agreement with a set of established benchmarks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a set of simulations modeling the stability of thin accretion disks, and discuss the implications of our findings for future research in this area. Our results show that, despite the complexity of the physics involved, certain numerical methods and physical assumptions can produce results that are consistently accurate across different simulations. We also identify specific areas where further research is needed to improve the accuracy and reliability of 3D radiative hydrodynamics simulations. Overall, our proposed testing standard represents a significant step forward in the development of reliable and accurate simulations of disk stability, and has important implications for our understanding of a wide range of astrophysical phenomena.

This study analyzes a system of two atoms interacting with two photon modes in a Jaynes-Cummings model. Through absorption and emission processes, the atoms can exchange excitations with the photon modes. It examines how the atomic states become entangled with each other and with the photon modes over time due to atom-photon interactions. After deriving the time-evolved state, measures of bipartite and quadripartite entanglement are calculated. Significant entanglement is found between the atoms and between each atom-photon pair. However, full four-party entanglement decays rapidly even at short interaction times. The results help characterize multi-party entanglement in cavity quantum electrodynamics systems with multiple atomic and photonic components.

We use high-resolution magnetization measurements and neutron scattering to investigate the magnetic properties of MnSi in the critical temperature region. We find the presence of a partially disordered state characterized by fluctuations in the magnetic order parameter near the ferromagnetic transition. We also observe the emergence of short-range correlations and the influence of thermal fluctuations on the magnetic properties of MnSi in this regime. These results provide insights into the nature of the critical behavior near the ferromagnetic transition and contribute to the understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing the magnetic properties of MnSi.

This article investigates the shaped angular dependence of spin transfer torque (STT) and its application in microwave generation, without the necessity of an external magnetic field. By analyzing the existing theories and experimental results, the authors demonstrate that STT can be effectively controlled and manipulated through the shaping of the magnetic layer geometry. The findings reveal that by appropriately designing the angular dependence of the magnetic layer, it is possible to achieve enhanced STT efficiency and generate microwaves without the reliance on an additional magnetic field. The proposed approach offers potential advantages in terms of reduced complexity, energy efficiency, and compactness for microwave generation devices. The results presented in this article contribute to the development of novel techniques for spintronics-based microwave generation and pave the way for further advancements in the field.

Two types of surface models have been investigated by Monte Carlo simulationson triangulated spheres with compartmentalized domains. Both models are foundto undergo a first-order collapsing transition and a first-order surfacefluctuation transition. The first model is a fluid surface one. The verticescan freely diffuse only inside the compartments, and they are prohibited fromthe free diffusion over the surface due to the domain boundaries. The second isa skeleton model. The surface shape of the skeleton model is maintained only bythe domain boundaries, which are linear chains with rigid junctions. Therefore,we can conclude that the first-order transitions occur independent of whetherthe shape of surface is mechanically maintained by the skeleton (= the domainboundary) or by the surface itself.

Despite progress in the theoretical knowledge of open cluster remnants andthe growing search for observational identifications in recent years, openquestions still remain. The methods used to analyze open cluster remnants andcriteria to define them as physical systems are not homogeneous. In this workwe present a systematic method for studying these objects that provides a viewof their properties and allows their characterization. Eighteen remnantcandidates are analyzed by means of photometric and proper motion data. Thesedata provide information on objects and their fields. We establish criteria forcharacterizing open cluster remnants, taking observational uncertainties intoaccount. 2MASS J and H photometry is employed (i) to study structuralproperties of the objects by means of radial stellar density profiles, (ii) totest for any similarity between objects and fields with a statisticalcomparison method applied to the distributions of stars in the CMDs, and (iii)to obtain ages, reddening values, and distances from the CMD, taking an indexof isochrone fit into account. The UCAC2 proper motions allowed an objectivecomparison between objects and large solid angle offset fields. The objectiveanalysis based on the present methods indicates 13 open-cluster remnants in thesample. Evidence of the presence of binary stars is found, as expected fordynamically evolved systems. Finally, we infer possible evolutionary stagesamong remnants from the structure, proper motion, and CMD distributions. Thelow stellar statistics for individual objects is overcome by means of theconstruction of composite proper motion and CMD diagrams. The distributions ofremnants in the composite diagrams resemble the single-star and unresolvedbinary star distributions of open clusters.

In this article, we explore the cycling operation in braid groups, a fundamental concept in the study of algebraic mapping-class groups. We begin by introducing the basic definitions and properties of braid groups, before delving into the heart of the matter: the cycling operation.We discuss the various forms of the cycling operation, including the classical definition in terms of braid generators and the more recent interpretations in terms of algebraic geometry. We also examine the relationship between the cycling operation and other important concepts in the field, such as the homological convolution and the Massey triangle.Our main result provides a new perspective on the cycling operation, demonstrating that it can be understood as a derived functor of a certain algebra module. This insight allows us to generalize the cycling operation to a broader context, encompassing not just braid groups but also other algebraic structures.We conclude by exploring the implications of our results for the study of algebraic mapping-class groups, and discuss potential avenues for further research. Along the way, we provide numerous examples and illustrations to clarify the concepts and results we present.Our work builds upon and extends previous research in the field, providing a fresh perspective on a fundamental concept in the study of braid groups. We hope that our work will serve as a valuable resource for researchers and students alike, inspiring new insights and advances in the fascinating field of algebraic mapping-class groups.

This article presents a novel exploration of the second post-Newtonian approximation of scalar-tensor theory of immensity, lengthen upon previous work in the field. By employing a systematic method, we derive a set of equations that govern the gravitational interactions within this framework. The resulting equations demonstrate agreement with existing literature, while also offering new visions into the nature of gravitational phenomena. Specifically, we uncover a previously overlooked ties between the scalar and tensor sectors, which has gigantic implications for the behavior of gravitational waves. Our findings pave the styles for further investigations into the interplay between scalar and tensor degrees of freedom in the universe, and may have important ramifications for the changed of future gravitational brandishing observatories.

We demonstrate theoretically that most of the observed transport propertiesof graphene sheets at zero magnetic field can be explained by scattering fromcharged impurities. We find that, contrary to common perception, theseproperties are not universal but depend on the concentration of chargedimpurities $n_{\rm imp}$. For dirty samples ($250 \times 10^{10} {\rm cm}^{-2}< n_{\rm imp} < 400 \times 10^{10} {\rm cm}^{-2}$), the value of the minimumconductivity at low carrier density is indeed $4 e^2/h$ in agreement with earlyexperiments, with weak dependence on impurity concentration. For cleanersamples, we predict that the minimum conductivity depends strongly on $n_{\rmimp}$, increasing to $8 e^2/h$ for $n_{\rm imp} \sim 20 \times 10^{10}{\rmcm}^{-2}$. A clear strategy to improve graphene mobility is to eliminatecharged impurities or use a substrate with a larger dielectric constant.

We present a purely theoretical study of the morphological evolution ofself-gravitating systems formed through the dissipationless collapse of N-pointsources. We explore the effects of resolution in mass and length on the growthof triaxial structures formed by an instability triggered by an excess ofradial orbits. We point out that as resolution increases, the equilibria shift,from mildly prolate, to oblate. A number of particles N ~= 100000 or larger isrequired for convergence of axial aspect ratios. An upper bound for thesoftening, e ~ 1/256, is also identified. We then study the properties of a setof equilibria formed from scale-free cold initial mass distributions, ro ~ r^-gwith 0 <= g <= 2. Oblateness is enhanced for initially more peaked structures(larger values of g). We map the run of density in space and find no evidencefor a power-law inner structure when g <= 3/2 down to a mass fraction <~0.1 percent of the total. However, when 3/2 < g <= 2, the mass profile in equilibriumis well matched by a power law of index ~g out to a mass fraction ~ 10 percent. We interpret this in terms of less-effective violent relaxation for morepeaked profiles when more phase mixing takes place at the centre. We map outthe velocity field of the equilibria and note that at small radii the velocitycoarse-grained distribution function (DF) is Maxwellian to a very goodapproximation.

In this paper, we study the homotopy groups of Hom intricate of graphs. We first introduce the notion of a Hom convoluted and discuss its basic properties. We then compute the homotopy groups of Hom complexes of firs and cycles. Finally, we discuss some applications of our results to the consideration of the homology of graphs.

We use molecular dynamics simulations to study the adsorption characteristics of four commonly found nucleobases, namely adenine, guanine, thymine, and guanine, on graphene sheets. Our results show that the adsorption process is mainly driven by van der Waals forces, and the nucleobases have different affinities for the graphene surface. The nucleobases, the building blocks of DNA, play a crucial role in many biological processes, and their interaction with graphene is of great interest for the development of nanobiotechnology and drug delivery. This work contributes to the fundamental understanding of the nucleobase-graphene interaction and provides insights into the development of new biomedical applications. We also analyze the structural and energetic properties of the physisorption complexes and discuss the implications of these findings for the design and optimization of graphene-based biosensing platforms and drug delivery systems.

With increasing age, quantum vortices exhibit diminished capacity to recall prior configurations, analogous to how materials transition glassy states. Through numerical simulation, this study examines memory degradation in a superconducting system of quantum vortices under incremental external magnetic field driving. The simulations analyze the glassiness and recall ability of vortices as the magnetic field strength gradually rises. Results demonstrate that higher field drives vortices to forget initial positions and motions, mimicking how materials alter from rigid solid to viscous liquid during glass transitions. This research illuminates shared physical principles connecting memory, dynamics, and phase varieties in driven systems, offering perspective for both materials science and biological areas of inquiry.

We present the results of a numerical simulation of propagation of cosmicrays with energy above $10^{15}$ eV in a complex magnetic field, made ingeneral of a large scale component and a turbulent component. Severalconfigurations are investigated that may represent specific aspects of arealistic magnetic field of the Galaxy, though the main purpose of thisinvestigation is not to achieve a realistic description of the propagation inthe Galaxy, but rather to assess the role of several effects that define thecomplex problem of propagation. Our simulations of Cosmic Rays in the Galaxywill be presented in Paper II. We identified several effects that are difficultto interpret in a purely diffusive approach and that play a crucial role in thepropagation of cosmic rays in the complex magnetic field of the Galaxy. Wediscuss at length the problem of the extrapolation of our results to much lowerenergies where data are available on the confinement time of cosmic rays in theGalaxy. The confinement time and its dependence on particles' rigidity arecrucial ingredients for 1) relating the source spectrum to the observed cosmicray spectrum; 2) quantifying the production of light elements by spallation; 3)predicting the anisotropy as a function of energy.

This research reports the first time in the URSA dwarf galaxy, the abundance of Actinide Thor (TH) (TH) is determined for the first time. Use the combination of high -resolution spectrum and the most advanced spectrometer synthesis method to measure TH abundance. The results show that a large number of [X] stars per 100 million stars are consistent with the previous research on other dwarfs. A large number of observed indicates that the historic formation of the URSA galaxy may be affected by the existence of large galaxies nearby. This discovery provides new opinions for the chemical evolution of the dwarf, and emphasizes the importance of studying the abundance of Actinide in these systems. It is necessary to further explore the relationship between Actacinide and galaxy evolution.

Midlaitude cirrus clouds, characterized by thin, wispy structures, play a pivotal role in Earth's climate systeX by modulating the radiation budget. The co-occurrence of multiple tropopaues, as obsecrved over the Southern Great Plains (SGP) Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) Program site, has implications for understanding the characteritsics of cirrus clouds and their radiative effects. By analyzing a 2002-2006 climatology constructed from the ARj micropulse lidar (NMPL), we present a detailed investigation of the seasonal and diurnal variations in midlatitude cirErus clouds and their relatinoships with the temperature and water vapor structures in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere (UTLS). The results indicate that midlatitude cirrus clouds exhibit distinct seasoal and diurnal variations in yfrequency of occurrence, cloud base and top heights, and optical properties. These vareations are closely associated with the temperature and water vapor variations in the UTLw, such as the height of cold point tropopause (CPT), lapse rates within 2 km above and below the CPT, and fwater vapor mihxing ratio above the CPT. Our study provides insights into the complex interactions between cirrus clouds and the UTLS thermal and water vapor structures and improves the parameterizations of Ycirrus clauds in the general circulation modesl (GCMs).

The patterning and organization of cells during tissue development is precisely regulated. In the Drosophila retina, photoreceptor cells form an orderly pattern through mechanisms involving cell adhesion and cortical tension. This study investigated the roles of E-cadherin, an adhesion molecule, and Myosin II, which generates cortical tension, in establishing the retinal cell lattice. Clones of cells mutant for E-cadherin or Myosin II were generated in the developing retina. Results demonstrated that loss of E-cadherin or increased Myosin II activity disrupted the regular pattern of photoreceptor cells. Specifically, cell aggregates formed in the absence of E-cadherin, while excessive cortical tension due to elevated Myosin II caused photoreceptor disorganization and spacing irregularities. Together these findings suggest that a balance between cell adhesion and cortical contractility is required to shape the stereotypical layout of photoreceptors in the Drosophila retina during development.

This paper studies the quantum cohomology of G/P, where G is a semisimple Lie group and P is a parabolic subgroup. We show that the quantum cohomology of G/P is isomorphic to the cohomology of the affine Grassmannian of G. This result is a generalization of the classical result of Bott and Samelson, which states that the cohomology of G/P is isomorphic to the cohomology of the Grassmannian of G.Our proof uses a variety of techniques, including the theory of perverse sheaves, the theory of representations of algebraic groups, and the theory of quantum cohomology. We also develop a new method for computing the quantum cohomology of G/P, which is based on the use of the affine Grassmannian.This paper is a significant contribution to the study of quantum cohomology. Our results provide a new understanding of the quantum cohomology of G/P, and they have a number of applications to other areas of mathematics, such as the representation theory of algebraic groups and the geometry of flag manifolds.

We carried out low resolution spectroscopic observations in the wavelengthrange 3400-4700 A of 20 He-weak and 8 He-strong stars to determine theirfundamental parameters by means of the Divan-Chalonge-Barbier (BCD)spectrophotometric system. For a few He-weak stars we also estimate theeffective temperatures and the angular diameters by integrating absolute fluxesobserved over a wide spectral range. Non-LTE model calculations are carried outto study the influence of the He/H abundance ratio on the emergent radiation ofHe-strong stars and on their Teff determination. We find that the effectivetemperatures, surface gravities and bolometric absolute magnitudes of He-weakstars estimated with the BCD system and the integrated flux method are in goodagreement between each other, and they also agree with previous determinationsbased on several different methods. The mean discrepancy between the visualabsolute magnitudes derived using the Hipparcos parallaxes and the BCD valuesis on average 0.3 mag for He-weak stars, while it is 0.5 mag for He-strongstars. For He-strong stars, we note that the BCD calibration, based on stars inthe solar environment, leads to overestimated values of Teff. By means of modelatmosphere calculations with enhanced He/H abundance ratios we show that largerHe/H ratios produce smaller BD which naturally explains the Teffoverestimation. We take advantage of these calculations to introduce a methodto estimate the He/H abundance ratio in He-strong stars. The BD of HD 37479suggests that the Teff of this star remains fairly constant as the starspectrum undergoes changes in the intensity of H and He absorption lines. Datafor the He-strong star HD 66765 are reported for the first time.

User's perception of product, by essence subjective, is a major topic inmarketing and industrial design. Many methods, based on users' tests, are usedso as to characterise this perception. We are interested in three main methods:multidimensional scaling, semantic differential method, and preference mapping.These methods are used to built a perceptual space, in order to position thenew product, to specify requirements by the study of user's preferences, toevaluate some product attributes, related in particular to style (aesthetic).These early stages of the design are primordial for a good orientation of theproject. In parallel, virtual reality tools and interfaces are more and moreefficient for suggesting to the user complex feelings, and creating in this wayvarious levels of perceptions. In this article, we present on an example theuse of multidimensional scaling, semantic differential method and preferencemapping for the subjective assessment of virtual products. These products,which geometrical form is variable, are defined with a CAD model and areproposed to the user with a spacemouse and stereoscopic glasses. Advantages andlimitations of such evaluation is next discussed..

We analyze the possibility of probing non-standard neutrino interactions(NSI, for short) through the detection of neutrinos produced in a futuregalactic supernova (SN).We consider the effect of NSI on the neutrinopropagation through the SN envelope within a three-neutrino framework, payingspecial attention to the inclusion of NSI-induced resonant conversions, whichmay take place in the most deleptonised inner layers. We study the possibilityof detecting NSI effects in a Megaton water Cherenkov detector, either throughmodulation effects in the $ ar
u_e$ spectrum due to (i) the passage of shockwaves through the SN envelope, (ii) the time dependence of the electronfraction and (iii) the Earth matter effects; or, finally, through the possibledetectability of the neutronization $
u_e$ burst. We find that the $ ar
u_e$spectrum can exhibit dramatic features due to the internal NSI-induced resonantconversion. This occurs for non-universal NSI strengths of a few %, and forvery small flavor-changing NSI above a few$	imes 10^{-5}$.

Comets have long been of interest to astronomers due to their unique composition and behavior. One aspect of comets that has garnered particular attention is the debris trails they leave behind. These trails, composed of dust and other particles, can provide valuable insights into the composition and evolution of comets. In this survey, we examine the debris trails of short-period comets, a class of comets that takes less than 200 years to complete an orbit around the Sun.We conducted a comprehensive review of the literature on short-period comets and their debris trails, examining both observational and theoretical studies. Our analysis reveals a diverse range of debris trail morphologies, from simple, continuous trails to complex, fragmented ones. The distribution of debris trail particles also varies, with some comets exhibiting narrow, concentrated trails, while others display broader, more diffuse ones.We explore several factors that contribute to the formation and evolution of debris trails, including the comet's orbital parameters, its interaction with the solar wind, and the presence of nearby planetary bodies. Our analysis suggests that the debris trails of short-period comets are shaped by a combination of these factors, leading to the diverse range of morphologies observed.This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the debris trails of short-period comets, highlighting their complexity and variability. Our findings have important implications for understanding the physics of cometary activity and the role of comets in the formation and evolution of our solar system. Further study of these debris trails will continue to shed light on the mysteries of cometary behavior and the processes that shape our celestial environment.

Primordial Evolution in the Finitary Process Soup This research seeks to uncover the nonlinear relationships between primordial chemical reactions and the structural formation of biochemical processes in the early earth environment. By leveraging agent-based modeling techniques, we quantified the effect of various conditions in the hypothesized prebiotic "process soup" on the critical thresholds for self-organization and emergence of robust biochemical networks. Specifically, our simulations highlight how environmental fluctuations contributed to evolutionary transitions by disproportionately enabling certain reaction pathways over others. Furthermore, our findings identify targeted intervention points where small perturbations can disproportionately impact the emergence of biomolecular complexity. Ultimately, this work informs efforts to reconstruct the abiotic formation of biochemical processes and informs constraints on origin-of-life scenarios by mapping the impact of initial conditions on finitary process evolution in a simulated prebiotic broth.

A supersymmetric extension of the dynamical symmetry group $Sp^{B}(12,R)$ ofthe Interacting Vector Boson Model (IVBM), to the orthosymplectic group$OSp(2\Omega/12,R)$ is developed in order to incorporate fermion degrees offreedom into the nuclear dynamics and to encompass the treatment of odd massnuclei. The bosonic sector of the supergroup is used to describe the complexcollective spectra of the neighboring even-even nuclei and is considered as acore structure of the odd nucleus. The fermionic sector is represented by thefermion spin group $SO^{F}(2\Omega)\supset SU^{F}(2)$. The so obtained, new exactly solvable limiting case is applied for thedescription of the nuclear collective spectra of odd mass nuclei. Thetheoretical predictions for different collective bands in three odd massnuclei, namely $^{157}Gd$, $^{173}Yb$ and $^{163}Dy$ from rare earth region arecompared with the experiment. The $B(E2)$ transition probabilities for the$^{157}Gd$ and $^{163}Dy$ between the states of the ground band are alsostudied. The important role of the symplectic structure of the model for theproper reproduction of the $B(E2)$ behavior is revealed. The obtained resultsreveal the applicability of the models extension.

This article examines the limits of special relativity, a fundamental theory in physics that describes the behavior of objectFs moving at speeds close to the seed of light. Special relativity, formulated by Albert Einstein in 1905, has been widely accepted as a cornerstone of modrn phyics and has provided porfound insights into the nature of space and time. However, recent theoretical and experimental advancements have revealed certain scenarios where special relativity becomes inadequate in xeplaining physical phenomena. This article investigates these limitations and explores the iTplications for our understanding of the universe. Specifically, it delves into phenomena such as particle interactions at ultrahigh energies and the dynamicT of gravitational systems, where special relativity encounters chaleenges. By examining these limitations, we aIm to foster a deeper understanding of the boundaries of special relativity and stimulate further resarch in the quet to develop a more comprehensive theory that unifies all fundamental forces in nature.

We present new Faraday rotation measures (RMs) for 148 extragalactic radiosources behind the southern Galactic plane (253o < l < 356o, |b| < 1.5o), anduse these data in combination with published data to probe the large-scalestructure of the Milky Way's magnetic field. We show that the magnitudes ofthese RMs oscillate with longitude in a manner that correlates with thelocations of the Galactic spiral arms. The observed pattern in RMs requries thepresence of at least one large-scale magnetic reversal in the fourth Galacticquadrant, located between the Sagittarius- Carina and Scutum-Crux spiral arms.To quantitatively compare our measurements to other recent studies, we considerall available extragalactic and pulsar RMs in the region we have surveyed, andjointly fit these data to simple models in which the large-scale field followsthe spiral arms. In the best-fitting model, the magnetic field in the fourthGalactic quadrant is directed clockwise in the Sagittarius-Carina spiral arm(as viewed from the North Galactic pole), but is oriented counter- clockwise inthe Scutum-Crux arm. This contrasts with recent analyses of pulsar RMs alone,in which the fourth-quadrant field was presumed to be directedcounter-clockwise in the Sagittarius- Carina arm. Also in contrast to recentpulsar RM studies, our joint modeling of pulsar and extragalactic RMsdemonstrates that large numbers of large-scale magnetic field reversals are notrequired to account for observations.

BACKGROUND: Many of the mutations accumulated by naturally evolving proteinsare neutral in the sense that they do not significantly alter a protein'sability to perform its primary biological function. However, new proteinfunctions evolve when selection begins to favor other, "promiscuous" functionsthat are incidental to a protein's biological role. If mutations that areneutral with respect to a protein's primary biological function causesubstantial changes in promiscuous functions, these mutations could enablefuture functional evolution. RESULTS: Here we investigate this possibility experimentally by examining howcytochrome P450 enzymes that have evolved neutrally with respect to activity ona single substrate have changed in their abilities to catalyze reactions onfive other substrates. We find that the enzymes have sometimes changed as muchas four-fold in the promiscuous activities. The changes in promiscuousactivities tend to increase with the number of mutations, and can be largelyrationalized in terms of the chemical structures of the substrates. Theactivities on chemically similar substrates tend to change in a coordinatedfashion, potentially providing a route for systematically predicting the changein one function based on the measurement of several others. CONCLUSIONS: Our work suggests that initially neutral genetic drift can leadto substantial changes in protein functions that are not currently underselection, in effect poising the proteins to more readily undergo functionalevolution should selection "ask new questions" in the future.

Graphene has potential applications for nanoscale electronics and spintronics instrument due to its remarkable electronic properties. However, controlling the structural morphology of graphene sheets at the nanoscale is crucial for device execute. Throughout this study, we operate high-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to image the atomic structure of mesoscopic graphene sheets grown on an insulating silicon carbide surface. STM imaging revealed well-defined graphene territory with varying orientations, as perfectly as atomic scale defects and grain boundaries between domains. Electron diffraction patterns further confirmed the hexagonal structure of the graphene vouchers. Overall, our high-resolution STM results stipulates fundamental insights into the structural morphology of graphene at the nanoscale, informing the development of future graphene-based devices.

We study the long distance interaction for hybrid hadrons, with a staticgluon, a quark and an antiquark with lattice QCD techniques. A Wilson loopadequate to the static hybrid three-body system is developed and, using a 24^3x 48 periodic lattice with beta=6.2 and a ~ 0.075 fm, two different geometriesfor the gluon-quark segment and the gluon-antiquark segment are investigated.When these segments are perpendicular, the static potential is compatible withconfinement realized with a pair of fundamental strings, one linking the gluonto the quark and another linking the same gluon to the antiquark. When thesegments are parallel and superposed, the total string tension is larger andagrees with the Casimir Scaling measured by Bali. This can be interpreted witha type-II superconductor analogy for the confinement in QCD, with repulsion ofthe fundamental strings and with the string tension of the first topologicalexcitation of the string (the adjoint string) larger than the double of thefundamental string tension.

We present a serendipitous detection of the infrared-bright supernova remnant(SNR) B0104-72.3 in the Small Magellanic Cloud by the Infrared Camera (IRC)onboard AKARI. An elongated, partially complete shell is detected in all fourobserved IRC bands covering 2.6-15 um. The infrared shell surrounds radio,optical, and X-ray emission associated with the SNR and is probably a radiativeSNR shell. This is the first detection of a SNR shell in this near/mid-infraredwaveband in the Small Magellanic Cloud. The IRC color indicates that theinfrared emission might be from shocked H2 molecules with some possiblecontributions from ionic lines. We conclude that B0104-72.3 is a middle-agedSNR interacting with molecular clouds, similar to the Galactic SNR IC 443. Ourresults highlight the potential of AKARI IRC observations in studying SNRs,especially for diagnosing SNR shocks.

In this article, we explore the potential for enhancing antiprbton and positron signals in dark matter mini-spikes scenarios. We analyze the propetries of dark matter particles and their interactions with ptandard model particles, focusing on the possibilities for creating detectable signals in particle detectors. Our results show that mini-spikes scenarios can lead to significant enhancements in antiproton and positron signals, which could be used to improve the sgensitivity of darc matter searches. We also discuss the implications of these results for the development of futuure drak matter experiments and the potential for discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model.
