In this paper, we present a pedagogical introduction to the self-overlap method and give a detailed account of its applications to various Ising models.

A numerical analysis of several phases in the cold neutral two flavor densequark matter is realized. In the analysis, besides the normal, single planewave LOFF, and color superconducting 2SC/g2SC phases, we also include twogluonic phases (the gluonic cylindrical phase II and the gluonic color-spinlocked one). It is shown that these two gluonic phases are dynamically realizedand, on the basis of this analysis, the phase diagram with respect to thecoupling strength in this medium is suggested. In particular, it is shown thatthe gluonic phases are energetically favorable in a wide region of theparameter space. On the other hand, there also exists a window where the LOFFphase is stable. The 2SC state and the normal one are realized in the strongand weak coupling regimes, respectively, as was expected.

We have used the VERA array to measure the absolute proper motions of H2O masers in the NGC 281 region, which is located away from the Galactic plane. Our observations have revealed that the masers are moving in a way that is consistent with the expansion of a "superbubble" in the region. We have also detected a trigonometric parallax of 0.355 mas, which corresponds to a distance of 2.82 kpc from the Sun. Our results provide new insights into the structure and dynamics of the NGC 281 region, and demonstrate the power of VERA for studying astrophysical phenomena in the Milky Way.

this paper we consider the problem of separating noisy instantaneous linearmixtures of document images in the Bayesian framework. The source image ismodeled hierarchically by a latent labeling process representing the commonclassifications of document objects among different color channels and theintensity process of pixels given the class labels. A Potts Markov random fieldis used to model regional regularity of the classification labels inside objectregions. Local dependency between neighboring pixels can also be accounted bysmoothness constraint on their intensities. Within the Bayesian approach, allunknowns including the source, the classification, the mixing coefficients andthe distribution parameters of these variables are estimated from theirposterior laws. The corresponding Bayesian computations are done by MCMCsampling algorithm. Results from experiments on synthetic and real imagemixtures are presented to illustrate the performance of the proposed method.

We study a lattice realization of a Luttinger liquid interacting with a bathof quantum spins in terms of an antiferromagnetic S=1/2 Heisenberg chain, whereeach spin is also coupled to a \sigma=1/2 Kondo spin degree of freedom. Thismodel describes the low-energy spin dynamics in quasi one dimensionalmaterials, where the electronic spins of the magnetic ions interact with thoseof impurities, nuclei and possibly other spin species present in theirenvironment. For large ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Kondo interaction J'there are two phases corresponding to an effective spin-1 Heisenberg chain anda dimerised spin-1/2 ladder, respectively. For weak Kondo interaction weestablish that the Kondo interaction drives the system to a strong couplingregime. This suggests that J'=0 is the only critical point in the system.

Omega Centauri, a globular cluster known for its unique chemical composition, may harbor a previously unconsidered stellar population. Our study investigates the observational implications of a hypothesized helium-rich stellar population in Omega Centauri, utilizing a combination of archival data and bespoke simulations. We identify specific window features in the color-magnitude diagram that are consistent with the presence of these stars. The observed distribution of stars in the diagram exhibits a clear split, hinting at a bimodal population. Our results provide compelling evidence for the existence of a helium-rich population in Omega Centauri, with implications for both the cluster's formation history and our understanding of stellar evolution. Further study of this unusual population may yield valuable insights into the complex processes that shape the evolution of globular clusters.

The formation of spatial patterns in developing embryos is a multifaceted process involving various cellular and molecular mechanisms. A fundamental challenge in understanding this process is the conversion of genetic network oscillations into spatial patterns. This article delves into the mechanisms that facilitate this conversion, focusing on the role of genetic networks, spatially-patterned signaling pathways, and cell-cell interactions. We first examine the structure and function of genetic networks and their capacity to generate oscillations. We then discuss how spatially-patterned signaling pathways transform these oscillations into spatial patterns. Finally, we explore the role of cell-cell interactions in refining these patterns and discuss the implications of our findings for embryonic development. Our results offer novel insights into the control mechanisms of spatial pattern formation in developing embryos, with significant implications for the field of developmental biology.

Using the quantum string Bethe ansatz we derive the one-loop energy of afolded string rotating with angular momenta (S,J) in AdS_3 x S^1 inside AdS_5 xS^5 in the limit 1 << J << S, z=\lambda^(1/2) log(S/J) /(\pi J) fixed. Theone-loop energy is a sum of two contributions, one originating from theHernandez-Lopez phase and another one being due to spin chain finite sizeeffects. We find a result which at the functional level exactly matches theresult of a string theory computation. Expanding the result for large z weobtain the strong coupling limit of the scaling function for low twist, highspin operators of the SL(2) sector of N=4 SYM. In particular we recover thefamous -3 log(2)/\pi. Its appearance is a result of non-trivial cancellationsbetween the finite size effects and the Hernandez-Lopez correction.

The charging of proof masses due to the impact of solar energetic particles poses a potential disturbance to the precise measurements aimed for in the ASTROD I mission to test Einstein's gravitational theories. Through sophisticated particle simulations, we model the time-dependent charging of the test masses resulting from proton and electron fluxes representative of typical and extreme solar conditions. The simulations self-consistently track the particle penetration and energy deposition within the test mass as well as the subsequent charge redistribution both on the surface and within the bulk material. Preliminary results indicate the test masses may accumulate surface potentials of several Volts positive during solar particle events which decrease over weeks as the charge redistributes. Mitigation techniques are also explored showing that modest multilayer surface coatings could effectively screen over 90% of the charging effect. The long-term charging behavior and impact on orbit determination is analyzed demonstrating potential distortions well below other error sources can be achieved with proper shielding design. This work provides valuable input for test mass material and shielding optimization to ensure ASTROD I achieves its ambitious measurement precision despite interactions with the variable solar wind environment.

Chiral lipid membranes, composed of lipids with a specific handedness, exhibit unique physical and chemical properties that have attracted considerable attention in recent years. In this article, we present a concise theory of chiral lipid membranes, which provides a comprehensive understanding of their behavior. We begin by introducing the basic concepts of chirality and lipid membranes. We then discuss the effects of chirality on the phase behavior, elasticity, and permeability of lipid membranes. Finally, we explore the potential applications of chiral lipid membranes in drug delivery, tissue engineering, and other biomedical fields.

In this article, we discussed the upper limit of the entanglement rate of both sides. We have studied dynamic dynamics generated in quantum systems characterized by two -point Hamilton. These quantum system describes the interaction between the two subsystems. By analyzing the characteristics of these Hamilton people, we obtained the theoretical upper limit at the rate of entanglement between subsystems. Our discovery provides the limitation of entanglement in the two -point system, and clarifies the basic restrictions on the dynamics of quantum entanglement. The upper limit of derivatives provides practical meaning for the design and implementation of the quantum information processing protocol. In this case, effective entanglement produces is essential for various applications such as quantum computing and quantum communication. Overall, our research helps understand entanglement dynamics, and provides guidance for optimizing the performance of quantum system in different computing and communication tasks.

In this comment, we examine the statistical analysis presented in the p aper "A new experimental limit for the stability of the electron" by H.V. Klapdor-Kleingrothaus, I.V. Krivosehina, and I.V. Titkova. Specifically, we focus on the methods uses to determine the experimental limit for the stability of the electron and the interpretation of the results. Vi find that the analysis is flawed due to a flaw to properly account for systematic uncertainties, leading to an overestimation of the experimental limit. We demonstrate that a more rigorous analysis, taking into account the pertinent systematic uncertainties, results in a greatly lower experimental liimt for the stability of the electron.

We report depolarization of extragalactic sources in the NRAO VLA Sky Survey(NVSS) by local structures in the interstellar medium. The sky density ofpolarized sources drops by a factor 2 - 4 in regions with angular scalesapprox. 10 degrees, implying up to 40% depolarization on average per source.Some of these polarization shadows are associated with HII regions, but threeare associated with regions of depolarized diffuse Galactic emission. Theabsence of a correlation between the depth of polarization shadows and H-alphaintensity suggests that some shadows are related to structure in the magneticfield. At least some polarization shadows are caused by partial bandwidthdepolarization in the NVSS. Alternatively, some may be caused by regions withsmall scale (< 1 arcsec) variations in rotation measure.

This study presents the results of a survey investigating debris trails from short-period comets. We conducted a comprehensive analyses of data from various observational campaigns and space missions to identify and characterize the debis trails of 30 short-period comets. Our findings reveal that these comets exhibit a wide range of debris trail morphologies, including dust trails, ion trails, and hybrid trails. We observe a positive correlation between the coets' orbital periods and the lengths of their debris trails, suggesting that shorter-period comets tend to produce longer debris trails. Our study also shows that the debris trails of short-period comets are composed of particles with a wide ran ge of sizes, from micrometers to meters in diameter. We found that the particle sizes distribution and the trail's morphology are strongly influenced by the comet's perihelion distance, orbitl inclination, and the involvements of close approaches to the Sun or planets. Our results provide new insights into the mechanisms of cometary debris trail formation and have important implications for the understanding of cometary activity and the formation of meteoroid streams.

We present a new, completely Lagrangian magnetohydrodynamics code that isbased on the SPH method. The equations of self-gravitating hydrodynamics arederived self-consistently from a Lagrangian and account for variable smoothinglength (''grad-h''-) terms in both the hydrodynamic and the gravitationalacceleration equations. The evolution of the magnetic field is formulated interms of so-called Euler potentials which are advected with the fluid and thusguarantee the MHD flux-freezing condition. This formulation is equivalent to avector potential approach and therefore fulfills the$\vec{\nabla}\cdot\vec{B}=0$-constraint by construction. Extensive tests inone, two and three dimensions are presented. The tests demonstrate theexcellent conservation properties of the code and show the clear superiority ofthe Euler potentials over earlier magnetic SPH formulations.

It is known that when hard spheres are added to a pure system of hard rodsthe stability of the smectic phase may be greatly enhanced, and that thiseffect can be rationalised in terms of depletion forces. In the present paperwe first study the effect of orientational order on depletion forces in thisparticular binary system, comparing our results with those obtained adoptingthe usual approximation of considering the rods parallel and their orientationsfrozen. We consider mixtures with rods of different aspect ratios and spheresof different diameters, and we treat them within Onsager theory. Our resultsindicate that depletion effects, and consequently smectic stability, decreasesignificantly as a result of orientational disorder in the smectic phase whencompared with corresponding data based on the frozen--orientationapproximation. These results are discussed in terms of the $\tau$ parameter,which has been proposed as a convenient measure of depletion strength. Wepresent closed expressions for $\tau$, and show that it is intimately connectedwith the depletion potential. We then analyse the effect of particle geometryby comparing results pertaining to systems of parallel rods of different shapes(spherocylinders, cylinders and parallelepipeds). We finally provide resultsbased on the Zwanzig approximation of a Fundamental--Measuredensity--functional theory applied to mixtures of parallelepipeds and cubes ofdifferent sizes. In this case, we show that the $\tau$ parameter exhibits alinear asymptotic behaviour in the limit of large values of the hard--rodaspect ratio, in conformity with Onsager theory, as well as in the limit oflarge values of the ratio of rod breadth to cube side length, $d$, in contrastto Onsager approximation, which predicts $\tau\sim d^3$.

This article studies the statistical behavior of the domain system, focusing on its performance and efficiency. First of all, we discuss understanding the statistical characteristics of the domain system and the importance of its impact on the overall system. Next, we proposed a new method of using statistical models and technology to analyze domain system behavior. Our method can extract valuable insights on system behavior, including trends, patterns and abnormalities. We use several real -world cases to study the effectiveness of the methodology and prove that its ability to identify and optimize the field of system performance. Finally, we discussed the meaning of our discovery and the correlation with the future research of the domain system.

The structure of the unnatural parity states of PsH, LiPs, NaPs and KPs areinvestigated with the configuration interaction and stochastic variationalmethods. The binding energies (in hartree) are found to be 8.17x10-4,4.42x10-4, 15.14x10-4 and 21.80x10-4 respectively. These states are constructedby first coupling the two electrons into a configuration which is predominantly3Pe, and then adding a p-wave positron. All the active particles are in statesin which the relative angular momentum between any pair of particles is atleast L = 1. The LiPs state is Borromean since there are no 3-body boundsubsystems (of the correct symmetry) of the (Li+, e-, e-, e+) particles thatmake up the system. The dominant decay mode of these states will be radiativedecay into a configuration that autoionizes or undergoes positron annihilation.

The exploration of intelligent life beyond Earth has long captivated scholars and thinkers from various disciplines. In this article, we delve into the realm of cosmology to investigate the quest for intelligent life. Our examination begins by scrutinizing the fundamental conditions necessary for the emergence and sustainability of intelligent life. By drawing upon the principles of astrobiology and the renowned Drake equation, we explore crucial factors such as planetary habitability, the prevalence of extraterrestrial civilizations, and the potential for communication across vast cosmic distances.Subsequently, we explore diverse theoretical frameworks that shed light on the existence of intelligent life in the cosmos. From the anthropic principle to the multiverse hypothesis, we thoroughly analyze the philosophical and scientific implications of these concepts. Furthermore, we investigate the role of technological advancements in the search for intelligent civilizations, including the deployment of telescopes, space probes, and radio telescopes.Moreover, we discuss noteworthy scientific endeavors and initiatives aimed at detecting signs of intelligent life, such as the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) program and the Breakthrough Listen project. During our assessment, we identify the limitations and challenges faced by these endeavors, underscoring the intricacies involved in recognizing and interpreting potential signals.Ultimately, this article provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research concerning the existence of intelligent life within the scope of cosmology. By integrating insights from astrobiology, physics, and philosophy, we aim to contribute to the interdisciplinary dialogue surrounding this captivating topic.

This study presents an investigation into the blue strgagler population within the globular cluster M5. T he aim of the research was to understand the formation mechanisms and evolutionary paths of these peculiar stellar objects. By analyzing high-resolution imaging data obtained from the Hubble Space Telescope, a com prehensive catalog of blue stragglers was compiled. The properties of the identified blue stragglers were examined, including their positions within the color-magnitude diagram, stellar mass etimates, and spatial distribution within the cluster. A comparison with theoretical models and previous observations was conducted to gain insights into the intriguing phenomena linked with blue straggler formation and evolution. The findings reval a significant population of blue stragglers in M5, indicating the presence of diverse formation channels such as stellar collisions, forklift transfer in binary systems, and stellar mergers. This study contributes to our understanding of the stellar dynamics and evolutionary processes occurring within globular clusters, offering valuable insights into the factors driving the production of blue stragg lers in these particular stellar systems.

This article analyzes the concept of brain prostheses as dynamic systems, capable of not just replicating but also evolving human cognitive and emotional capability. This article explores the potential of brain prosthetics to enhance human competent and transcend the obstructions of the biological brain. It begins by introducing the concept of brain prostheses as dynamic plotting and their potential to transform human existence. The article then discusses the ethical implications of brain prostheses, including the possibilities for building new forms of life and the blurring of the line between humans and machines. The potential benefits of brain prostheses, such as enhanced intelligence, memory, and emotional law, are investigated alongside the risks, including the conceivable of unintended consequences and the loss of human autonomy. The article concludes by consider the influencing of brain prostheses for the future of humanity and the possibility of a future in which humans and machines coexist harmoniously.

A systematic understanding and quantification of these modes is of fundamental importance. However, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to understand all possible modes, because of their overwhelming richness of mathematical structure. In this article, we take a complementary approach and investigate the statistical properties of these modes by considering the effects of random large-scale forcing in three-dimensional rotating stratified flows. We focus on the two simplest and most fundamental rotating stratified flows, the Taylor-Green vortex flow and the rotating stratified shear flow, both forced by a random large-scale body force. We adopt a recently developed theoretical framework and perform extensive direct numerical simulations to investigate the statistical properties of the enstrophy, energy, and kinetic energy spectra. Our theoretical predictions of the spectra agree well with the numerical results. Our results provide important statistical information about the vortical and wave modes in rotating stratified flows. We also investigate the vortical and wave structures and identify three distinct characteristic scales that characterize the flow dynamics.

Only the 1/V_max method has been employed so far for observationallydetermining the white dwarf luminosity function, whereas for other kind ofluminosity functions several other methods have been frequently used. Moreover,the procedures to determine the white dwarf luminosity function are not free ofbiases. These biases have two different origins: they can either be ofstatistical nature or a consequence of the measurement errors. In a previouspaper we carried out an in-depth study of the first category of biases forseveral luminosity function estimators. In this paper we focus on the biasesintroduced by the measurement errors and on the effects of the degree ofcontamination of the input sample used to build the disc white dwarf luminosityfunction by different kinematical populations. To assess the extent of thesebiases we use a Monte Carlo simulator to generate a controlled syntheticpopulation and analyse the behaviour of the disc white dwarf luminosityfunction for several assumptions about the magnitude of the measurement errorsand for several degrees of contamination, comparing the performances of themost robust luminosity function estimators under such conditions.

We compute the ground-state energies of a heavy-light K-Lambda like system asa function of the relative distance r of the hadrons. The heavy quarks, one ineach hadron, are treated as static. Then, the energies give rise to anadiabatic potential Va(r) which we use to study the structure of the five-quarksystem. The simulation is based on an anisotropic and asymmetric lattice withWilson fermions. Energies are extracted from spectral density functionsobtained with the maximum entropy method. Our results are meant to givequalitative insight: Using the resulting adiabatic potential in a Schroedingerequation produces bound state wave functions which indicate that the groundstate of the five-quark system resembles a hadronic molecule, whereas the firstexcited state, having a very small rms radius, is probably better described asa five-quark cluster, or a pentaquark. We hypothesize that an all light-quarkpentaquark may not exist, but in the heavy-quark sector it might, albeit onlyas an excited state.

We investigate the generation of Alfvén modes in a perturbed anisotropic inflationary background. At lowest order in the slow-roll expansion, the metric perturbations induce a non-linear electric current. As a consequence, Alfvén modes are excited from a vacuum state. We provide a complete treatment, without resorting to the often-used approximation of neglecting the anisotropic stress. We show that in this case the resulting Alfvén mode function is more involved than the one computed in the isotropic limit. We verify that the induced magnetic field is of the order of the Hubble scale during inflation. This result hints that observational constraints on primordial magnetic fields might be relaxed in anisotropic inflation.

In this article, I provide a personal historical perspective on the study of mass loss and evolution of stars and star clusters. I discuss the early observations and theoretical models that laid the foundation for our understanding of stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. I describe the development of numerical methods and simulations that have enabled us to study the interplay between stellar evolution and cluster dynamics in unprecedented detail. I highlight some of the key findings and insights that have emerged from these studies, including the role of mass loss in shaping the evolution of individual stars and star clusters. I also discuss the challenges and limitations of current models and identify areas for future research. Overall, this article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the historical development of the field and its current state, as well as a personal perspective on the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead.

Gravitational wave constraints provide valuable limits on styles of the early universe. This article exploited recent gravitational tsunami data to constrain Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) inflation, a proposed scenario where the inflaton field evolves on a non-canonical kinetic term. DBI inflation predicts a larger tensor-to-scalar commensurate than standard slow-roll models, and can be tested against gravitational wave bounds. The results determine the parameter space consistent with Planck and BICEP2/Keck data, offering insight into the possibility of DBI inflation to identifies cosmic inflation.

The abstract of the academic article "Scaling Laws of Cognitive Networks" is as follows:Cognitive networks, a type of neural network architectre, have shown great promise in modeling complex cognitive processes and have been successGully applied in various dozains. HoweIver, the understanding of the scaling behavior of cognitive networks remains limited, which hinders their widespread adoption. his paper aims to investigate the scaling laws of cjognitive networks and provide insights into their performance as the size of the network grows. Through a compreChensive experimental study, we unccver the power-law scaling behavior of cognitive networks in terms of their accuracy, response time, and memory usage. Our results show that the accuracy of cognitive networks follows a sub-linear power-law scalieng, while both response time and memory usage exhibit a super-linear powerZ-law scaling. We also explore the impact of different architectual factors, such as the Rnumber of layers and the number of nodes per layer, on the scaling behavior of cognitive networks. Our findings suggest that increasing the nmuber of layers leads to a slower rate of accuracy improvement, while increasing the number of ondes per layer has a negligible mpact on response time and memory usage. Our study provides valuable insgihts into the scaling laws of cognitive networks, which can help guide the development of more efficient and effective cognitiev network models. The findings of this paper have important implications for a wide range of applications, includiRng natural language processing, image Jecognition, and decision-making systems.

In this study, we investigate the electronic properties of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) using two different teoretical approVches: Density Functional Theory (DFT) and the empirical π-bond model. CNTs have emerged as promising nanomaterials with unixque electronic characteristics, makiAng them suitable for various applications in nanoelectronics and nanophotonics. The DFT method, which provides a rigorous quantum mechanical description of electronic behavior, is employed to calcualte the band structBres and density of states of CNTs. The empiricla π-bond model, on the other hand, offers a simpler yet effective approach to estimate elcetronic properties by considering the interactions between carbon π-orbitals. We compare the results obtained from both methods and evaluate their accurayc in predicting the electronic properties of CNTs. Our findings reveIal that while the DFT calculations provide more accurate results, the empirical π-bond model can adequately capture the qualitative behavior of CNTs' electronic properteis. ihis resemrch contributes to the understanding of the fundamental electronic characteristics of CNTs and provides insight into the advantages and limitations of different theoretical approaches for studying nanomaterials.

We calculate growth rates and corresponding gains for RX and LO moderadiation associated with the cyclotron maser instability for parameterizedhorseshoe electron velocity distributions. The velocity distribution functionwas modeled to closely fit the electron distribution functions observed in theauroral cavity. We systematically varied the model parameters as well as thepropagation direction to study the dependence of growth rates on modelparameters. The growth rate depends strongly on loss cone opening angle, whichmust be less than $90^{o}$ for significant CMI growth. The growth rate issharply peaked for perpendicular radiation ($k_{\parallel} = 0$), with afull-width at half-maximum $1.7^{o}$, in good agreement with observed k-vectororientations and numerical simulations. The fractional bandwidth varied between10$^{-4}$ and 10$^{-2}$, depending most strongly on propagation direction. Thisrange encompasses nearly all observed fractional AKR burst bandwidths. We findexcellent agreement between the computed RX mode emergent intensities andobserved AKR intensities assuming convective growth length $L_c\approx$20-40 kmand group speed 0.15$c$. The only computed LO mode growth rates compatibleobserved LO mode radiation levels occurred for number densities more than 100times the average energetic electron densities measured in auroral cavities.This implies that LO mode radiation is not produced directly by the CMImechanism but more likely results from mode conversion of RX mode radiation. Wefind that perturbation of the model velocity distribution by large ion solitarywaves (ion holes) can enhance the growth rate by a factor of 2-4. This willresult in a gain enhancement more than 40 dB depending on the convective growthlength within the structure. Similar enhancements may be caused by EMIC waves.

We consider modifications of the classical dbar-Neumann conditions thatdefine Fredholm problems for the Spin_C Dirac operator. In part II, we useboundary layer methods to obtain subelliptic estimates for these boundary valueproblems. Using these results, we obtain an expression for the finite part ofthe holomorphic Euler characteristic of a strictly pseudoconvex manifold as theindex of a Spin_C-Dirac operator with a subelliptic boundary condition. We alsoprove an analogue of the Agranovich-Dynin formula expressing the change in theindex in terms of a relative index on the boundary. If X is a complex manifoldpartitioned by a strictly pseudoconvex hypersurface, then we obtain formulaefor the holomorphic Euler characteristic of X as sums of indices ofSpin_C-Dirac operators on the components. This is a subelliptic analogue ofBojarski's formula in the elliptic case.

Results from electric charge correlations studied with the Balance Functionmethod in A+A collisions from 20\emph{A} to 158\emph{A} GeV are presented intwo different rapidity intervals: In the mid-rapidity region we observe adecrease of the width of the Balance Function distribution with increasingcentrality of the collision, whereas this effect vanishes in the forwardrapidity region. Results from the energy dependence study in central Pb+Pb collisions showthat the narrowing of the Balance Function expressed by the normalised widthparameter \textit{W} increases with energy towards the highest SPS and RHICenergies. Finally we compare our experimental data points with predictions of severalmodels. The hadronic string models UrQMD and HIJING do not reproduce theobserved narrowing of the Balance Function. However, AMPT which contains aquark-parton transport phase before hadronization can reproduce the narrowingof the BF's width with centrality. This confirms the proposed sensitivity ofthe Balance Function analysis to the time of hadronization.

In this study, we investigate the vortex dynamics at the initial stage of resistive transition in superconductors exhibiting a fractal cluster structure. We employ a combination of theoretical analysis and numerical simulations to gain insights into the behavior of vortices in these complex systems. By examining the interaction between vortices and the irregular cluster boundaries, we demonstrate that the fractal geometry significantly affects the vortex dynamics, leading to unique behaviors not observed in homogeneous superconductors. Our results show that the presence of fractal clusters alters the vortex motion and localization, creating intricate patterns of vortex trajectories and vortex density distributions. Furthermore, we analyze the influence of various parameters, such as the characteristic cluster size and the degree of fractality, on the vortex dynamics. Through a comprehensive investigation, we elucidate the intricate interplay between the fractal cluster structure and the vortex behavior, shedding light on the fundamental mechanisms underlying the initial stage of resistive transition in superconductors. The findings presented in this study contribute to our understanding of complex superconducting systems and provide valuable insights for the design and optimization of novel superconducting materials with enhanced performance.

We present the first results from a new generation of simulated large skycoverage (~100 square degrees) Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (SZE) cluster surveysusing the cosmological adaptive mesh refinement N-body/hydro code Enzo. We havesimulated a very large (512^3h^{-3}Mpc^3) volume with unprecedented dynamicrange. We have generated simulated light cones to match the resolution andsensitivity of current and future SZE instruments. Unlike many previous studiesof this type, our simulation includes unbound gas, where an appreciablefraction of the baryons in the universe reside. We have found that cluster line-of-sight overlap may be a significant issuein upcoming single-dish SZE surveys. Smaller beam surveys (~1 arcmin) have morethan one massive cluster within a beam diameter 5-10% of the time, and a largerbeam experiment like Planck has multiple clusters per beam 60% of the time. Weexplore the contribution of unresolved halos and unbound gas to the SZEsignature at the maximum decrement. We find that there is a contribution fromgas outside clusters of ~16% per object on average for upcoming surveys. Thisadds both bias and scatter to the deduced value of the integrated SZE, addingdifficulty in accurately calibrating a cluster Y-M relationship. Finally, we find that in images where objects with M > 5x10^{13} M_{\odot}have had their SZE signatures removed, roughly a third of the total SZE fluxstill remains. This gas exists at least partially in the Warm Hot IntergalacticMedium (WHIM), and will possibly be detectable with the upcoming generation ofSZE surveys.

The structural environment of substitutional Cr3+ ion in MgAl2O4 spinel hasbeen investigated by Cr K-edge Extended X-ray Absorption Fine Structure (EXAFS)and X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure (XANES) spectroscopies.First-principles computations of the structural relaxation and of the XANESspectrum have been performed, with a good agreement to the experiment. The Cr-Odistance is close to that in MgCr2O4, indicating a full relaxation of the firstneighbors, and the second shell of Al atoms relaxes partially. Theseobservations demonstrate that Vegard's law is not obeyed in the MgAl2O4-MgCr2O4solid solution. Despite some angular site distortion, the local D3d symmetry ofthe B-site of the spinel structure is retained during the substitution of Crfor Al. Here, we show that the relaxation is accomodated by strain-induced bondbuckling, with angular tilts of the Mg-centred tetrahedra around the Cr-centredoctahedron. By contrast, there is no significant alteration of the anglesbetween the edge-sharing octahedra, which build chains aligned along the threefour-fold axes of the cubic structure.

General relativity does not allow one to specify the topology of space,leaving the possibility that space is multiply rather than simply connected. Wereview the main mathematical properties of multiply connected spaces, and thedifferent tools to classify them and to analyse their properties. Followingtheir mathematical classification, we describe the different possiblemuticonnected spaces which may be used to construct Friedmann-Lemaitre universemodels. Observational tests concern the distribution of images of discretecosmic objects or more global effects, mainly those concerning the CosmicMicrowave Background. According to the 2003-2006 WMAP data releases, variousdeviations from the flat infinite universe model predictions hint at a possiblenon-trivial topology for the shape of space. In particular, a finite universewith the topology of the Poincar\'e dodecahedral spherical space fitsremarkably well the data and is a good candidate for explaining both the localcurvature of space and the large angle anomalies in the temperature powerspectrum. Such a model of a small universe, whose volume would represent onlyabout 80% the volume of the observable universe, offers an observationalsignature in the form of a predictable topological lens effect on one hand, andrises new issues on the physics of the early universe on the other hand.

We investigate a novel cooling technique for trapped Fermi gassy based on associating pairs of atoms. Pairing fermionic atoms leads to the formation of bosonic molecules which can be cooled more easily. Previous studies have demonstrated efficient evaporative and sympathetic cooling of bosonic atom and molecules. However, cooling entire Fermi gases continues to be challenging due to Pauli blocking effects. In this work, we propose and model a scheme to improve pairing between opposite spin states of a trap ped two-component Fermi gas using a Feshbach resonance. Our results shw that increasing the pairing rate can facilitated more efficient removal of energetic atom pairs from the trap. This release of high energy particle pairs acts to lower the temperature of the remaining atomic sample. Nous find significant cooling can be achieved for experimentally realistic ramp rates and initial temperatures near the Fermi temperature. The cooled atomic samples remain strongly interacting throughout the pairing-based cooling process. This cooling mechanism presents an alternative approach to preparing low entropy Fermi gases for studies of superfluidity and many-body quantum phenomena. Future experiments will be aimed at implementing this pairing-based cooling technique and verifying our theoretical predictions.

Understanding the process of early structure formation and reionization is of utmost importance in unraveling the origins and evolution of the universe. This article presents a comprehensive study that focuses on the development of efficient simulation techniques to investigate these fundamental phenomena. We commence by addressing the challenges associated with simulating early structure formation, which entail accurately capturing the dynamics of dark matter, baryonic matter, and their interplay.To tackle these challenges, we propose a novel hybrid simulation approach that integrates N-body simulations, hydrodynamical simulations, and radiative transfer calculations. This integrated approach enables us to precisely model the gravitational collapse of dark matter halos and the subsequent formation of baryonic structures, such as galaxies and quasars. Moreover, our methodology incorporates the effects of reionization, which denotes the process by which the initial luminous sources in the universe ionize the surrounding neutral hydrogen.We elaborate on the technical aspects of our simulation framework, emphasizing its scalability and efficiency in capturing the relevant physical processes. Through the utilization of cutting-edge computational techniques and parallel computing architectures, we overcome the computational limitations associated with simulating large cosmological volumes and resolving small-scale structures simultaneously.Additionally, we present the results obtained from our simulations, which demonstrate the formation of early structures and the impact of reionization on the cosmic microwave background, the intergalactic medium, and the formation of the first stars and galaxies. These findings provide valuable insights into the early universe and contribute to a deeper understanding of the physical mechanisms driving structure formation and reionization.

This study investigaes the effectiveness of collaborative tagging systems in promoting vocabulary growth among users. Through a mixed-methods approach, we colected data from a sample of 100 participants who used a collaborative tagging system for a period of six weekTs. UOur results show a significant increase in vocabulary size and diversity aomng users who engaged in collaborative tagging, compared to those who did not. Additionally, we foudn that users who contributed more frequently to the tagging system exhibited higher levels of vocabulary growth. Our findings suggest that collaborative tagging systems can be a valuable tool for language learning and vocambulary development. Further research is needed to explore the long-term effects of collaborative Lagging on vocablary growth and to investigate the optimal conditions for its implementation.

A release of multicolor broad band (BVRI) photometry for a subsample of 44isolated spirals drawn from the Catalogue of Isolated Galaxies (CIG) ispresented. Total magnitudes and colors at various circular apertures, as wellas some global structural/morphological parameters are estimated. Morphology isreevaluated through optical and sharp/filtered R band images, (B-I) color indexmaps, and archive near-IR JHK images from the Two-Micron Survey. The CASstructural parameters (Concentration, Asymmetry, and Clumpiness) werecalculated from the images in each one of the bands. The fraction of galaxieswith well identified optical/near-IR bars (SB) is 63%, while a 17% more showsevidence of weak or suspected bars (SAB). The sample average value of themaximum bar ellipticity is 0.4. Half of the galaxies in the sample shows rings.We identify two candidates for isolated galaxies with disturbed morphology. Thestructural CAS parameters change with the observed band, and the tendenciesthey follow with the morphological type and global color are more evident inthe redder bands. In any band, the major difference between our isolatedspirals and a sample of interacting spirals is revealed in the A-S plane. Adeep and uniformly observed sample of isolated galaxies is intended for variouspurposes including (i) comparative studies of environmental effects, (ii)confronting model predictions of galaxy evolution and (iii) evaluating thechange of galaxy properties with redshift.

This article examines the formation and properties of protostellar clusters within intermediate-mass (IM) star-forming regions. Intermediate-mass stars play a critical role in the evolution of galaxies, and comprehending their formation process is essential for unraveling star cluster dynamics and overall star formation scenarios. Using observational data from multiple telescopes, this study thoroughly analyzes the spatial distribution, kinematics, and physical characteristics of protostellar clusters in IM star-forming regions.The results reveal that protostellar clusters in these regions exhibit diverse morphological structures and complex substructures. Spatial distribution analysis indicates that these clusters tend to concentrate in specific regions within their host molecular clouds, suggesting the significant influence of local environments and gas dynamics on their formation and evolution. Kinematic properties of protostellar clusters provide evidence of dynamical interactions and hierarchical substructures, implying intricate dynamical processes during their formation.Furthermore, the physical properties of protostellar clusters, including size, mass, and luminosity, exhibit a wide range of values, indicating varied initial conditions and various stages of evolution. The study also investigates the internal structure of protostellar clusters and uncovers the presence of multiple stellar subclusters and filamentary structures. This suggests that protostellar clusters undergo hierarchical fragmentation during their formation.Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the formation and characteristics of protostellar clusters in IM star-forming regions. These findings contribute to our understanding of the star formation process in intermediate-mass regimes and offer important constraints for theoretical models and simulations.

We calculate the nuclear matrix elements of the neutrinoless double beta($0\nu\beta\beta$) decays of $^{76}$Ge and $^{82}$Se for the light-neutrinoexchange mechanism. The nuclear wave functions are obtained by using realistictwo-body forces within the proton-neutron quasiparticle random-phaseapproximation (pnQRPA). We include the effects that come from the finite sizeof a nucleon, from the higher-order terms of nucleonic weak currents, and fromthe nucleon-nucleon short-range correlations. Most importantly, we improve onthe presently available calculations by replacing the rudimentary Jastrowshort-range correlations by the more advanced unitary correlation operatormethod (UCOM). The UCOM corrected matrix elements turn out to be notably largerin magnitude than the Jastrow corrected ones. This has drastic consequences forthe detectability of $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay in the present and future doublebeta experiments.

In this study, we investigate the radial density profiles of galaxies show time-delay lensing, a phenomenon caused by the bending of light around massive commodities. We analyze a sample of 20 time-delay lensing galaxies, utilizing high-resolution Hubble Space Telescope imaging data to evaluating their surface gloria profiles. Our culmination show that the radial density profiles of these galaxies are typically characterized by a central concentration of light, followed by a gradual decline in surface dazzle with enhancing distance from the center. We find that the slope of the radial density characterize is strongly correlated with the amount of time delay avowed in the lensing effect, illustrate a direct relationship between the broadcast of matter in the galaxy and the bending of light around it. Our findings supplying new insights into the properties of dark matter and its role in the devising and evolution of galaxies. Anymore, we demonstrate that the radial density profiles of time-delay lensing galaxies can be used to constrain models of galaxy formation and evolution, offering a novel tool for probe the erected and composition of galaxies.

Continuous quantum error correction (CQEC) is a significant technique to mitigate the effects of decoherence in quantum systems. In this work, a CQEC scheme is proposed to protect quantum systems from non-Markovian decoherence. A master equation approach is utilized to derive the effective Lindblad operators for the non-Markovian decoherence. Furthermore, a CQEC code is designed to correct these errors. The proposed scheme can effectively suppress the decoherence effects and enhance the performance of quantum systems. This work provides a novel approach for safeguarding quantum systems from non-Markovian decoherence, with potential applications in quantum information processing and quantum communication.The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the fundamental concepts of CQEC and non-Markovian decoherence. Section III derives the effective Lindblad operators for the non-Markovian decoherence. Section IV designs a CQEC code to correct these errors. Section V presents simulation results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

We study the connection between the appearance of a 'metastable' behavior ofweakly chaotic orbits, characterized by a constant rate of increase of theTsallis q-entropy (Tsallis 1988), and the solutions of the variationalequations of motion for the same orbits. We demonstrate that the variationalequations yield transient solutions, lasting for long time intervals, duringwhich the length of deviation vectors of nearby orbits grows in time almost asa power-law. The associated power exponent can be simply related to theentropic exponent for which the q-entropy exhibits a constant rate of increase.This analysis leads to the definition of a new sensitive indicatordistinguishing regular from weakly chaotic orbits, that we call 'Average PowerLaw Exponent' (APLE). We compare the APLE with other established indicators ofthe literature. In particular, we give examples of application of the APLE ina) a thin separatrix layer of the standard map, b) the stickiness region aroundan island of stability in the same map, and c) the web of resonances of a 4Dsymplectic map. In all these cases we identify weakly chaotic orbits exhibitingthe 'metastable' behavior associated with the Tsallis q-entropy.

We performed the first scanning tunneling spectroscopy measurements on thepyrochlore superconductor KOs2O6 (Tc = 9.6 K) in both zero magnetic field andthe vortex state at several temperatures above 1.95 K. This material presentsatomically flat surfaces, yielding spatially homogeneous spectra which revealfully-gapped superconductivity with a gap anisotropy of 30%. Measurementsperformed at fields of 2 and 6 T display a hexagonal Abrikosov flux linelattice. From the shape of the vortex cores, we extract a coherence length of31-40 {\AA}, in agreement with the value derived from the upper critical fieldHc2. We observe a reduction in size of the vortex cores (and hence thecoherence length) with increasing field which is consistent with theunexpectedly high and unsaturated upper critical field reported.

We study Gaussian valence bond states of continuous variable systems,obtained as the outputs of projection operations from an ancillary space of Minfinitely entangled bonds connecting neighboring sites, applied at each of $N$sites of an harmonic chain. The entanglement distribution in Gaussian valencebond states can be controlled by varying the input amount of entanglementengineered in a (2M+1)-mode Gaussian state known as the building block, whichis isomorphic to the projector applied at a given site. We show how thismechanism can be interpreted in terms of multiple entanglement swapping fromthe chain of ancillary bonds, through the building blocks. We provide opticalschemes to produce bisymmetric three-mode Gaussian building blocks (whichcorrespond to a single bond, M=1), and study the entanglement structure in theoutput Gaussian valence bond states. The usefulness of such states for quantumcommunication protocols with continuous variables, like telecloning andteleportation networks, is finally discussed.

With the use of the AdS/CFT dictionary, a five-dimensional effectivedescription of dynamical electro-weak symmetry breaking with walking behavioris constructed. The minimal model contains only two new parameters, theconfinement scale and the effective coupling of the new strong sector. Thisparameter space is restricted by the precision electro-weak constraints and bythe requirement that the five-dimensional coupling be perturbative(corresponding to the large-N regime in four-dimensional language). Thelightest observable new states are a set of four nearly degenerate spin-1states with the same quantum numbers as the standard-model electro-weak gaugebosons, and masses in the few TeV range. Their decay rate is dominated bytwo-fermion final states. The number of pp -> mu mu and pp -> mu nu events isstudied as a function of the LHC integrated luminosity and of the two freeparameters. Discovery at the LHC is possible over a significant part of theallowed parameter space up to masses of 4 TeV already with 10/fm of integratedluminosity.

Our method uses a Bayesian framework to ensure that the results are reliable and accurate. We show the effectiveness of our method by simulations and real-world examples, which show that it outperforms traditional methods in terms of both detection accuracy and computational efficiency. Our method has important implications for signal processing, machine learning, and hypothesis testing, where accurate detection of signals in noisy data is critical.

Conditional independence models in the Gaussian case are algebraic varietiesin the cone of positive definite covariance matrices. We study these varietiesin the case of Bayesian networks, with a view towards generalizing therecursive factorization theorem to situations with hidden variables. In thecase when the underlying graph is a tree, we show that the vanishing ideal ofthe model is generated by the conditional independence statements implied bygraph. We also show that the ideal of any Bayesian network is homogeneous withrespect to a multigrading induced by a collection of upstream random variables.This has a number of important consequences for hidden variable models.Finally, we relate the ideals of Bayesian networks to a number of classicalconstructions in algebraic geometry including toric degenerations of theGrassmannian, matrix Schubert varieties, and secant varieties.

The cross-correlations between price fluctuations of 201 frequently tradedstocks in the National Stock Exchange (NSE) of India are analyzed in thispaper. We use daily closing prices for the period 1996-2006, which coincideswith the period of rapid transformation of the market following liberalization.The eigenvalue distribution of the cross-correlation matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, ofNSE is found to be similar to that of developed markets, such as the New YorkStock Exchange (NYSE): the majority of eigenvalues fall within the boundsexpected for a random matrix constructed from mutually uncorrelated timeseries. Of the few largest eigenvalues that deviate from the bulk, the largestis identified with market-wide movements. The intermediate eigenvalues thatoccur between the largest and the bulk have been associated in NYSE withspecific business sectors with strong intra-group interactions. However, in theIndian market, these deviating eigenvalues are comparatively very few and liemuch closer to the bulk. We propose that this is because of the relative lackof distinct sector identity in the market, with the movement of stocksdominantly influenced by the overall market trend. This is shown by explicitconstruction of the interaction network in the market, first by generating theminimum spanning tree from the unfiltered correlation matrix, and later, usingan improved method of generating the graph after filtering out the market modeand random effects from the data. Both methods show, compared to developedmarkets, the relative absence of clusters of co-moving stocks that belong tothe same business sector. This is consistent with the general belief thatemerging markets tend to be more correlated than developed markets.

The Millennium Galaxy Catalogue (MGC) provides a wealth of information about the properties of galaxies, including their B-band attenuation, which is a measure of the amount of light absorbed by dust and gas in the galaxy. In this study, we use the MGC to investigate the B-band attenuation of bulge and disc light in a sample of galaxies and explore its implications for the cosmic dust and stellar mass densities.We find that the B-band attenuation of bulge light is significantly higher than that of disc light, indicating that bulges are more heavily obscured by dust and gas. This suggests that bulges may have formed through a different process than discs, such as through the merger of smaller galaxies.We also find a strong correlation between the B-band attenuation and the stellar mass density of galaxies, indicating that galaxies with higher stellar masses tend to have higher levels of dust extinction. This is consistent with the idea that dust is an important component of galaxy evolution, playing a role in the formation and growth of galaxies.Furthermore, we use the MGC to estimate the cosmic dust density, which is found to be consistent with previous estimates based on observations of the cosmic microwave background radiation. This suggests that the MGC provides a reliable measure of the dust content of galaxies.Our results have important implications for our understanding of galaxy evolution and the role of dust in shaping the properties of galaxies. They also highlight the importance of considering the effects of dust extinction when interpreting observations of galaxy properties.Overall, this study demonstrates the power of the MGC for investigating the properties of galaxies and the role of dust in shaping their evolution. The catalogue provides a valuable resource for future studies of galaxy evolution and cosmology.

In this paper, the error performance of on-off frequency shift keying (OOFSK)modulation over fading channels is analyzed when the receiver is equipped withmultiple antennas. The analysis is conducted in two cases: the coherentscenario where the fading is perfectly known at the receiver, and thenoncoherent scenario where neither the receiver nor the transmitter knows thefading coefficients. For both cases, the maximum a posteriori probability (MAP)detection rule is derived and analytical probability of error expressions areobtained. The effect of fading correlation among the receiver antennas is alsostudied. Simulation results indicate that for sufficiently low duty cyclevalues, lower probability of error values with respect to FSK signaling areachieved. Equivalently, when compared to FSK modulation, OOFSK with low dutycycle requires less energy to achieve the same probability of error, whichrenders this modulation a more energy efficient transmission technique.

We study spontaneous symmetry breaking in a system of two parallelquasi-one-dimensional traps, equipped with optical lattices (OLs) and filledwith a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC). The cores are linearly coupled bytunneling. Analysis of the corresponding system of linearly coupledGross-Pitaevskii equations (GPEs) reveals that spectral bandgaps of the singleGPE split into subgaps. Symmetry breaking in two-component BEC solitons isstudied in cases of the attractive (AA) and repulsive (RR) nonlinearity in bothtraps; the mixed situation, with repulsion in one trap and attraction in theother (RA), is considered too. In all the cases, stable asymmetric solitons arefound, bifurcating from symmetric or antisymmetric ones (and destabilizingthem), in the AA and RR systems, respectively. In either case, bi-stability ispredicted, with a nonbifurcating stable branch, either antisymmetric orsymmetric, coexisting with asymmetric ones. Solitons destabilized by thebifurcation tend to rearrange themselves into their stable asymmetriccounterparts. The impact of a phase mismatch, between the OLs in the two coresis also studied. Also considered is a related model, for a binary BEC in asingle-core trap with the OL, assuming that the two species (representingdifferent spin states of the same atom) are coupled by linear interconversion.In that case, the symmetry-breaking bifurcations in the AA and RR models switchtheir character, if the inter-species nonlinear interaction becomes strongerthan the intra-species nonlinearity.

We make a further study of the very deep Chandra observation of the X-raybrightest galaxy cluster, A426 in Perseus. We examine the radial distributionof energy flux inferred by the quasi-concentric ripples in surface brightness,assuming they are due to sound waves, and show that it is a significantfraction of the energy lost by radiative cooling within the inner 75-100 kpc,where the cooling time is 4-5 Gyr, respectively. The wave flux decreasesoutward with radius, consistent with energy being dissipated. Some newlydiscovered large ripples beyond 100 kpc, and a possible intact bubble at 170kpc radius, may indicate a larger level of activity by the nucleus a few 100Myr ago. The distribution of metals in the intracluster gas peaks at a radiusof about 40 kpc and is significantly clumpy on scales of 5 kpc. The temperaturedistribution of the soft X-ray filaments and the hard X-ray emission componentfound within the inner 50 kpc are analysed in detail. The pressure due to thenonthermal electrons, responsible for a spectral component interpreted asinverse Compton emission, is high within 40 kpc of the centre and boosts thepower in sound waves there; it drops steeply beyond 40 kpc. We find no thermalemission from the radio bubbles; in order for any thermal gas to have a fillingfactor within the bubbles exceeding 50 per cent, the temperature of that gashas to exceed 50 keV.

This study aims to investigate the rotation of sub-populations in Omega Centauri using observational data and numerical simulations. The rotation of sub-populations is influenced by a combination of factors, such as the mass of the sub-population, the density of the cluster, and the presence of dark matter. The results show that the rotation of sub-populations in Omega Centauri is a complex phenomenon, and some sub-populations rotate quickly, while others rotate slowly or even retrograde. Our results have important implications for our understanding of the formation and evolution of globular clusters and the role of sub-populations in these clusters.

Exomoons, or moons orbiting planets outside our solar system, could be widespread in the galaxy. Their detection could provide perceptions into the formation and evolution of planetary systems. However, directly imaging exomoons with current telescopes is extremely challenging due to their small pruning and large distance from Territorial. Here we analyzed an alternative method for characterizing exomoons based on photometric transit timing variations. We develop a theoretical model to predict the timing deviations caused by an exomoon as its host mundos transits its host stars. We show that the amplitude of these distinctions scales predictably with the exomoon's physical trait including its mass, radius, and orbital parameters. We test our model using numerical simulations of transiting planetary systems containing exomoons with a gama of weights and orbits. We then attempt to recover the exomoon properties by appraisals the simulated transit light curves. Our results demonstrate that it is conceivable to constrain an exomoon's mass to within 50% and radius to within 20% for objects larger than 0.5 Earth radii exploited this technique with current plant. We discuss the factors that determine the measurement precision such as exomoon size, orbital fracture, and banners to noise of the observations. This method holds promise for establishing the prevalence of exomoons and earns new insights into the formation of satellites outside our solar regime.

In this article, we studied the count in the theory of the BPS computing in N = 4 Super Yang-Mills (SYM). We explore extensions of hybrid inflationary models in the context ofsupersymmetric D-term inflation. We point out that a large variety ofinflationary scenarios can be encountered when the field content is extended.It is not only possible to get curvaton type models but also scenarios in whichdifferent fields, with nontrivial statistical properties, contribute to theprimordial curvature fluctuations. We explore more particularly the parameterspace of these multiple field inflationary models. It is shown that thereexists a large domain in which significant primordial non-Gaussianities can beproduced while preserving a scale free power spectrum for the metricfluctuations. In particular we explicitly compute the expected bi- andtrispectrum for such models and compared the results to the current andexpected observational constraints. It is shown that it is necessary to useboth the bi- and tri-spectra of CMB anisotropies to efficiently reduce theirparameter space.

Photonic molecules, named by analogy with chemical molecules, are clusters ofclosely located electromagnetically interacting microcavities or "photonicatoms". As two or several microcavities are brought close together, theiroptical modes interact, and a rich spectrum of photonic molecule supermodesemerges, which depends both on geometrical and material properties ofindividual cavities and on their mutual interactions. Here, we discuss ways ofcontrollable manipulation of photonic molecule supermodes, which improve or addnew functionalities to microcavity-based optical components. We present severaloptimally-tuned photonic molecule designs for lowering thresholds ofsemiconductor microlasers, producing directional light emission, enhancingsensitivity of microcavity-based bio(chemical)sensors, and optimizingelectromagnetic energy transfer around bends of coupled-cavity waveguides.Photonic molecules composed of identical microcavities as well as ofmicrocavities with various degrees of size or material detuning are discussed.Microwave experiments on scaled photonic molecule structures are currentlyunder way to confirm our theoretical predictions.

Electronic properties of bilayer and multilayer graphene have generally beeninterpreted in terms of AB or Bernal stacking. However, it is known that manytypes of stacking defects can occur in natural and synthetic graphite; rotationof the top layer is often seen in scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) studiesof graphite. In this paper we consider a graphene bilayer with a relative smallangle rotation between the layers and calculate the electronic structure nearzero energy in a continuum approximation. Contrary to what happens in a ABstacked bilayer and in accord with observations in epitaxial graphene we find:(a) the low energy dispersion is linear, as in a single layer, but the Fermivelocity can be significantly smaller than the single layer value; (b) anexternal electric field, perpendicular to the layers, does not open anelectronic gap

Contact patterns in populations fundamentally influence the spread ofinfectious diseases. Current mathematical methods for epidemiologicalforecasting on networks largely assume that contacts between individuals arefixed, at least for the duration of an outbreak. In reality, contact patternsmay be quite fluid, with individuals frequently making and breaking social orsexual relationships. Here we develop a mathematical approach to predictingdisease transmission on dynamic networks in which each individual has acharacteristic behavior (typical contact number), but the identities of theircontacts change in time. We show that dynamic contact patterns shapeepidemiological dynamics in ways that cannot be adequately captured in staticnetwork models or mass-action models. Our new model interpolates smoothlybetween static network models and mass-action models using a mixing parameter,thereby providing a bridge between disparate classes of epidemiological models.Using epidemiological and sexual contact data from an Atlanta high school, wethen demonstrate the utility of this method for forecasting and controllingsexually transmitted disease outbreaks.

This study presents an investigaion into the phenomenon of color reconnection in WW events uTsing data obtained from the DELPHI detector at LEP-2. A comparison is made between data and Monte JCarlo simulations, both with and without color reconnection effects. The results indicate that the inclusion of colo reconnection in the simulations provides a better description of the dataa, as evidenced by the improved agreement between the simulation and experimental observableu. These fidings contribute to our uBnderstanding of the hadronization process and provide valuable insights for future studies of color reconnection in high-energy physics.

A large acceptance scintillator detector with wavelength shifting fibre read-out for search of eta-nucleus bound statesWe propose to construct a large acceptance detector for the search for eta-nucleus bound states in the reaction eta + nucleus --> nսcleus + X by using the missing mass teshnique. We present the first resuts from a survey of luminous red galaxy (LRG) clustering at intermediate redshift suing the AAOmega multi-object spectrograph on the Anglo-Australian Telescope. Spectra for over 3000 LRGs were obtained in the redshift range 0.5<z<0.8 over a ottal surevy area of 50 square degrees. Redshifts were measured from the spectra and used to stuy the spatia clustering of LRGs through the calculation of the two-point correlation function. On small scales we detect strong clustering consistent with the prsferential formation of LRGs in dense environments. On larger scales the correlation functUon provides new constraints on cosmological parameters and galaxy bias evolution. The LRG clustering strength is found to remain pproximately constant with redshift in the surveyed epoch. We perform a prelminary analysis of the clustering aBplitude as a function of LRG luminosity and find hints of an increased clustering for more luminous LRGs. Overall our wrk demonstrates the poewr of AAOmega for studying the intermediate-redshift universe and provides a reference sample for future galaxy clustering studies at z~0.7.

Polarization-selective excitation of nitrogen-vacancy (N-V) centers in diamond is a powerful technique for studying the electronic structure of defects in solids and for realizing novel quantum technologies. In this work, we investigate the polarization dependence of the excitation efficiency of N-V centers in diamond using a variety of optical techniques. We find that the excitation efficiency is strongly dependent on the polarization of the incident light, with the N-V centers being most efficiently excited by light polarized parallel to the [111] crystal axis. We also observe a significant decrease in the excitation efficiency for light polarized parallel to the [100] crystal axis. These results are explained in terms of the symmetry of the N-V center and the selection rules for optical transitions. Our findings have important implications for the design of experiments using N-V centers in diamond, as well as for the development of novel quantum technologies based on these defects.

In the fruit flies, the photoretically sensitive cells form an orderly mode through the mechanism involving cell adhesion and cortex tension.
