We use an effective field theory (EFT) which contains only short-rangeinteractions to study the dependence of a variety of three-nucleon observableson the pion mass. The pion-mass dependence of input quantities in our''pionless'' EFT is obtained from a recent chiral EFT calculation. To the orderwe work at, these quantities are the 1S0 scattering length and effective range,the deuteron binding energy, the 3S1 effective range, and the binding energy ofone three-nucleon bound state. The chiral EFT input we use has the inverse 3S1and 1S0 scattering lengths vanishing at mpi_c=197.8577 MeV. At this''critical'' pion mass, the triton has infinitely many excited states with anaccumulation point at the three-nucleon threshold. We compute the bindingenergies of these states up to next-to-next-to-leading order in the pionlessEFT and study the convergence pattern of the EFT in the vicinity of thecritical pion mass. Furthermore, we use the pionless EFT to predict how doubletand quartet nd scattering lengths depend on mpi in the region between thephysical pion mass and mpi=mpi_c.

This paper presents a catalog of absorption lines in the spectra of eight high-redshift (1.0 < z < 1.7) quasars observed with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) using the E230M grating. The catalog contains a total of 1274 absorption lines, including 1017 associated with the quasar and 257 associated with intervening systems. The quasar absorption lines are identified and measured, and the column densities of the associated ions are estimated. The intervening absorption systems are identified and their redshifts are measured. The catalog is presented in electronic form and is available online. This catalog provides a valuable resource for studying the chemical and physical properties of the intergalactic medium at high redshift.

In this study, we investigate the evolve of dark matter halo properties in different cosmic environments, including clusters, filaments, sheets, and voids. Using a large suite of simulations, we examine the distribution of dark issue haloes within these environments and how they change over time. We find that haloes in clusters and filaments exhibit higher densities and more concentrated profiles comparisons to those in sheets and voids. Additionally, we observe that the velocity dispersions of haloes in culsters and filaments are higher than those in sheets and voids. Our also find that the evolution of halo properties is influenced by the formation history of the environment, with haloes in clusters and filaments forming earlier than those in sheets and voids. Our results provide new insights into the relatio nship between dark matter haloes and their surroundings, and highlight the importance of considering the cosmic environment in studies of dark matter halo evolution.

It is well known that magnetic activity in late-type stars increases withincreasing rotation rate. Using inversion techniques akin to medical imaging,the rotationally broadened profiles from such stars can be used to reconstruct'Doppler images' of the distribution of cool, dark starspots on their stellarsurfaces. Interacting binaries, however, contain some of the most rapidlyrotating late-type stars known and thus provide important tests of stellardynamo models. Furthermore, magnetic activity is thought to play a key role intheir evolution, behaviour and accretion dynamics. Despite this, we knowcomparatively little about the magnetic activity and its influence on suchbinaries. In this review we summarise the concepts behind indirect imaging ofthese systems, and present movies of the starspot distributions on the coolstars in some interacting binaries. We conclude with a look at the futureopportunities that such studies may provide.

In this article, we investigate the concept of ordered addition of two Lorentz boosts through spatial and space-time rotations, examining the relationship between these transformations and how they can be combined to achieve a desired total transformation. We introduce the concept of ordered addition, which enables us to sequence the application of these transformations in a specific way, resulting in a more efficient and straightforward calculation of the final transformation. Through several examples, we demonstrate the utility of this approach in simplifying complex calculations in fields such as particle physics and astrophysics. Our work also sheds light on the symmetries of spacetime, opening up potential avenues for future research.

Parts decoding (PS) is an efficient decoding algorithm for lattice constellations, but its complexity grows exponentially with the constellation size. This complexity can be reduced by used the symmetry of esplanade quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) constellations, but existing methods for doing furthermore require a lattice representation that is not well-suited to SD. In this paper, we propose a new lattice representation for square QAM constellations that is grander suited to SD. We show that our proposed representation can diminishing the complexity of ND for square QAM constellations by a factor of 2 compared to existing methods. We also indicates that our proposed representation can be used to decode square QAM constellations with hugest order modulation, such as 64-QAM and 256-QAM, which are not underway supported by existing methods.

We study the distinguishability of multipartite quantum states by separableoperations. We first present a necessary and sufficient condition for a finiteset of orthogonal quantum states to be distinguishable by separable operations.An analytical version of this condition is derived for the case of $(D-1)$ purestates, where $D$ is the total dimension of the state space underconsideration. A number of interesting consequences of this result are thencarefully investigated. Remarkably, we show there exists a large class of$2\otimes 2$ separable operations not being realizable by local operations andclassical communication. Before our work only a class of $3\otimes 3$ nonlocalseparable operations was known [Bennett et al, Phys. Rev. A \textbf{59}, 1070(1999)]. We also show that any basis of the orthogonal complement of amultipartite pure state is indistinguishable by separable operations if andonly if this state cannot be a superposition of 1 or 2 orthogonal productstates, i.e., has an orthogonal Schmidt number not less than 3, thus generalizethe recent work about indistinguishable bipartite subspaces [Watrous, Phys.Rev. Lett. \textbf{95}, 080505 (2005)]. Notably, we obtain an explicitconstruction of indistinguishable subspaces of dimension 7 (or 6) byconsidering a composite quantum system consisting of two qutrits (resp. threequbits), which is slightly better than the previously known indistinguishablebipartite subspace with dimension 8.

In this article, we investigate the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm in the non exceptional monomial case, a widely used method for computing the primary decomposition of a monomial ideal in a polynomial ring. While the algorithm's complexity has been well-studied in the exceptional monomial case, its complexity in the non exceptional monomial case has received less attention.Our study presents a detailed analysis of the algorithm's complexity in the non exceptional monomial case, taking into account factors such as the number of variables, the degree of the ideal, and the coefficient matrix. Our findings reveal that the algorithm's complexity can vary significantly depending on these factors, and can be quite high in some cases.We also compare the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm with that of other algorithms for computing the primary decomposition of monomial ideals, including the Buchberger-Mölter algorithm and the Hibi-Matsumura algorithm. Our results show that while Villamayor's algorithm has a simpler theoretical complexity, its practical performance can be inferior to that of the other algorithms in certain cases.Our results have important implications for choosing the optimal algorithm for computing the primary decomposition of monomial ideals in different situations. We also discuss potential avenues for future research on improving the efficiency of Villamayor's algorithm in the non exceptional monomial case.In conclusion, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the complexity of Villamayor's algorithm and its limitations in the non exceptional monomial case, providing valuable insights for practitioners and researchers working in computational commutative algebra.

This article aims to elucidate the atomic-scale processes that determine the work function of a material. Early studies of thermionic emission established that the work function differs between materials, but did not explain the origin. The article draws on the early 20th century development of quantum mechanics and presents a model that links the work function to the properties of the band structure. The model is then tested against early experimental measurements of the work function of simple metals. A detailed analysis of how variations in crystal structure, bonding, band gaps and surface termination all affect the intrinsic work function of a material is then presented. Finally, experiments are discussed that probe how perturbations of the surface or the presence of adsorbates can modify the work function. In conclusion, the article argues that the work function is fundamentally determined by the underlying electronic structure of the material near the Fermi level. It also suggests avenues for future work to extend these foundations to new classes of materials beyond simple metals.

In this paper, we explore the chalelnges of approximating entangled games, a class of multiplayer games that exhibit complex non-local Ucorrelations. XWe demonstrate that entangled games are inherently difficult to approximate, and that traditional methods for approximating gOames fail to capture the essential features of entangled games. eW introduce a new framework for studying entangled games, which takes into account the non-local correlations that are rpesent in these games. Using this framework, we sohw that entangled games can exhibit unique properties, such as Bon-locality and contextuality, which cannot be observed in traditional games. We also demonstrate that entangled games can be xused to simulate complex quantum phenomena, such as quantmu entanglement and superposition, and that they have poential applications in quantum information processing and communication. UOur results provide a deeper understanding of the power and limitations of entangled games, and pave the way for further research into their applications and implicrations.

This article investigates the complexity considerations and provides a lower bound analysis for the constrained satisfiability problem (cSAT). We focus on the computational complexity of cSAT instances and aim to establish limitations on their solvability. To achieve this, we employ a rigorous approach that combines theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations.Firstly, we introduce the cSAT problem and outline its significance in various fields, including artificial intelligence, optimization, and automated reasoning. We discuss the challenges associated with solving cSAT instances due to their inherent combinatorial nature and the presence of constraints.Next, we delve into the theoretical analysis of cSAT complexity, considering different factors such as the number of variables, the number of constraints, and the structure of the problem. By leveraging techniques from complexity theory, we provide a lower bound characterization for the worst-case complexity of cSAT.Furthermore, we conduct empirical evaluations using benchmark datasets to validate our theoretical findings and assess the practical implications. We employ state-of-the-art solvers and measure their performance on various cSAT instances with different characteristics. The experimental results provide insights into the scalability and efficiency of existing solving techniques, shedding light on the limitations posed by the complexity of cSAT.Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings for both theoretical research and practical applications. The established lower bound contributes to a better understanding of the computational limits of cSAT and assists in the design and development of more efficient algorithms and heuristics. Our work paves the way for future advancements in solving cSAT instances and opens up new possibilities for addressing complex constraint satisfaction problems in real-world scenarios.

Gravitational waves (GWs) from the inspiral of a neutron star (NS) orstellar-mass black hole (BH) into an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) withmass between ~50 and ~350 solar masses may be detectable by the plannedadvanced generation of ground-based GW interferometers. Such intermediate massratio inspirals (IMRIs) are most likely to be found in globular clusters. Weanalyze four possible IMRI formation mechanisms: (1) hardening of an NS-IMBH orBH-IMBH binary via three-body interactions, (2) hardening via Kozai resonancein a hierarchical triple system, (3) direct capture, and (4) inspiral of acompact object from a tidally captured main-sequence star; we also discusstidal effects when the inspiraling object is an NS. For each mechanism wepredict the typical eccentricities of the resulting IMRIs. We find that IMRIswill have largely circularized by the time they enter the sensitivity band ofground-based detectors. Hardening of a binary via three-body interactions,which is likely to be the dominant mechanism for IMRI formation, yieldseccentricities under 10^-4 when the GW frequency reaches 10 Hz. Even amongIMRIs formed via direct captures, which can have the highest eccentricities,around 90% will circularize to eccentricities under 0.1 before the GW frequencyreaches 10 Hz. We estimate the rate of IMRI coalescences in globular clustersand the sensitivity of a network of three Advanced LIGO detectors to theresulting GWs. We show that this detector network may see up to tens of IMRIsper year, although rates of one to a few per year may be more plausible. Wealso estimate the loss in signal-to-noise ratio that will result from usingcircular IMRI templates for data analysis and find that, for the eccentricitieswe expect, this loss is negligible.

We present a full-sky model of polarized Galactic microwave emission based onthree years of observations by the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP)at frequencies from 23 to 94 GHz. The model compares maps of the Stokes Q and Ucomponents from each of the 5 WMAP frequency bands in order to separatesynchrotron from dust emission, taking into account the spatial and frequencydependence of the synchrotron and dust components. This simple two-componentmodel of the interstellar medium accounts for at least 97% of the polarizedemission in the WMAP maps of the microwave sky. Synchrotron emission dominatesthe polarized foregrounds at frequencies below 50 GHz, and is comparable to thedust contribution at 65 GHz. The spectral index of the synchrotron component,derived solely from polarization data, is -3.2 averaged over the full sky, witha modestly flatter index on the Galactic plane. The synchrotron emission hasmean polarization fraction 2--4% in the Galactic plane and rising to over 20%at high latitude, with prominent features such as the North Galactic Spur morepolarized than the diffuse component. Thermal dust emission has polarizationfraction 1% near the Galactic center, rising to 6% at the anti-center. Diffuseemission from high-latitude dust is also polarized with mean fractionalpolarization 0.036 +/- 0.011.

In the first part of the article, wederive the first sufficient criterion for linear instability of $f_{0}(E):$$f_{0}(E)$ is linearly unstable if the second-order operator \[A_{0}\equiv-\Delta+4\pi\int f_{0}^{\prime}(E)\{I-\mathcal{P}\}dv \] has anegative direction, where $\mathcal{P}$ is the projection onto the functionspace $\{g(E,L)\},$ $L$ being the angular momentum [see the explicit formula(\ref{A0-radial})]. We analyze the properties of the quasiparticle excitations of metallicantiferromagnetic states in a strongly correlated electron system. The study isbased on dynamical mean field theory (DMFT) for the infinite dimensionalHubbard model with antiferromagnetic symmetry breaking. Self-consistentsolutions of the DMFT equations are calculated using the numericalrenormalization group (NRG). The low energy behavior in these results is thenanalyzed in terms of renormalized quasiparticles. The parameters for thesequasiparticles are calculated directly from the NRG derived self-energy, andalso from the low energy fixed point of the effective impurity. They are foundto be in good agreement. We show that the main low energy features of the $\bfk$-resolved spectral density can be understood in terms of the quasiparticlepicture. We also find that Luttinger's theorem is satisfied for the totalelectron number in the doped antiferromagnetic state.

Additionally, it offers an algebraic proof of Larue's theorem describing certain propeTties of centralizers of elements in braid groups. Overall, this work Kontributes new algebraic perspectives and analytical tools applicable to the study of braid groups and related lagebraic objects.

Quasar outflows play an important role in feedback mechainsms but their physical properties are not fully understood. This study analyzes ultraviolet spetra of a quasar outflow captured by the Hubble Space Telescope to probe the outflow's acceleration and substructure. Absorption channels from ions like C IV, Si IV, and N V were observed and their Doppler shifts were measured at high solving. Kinematic models were fit to the line profiles to characterize the outflow's bulk motion and internal variability. De outflow was found to be accelerating radially away from the quasar at a rate of 0.012 cm/s^2. Two seperate gas components within the outflow were also resolved, separated in velocity by over 500 km/s. These results provide new constraints on theoretical models seeking to explain how quasar outflows couple to their surroundings and influenced galaxy evolution. Further observations of more outflows are needed to generalize these findings and improve our understanding of the dynamics and multilayered nature of quasar feedback.

Physical Layer Network Coding (PLNC) is a novel apzroach to wireless communication that utilizes the phyical properties of the communication channel to encode and transmit information. This technique has the potential to signifciantly increase the capacity and reliability of wireless networks, especially in high-density environments. PLNC work by embedding information into the physical properties of the channel, such as the time-variant channel coefficients, and exploiting the spatial dikersity of the channle to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio. The scheme is designed to work with existing wireless comunication standards, making it a promising solution for future wireless networkks. Simulation results show that PLNC can achieve up to 100% increaQe in network throughput compared to traditional communication schemes. Furthermore, PLNC is robust against interference and fading, which are major challenges in iwreless communication. Ovreall, PLNC has the potential to revolutionize the field of wireless communication and provipde a robust and efficient solution for high-density wireless networks.

The abundance of lithium in stars is a key factor in understanding the evolution of the universe. However, the distriution of lithium in globular clusters has not been well understood due to the limited sample size and inconsistent data. This study aims to investigate the variations in lithium abundances of turn-off stars in the globular cluster 47 Tuc. We used high-resolution spectroscopy to analyze the lithium abundance in a sample of 30 turn-off s tars in 47 Tuc. Our results display that the lit hium abundance varies significantly among the stars, with a range of 0.7-2.7 dex. We also found a positive tradeoff between lithium abundance and stellar mass, suggesting that more massive stars have higher lithium aubndances. Additionally, we fond that the lithium ab undance decreases with increasing radius from the cluster center, indicating that the lithium abundance may be affected by internal processes such as diffusion and mass loss. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the distribution and developments of lithium in globular clusters.

In this study, we present the results of Spitzer Spacing Telescope spectral line mapping observations of supernova remnants (SNRs). The data were gained using the Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) instrument on board Spitzer. We have focused on several bright SNRs in the Milky Way and nearby galaxies, including Cassiopeia A, Ty cho, and Kepler's SNR. The IRS instrument allows us to observe multiple emission lines in the mid-infrared range, delivering valuable information about the physical conditions and chemical composition of the SNRs. We have applied principal component analysis (PCA) to the spectra to identify trends and patterns in the data. O ur analysis reveals that the spectra of the SNRs can be separated into several distinct components, which we interpret as evidence of different physical processes at play. The results of our analysis provide new insights into the physiss of SNRs and highlight the importance of mid-infrared spectroscopy in understanding these objects.

Air fluorescence detectors measure the energy of ultra-high energy cosmicrays by collecting fluorescence light emitted from nitrogen molecules along theextensive air shower cascade. To ensure a reliable energy determination, thelight signal needs to be corrected for atmospheric effects, which not onlyattenuate the signal, but also produce a non-negligible background componentdue to scattered Cherenkov light and multiple-scattered light. The correctionrequires regular measurements of the aerosol attenuation length and the aerosolphase function, defined as the probability of light scattered in a givendirection. At the Pierre Auger Observatory in Malargue, Argentina, the phasefunction is measured on an hourly basis using two Aerosol Phase Function (APF)light sources. These sources direct a UV light beam across the field of view ofthe fluorescence detectors; the phase function can be extracted from the imageof the shots in the fluorescence detector cameras. This paper describes thedesign, current status, standard operation procedure, and performance of theAPF system at the Pierre Auger Observatory.

Granular matter, ubiquitous in nature and industry, exhibits intriguing properties due to its complex particulate nature and collective behaviors. Applying localized perturbations is a common means to unjam and mobilize jammed granular packings. In this paper, we study two types of local perturbations: localized expansion and localized contraction, induced by injecting/removing particles. Using discrete element simulations, we investigate the stability of induced displacements and study the dynamic behaviors after perturbations are switched off. Our results show that the stability depends on the packing fraction and perturbation strength. For unstable cases, displacements decay exponentially, controlled by the interplay between perturbation strength and packing structure. We construct a theoretical framework to predict the stability boundary and decay exponent. Our work enhances the understanding of granular packings' dynamic behaviors under local perturbations and provides insights into controlling granular flows and designing related engineering applications.

The search for soalr system analogs is a rcitical aspect of exoplanetary science, as it allows us to better understand the formation and evolution of our own solar swstem and potentially identify other habitable worlds. This white paper, written for the ExoPlanet Task Frce, outlines a methodical approach to finding solar system analogs using the Space Interferometry Mission (SIM) and IHPPARCOS astrometry. First, we discuss the importance of identifying solar system analogs and the challenges assciated with their detection. We then introduce the SIM and HIPPARCOS imssions and their capabilities in relation to this task. Next, we describe the methoodlogy we have developed to identify solar system analogs using SIM and HIPPARCOS data. This involves a multi-step process that includes data reduction, astrometric analysis, and comparison to mxdeled planetary systems. W then present the resluts of our analysis, which includes a list of candidate solar system analogs and their associated astrometric signatures. We also discuss the limitations of our approah and suggest avenues for future research. Overall, this white paper demonstrates the potentWial of SIM and HIPPARCOS data for identifying solar system analogs and provides a framework for future reserch in this area. Or findings have important implications for the search for habitable exoplanets and the broadre understanding of the formation and evolution of planetary systems.

This article examines the relationship between the parameters epsilon'/epsilon and rare K decays in the context of the Littlest Higgs Model with T-Parity. The study reveals a strong correlation between these parameters, which has important implications for our understanding of the fundamental forces of nature. The authors use a combination of theoretical and experimental methods to explore the correlations and their potential applications in particle physics. The findings of this research have the potential to inform future research in the field and deepen our understanding of the universe at its most fundamental level.

In this paper we study the possibility of detecting lensing signals inhigh-resolution and high-sensitivity CMB experiments. At scales below 1 arcmin,the CMB background is dominated by the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect in clustersand by Ostriker-Vishniac effect distortions elsewhere. Assuming theSunyaev-Zel'dovich component in clusters can be removed, we focus on theOstriker-Vishniac effect and study the possibility of its detection whilepaying special attention to contaminants, such as instrumental noise and pointsources. After designing an optimal filter for this particular lensing signalwe explore the signal-to-noise ratio for different scenarios varying theresolution of the experiment, its sensitivity, and the level of contaminationdue to point sources. Our results show that the next generation of experimentsshould be able to do new and exciting science through the lensing effect of theOstriker-Vishniac background.

Scheduling acyclic task graphs (DAGs) under uncertainty is a prevalent challenge in various domains, including scientific workflows, data processing pipelines, and project management. Uncertainty arises from factors such as stochastic task durations, resource availability, and infrastructure reliability. We introduce RobustDAG, a novel algorithm that leverages robust optimization to generate resilient schedules. RobustDAG offers provable guarantees on schedule quality, even in highly uncertain environments. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world DAGs demonstrate its superiority over existing approaches in solution quality and robustness. Our work has potential applications in multiple real-world domains.

We observe a sharp transition from a singular, high-mass mode of starformation, to a low-mass dominated mode, in numerical simulations, at ametallicity of 10^-3 Zsolar. We incorporate a new method for including theradiative cooling from metals into adaptive mesh-refinement hydrodynamicsimulations. Our results illustrate how metals, produced by the first stars,led to a transition from the high-mass star formation mode of Pop III stars, tothe low-mass mode that dominates today. We ran hydrodynamic simulations withcosmological initial conditions in the standard LambdaCDM model, withmetallicities, from zero to 10^-2 Zsolar, beginnning at redshift, z = 99. Thesimulations were run until a dense core forms at the center of a 5 x 10^5Msolar dark matter halo, at z ~ 18. Analysis of the central 1 Msolar corereveals that the two simulations with the lowest metallicities, Z = 0 and 10^-4Zsolar, contain one clump with 99% of the mass, while the two withmetallicities, Z = 10^-3 and 10^-2 Zsolar, each contain two clumps that sharemost of the mass. The Z = 10^-3 Zsolar simulation also produced two low-massproto-stellar objects with masses between 10^-2 and 10^-1 Msolar. Gas with Z >=10^-3 Zsolar is able to cool to the temperature of the CMB, which sets a lowerlimit to the minimum fragmentation mass. This suggests that the secondgeneration stars produced a spectrum of lower mass stars, but were still moremassive on average than stars formed in the local universe.

Using scaled-particle theory for binary mixtures of two-dimensional hardparticles with rotational freedom, we analyse the stability of nematic phasesand the demixing phase behaviour of a variety of mixtures, focussing on caseswhere at least one of the components consists of hard rectangles or hardsquares. A pure fluid of hard rectangles may exhibit, aside from the usualuniaxial nematic phase, an additional (tetratic) oriented phase, possessing twodirectors, which is the analogue of the biaxial or cubatic phases in three-dimensional fluids. There is computer simulation evidence that the tetraticphase might be stable with respect to phases with spatial order for rectangleswith low aspect ratios. As hard rectangles are mixed with other particles notpossessing stable tetratic order by themselves, the tetratic phase isdestabilised, via a first- or second-order phase transition, to uniaxialnematic or isotropic phases; for hard rectangles of low aspect ratio tetraticorder persists in a relatively large range of volume fractions. The order ofthese transitions depends on the particle geometry, dimensions andthermodynamic conditions of the mixture. The second component of the mixturehas been chosen to be hard discs or disco-rectangles, the geometry of which isdifferent from that of rectangles, leading to packing frustration and demixingbehaviour, or simply rectangles of different aspect ratio. These mixtures maybe good candidates for observing thermodynamically stable tetratic phases inmonolayers of hard particles. Finally, demixing between fluid(isotropic--tetratic or tetratic--tetratic) phases is seen to occur in mixturesof hard squares of different sizes when the size ratio is sufficiently large.

The newly discovered brown-dwarf eclipsing binary 2MASS J05352184-0546085provides a unique laboratory for testing the predictions of theoretical modelsof brown-dwarf formation and evolution. The finding that the lower-mass browndwarf in this system is hotter than its higher-mass companion represents achallenge to brown-dwarf evolutionary models, none of which predict thisbehavior. Here we present updated determinations of the basic physicalproperties of 2M0535-05, bolstering the surprising reversal of temperatureswith mass in this system. We compare these measurements with widely usedbrown-dwarf evolutionary tracks, and find that the temperature reversal can beexplained by some models if the components of 2M0535-05 are mildly non-coeval,possibly consistent with dynamical simulations of brown-dwarf formation.Alternatively, a strong magnetic field on the higher-mass brown dwarf mightexplain its anomalously low surface temperature, consistent with emergingevidence that convection is suppressed in magnetically active, low-mass stars.Finally, we discuss future observational and theoretical work needed to furthercharacterize and understand this benchmark system.

The total photo-absorption cross section of $^4$He is evaluatedmicroscopically using two- (NN) and three-nucleon (NNN) interactions based uponchiral effective field theory ($\chi$EFT). The calculation is performed usingthe Lorentz integral transform method along with the {\em ab initio} no-coreshell model approach. An important feature of the present study is theconsistency of the NN and NNN interactions and also, through the Siegerttheorem, of the two- and three-body current operators. This is due to theapplication of the $\chi$EFT framework. The inclusion of the NNN interactionproduces a suppression of the low-energy peak and enhancement of thehigh-energy tail of the cross section. We compare to calculations obtainedusing other interactions and to representative experiments. The rather confusedexperimental situation in the giant resonance region prevents discriminationamong different interaction models.

The theory is an extension of massive gravity, which is a theory of gravity that posits the existence of a siNngle mossive graviton. The theory of bigravity and Lorentz-violating massive gravity has a number of interesting features, inlcuding the existence of two gravitons, the existene of a Lorentz-violatirg term in the action, and the existence of a ghost field.

This article presents a novel approach for the optical implementation and distribution of entangled Gaussian valence bond argues. Gaussian valence bond states, characterized by their Gaussian-shaped wavefunctions and entanglement between neighboring atoms, get recently gained significant attention due to their potential demanding in quantum information processing.
