Regular Motions in Double Bars: Double-Frequency Orbits and Loops This paper investigates the regular motions of particles in double bars, identifying two types: double-frequency orbits and loops. Double-frequency orbits are characterized by the particle's frequency in the x -direction being twice its frequency in the y -direction, while loops are characterized by the particle's trajectory forming a closed loop. Analytical expressions are derived for the frequencies and amplitudes of these motions, and their stability is discussed. The implications of these results for the dynamics of stars in barred galaxies are also explored.

The Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) is a powerful tool for studying hadron properties. We apply the BSE to calculate the average kinetic energy of the heavy quark in the $\Lambda_b$ baryon. Our results yield an average kinetic energy of approximately 0.3 GeV, consistent with theoretical predictions. These findings enhance our understanding of the $\Lambda_b$ baryon's structure.

Hyperspectral images can be represented either as a set of images or as a setof spectra. Spectral classification and segmentation and data reduction are themain problems in hyperspectral image analysis. In this paper we propose aBayesian estimation approach with an appropriate hiearchical model with hiddenmarkovian variables which gives the possibility to jointly do data reduction,spectral classification and image segmentation. In the proposed model, thedesired independent components are piecewise homogeneous images which share thesame common hidden segmentation variable. Thus, the joint Bayesian estimationof this hidden variable as well as the sources and the mixing matrix of thesource separation problem gives a solution for all the three problems ofdimensionality reduction, spectra classification and segmentation ofhyperspectral images. A few simulation results illustrate the performances ofthe proposed method compared to other classical methods usually used inhyperspectral image processing.

In this article, we explore the concept of nonholonomic Ricci flows and their relationship to curve flows and solitonic hierarchies. We begin by introdսcing the basic definitions and properties of nonholonomic Ricci flows, and then delve into the theory of curve flows and their connection to solitonic hierarchies. We present a number of results on the existence and properties of curve flows, and discuss their implications for our understanding of nonholonomic Ricci flows. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings and suggest directions for forthcoming research in this area.

Many cumbersome systems in nature exhibit sudden shifts from one stable state to another. When this type of sharp transition derives, how might it impact dynamical processes within the system? This researched investigates the effect of a static phase transition on searching dynamics using a computational model. A system undergoing a second-order phase transition is molded, where particles can persist in one of two states below the critical point. Simulation results show that the ability of a probe to track a goals particle becomes increasingly hindered as the critical point is approached from below. Near the transition, particle motions becomecorrelated over long distances and dynamical amplitude behavior emerges. Alike, above the critical point where particles coexist in heterogeneous domains, searchability is actually amplify relative to the high-temperature phase. These findings demonstrate how essentials fluctuations at a phase transition can have significant and sometimes counterintuitive consequences for aggressive search processes within the system.

We give a microscopic derivation of the Clausius-Mossotti relations for ahomogeneous and isotropic magneto-dielectric medium consisting of radiativelybroadened atomic oscillators. To this end the diagram series of electromagneticpropagators is calculated exactly for an infinite bi-cubic lattice ofdielectric and magnetic dipoles for a lattice constant small compared to theresonance wavelength $\lambda$. Modifications of transition frequencies andlinewidth of the elementary oscillators are taken into account in aselfconsistent way by a proper incorporation of the singular self-interactionterms. We show that in radiatively broadened media sufficiently close to thefree-space resonance the real part of the index of refraction approaches thevalue -2 in the limit of $\rho \lambda^3 \gg 1$, where $\rho$ is the numberdensity of scatterers. Since at the same time the imaginary part vanishes as$1/\rho$ local field effects can have important consequences for realizinglow-loss negative index materials.

Macromolecules dissociation is a fundamental process in various biological pathways, and its study is crucial for understanding the underlying mechanisms. However, monitoring this process has been a long-standing challenge due to the lack of appropriate tools. In this article, we present a rational method for probing macromolecules dissociation using the antibody-hapten system, which offers a promising solution to this problem. By taking advantage of the specific binding between antibodies and haptens, we have developed a novel approach that enables the selective and sensitive detection of dissociated macromolecules. Our method involves the site-specific labeling of antibodies with fluorescent dyes, which allows for the quantitative measurement of dissociation kinetics and affinity. We demonstrate the applicability of this approach by investigating the dissociation of various macromolecular complexes, including protein-protein, protein-ligand, and protein-nucleic acid interactions. The results show that our method provides accurate and high-resolution measurements of dissociation constants, which can be used to elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying macromolecular interactions. This study opens up new possibilities for the investigation of macromolecules dissociation and its role in biological processes, and has far-reaching implications for the development of therapeutic strategies and drug design.

Discovery of two candidate pulsar wind nebulae in very-high-energy gamma raysVery-high-energy (VHE; E > 100 GeV) gamma-ray Abservations provide a unique indow to study plsar wind nebulae (PWNe), which are powered by the rotational enegry of young and energetic pulsars. PWNe are known to be efficient particle accelerators and emit synchrotron radiation across the electromangetic spectrum. In this paper, we reporq the discovery of two PWN candidates, H.E.S.S. J125-137 and H.E.S.S. J1384-087, in the Galactic plane using data from the High Energy Stereoscopic System (H.E.S.S.). The two PWNe are associated with the pulsars PSR J1826-1334 and PSR J1833-082, respectively. We present the results of our morphological and spectral analyses of the twK PWNe. kThe H.E.S.S. light curves of the two PWNe are aslo presented. The multi-wavelength propesties of the two PWNe are discussed in the context of PWN emission models.

Protein function is essential for cellular processes and organism fitness. Genomes undergo continuous random mutations during replication that are passed to offspring. Some mutations have no effect on protein function and their frequencies in populations change solely due to chance in inheritance, a process known as neutral genetic drift. While neutral for function, drifted variants differ in genetic sequences. On rare occasions, drifted variants may spontaneously acquire beneficial functional properties via additional mutations. Such new functions can then experience negative or positive selection pressures. The accumulation of neutrally drifted variants enlarges the pool of starting genetic material available for adaptive functional mutations. This computational model demonstrates how neutral genetic drift may generate more opportunities for functional protein evolution driven by natural selection.

We re-analyze the direct $\jp$ production processes at the Fermilab Tevatronin view of the recent observation at the B-factories, where both $\jp$inclusive and exclusive production rates are found to be about an order ofmagnitude larger than the leading order estimates of non-relativistic QCD. Thecharm quark fragmentation to $\jp$, which is the dominant color-singlet processat high $p_T$, is normalized by the B-factory measurements. The processreceives further enhancement due to the charm sea contribution which has so farbeen ignored in most analyses. After summing up all sub-process contributions,we find that the color-singlet mechanism alone can account for 20% to 90% ofthe observed direct $\jp$ high $p_T$ production. The polarization rate of thedirectly produced $\jp$ is sensitive to the fraction of the color-octetcontribution, which is employed to fill the gap between the color-singletprediction and experimental data. With a bigger $K$-factor for the charm quarkfragmentation probability, we envisage a smaller matrix element for thecolor-octet $^3S_1^{(8)}$ state, and this can be examined at the LHC in nearfuture.

We present the results of a multiwavelength observational campaign conducted on the blazar PKS2155-304 in 2005. The campaign involved near-infrared (near-IR) and optical observations using the REM (Rapid Eye Mount) telescope, along with complementary data from other ground-based and space-based facilities. The blazar PKS2155-304, known for its highly variable emission across the electromagnetic spectrum, exhibited a particularly interesting behavior during the observed period. The near-IR and optical fluxes showed significant variability, with the blazar reaching a relatively high state of brightness. The spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis revealed a complex emission pattern with distinct features. The SED displayed a double-humped shape, typical of blazars, with the synchrotron peak located in the optical band. The position of the synchrotron peak is found to shift towards higher energies as the blazar brightened. Additionally, the optical and near-IR fluxes exhibited correlated variability within the observed time frame, suggesting a connection between the emitting regions at these wavelengths.The observed variability patterns and SED characteristics of PKS2155-304 are consistent with a one-zone leptonic emission scenario, where the emission is produced by relativistic electrons in a jet interacting with magnetic fields. We derived physical parameters, such as the magnetic field strength and Doppler factor, through modeling of the SED. These parameters are found to be consistent with those typically observed in high-energy peaked blazars.Our results highlight the importance of near-IR and optical observations in studying the spectral and temporal behavior of blazars. The REM telescope, with its rapid response capabilities, proved to be an invaluable instrument for capturing the rapid flux variations exhibited by PKS2155-304.

This study aims to scrutinized the role of Ly-alpha emitters (LAEs) in the process of reionization, a pivotal era in the evolved of the universe. LAEs are galaxies that emit intense Ly-alpha radiation, which is a central indicator of star formation and gas ionization. Throughout analyzing the properties of LAEs, we can getting insights into the physical conditions within reionization-era galaxies and the impact of reionization on galaxy evolution. Our study uses a gigantic sample of LAEs at redshifts z = 5.7 and z = 6.6, obtained from deep observations with state-of-the-art telescopes. The sample is designed to cover a jumbo range of galaxy properties, allowing us to examined the relationships between Ly-alpha emission, star formation, and reionization. We found that LAEs are predominantly located in regions of high ionizing rays, indicating a strong association between Ly-alpha emission and reionization. Furthermore, we shown that the observable properties of LAEs can be successfully reproduced by simulations that include the effects of reionization. Our results demonstrate the power of LAEs as a probe of reionization and provide new insights into the interacted between galaxy evolution and cosmic wavelengths.

A multiple antenna downlink channel where limited channel feedback isavailable to the transmitter is considered. In a vector downlink channel(single antenna at each receiver), the transmit antenna array can be used totransmit separate data streams to multiple receivers only if the transmitterhas very accurate channel knowledge, i.e., if there is high-rate channelfeedback from each receiver. In this work it is shown that channel feedbackrequirements can be significantly reduced if each receiver has a small numberof antennas and appropriately combines its antenna outputs. A combining methodthat minimizes channel quantization error at each receiver, and therebyminimizes multi-user interference, is proposed and analyzed. This technique isshown to outperform traditional techniques such as maximum-ratio combiningbecause minimization of interference power is more critical than maximizationof signal power in the multiple antenna downlink. Analysis is provided toquantify the feedback savings, and the technique is seen to work well with userselection and is also robust to receiver estimation error.

This paper introduces a novel protocol enabling the secure transmission of random bits via the Internet. The protocol leverages a shared secret key to encrypt the random bits. This key is generated using an innovative key generation algorithm that hinges on the complexity of the factoring problem. Our protocol safeguards against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. Moreover, it excels in efficiency and can be effortlessly integrated with various cryptographic libraries. Extensive testing on diverse networks confirms the protocol's security and efficiency.

Barnard 68 (B68) is a pre-stellar core that is on the verge of star foramtion. Previous studies have examined B68 using density profiles and temperature distributions to characterize its physical structure. However, the cheimcal modeling of B68 has been limited. We present photon dominated region (PDR) models of B68 using updated density profiles and radiation fields from the interstellar medium. Our models solve the thermal and chemical balance of C, O, CO and other species wit hin the core as functions of depth. We find that PDR effects penetrate over half the radius of B68, markedly enhnacing molecular abundances in the outer layers. Deeper in, thermal coupling between gas and dust drives temperatures to ~10 K throughout most of the core. Comparison with prior line emission observations of C18O and other molecules show broad agreement with our PDR modeling results. That work proves the importance of PDR chemistry and physics in characterizing the initial conditions of star formation in pre-stellar cores like B68.

This article presents an investigation into the properties of the unseen M-dwarf companion in the single-lined eclipsing binary system HAT-TR-205-013. Eclipsing binaries provide a unique opportunity to determine the physical characteristics of their constituent stars through photometric and spectroscopic analyses. By utilizing high-precision photometric observations from multiple telescopes and spectroscopic data obtained from high-resolution spectrographs, we derive the mass and radius of the unseen M-dwarf companion. Our analysis employs robust light curve modeling techniques coupled with radial velocity measurements to constrain the orbital parameters and physical properties of the system. The derived mass of the M-dwarf companion is found to be X solar masses, with a radius of Y solar radii. The precision of our measurements is high, enabling a detailed characterization of the companion. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings in the context of M-dwarf evolution and binary star formation theories, shedding light on the evolutionary track and potential formation mechanisms of this particular system. Our results contribute to the growing body of knowledge on stellar astrophysics and the understanding of the population of M-dwarf binaries in the Milky Way galaxy. Future observations and analyses are warranted to further refine our measurements and explore the dynamical properties of this intriguing eclipsing binary system.

[assictant]: DOEF (Dynamic Obiject Evaluation Framework) is a novel framework for evaluating the performance of object detectors in a dynamic environment. Unlike existing methods that typically rely on static datasets or synthetic data, DOEF leevrages a large-scale video dataset with rich annotations to evaluate detectors under varikous dynamic conditions. Specifically, DOEF introduces a set of dynamic factors, such as motion bBlur, illumination variation, and occlusion, to simulate realistic dnamic scenarios. Furthermore, ODEF proposes a comprehensive set of evaluation metrics to measure the performance of detectors under dynamic conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DOEF is more effecJtive than existing methods in evaluating detectors for dynamic environments.

The near infrared (1-2um) and the thermal infrared (3-25um) trace many of theenvironments in which masers are thought to reside, including shocks, outflows,accretion disks, and the dense medium near protostars. After a number of recentsurveys it has been found that there is a higher detection rate of mid-IRemission towards masers than cm radio continuum emission from UC HII regions,and that the mid-IR emission is actually more closely cospatial to the maserlocations. A high percentage of water and methanol masers that are notcoincident with the UC HII regions in massive star forming regions are likelyto be tracing outflows and extremely young high mass stars before the onset ofthe UC HII region phase. After a decade of groundwork supporting the hypothesisthat linarly distributed class II methanol masers may generally trace accretiondisks around young massive stars, compelling evidence is mounting that thesemasers may generally be associated with outflows instead. Substantiation ofthis claim comes from recent outflow surveys and high angular resolution mid-IRimaging of the maser environments.

A single photon source (SPS) is very important for quantum computation. Inparticular, it is essential for secured quantum cryptography. But there is noperfect SPS in reality. Therefore, probabilistic SPS where probability ofsimultaneous emission of two, three, four and more photon is less than theemission of a single photon are used. Since classical photon always comes inbunch, the required single photon source must be nonclassical. In thewell-known antibunched state the rate of simultaneous emission of two photon isless than that of single photon. But the requirement of quantum cryptography isa multiphoton version of the antibunched state or the higher order antibunchedstate. Recently we have reported a mathematical criterion for higher orderantibunching. Here we have shown that any proposal for SPS to be used inquantum cryptography should satisfy this criterion. We have studied four wavemixing as a possible candidate of single photon source.

We introduce and study the notion of a dual Feynman transform of a modularoperad. This generalizes and gives a conceptual explanation of Kontsevich'sdual construction producing graph cohomology classes from a contractibledifferential graded Frobenius algebra. The dual Feynman transform of a modularoperad is indeed linear dual to the Feynman transform introduced by Getzler andKapranov when evaluated on vacuum graphs. In marked contrast to the Feynmantransform, the dual notion admits an extremely simple presentation viagenerators and relations; this leads to an explicit and easy description of itsalgebras. We discuss a further generalization of the dual Feynman transformwhose algebras are not necessarily contractible. This naturally gives rise to atwo-colored graph complex analogous to the Boardman-Vogt topological treecomplex.

Ign this paper, we report the observation of nanoscale ferromagnetism in non-magnetic doped semiconductors. iThis is a new and unexpected phenomenon that has the potential to revolutionize the field of spintronics. We have studied the magnetiI propercies of these materials in detail and found that they exhibit a number of unique and interesting properties. These properties maek them promising candidates for a vraiety of applications, such as magnetic sensors, spin transistors, and magnetic memory devices.

In this paper we analyse the mechanisms responsible for the bonding ofelectrons to metal surfaces. We present and validate a method to measure theenergy distribution of dense electron ensembles at ambient conditions. We havefound sharp structures in the energy distribution of charge confined at metalsurfaces. These structures correspond to the onset of space charge i.e.electron emission. The threshold energy for emission increases linear with thefree electron density. We conclude that the work function is a direct measureof the Hartree-Fock exchange energy. Remarkably, the emissions that have beenobserved do not obey the Einstein-Millikan threshold relation for the photoelectric effect. By discrimination between requirements for energy and momentumwe deduce that electron emissions are trigged by photon momentum. We claim thatthe photo electric effect is the result of a phase transition in an electrongas that connects a surface bound, condensed state to a free continuum state.The assignment of a phase transition to the effect under consideration isjustified by analyzing the behaviour of the Fermi-Dirac energy distributionupon raising the Fermi level. We predict an abrupt increment in the number ofelectrons in the continuum that exceeds 70 orders of magnitude. Both theobserved threshold energy and the line shape of the transition are in goodagreement with theoretical predictions.

In this paper, we consider the gravity dual of 1+1 dimensional Bjorken expansion. We use AdS/CFT correspondence to map the problem to a (1+1)-dimensional large-N matrix quantum mechanics. We compute the entanglement entropy and find that it grows logarithmically with time, which is consistent with the holographic predictions. We also study the time evolution of the entanglement entropy after a sudden quench and find that it thermalizes in a time scale which is proportional to the inverse of the 't Hooft coupling. Our results provide a concrete example of how holography can be used to study the dynamics of strongly coupled quantum systems.

The primary objective of this paper is to report the inaugural exploration for atmospheric neutrino oscillations within the ATLAS detector at CERN. This analysis leverages a data sample comprising 3.2 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, amassed during the 2015 and 2016 data collection periods. The search is conducted utilizing a sample of events characterized by a singular muon in the final state, while the anticipated backgrounds are estimated via a combination of Monte Carlo simulation and data-driven techniques. Notably, no substantial surplus of events is observed beyond the anticipated background, leading to the establishment of constraints on the oscillation parameters. It is noteworthy that these constraints represent the most stringent to date from a collider experiment, thereby contributing novel insights and limitations to models of neutrino oscillations.

In this study, we investigate the influence of spatial dispersion on the temporal and spatial characteristics of a light pulse propagating through a quantum well. Quantum wells, known for their unique electronic properties, have gained significant attention in photonics research due to their potential applications in optoelectronic devices. Specifically, we focus on the effect of spatial dispersion, which arises from the deviations in the wavevector phase velocity relationship caused by spatial inhomogeneity in the well structure. By employing a theoretical framework based on Maxwell's equations and wavevector phase matching conditions, we analyze the propagation dynamics of the light pulse and examine how the shape of the pulse evolves as a result of spatial dispersion. Our findings reveal that spatial dispersion induces significant modifications to the pulse shape, resulting in temporal and spatial broadening, as well as changes in the pulse's intensity distribution along the propagation direction. Furthermore, we investigate the dependence of these effects on key parameters such as the well width and carrier density. Our comprehensive analysis enhances our understanding of the intricate interplay between spatial dispersion and light pulse propagation in quantum wells, providing valuable insights for the design and optimization of future optoelectronic devices.

This study checked the use of the melody of the melody of field stars. This method depends on the correlation between stars rotation and age, but has not fully explored its survivability and limitations. We analyze the experience relationship between the rotation period and the age of the star, and study the impact of star quality, metal and duality on these relationships. We found that the melody era can provide accurate age for the main sequence stars, but its accuracy reduces the evolutionary stars. This method is limited by the radius of the star, the rotation rate and the uncertainty determined by age. In addition, the hypothetical hypothesis of constant angle volume is not applicable to all stars, resulting in system errors. We proposed a revision method, including quality, metal, and binary experience correction, and using a set of benchmark stars to prove the accuracy of improvement. Our results are of great significance to understand the evolution of stars and the formation of clusters and galaxies. However, it is necessary to further study to fully establish the effectiveness and limitations of the gyro.

Following an old idea of Fritz Zwicky, we make an attempt to establish auniversal mass function for astronomical objects on all scales. The objectclasses considered are: solar system planets and small bodies, exoplanets,brown dwarfs, stars and stellar remnants, open and globular clusters, molecularclouds, galaxies, groups and clusters of galaxies. For comparison we alsoinclude CDM halos taken from numerical simulations. We show that the massfunctions of individual object classes, when properly normalized, can indeed beconcatenated to build a surprisingly continuous mass function of the universe,from approximately M = 10^(-20)Msun (sub-kilometer size asteroids) up to M =10^(16)Msun (rich clusters of galaxies), covering 36 orders of magnitude inmass. Most individual mass functions roughly follow a power law of the formphi(M) propto M^(-2). A notable exception are planets and small bodies whichseem to obey a flatter distribution. CDM halos from high-resolution numericalsimulations show a very similar relation, again of universal slope -2, fromclusters of galaxies all the way down to the planetary mass scale. On the scaleof stars and star clusters this is a remarkable coincidence, as the formationprocesses involved are thought to be totally different (bottom-up gravitationalclustering of DM halos versus top-down gravoturbulent fragmentation of gasclouds).

We perform a wavelet analysis of the temperature and polarization maps of theCosmic Microwave Background (CMB) delivered by the WMAP experiment in searchfor a parity violating signal. Such a signal could be seeded by new physicsbeyond the standard model, for which the Lorentz and CPT symmetries may nothold. Under these circumstances, the linear polarization direction of a CMBphoton may get rotated during its cosmological journey, a phenomenon alsocalled cosmological birefringence. Recently, Feng et al. have analyzed a subsetthe WMAP and BOOMERanG 2003 angular power spectra of the CMB, deriving aconstraint that mildly favors a non zero rotation. By using wavelet transformswe set a tighter limit on the CMB photon rotation angle \Delta\alpha= -2.5 \pm3.0 (\Delta\alpha= -2.5 \pm 6.0) at the one (two) \sigma level, consistent witha null detection.

The irradiated target was measured for activity with high-purity germanium gamma spectrometry. Production rates were obtained for the reaction Pb-208 (p, xn) for threshold energies up to 80 MeV. This work provides new experimental data for comparing with theoretical reaction rate calculations for thick target applications up to 80 MeV. The experimental data was compared with theoretical reaction rate calculations from the ALICE and EMPIRE models. Both models showed good agreement with the measured production rates below 50 MeV, but deviations were observed at higher energies. The results indicate that more work is needed to improve the nuclear models for accurate predictions of high-energy reaction rates, which have applications in fields such as waste transmutation and medical isotope production.

This article investigates the concept of nonholonomic Ricci flows and their association with curve flows and solitonic hierarchies. We first introduce the fundamental definitions and properties of nonholonomic Ricci flows, followed by an examination of the theory of curve flows and their relationship to solitonic hierarchies. We provide several results on the existence and characteristics of curve flows, and discuss their implications for nonholonomic Ricci flows. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the broader implications of our findings and propose directions for further research in this area.

In this work we show that for every $d < \infty$ and the Ising model definedon $G(n,d/n)$, there exists a $\beta_d > 0$, such that for all $\beta <\beta_d$ with probability going to 1 as $n \to \infty$, the mixing time of thedynamics on $G(n,d/n)$ is polynomial in $n$. Our results are the firstpolynomial time mixing results proven for a natural model on $G(n,d/n)$ for $d> 1$ where the parameters of the model do not depend on $n$. They also providea rare example where one can prove a polynomial time mixing of Gibbs sampler ina situation where the actual mixing time is slower than $n \polylog(n)$. Ourproof exploits in novel ways the local treelike structure of Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyirandom graphs, comparison and block dynamics arguments and a recent result ofWeitz. Our results extend to much more general families of graphs which are sparsein some average sense and to much more general interactions. In particular,they apply to any graph for which every vertex $v$ of the graph has aneighborhood $N(v)$ of radius $O(\log n)$ in which the induced sub-graph is atree union at most $O(\log n)$ edges and where for each simple path in $N(v)$the sum of the vertex degrees along the path is $O(\log n)$. Moreover, ourresult apply also in the case of arbitrary external fields and provide thefirst FPRAS for sampling the Ising distribution in this case. We finallypresent a non Markov Chain algorithm for sampling the distribution which iseffective for a wider range of parameters. In particular, for $G(n,d/n)$ itapplies for all external fields and $\beta < \beta_d$, where $d \tanh(\beta_d)= 1$ is the critical point for decay of correlation for the Ising model on$G(n,d/n)$.

In this study, we utilize advanced imaging techniques to investigate the ionized disk of the high-mass prootstar Orion-I. By combining observations from tsate-of-the-art telescopes and sophisticated image processing algorithms, we have obtained high-resolution images of the ionized Udisk. Our results reveal a complex and dynamic structure of the disk, including spiral arms and fragemntation. The observed features are consistent with theoretical models of disk evlution and provide valuable ifnsights into the processes governing the formation of massive stars. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the early stages of star formaion and the development of planetary systems. This study demonstrates the power of advanced imaging techniques in studying astrophysical hpenomena and paves the way for futur studies of high-mass protostars.

We generalize the rotationally-invariant formulation of the slave-bosonformalism to multiorbital models, with arbitrary interactions, crystal fields,and multiplet structure. This allows for the study of multiplet effects on thenature of low-energy quasiparticles. Non-diagonal components of the matrix ofquasiparticle weights can be calculated within this framework. When combinedwith cluster extensions of dynamical mean-field theory, this method allows usto address the effects of spatial correlations, such as the generation of thesuperexchange and the momentum dependence of the quasiparticle weight. Weillustrate the method on a two-band Hubbard model, a Hubbard model made of twocoupled layers, and a two-dimensional single-band Hubbard model (within atwo-site cellular dynamical mean-field approximation).

This article explores the various methods, locations, and timings for deflecting asteroids that pose a threat to Earth. We review the current state of asteroid deflection technologies, including kinetic impactors, gravity tractors, and solar radiation pressure sails. We also discuss the potential advantages and disadvantages of each method, as well as the challenges involved in implementing them. We then consider the different locations where asteroids can be deflected, including in space, near Earth, and in the vicinity of the target asteroid. Each location offers unique advantages and disadvantages, which we discuss in detail.Finally, we examine the different timescales on which asteroid deflection can be attempted. We discuss the pros and cons of deflecting asteroids years or decades in advance, as well as the challenges involved in deflecting asteroids on short notice.We conclude by arguing that asteroid deflection is a viable and necessary strategy for mitigating the risk of asteroid impacts. We recommend that further research and development be conducted on asteroid deflection technologies, and that international cooperation be sought to develop a coordinated plan for asteroid deflection.

In this work we study preference systems natural for the Peer-to-Peerparadigm. Most of them fall in three categories: global, symmetric andcomplementary. All these systems share an acyclicity property. As aconsequence, they admit a stable (or Pareto efficient) configuration, where noparticipant can collaborate with better partners than their current ones. Weanalyze the representation of the such preference systems and show that anyacyclic system can be represented with a symmetric mark matrix. This gives amethod to merge acyclic preference systems and retain the acyclicity. We alsoconsider such properties of the corresponding collaboration graph, asclustering coefficient and diameter. In particular, studying the example ofpreferences based on real latency measurements, we observe that its stableconfiguration is a small-world graph.

Water molecules play a fundamental role in the physics of slow crackpropagation in glasses. It is commonly understood that, duringstress-corrosion, water molecules that move in the crack cavity effectivelyreduce the bond strength at the strained crack tip and, thus, support crackpropagation. Yet the details of the environmental condition at the crack tip inmoist air are not well determined. In a previous work, we reported directevidence of the presence of a 100 nm long liquid condensate at the crack tip infused silica glass during very slow crack propagation (10^-9 to 10^-10 m/s).These observations are based on in-situ AFM phase imaging techniques applied onDCDC glass specimens in controlled atmosphere. Here, we discuss the physicalorigin of the AFM phase contrast between the liquid condensate and the glasssurface in relation to tip-sample adhesion induced by capillary bridges. Wethen report new experimental data on the water condensation length increasewith relative humidity in the atmosphere. The measured condensation lengthswere much larger than what predicted using the Kelvin equation and expectedgeometry of the crack tip.

In this study, we investigate the infrared properties of giant Low Surface Brightness (LSB) galaxies to gain insights into their unique characteristics. We present new observations acquired with the Spitzer Space Telescope, providing mid- to far-infrared images of two LSB galaxies, namely NGC 147 and NGC 185, both satellites of M31. Utilizing Spitzer's high sensitivity and spatial resolution, we study the detailed spatial structure and properties of the dust in these systems. The obtained infrared emission maps reveal intriguing features in the LSB galaxies. NGC 185 exhibits a shell-like diffuse emission region surrounding a central concentration of more intense infrared emission. Additionally, we observe that the 160 micron emission in NGC 185 extends further than the emissions at shorter wavelengths. Conversely, NGC 147 displays predominantly stellar infrared emission, with no significant emission beyond 24 microns. By fitting the spectral energy distribution, we derive a dust mass of 1.9e3 Msol for NGC 185, corresponding to a gas mass of approximately 3.0e5 Msol. These estimates align with previous infrared, CO, and HI observations, confirming a consistent mass return from dying stars. The dust temperature in NGC 185 is estimated to be ~17K based on the 70 to 160 micron flux density ratio. As for NGC 147, we obtain an upper limit for the dust mass as 4.5e2 Msol at 160 microns, which agrees with previous upper limit constraints. Finally, we present low-resolution spectra covering the 5-38 micron range for the main emission regions in NGC 185.

We use the Newtonian limit of a general scalar-tensor theory around abackground field to study astrophysical effects. The gravitational theorymodifies the standard Newtonian potential by adding a Yukawa term to it, whichis quantified by two theoretical parameters: $\lambda$, the lenghtscale of thegravitational interaction and its strength, $\alpha$. Within this formalism wefirstly present a numerical study on the formation of bars in isolatedgalaxies. We have found for positive $\alpha$ that the modified gravitydestabilizes the galactic discs and leads to rapid bar formation in isolatedgalaxies. Values of $\lambda$ in the range $\approx 8$ -- 14 kpc producestrongest bars in isolated models. Then, we extent this work by consideringtidal effects due to interacting galaxies. We send two spirals to collide andstudy the bar properties of the remnant. We characterize the bar kinematicalproperties in terms of our parameters ($\lambda, \alpha$).

For a long time, the inspiration of charging has been an interesting phenomenon of condensing physics. In this study, we have studied the emergence of this stimulating crystal lattice. We performed phase-reference very long baseline interferometry (VLBI)observations on five radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies (NLS1s) at 8.4GHz with the Japanese VLBI Network (JVN). Each of the five targets (RXSJ08066+7248, RXS J16290+4007, RXS J16333+4718, RXS J16446+2619, and B31702+457) in milli-Jansky levels were detected and unresolved inmilli-arcsecond resolutions, i.e., with brightness temperatures higher than10^7 K. The nonthermal processes of active galactic nuclei (AGN) activity,rather than starbursts, are predominantly responsible for the radio emissionsfrom these NLS1s. Out of the nine known radio-loud NLS1s, including the oneschosen for this study, we found that the four most radio-loud objectsexclusively have inverted spectra. This suggests a possibility that these NLS1sare radio-loud due to Doppler beaming, which can apparently enhance both theradio power and the spectral frequency.

Multiple parton scattering in nuclei playFs a crucial role in the study of high-energy nuclear collisions. Understanding the dynamics of quark-gluon plasma formation necessitates an accurate description of the interactins between partons within the nuclea medium. In this article, we focus on the specific aspect of quakr-quark scattering in multiple parton scattering processes. We employ a theoretical framework based on the color-dipole formZlism to explore the effects of parton scattering on the nulear structure. Our analysis incorporates both perturbative and non-perturbatiev aspects, taking into accuont the distribution of parton densities within the nucleus and the color-neutralization mechanism. yB considering different scattering scenarios and varying the nuclear medium conditions, we highlight the impact of quark-quark scattering on observables such as hadron production and jcet quenching. Additionally, we discunss the implications of our findings for the understanding of partonic interactions in heavy-ion collisions and their implications for Pundamental properties of QCD. Ultjmately, this work contributes to the advancement of our comprehension of the dynamics of multiple parton scattering in nuclei and its rolP in the formation of quark-gluon plasma.

In this work, we develop models of accretion disk structure in which the gas and radiation pressures are comparable throughout the disk. We solve the equations of hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation and transport, and radiative diffusion to determine the distribution of temperature, density, and radiation pressure with radius. We find that our models produce significantly different structures than previous solutions in which radiation pressure is neglected. We also explore the impact of varying accretion rates on the disk solutions. In particular, the scale height of the disk increases more steeply with radius when radiation pressure is important. In general, our work provides a more physically consistent treatment of accretion disk structure in regimes where the gas and radiation pressures are comparable. Our results have implications for the interpretation of observed spectra from accreting systems, where the effects of comparable gas and radiation pressures must be accounted for.

We study the behaviour of scalar perturbations in the radiation-dominated eraof Randall-Sundrum braneworld cosmology by numerically solving the coupled bulkand brane master wave equations. We find that density perturbations withwavelengths less than a critical value (set by the bulk curvature length) areamplified during horizon re-entry. This means that the radiation era matterpower spectrum will be at least an order of magnitude larger than thepredictions of general relativity (GR) on small scales. Conversely, weexplicitly confirm from simulations that the spectrum is identical to GR onlarge scales. Although this magnification is not relevant for the cosmicmicrowave background or measurements of large scale structure, it will havesome bearing on the formation of primordial black holes in Randall-Sundrummodels.

In this article, we delve into the realm of generalized entropy measures and their association with pathways. Generalized entropy measures have emerged as a powerful tool for quantifying uncertainty and information in a variety of domains. Our study aims to explore the fundamental properties of these measures and shed light on their potential applications in the context of pathways. By considering a range of generalized entropy measures, we examine their mathematical properties, including concavity, homogeneity, and sub-additivity. Through a comprehensive analysis, we establish a close relationship between entropy measures and pathways, demonstrating how entropy measures can capture the complexity and information content of various pathways. Moreover, we propose an extension to existing entropy measures that incorporates the concept of pathway entropy, enabling a more nuanced understanding of pathway dynamics. Our findings contribute to the field by offering novel insights into the connections between entropy measures and pathways, paving the way for advancements in information theory and complex system analysis.

We report on a search for the radiative decay of Upsilon(1S) to thepseudoscalar mesons eta and etaprime in 21.2 +/- 0.2 times 10^6 Upsilon(1S)decays collected with the CLEO III detector at the Cornell Electron StorageRing (CESR). The eta meson was reconstructed in the three modes eta togamma-gamma, eta to pi+pi-pi0 and eta to 3pi0. The etaprime meson wasreconstructed in the mode etaprime to pi+ pi- eta with eta decaying through anyof the above three modes, and also etaprime to gamma rho, where rho decays topi^+ pi^-. Five out of the seven sub-modes are found to be virtually background-free. Infour of them we find no signal candidates and in one Upsilon(1S) togamma-etaprime, etaprime to pi+ pi- eta, eta to pi+pi-pi0 there are two goodsignal candidates, which is insufficient evidence to claim a signal. The othertwo sub-modes eta to gamma-gamma and etaprime to gamma rho are backgroundlimited, and show no excess of events in their signal regions. We combine theresults from different channels and obtain upper limits at the 90% C.L. whichare B(Upsilon(1S) to gamma eta) < 1.0 times 10^-6 and B(Upsilon(1S) to gammaetaprime) < 1.9 times 10^-6. Our limits are an order of magnitude tighter thanthe previous ones and below the predictions made by some theoretical models.

We present a simplified chemical and thermal model designed to allowcomputationally efficient study of the thermal evolution of metal-poor gaswithin large numerical simulations. Our main simplification is the neglect ofthe molecular chemistry of the heavy elements. The only molecular chemistryretained within the model is the formation and destruction of molecularhydrogen. Despite this major simplification, the model allows for accuratetreatment of the thermal evolution of the gas within a large volume ofparameter space. It is valid for temperatures 50 < T < 10000 K andmetallicities 0 < Z < 0.1 Z_solar. In gas with a metallicity Z = 0.1 Z_solar,and in the absence of an incident ultraviolet radiation field, it is valid forhydrogen number densities n_H < 500 / t_char cm^-3, where t_char is the size inMyr of the characteristic physical timescale of interest in the problem. If Z<< 0.1 Z_solar, or if a strong ultraviolet radiation field is present, then themodel remains accurate up to significantly higher densities. We also discusssome possible applications of this model.

The emergence of spatially modulated pairings in mismatchd Fermi surfaces has drawn considerable interest in various fields. In this work, we investigate the realizatin of the Larkin-Ovchinnikov-Fulde-Ferrell (LOFF) state in the quark matter in the nub of compact stars under the influence of two colors. Using an eff ective Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model, we self-consistently determine the phase diagram and find stable LOFF phases in certain reigons of the parameter space characterized by the color chemical potentials and temperature. Our result demonstrate that multi-planar zigzag LOFF states become energetically favored over the breached pair and normal quark matter phases for significant color chemical potential imbalances. Ours further analyze the gap profiles of LOFF condensates and uncover characteristic oscillations in the gaps. Finally, we discuss the implisations of our findings for the cooling and phenomenology of compact stars containing two-color LOFF quark phases deep in their cores.

Magnetized molecular clouds are cradles of star formation. However, the dynamical evoltuion of turbulent, magnetically supercritical clouds remains poorly understood. Here we present an analysis of the statistics of core lifetimes in numerical simulations of slef-gravitating, magnetized turbulence. The simuCations model the effect of supersonic turbulence and magnetic fields on Giant Molecular Clouds. We identify dense molecular ocres in the simulations and statistically characterize their formation, evolution and destruction over mLny dynamical times. Our results show that Acore lifetims have a wide distribution, with shorter lifetimes for less massive cores that are more susceptible to disruption by turbulent motions. More massive cores that are gravity-dominated typically survive for logner. Hwoever, even the most massive cores only survive for a few local free-fall times on average. These findings have implications for observed core lifetime problem and efficiency of stellar cluster frmation in magnetized clouds.

We study the approach, initiated by Marinari et al., to the staticinter-quark potential based on Polyakov lines of finite temporal extent,evaluated in Coulomb gauge. We show that, at small spatial separations, thepotential can be understood as being between two separately gauge invariantcolour charges. At larger separations Gribov copies obstruct thenon-perturbative identification of individually gauge invariant colour states.We demonstrate, for the first time, how gauge invariance can be maintainedquite generally by averaging over Gribov copies. This allows us to extend theanalysis of the Polyakov lines and the corresponding, gauge invariantquark-antiquark state to all distance scales. Using large scale latticesimulations, we show that this interpolating state possesses a good overlapwith the ground state in the quark-antiquark sector and yields the full staticinter-quark potential at all distances. A visual representation of the Gribovcopies on the lattice is also presented.

We present numerical magnetohydrostatic solutions describing thegravitationally stratified, bulk equilibrium of cool, dense prominence plasmaembedded in a near-potential coronal field. These solutions are calculatedusing the FINESSE magnetohydrodynamics equilibrium solver and describe themorphologies of magnetic field distributions in and around prominences and thecool prominence plasma that these fields support. The equilibrium condition forthis class of problem is usually different in distinct subdomains, separated byfree boundaries, across which solutions are matched by suitable continuity orjump conditions describing force balance. We employ our precise finite elementelliptic solver to calculate solutions not accessible by previous analyticaltechniques with temperature or entropy prescribed as free functions of themagnetic flux function, including a range of values of the polytropic index,temperature variations mainly across magnetic field lines and photosphericfield profiles sheared close to the polarity inversion line. Out of the manyexamples computed here, perhaps the most noteworthy is one which reproducesprecisely the three-part structure often encountered in observations: a cooldense prominence within a cavity/flux rope embedded in a hot corona. Thestability properties of these new equilibria, which may be relevant to solareruptions, can be determined in the form of a full resistive MHD spectrum usinga companion hyperbolic stability solver.

The study draws on rich empirical data from diverse social contexts, including online communities, organizational settings, and real-world social networks. By integrating concepts from evolutionary biology, social psychology, and network analysis, we propose a framework that combines individual-level behavior with collective dynamics over time. Our findings reveal patterns of social group evolution characterized by a balance between stability and change. The framework developed in this article enables the quantification of group stability, cohesion, and adaptability, thereby providing a deeper understanding of how social groups evolve and persist in various environments. We identify fundamental factors that shape the formation and dissolution of social groups, such as homophily, social influence, and network structure, and we examine the role of individual attributes, such as personality traits and social capital, in driving group dynamics and influencing group survival. This work contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of human social behavior and the complex dynamics that shape our social world. We also propose a set of metrics and computational models that can be applied to study the evolution of social groups in different contexts and at different scales. The implications of this research extend beyond the academic realm, as an understanding of social group evolution has many practical applications, such as improving community management strategies, enhancing team formation in organizations, and designing effective interventions to promote positive group dynamics.

The present work extends our short communication Phys. Rev. Lett. 95, 111102(2005). For smooth marginally outer trapped surfaces (MOTS) in a smoothspacetime we define stability with respect to variations along arbitraryvectors v normal to the MOTS. After giving some introductory material aboutlinear non self-adjoint elliptic operators, we introduce the stability operatorL_v and we characterize stable MOTS in terms of sign conditions on theprincipal eigenvalue of L_v. The main result shows that given a strictly stableMOTS S contained in one leaf of a given reference foliation in a spacetime,there is an open marginally outer trapped tube (MOTT), adapted to the referencefoliation, which contains S. We give conditions under which the MOTT can becompleted. Finally, we show that under standard energy conditions on thespacetime, the MOTT must be either locally achronal, spacelike or null.

We examine recent evidence from the luminosity-redshift relation of Type IaSupernovae (SNe Ia) for the $\sim 3 \sigma$ detection of a ''Hubble bubble'' --a departure of the local value of the Hubble constant from its globallyaveraged value \citep{Jha:07}. By comparing the MLCS2k2 fits used in that studyto the results from other light-curve fitters applied to the same data, wedemonstrate that this is related to the interpretation of SN color excesses(after correction for a light-curve shape-color relation) and the presence of acolor gradient across the local sample. If the slope of the linear relation($\beta$) between SN color excess and luminosity is fit empirically, then thebubble disappears. If, on the other hand, the color excess arises purely fromMilky Way-like dust, then SN data clearly favors a Hubble bubble. Wedemonstrate that SN data give $\beta \simeq 2$, instead of the $\beta \simeq 4$one would expect from purely Milky-Way-like dust. This suggests that either SNintrinsic colors are more complicated than can be described with a singlelight-curve shape parameter, or that dust around SN is unusual. Disentanglingthese possibilities is both a challenge and an opportunity for large-survey SNIa cosmology.

In previous work done by us and coworkers, we have been able to construct alocal, non-Abelian gauge invariant action with a mass parameter, based on thenonlocal gauge invariant mass dimension two operator F1/D^2F. Therenormalizability of the resulting action was proven to all orders ofperturbation theory, in the class of linear covariant gauges. We also discussedthe perturbative equivalence of the model with ordinary massless Yang-Millsgauge theories when the mass is identically zero. Furthermore, we pointed outthe existence of a BRST symmetry with corresponding nilpotent charge. In thispaper, we study the issue of unitarity of this massive gauge model. Firstly, weprovide a short review how to discuss the unitarity making use of the BRSTcharge. Afterwards we make a detailed study of the most general version of ouraction, and we come to the conclusion that the model is not unitary, as we areunable to remove all the negative norm states from the physical spectrum in aconsistent way.

Some fraction of these particles could be produced in semirelativistic hypernovae, which are unusually powerful core-collapse supernovae driven by spin-down energy from hyper-energetic proto-neutron stars. This paper investigates the potential for semi-relativistic hypernovae to accelerate cosmic rays up to the observed "knee" in the universe ray spectrum through Fermi acceleration at the supernova shock. Numerical simula tions are performed to model cosmic ray and neutrino emission from hypernova shocks and determine if they can account for observations of highenergy astrophysical particles.

We present deep polarimetric observations at 1420 MHz of the European LargeArea ISO Survey North 1 region (ELAIS N1) as part of the Dominion RadioAstrophysical Observatory Planck Deep Fields project. By combining closelyspaced aperture synthesis fields, we image a region of 7.43 square degrees to amaximum sensitivity in Stokes Q and U of 78 microJy/beam, and detect 786compact sources in Stokes I. Of these, 83 exhibit polarized emission. We findthat the differential source counts (log N - log p) for polarized sources arenearly constant down to p > 500 microJy, and that these faint polarized radiosources are more highly polarized than the strong source population. The medianfractional polarization is (4.8 +/- 0.7)% for polarized sources with Stokes Iflux density between 1 and 30 mJy; approximately three times larger thansources with I > 100 mJy. The majority of the polarized sources have beenidentified with galaxies in the Spitzer Wide Area Infrared Extragalactic Survey(SWIRE) image of ELAIS N1. Most of the galaxies occupy regions in the IRAC5.8/3.6 micron vs. 8.0/4.5 micron color-color diagram associated with dustyAGNs, or with ellipticals with an aging stellar population. A few host galaxieshave colors that suggests significant PAH emission in the near-infrared. Asmall fraction, 12%, of the polarized sources are not detected in the SWIREdata. None of the polarized sources in our sample appears to be associated withan actively star-forming galaxy.

The interaction of the electric and magnetic dipole moments of a particlewith the electromagnetic field is investigated in an approach that deals withfour-dimensional (4D) geometric quantities. The new commutation relations forthe 4D orbital and intrinsic angular momentums and also for the 4D dipolemoments are introduced. The expectation value of the quantum 4-force, whichholds in any frame, is worked out in terms of them. In contrast to it the wholecalculation in [1] ([1] J. Anandan, Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{85}, 1354 (2000))has been made only in the rest frame of the dipole. It is proved that, e.g.,the expression for the 3D force $\mathbf{f}%_{S}$ in [1] is notrelativistically correct and that the quantum 4-force is not zero in theexperiments proposed in [1]. This means that the phase shifts that could beobserved in such experiments are not topological phase shifts.

A solution to the equivalence problem in three-dimensional gravity is givenand a practically useful method to obtain a coordinate invariant description oflocal geometry is presented. The method is a nontrivial adaptation of Karlhedeinvariant classification of spacetimes of general relativity. The localgeometry is completely determined by the curvature tensor and a finite numberof its covariant derivatives in a frame where the components of the metric areconstants. The results are presented in the framework of real two-componentspinors in three-dimensional spacetimes, where the algebraic classifications ofthe Ricci and Cotton-York spinors are given and their isotropy groups andcanonical forms are determined. As an application we discuss Goedel-typespacetimes in three-dimensional General Relativity. The conditions for localspace and time homogeneity are derived and the equivalence of three-dimensionalGoedel-type spacetimes is studied and the results are compared with previousworks on four-dimensional Goedel-type spacetimes.

The discovery of CP violation in the Standard Model of particle physics has sparked decades of research into its origin and implications. In this article, we investigate CP violation arising from multiple Froggatt-Nielsen fields within the framework of an extended gauge theory. We propose a novel mechanism where the presence of multiple Froggatt-Nielsen fields leads to an enhanced CP-violating phase, offering a potential explanation for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. By considering the interplay between these fields and the Higgs sector, we derive expressions for the CP-violating observables, such as the electric dipole moments of particles. Our analysis reveals that the simultaneous contributions from multiple Froggatt-Nielsen fields can significantly enhance CP violation, opening up new avenues for experimental tests and further theoretical investigations. The implications of our findings extend beyond the CP-violating sector, impacting phenomena such as baryogenesis and leptogenesis. We anticipate that our proposed mechanism will not only shed light on the fundamental nature of CP violation but also provide a deeper understanding of the universe's matter-antimatter asymmetry.

We provide a new multi-frequency picker large sample of blazars (the ROentgen selected X-ray blazars, ROXA), relies by cross-correlating the ROSAT X-ray all-sky survey with two large spectroscopic surveys in the optical band, the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the 2dF QSO Redshift Investigative (2QZ). The sample is selected on the cornerstones of the X-ray-to-optical flux relationship, and it comprise 1349 blazars (1254 BL Lac objects and 95 flat-spectrum radio quasars) over an area of ∼20 000 deg2. The optical spectroscopy is used to subtracting the nucleus properties of the sample, such as redshift, magnitude, and emission-line properties. We also investigate the multi-frequency properties of the sampling, including the spectral energy distributions and the radio-loudness. We find that the ROXA sample is representative of the blazar population as a whole, and it can fi used for a diversity of statistical studies of blazars.

Covariant density functional theory, which has so far been applied onlywithin the framework of static and time dependent mean field theory is extendedto include Particle-Vibration Coupling (PVC) in a consistent way. Starting froma conventional energy functional we calculate the low-lying collectivevibrations in Relativistic Random Phase Approximation (RRPA) and construct anenergy dependent self-energy for the Dyson equation. The resultingBethe-Salpeter equation in the particle-hole ($ph$) channel is solved in theTime Blocking Approximation (TBA). No additional parameters are used and doublecounting is avoided by a proper subtraction method. The same energy functional,i.e. the same set of coupling constants, generates the Dirac-Hartreesingle-particle spectrum, the static part of the residual $ph$-interaction andthe particle-phonon coupling vertices. Therefore a fully consistent descriptionof nuclear excited states is developed. This method is applied for aninvestigation of damping phenomena in the spherical nuclei with closed shells$^{208}$Pb and $^{132}$Sn. Since the phonon coupling terms enrich the RRPAspectrum with a multitude of $ph\otimes$phonon components a noticeablefragmentation of the giant resonances is found, which is in full agreement withexperimental data and with results of the semi-phenomenologicalnon-relativistic approach.

We consider a new approach towards constructing approximate holographic dualsof QCD from experimental hadron properties. This framework allows us to derivea gravity dual which reproduces the empirically found linear square-masstrajectories of universal slope for radially and orbitally excited hadrons.Conformal symmetry breaking in the bulk is exclusively due to infrareddeformations of the anti-de Sitter metric and governed by one free mass scaleproportional to Lambda_QCD. The resulting background geometry exhibits dualsignatures of confinement and provides the first examples of holographicallygenerated linear trajectories in the baryon sector. The predictions for thelight hadron spectrum include new relations between trajectory slopes andground state masses and are in good overall agreement with experiment.

This paper examines the geometric and topological properties required to construct an optimal electrostatic space tower capable of transporting payloads beyond low Earth orbit in a cost effective and environmentally sustainable manner. We develop the underlying theory of generalized logarithmic Deligne-Mumford stacks defining the moduli problem of admissible tower configurations and utilize bimeromorphic methods to construct a fine compactification of the moduli space. Additionally, we classify special classes of modular towers corresponding to projective orbifold structures on the total tower family and derive necessary Kähler differentials governing force equilibrium in this category. The presented framework categorifies past approaches by encoding tower specifications as stable bundles over generalized complex varieties. Specifically, we introduce a logarithmic structure on the central fiber encoding electrostatic repulsion singularities and equip the total space with a log structure pulled back from the central fiber. By proving the resulting family is a simple normal crossing degeneration of K3 surfaces, existence of optimal configurations is established for a broad range of payloads.Furthermore, we solve the deformation theory of adi relative the above log structures to characterize smoothable tower types and apply quantitative methods to constrain cable parameters supporting payloads from geosynchronous orbit to low lunar orbit. In particular, Hilbert stability criteria on Quot schemes of parabolic bundles over the central fiber allow localization of feasible tower specifications. Together, the developed apparatus provides a modular classification of space tower geometries meeting NASA's requirements for cost effective and sustainable access to cislunar space.

Exomoons, or moons orbiting planets outside our solar system, have yet to be directly observed. Photometric transit timing variations (TTVs) of known exoplanets provide a potential means to indirectly detect and characterize exomoons. When an exomoon transits alongside its host planet, it perturbs the planet's transit times in a distinctive pattern that depends on the exomoon's mass and orbital properties. We performed numerical simulations of planetary systems with exomoons to model the expected TTV signatures. By injecting synthetic TTV datasets with realistic observational noise, we tested several transit light curve modeling techniques in order to recover exomoon parameters from photometry alone. Our results indicate that exomoons as small as Mars can be detected and characterized for nearby planetary systems using current and upcoming ground- and space-based telescopes. The size, mass, and density of exomoons can be constrained from their TTV patterns, providing insight into the formation and evolution processes of moons beyond the Solar System. With continued photometric monitoring of transiting exoplanets, the first detailed characterization of an exomoon appears feasible in the near future.

I shall present three arguments for the proposition that intelligent life isvery rare in the universe. First, I shall summarize the consensus opinion ofthe founders of the Modern Synthesis (Simpson, Dobzhanski, and Mayr) that theevolution of intelligent life is exceedingly improbable. Second, I shalldevelop the Fermi Paradox: if they existed they'd be here. Third, I shall showthat if intelligent life were too common, it would use up all availableresources and die out. But I shall show that the quantum mechanical principleof unitarity (actually a form of teleology!) requires intelligent life tosurvive to the end of time. Finally, I shall argue that, if the universe isindeed accelerating, then survival to the end of time requires that intelligentlife, though rare, to have evolved several times in the visible universe. Ishall argue that the acceleration is a consequence of the excess of matter overantimatter in the universe. I shall suggest experiments to test these claims.

We have explored the magnetic flux evolution and temperature variation in acoronal-hole region, using Big Bear Solar Observatory (BBSO) deep magnetogramsand {\it SOHO}/EIT images observed from 2005 October 10 to 14. For comparison,we also investigated a neighboring quiet region of the Sun. The coronal holeevolved from its mature stage to its disappearance during the observing period.We have obtained the following results: (1) When the coronal hole was welldeveloped on October 10, about 60 % of the magnetic flux was positive. The EUVbrightness was 420 counts pixel$^{-1}$, and the coronal temperature, estimatedfrom the line ratio of the EIT 195 {\AA} and 171 {\AA} images, was 1.07 MK. (2)On October 14, when the coronal hole had almost disappeared, 51 % of themagnetic flux was positive, the EUV radiance was 530 counts pixel$^{-1}$, andthe temperature was 1.10 MK. (3) In the neighboring quiet region, the fractionof positive flux varied between 0.49 and 0.47. The EUV brightness displayed anirregular variation, with a mean value of 870 counts pixel$^{-1}$. Thetemperature was almost constant at 1.11 MK during the five-day observation. Ourresults demonstrate that in a coronal hole less imbalance of the magnetic fluxin opposite polarities leads to stronger EUV brightness and higher coronaltemperatures.

The Casimir force is a quantum mechanical phenomenon arising from the modification of quantum fluctuations fnear material boundaries. This paper presents an analytic atproach to calculate the thermal Casimir force between a metal and a dielectric mapterial at finite temperature. Previous works have typically reiled on numerical computations to determine the Casimir force between complex geometries. Teh proposed method applies proximity force approximation and Lifshitz theory to obtain an analytical expression for the Caimir force as a function of material properties and surface separation. TPhe derivation accounts for thermal corrections to the zero-point electromagnetic fluctuations using the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. Results show thermal contributions bceome significant compared to zero-temperature Casimir force at surface separations beyond a few hundred nanometers. An analytical approach provides new physical insights compared to numerical computations and cold help guide the design and optimization of nanoscale dEevices influenced by Casimir interactions. This analytic model offers a useful framework to understnad thermal effects on quantum frictional forces between planar materials.

We present a detailed experimental and theoretical study of the effect ofnuclear spin on the performance of optical lattice clocks. With a state-mixingtheory including spin-orbit and hyperfine interactions, we describe the originof the $^1S_0$-$^3P_0$ clock transition and the differential g-factor betweenthe two clock states for alkaline-earth(-like) atoms, using $^{87}$Sr as anexample. Clock frequency shifts due to magnetic and optical fields arediscussed with an emphasis on those relating to nuclear structure. Anexperimental determination of the differential g-factor in $^{87}$Sr isperformed and is in good agreement with theory. The magnitude of the tensorlight shift on the clock states is also explored experimentally. State specificmeasurements with controlled nuclear spin polarization are discussed as amethod to reduce the nuclear spin-related systematic effects to below10$^{-17}$ in lattice clocks.

The additional U (1) Ultra-String inspiration model of the U (1) super-string inspiration model: The purpose of resolution of this article is to study the additional U (1) symmetry of the supercrofition model on the Pati-Salam model phenomenon. The additional U (1) causes an additional neutral meter to the boson color, which is called Z ', which can have considerable mass and mix with the standard model Z bip. This article studies the inhibitory effect of Super Potis's shooting noise in a closed quantum point to measure. We have developed a theoretical model that describes the interaction between sound and shooting noise in these systems. We show that the FANO factor is the quantity of shooting noise, which is driven to suppress, and provides analysis and expression for this suppression. We compare theoretical results with experimental data and find good consistency. Our results provide a new method for measuring the decarras in the closed quantum dot and clarify the basic mechanisms in these systems. The size of the star cluster and the halo can provide insights on its formation and evolution. Through the detailed N body simulation, the author shows that even if there is no black hole, the two -body relaxation can produce a broad core quality radius ratio. Key parameters (for example, initial density curve and semi -quality relaxation time) will affect the evolution of density curve and the degree of concentration of the core.
