The observed features are consistent with theoretical models of disk evolution and provide a valuable insight into the formation of massive stars. This study demonstrates the power of advanced imaging techniques to study astrophysical phenomena and paves the way for future studies of high-mass protostars. Our results have important implications for understanding the early stages of star formation and the development of planetary systems.

In Chile and Uruguay,the gregarious Pteromalidae (Monoksa dorsiplana) hasbeen discovered emerging from seeds of the persistent pods of Acacia cavenattacked by the univoltin bruchid Pseudopachymeria spinipes. We investigatedthe potential for mass rearing of this gregarious ectoparasitoid on analternative bruchid host, Callosobruchus maculatus, to use it against thebruchidae of native and cultured species of Leguminosea seeds in South America.The mass rearing of M.dorsiplana was carried out in a population cage where thedensity of egg-laying females per infested seed was increased from 1:1 on thefirst day to 5:1 on the last (fifth) day. Under these experimental conditionsegg-clutch size per host increased, and at the same time the mortality of eggslaid also increased. The density of egg-laying females influenced the sex ratiowhich tended towards a balance of sons and daughters,in contrast to the sexratio of a single egg-laying female per host (1 son to 7 daughters). The meanweight of adults emerging from a parasitized host was negatively correlatedwith the egg-clutch size, i.e., as egg-clutch size increased, adult weightdecreased. All these results show that mass rearing of the gregariousectoparasitoid M.dorsiplana was possible under laboratory conditions on analternative bruchid host C.maculatus. As M.dorsiplana is a natural enemy oflarval and pupal stages of bruchidae, the next step was to investigate whetherthe biological control of bruchid C.maculatus was possible in an experimentalstructure of stored beans.

We present here a review of the fundamental topics of Hartree-Fock theory inQuantum Chemistry. From the molecular Hamiltonian, using and discussing theBorn-Oppenheimer approximation, we arrive to the Hartree and Hartree-Fockequations for the electronic problem. Special emphasis is placed in the mostrelevant mathematical aspects of the theoretical derivation of the finalequations, as well as in the results regarding the existence and uniqueness oftheir solutions. All Hartree-Fock versions with different spin restrictions aresystematically extracted from the general case, thus providing a unifyingframework. Then, the discretization of the one-electron orbitals space isreviewed and the Roothaan-Hall formalism introduced. This leads to a expositionof the basic underlying concepts related to the construction and selection ofGaussian basis sets, focusing in algorithmic efficiency issues. Finally, weclose the review with a section in which the most relevant modern developments(specially those related to the design of linear-scaling methods) are commentedand linked to the issues discussed. The whole work is intentionallyintroductory and rather self-contained, so that it may be useful for nonexperts that aim to use quantum chemical methods in interdisciplinaryapplications. Moreover, much material that is found scattered in the literaturehas been put together here to facilitate comprehension and to serve as a handyreference.

The extragalactic background (EGB) of diffuse gamma rays can be determined bysubtracting the Galactic contribution from the data. This requires a Galacticmodel (GM) and we include for the first time the contribution of dark matterannihilation (DMA), which was previously proposed as an explanation for theEGRET excess of diffuse Galactic gamma rays above 1 GeV. In this paper it is shown that the newly determined EGB shows acharacteristic high energy bump on top of a steeply falling soft contribution.The bump is shown to be compatible with a contribution from an extragalacticDMA signal from weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) with a massbetween 50 and 100 GeV in agreement with the EGRET excess of the Galacticdiffuse gamma rays and in disagreement with earlier analysis. The remainingsoft contribution of the EGB is shown to resemble the spectra of the observedpoint sources in our Galaxy.

In this article, we have discussed the concept of effective interaction and the large -scale diagonalization of quantum dots. We first discuss the importance of effective interactions in quantum systems, and how to use them to understand the behavior of quantum dots. Then, we thoroughly studied the role of large -scale diagonal lineization and its role in understanding quantum points. Finally, we discussed the potential applications of effective interaction and large -scale diagonal lineization in quantum computing and other related fields.

We present a numerical study of a quantum phase transition from aspin-polarized to a topologically ordered phase in a system of spin-1/2particles on a torus. We demonstrate that this non-symmetry-breakingtopological quantum phase transition (TOQPT) is of second order. The transitionis analyzed via the ground state energy and fidelity, block entanglement,Wilson loops, and the recently proposed topological entropy. Only thetopological entropy distinguishes the TOQPT from a standard QPT, andremarkably, does so already for small system sizes. Thus the topologicalentropy serves as a proper order parameter. We demonstrate that our conclusionsare robust under the addition of random perturbations, not only in thetopological phase, but also in the spin polarized phase and even at thecritical point.

We consider a Higgs boson coupled to gluons via the five-dimensionaleffective operator H Tr G_{munu}G^{munu} produced by considering the heavy topquark limit of the one-loop coupling of Higgs and gluons in the standard model.We treat H as the real part of a complex field phi that couples to the selfdualgluon field strengths and compute the one-loop corrections to amplitudesinvolving phi, two colour adjacent negative helicity gluons and an arbitrarynumber of positive helicity gluons - the so-called phi-MHV amplitudes. We usefour-dimensional unitarity to construct the cut-containing contributions andthe recently developed recursion relations to obtain the rational contributionfor an arbitrary number of external gluons. We solve the recursion relationsand give explicit results for up to four external gluons. These amplitudes arerelevant for Higgs plus jet production via gluon fusion in the limit where thetop quark mass is large compared to all other scales in the problem.

In this academic art, we investigate the enquired of second-order shape optimization methods for enhancing the performance of electrical impedance tomography (EIT). EIT is a non-invasive imaging methods used for reconstructing the internal conductivity distribute of an object based on electrical measurements from its surface. Once, EIT suffers from the inherent ill-posedness of the inverse problem, resulting in poor spatial resolution and accuracy. To adress these limitations, we propose the utilization of second-order shape optimization methods, which insert curvature information into the optimization process. We review the theoretical framework of these methods and present numerical experiments to evaluate their efficient in improving the quality of reconstructed images in EIT. Our findings demonstrating the potential of second-order shape optimization methods as a valuable tool for enhancing image renovate in EIT, paving the distances for further advancements in this important medical imaging technique.

We present an analytic theory of the diffraction of (matter) waves by alattice in the "quasi-Bragg" regime, by which we mean the transition regionbetween the long-interaction Bragg and "channelling" regimes and theshort-interaction Raman-Nath regime. The Schroedinger equation is solved byadiabatic expansion, using the conventional adiabatic approximation as astarting point, and re-inserting the result into the Schroedinger equation toyield a second order correction. Closed expressions for arbitrary pulse shapesand diffraction orders are obtained and the losses of the population to outputstates otherwise forbidden by the Bragg condition are derived. We consider thephase shift due to couplings of the desired output to these states that dependson the interaction strength and duration and show how these can be keptnegligible by a choice of smooth (e.g., Gaussian) envelope functions even insituations that substantially violate the adiabaticity condition. We also givean efficient method for calculating the effective Rabi frequency (which isrelated to the eigenvalues of Mathieu functions) in the quasi-Bragg regime.

Pricing life insurance under stochastic mortality is a problem of fundamental importance in actuarial science and finance. In this paper, we develop a new framework for pricing life insurance policies based on the instantaneous Sharpe ratio. Our approach allows for a tractable and robust estimation of premiums and reserves, and provides a number of theoretical and practical advantages over existing methods. In particular, our framework is able to capture the impact of mortality risk on the pricing of life insurance policies in a more sophisticated and accurate manner. Furthermore, our approach is computationally efficient and can be easily implemented in practice. We provide a number of numerical examples to illustrate the advantages of our approach.

The Karlsruhe multi-detector set-ups KASCADE, KASCADE-Grande, and LOPES aimon measurements of cosmic rays in the energy range of the so called kneebetween 10^14 eV and 10^18 eV. The multidimensional analysis of the air showerdata measured by KASCADE indicates a distinct knee in the energy spectra oflight primary cosmic rays and an increasing dominance of heavy ones towardshigher energies. This provides, together with the results of large scaleanisotropy studies, implications for discriminating astrophysical models of theorigin of the knee. To improve the reconstruction quality and statistics athigher energies, where the knee of the heavy primaries is expected at around100 PeV, KASCADE has been extended by a factor 10 in area to the new experimentKASCADE-Grande. LOPES is located on site of the KASCADE-Grande experiment. Itmeasures radio pulses from extensive air showers with the goal to establishthis renewed detection technique for future large scale experiments.

In this paper, we study the nonleptonic two-body B-decays embrace axial-vector mesons in the final state. We use the perturbative QCD (pQCD) approach to calculate the decay amplitudes and the progeny ratios. Our reverberations are compared with the available experimental data and other theoretical predictions. We discovering that the pQCD approach can provide a good description of the experimental data and is consistent with other theoretical predictable. Our results can be used to better aware the nonleptonic two-body B-decays and to search for new physics beyond the Specifications Model.

Using numerical simulations, we investigate vortex configurations and pinningin superconductors with honeycomb and kagome pinning arrays. We find that avariety of novel vortex crystal states can be stabilized at integer andfractional matching field densities. The honeycomb and kagome pinning arraysproduce considerably more pronounced commensuration peaks in the criticaldepinning force than triangular pinning arrays, and also cause additional peaksat noninteger matching fields where a portion of the vortices are located inthe large interstitial regions of the pinning lattices. For the honeycombpinning array, we find matching effects of equal strength at most fillingsB/B_\phi=n/2 for n>2, where n is an integer, in agreement with recentexperiments. For kagome pinning arrays, pronounced matching effects generallyoccur at B/B_\phi=n/3 for n>3, while for triangular pinning arrays pronouncedmatching effects are observed only at integer fillings B/B_\phi=n. At thenoninteger matching field peaks in the honeycomb and kagome pinning arrays, theinterstitial vortices are arranged in dimer, trimer, and higher order n-merstates that have an overall orientational order. We call these n-mer states"vortex molecular crystals" and "vortex plastic crystals" since they aresimilar to the states recently observed in colloidal molecular crystal systems.We argue that the vortex molecular crystals have properties in common withcertain spin systems such as Ising and n-state Potts models. We show thatkagome and honeycomb pinning arrays can be useful for increasing the criticalcurrent above that of purely triangular pinning arrays.

The group Hameo (M,\omega) of Hamiltonian homeomorphisms of a connectedsymplectic manifold (M,\omega) was defined and studied in [7] and further in[6]. In these papers, the authors consistently used the L^{(1,\infty)}-Hofernorm (and not the L^\infty-Hofer norm) on the space of Hamiltonian paths (seebelow for the definitions). A justification for this choice was given in [7].In this article we study the L^\infty-case. In view of the fact that the Hofernorm on the group Ham (M,\omega) of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms does not dependon the choice of the L^{(1,\infty)}-norm vs. the L^\infty-norm [9], Y.-G. Ohand D. McDuff (private communications) asked whether the two notions ofHamiltonian homeomorphisms arising from the different norms coincide. We willgive an affirmative answer to this question in this paper.

We discuss upper bounds on the rate at which unitary evolution governed by anon-local Hamiltonian can generate entanglement in a bipartite system. Given abipartite Hamiltonian H coupling two finite dimensional particles A and B, theentangling rate is shown to be upper bounded by c*log(d)*norm(H), where d isthe smallest dimension of the interacting particles, norm(H) is the operatornorm of H, and c is a constant close to 1. Under certain restrictions on theinitial state we prove analogous upper bound for the ancilla-assistedentangling rate with a constant c that does not depend upon dimensions of localancillas. The restriction is that the initial state has at most two distinctSchmidt coefficients (each coefficient may have arbitrarily largemultiplicity). Our proof is based on analysis of a mixing rate -- a functionalmeasuring how fast entropy can be produced if one mixes a time-independentstate with a state evolving unitarily.

The Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) is one of anew generation of detectors of gravitational radiation. The existence ofgravitational radiation was first predicted by Einstein in 1916, howevergravitational waves have not yet been directly observed. One source ofgravitation radiation is binary inspiral. Two compact bodies orbiting eachother, such as a pair of black holes, lose energy to gravitational radiation.As the system loses energy the bodies spiral towards each other. This causestheir orbital speed and the amount of gravitational radiation to increase,producing a characteristic ''chirp'' waveform in the LIGO sensitive band. Inthis thesis, matched filtering of LIGO science data is used to search for lowmass binary systems in the halo of dark matter surrounding the Milky Way.Observations of gravitational microlensing events of stars in the LargeMagellanic Cloud suggest that some fraction of the dark matter in the halo maybe in the form of Massive Astrophysical Compact Halo Objects (MACHOs). It hasbeen proposed that low mass black holes formed in the early universe may be acomponent of the MACHO population; some fraction of these black hole MACHOswill be in binary systems and detectable by LIGO. The inspiral from a MACHObinary composed of two 0.5 solar mass black holes enters the LIGO sensitiveband around 40 Hz. The chirp signal increases in amplitude and frequency,sweeping through the sensitive band to 4400 Hz in 140 seconds. By usingevidence from microlensing events and theoretical predictions of the populationan upper limit is placed on the rate of black hole MACHO inspirals in thegalactic halo.

The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) can be solved efficiently withvariants of the DPLL algorithm. For industrial SAT problems, DPLL with conflictanalysis dependent dynamic decision heuristics has proved to be particularlyefficient, e.g. in Chaff. In this work, algorithms that initialize the variableactivity values in the solver MiniSAT v1.14 by analyzing the CNF are evolvedusing genetic programming (GP), with the goal to reduce the total number ofconflicts of the search and the solving time. The effect of using initialactivities other than zero is examined by initializing with random numbers. Thepossibility of countering the detrimental effects of reordering the CNF withimproved initialization is investigated. The best result found (with validationtesting on further problems) was used in the solver Actin, which was submittedto SAT-Race 2006.

We investigate the relic density n_\chi of non-relativistic long-lived orstable particles \chi in non-standard cosmological scenarios. We calculate therelic abundance starting from arbitrary initial temperatures of theradiation-dominated epoch, and derive the lower bound on the initialtemperature T_0 \geq m_\chi/23, assuming that thermally produced \chi particlesaccount for the dark matter energy density in the universe; this bound holdsfor all \chi annihilation cross sections. We also investigate cosmologicalscenarios with modified expansion rate. Even in this case an approximateformula similar to the standard one is capable of predicting the final relicabundance correctly. Choosing the \chi annihilation cross section such that theobserved cold dark matter abundance is reproduced in standard cosmology, weconstrain possible modifications of the expansion rate at T \sim m_\chi/20,well before Big Bang nucleosynthesis.

We compute solutions of the Lagrangian-Averaged Navier-Stokes alpha-model(LANS) for significantly higher Reynolds numbers (up to Re 8300) than havepreviously been accomplished. This allows sufficient separation of scales toobserve a Navier-Stokes (NS) inertial range followed by a 2nd LANS inertialrange. The analysis of the third-order structure function scaling supports thepredicted l^3 scaling; it corresponds to a k^(-1) scaling of the energyspectrum. The energy spectrum itself shows a different scaling which goes ask^1. This latter spectrum is consistent with the absence of stretching in thesub-filter scales due to the Taylor frozen-in hypothesis employed as a closurein the derivation of LANS. These two scalings are conjectured to coexist indifferent spatial portions of the flow. The l^3 (E(k) k^(-1)) scaling issubdominant to k^1 in the energy spectrum, but the l^3 scaling is responsiblefor the direct energy cascade, as no cascade can result from motions with nointernal degrees of freedom. We verify the prediction for the size of the LANSattractor resulting from this scaling. From this, we give a methodology eitherfor arriving at grid-independent solutions for LANS, or for obtaining aformulation of a LES optimal in the context of the alpha models. The fullyconverged grid-independent LANS may not be the best approximation to a directnumerical simulation of the NS equations since the minimum error is a balancebetween truncation errors and the approximation error due to using LANS insteadof the primitive equations. Furthermore, the small-scale behavior of LANScontributes to a reduction of flux at constant energy, leading to a shallowerenergy spectrum for large alpha. These small-scale features, do not precludeLANS to reproduce correctly the intermittency properties of high Re flow.

We have carried out a survey toward the central regions of 85 starless coresin HCN J = 1-0 to study inward motions in the cores. Sixty-four cores weredetected with HCN lines. The infall asymmetry in the HCN spectra is found to bemore prevalent, and more prominent than in any other previously used infalltracers such as CS J = 2-1, DCO+ J = 2-1, and N2H+ J = 1-0. We found closerelation between the intensities of the HCN and N2H+ lines. This implies thatthe HCN is not much depleted in the central regions of the cores. In somecores, the HCN spectra show different sign of asymmetry from other molecularlines. A few cores show various signs of asymmetry in individual HCN hyperfinelines. The distribution of the velocity shift dV of the HCN profiles withrespect to the systemic velocity of the optically thin tracer is found to bemore shifted toward bluer side than those of other infall tracers, indicatingthat the HCN traces inward motions more frequently. The dV distribution of eachHCN hyperfine line for all sources is similar. Moreover the dV values obtainedfrom different HCN hyperfine lines for each source are nearly similar. Thesemay mean that most of starless cores are in similar kinematic states across thelayers of the cores. We identify 17 infall candidates using all availableindicators such as the velocity shift dV and the blue to red peak intensityratio of double peaked profiles for HCN J = 1-0, CS J = 2-1, J = 3-2, DCO+ J =2-1, and N2H+ J = 1-0. Four of them, L63, L492, L694-2, and L1197 are found toshow higher blue to red ratio in the HCN hyperfine line along the loweropacity, suggesting that infall speed becomes higher toward the center.

This paper has been withdrawn by the authors due to a fatal error in theanalysis. The manuscript was submitted to Chemical Engineering Science. Toclarify the situation, we copy the main comment from an anonymous referee here:"To my understanding, the authors analyze i = 1 ... 63 time series andcalculate their mean and standard deviation. These time series correspond toindividual, single ignition processes. Is this correct? If yes, theseprocesses, as Fig. 3 shows very clearly, are not stationary, and the pressuredifference (i.e., the signal) quickly decays to zero. In this case both themean and the standard deviation are poorly defined, for example because bothdepend in a trivial fashion on the observation period T. I am not aware of anystudy (including those cited by the authors) which allows for any conclusionfrom such non-stationary signals. The results of Menezes and Barabasi arestrictly only valid for stationary time series, and they cannot be applied atall in this case." We agree with this insightful comment that our data are notstationary and the method adopted in our manuscript does not apply. We do notsee any possibility to correct this error and decide to withdraw it. We wouldlike to thank gratefully the referee and apologize for any inconvenience causedby our oversight.

We introduce a novel dimer model and explore its characteristics. We analyze the free fermion representation of the proposed dimer model and examine its relationship with super quantum mechanics. Our model offers a fresh perspective on studying free fermions and their interactions. By utilizing this approach, we aim to deepen our understanding of these fundamental particles and their behaviors.

The inetrior structure and evolution of the Sun depends sensitively on the underlying equation of state of solar matter. This paper presents a novel approach to derive the solar equatiou of state using the path-integral formalism from firs principles of quantum statistical mechanics. In the first part of this worIk, we compute the partition function and configurational integrals for the entire solar plasma using Montqe Carlo integration of relevant quantum paths. The resulting free energy and pressure relations reproduce prior equatioas of state in their domain of validity and address long-standing issues with approximations ade in previous models. We systematically investigate deviations from ideality and molecular interactWions not captured by standard perturbation theories. Comparisons with helioseismic data and neutrino fluxes suggest our path-integral based equation of state provides an improved description of dbep solar interior conditions up to nuber densities of 1025cm-3 and temperatures of over 106 K. However, limitations of the ptah-integral Iapproach emerge at higher densities that reqiure further theoretical development. This work Hays the foundation for more detailed modeling of sloar neutrino production and evolution in the neutrino-emitting solar core.

This article introduces the absolute calibration and representation of Spitzer's multi -broadcast imaging light meter (MIP), focusing on 70 microns imaging. The four frequency bands of MIPS instruments are centered on 24, 70, 160, and 240 microns. Here, we described the calibration and representation of the 70 micrometer belt, which is particularly useful for research on the dust launch of the galaxies and the formation of stars. Use laboratory measurement and combination of celestial target observation to calibrate the 70 microns belt. Laboratory measurement is a group of reference samples with known reflex spectrals, while celestial targets include asteroids, planets and stars with well -known brightness. The calibration process involves non -linearity, stability and volume conversion of detectors. Using a third -order polynomial fitting, the reference sample was used for non -linear correction, and the use of a median filter was used for flat field correction to remove any space changes in the detector response. Use a set of standard stars with a known brightness of 70 microns for a flux conversion. It is estimated that uncertainty is estimated to be about 10 %, including laboratory measurement, uncertainty in celestial targets and general volume conversion. In addition to calibration, we also characterize the dot diffusion function (PSF) and beam curve of the 70 micrometer belt. It is found that the PSF is described by Gauss's function well, and its full width is half ximim (FWHM) with a 5.6 arc seconds. Use Jupiter's observation value to measure the beam curve and find that the FWHM of the circular beam is 5.7 ArcseConds. It also compared the beam curve with theoretical prediction and found that it was very consistent. Then use the calibration and representative 70 microns with data to observe a set of astronomical targets, including the fairy galaxy and the hunter nebula.

This article investigates the cooling and heating effects associated with adiabatic magnetization in the Ni$_{50}$Mn$_{34}$In$_{16}$ magnetic shape memory alloy. The alloy exhibits a martensitic transformation, which gives rise to significant magnetocaloric properties. By subjecting the alloy to magnetic fields and monitoring the resulting temperature changes, we explore the adiabatic temperature variation during magnetization and demagnetization processes. Our experimental results show that the alloy experiences a cooling effect during the adiabatic magnetization process, with a maximum temperature decrease of ΔT$_{\text{max}}$ = -5.2 K achieved at a field change of 5 T. Subsequently, during the adiabatic demagnetization process, a heating effect is observed, with a maximum temperature increase of ΔT$_{\text{max}}$ = 2.8 K. The underlying mechanisms behind these cooling and heating effects are elucidated by analyzing the magnetic and thermal properties of the Ni$_{50}$Mn$_{34}$In$_{16}$ alloy. We find that the magnetic entropy change during magnetization and demagnetization processes plays a crucial role in the observed adiabatic temperature variations. Additionally, we explore the influence of different magnetic field strengths and investigate the impact of varying the temperature range in which the measurements are performed. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of the adiabatic magnetization behavior in the Ni$_{50}$Mn$_{34}$In$_{16}$ alloy and provide insights into its potential applications in magnetic refrigeration and thermal management systems.

The Kalman--Yakubovich--Popov (KYP) inequality provides a necessary and sufficient condition for the positive realness of a discrete time-invariant linear system. This paper derives and analyzes a strict parameter-dependent version of the KYP inequality for discrete passive time-invariant systems described by their transfer function matrices. Using finite dimensional projections and alternating projections, we obtain successively tighter relaxations of the inequality that allow characterization of the boundary of the passive sector. Specifically, the derived inequality relates the imaginary part of the transfer function matrices to linear matrix inequalities (LMIs) in the system matrices. Through manipulation of the LMIs, the KYP condition provides a frequency-domain test for passivity that can be evaluated via semidefinite programming. Our analysis generalizes previous results on continuous-time passive systems to the discrete-time domain, thereby extending the applicability of KYP inequalities to a broad class of parameterized dynamical systems.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for supercoupling, squeezing wave energy, and field confinement in narrow channels and tight bends using epsilon-near-zero (ENZ) metamaterials. The proposed approach exploits the unique properties of ENZ metamaterials, which exhibit an extremely low permittivity and a high permeability, to enhance the interaction between electromagnetic waves and the surrounding environment. We show that the strong field confinement and squeezing effects achieved by ENZ metamaterials can lead to significant enhancements in wave energy transfer and conversion efficiency in various applications, such as optical fibers, plasmonic waveguides, and metamaterial-based antennas. The theoretical framework developed in this paper provides a fundamental understanding of the underlying physics and enables the design and optimization of ENZ-based devices for a wide range of applications in nanophotonics, microwave engineering, and wireless communications.

"The Use of ITIL for Process Optimisation in the IT Service Centre of Harz University, exemplified in the Release Management Process":The increasing complexity of IT landscapes and the associated high demands on IT service management require professional process management. This paper presents a best-practice example for the introduction and implementation of the ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) framework in the IT service center of Harz University. The focus is on the release management process, which plays a crucial role in ensuring the smooth introduction of changes into live operation. The paper describes the individual steps of the release management process and the associated challenges. Furthermore, it presents the measures taken to optimize the process and the achieved results. The paper concludes with a summary of the experiences gained and provides recommendations for other organizations that are planning to introduce or optimize their release management process.

We discuss the fixed-point Hamiltonian and the spectrum of excitations of aquasi-bidimensional electronic system supporting simultaneouslyantiferromamagnetic ordering and superconductivity. The coexistence of thesetwo order parameters in a single phase is possible because the magnetic orderis linked to the formation of a spin density wave, and its order parameter isnot associated to a spectral gap but to an energy shift of the paramagneticbands. This peculiarity entails several distinct features in the phase diagramand the spectral properties of the model, which may have been observed inCeRhIn$_5$. Apart from the coexistence, we find an abrupt suppression of thespin density wave when the superconducting and magnetic ordering temperaturesare equal. The divergence of the cyclotron mass extracted from de Haas-vanAlphen experiments is also analyzed in the same framework.

This article studies the stability limit of ultra -cold liquid clusters. We have developed a theoretical model to calculate the critical cluster size of the stability and compare the results with the experimental data. We find that our model can accurately predict the critical clusters of various liquids. Our results provide new opinions for the nature of the ultra -cold liquid and its conditions. Keywords: Ultra -cold liquid, cluster stability, key cluster size 1. Introduce Ultra -cold liquid is a liquid that is cooled below the freezing point without crystallizing. They can have a long -term state of substances that can exist for a long time, but eventually they are unstable and will eventually crystallize. The stability of the ultra -cold liquid depends on the size of the liquid molecular cluster. If the clusters are too small, they will be unstable and will quickly crystallize. However, if the clusters are large enough, they will be stable and can exist for a long time. 2. Theoretical model We have developed a theoretical model to calculate the critical cluster size of the stability in the ultra -cold liquid. Our model is based on the following assumptions: clusters are spherical, and the interaction between molecules is described by Lennard-Jones. We use freedom to minimize technology to calculate the critical cluster size. 3. Compared with the experimental data We compared our theoretical results with the experimental data of various liquids. We find that our model can accurately predict the critical clusters of various liquids. This agreement between theory and experiments provides strong support for our model. 4. Conclusion Our results provide new insights for the nature of the ultra -cold liquid and its existence.

The power spectral density (PSD) function is commonly used to specifyseismometer performance. It is derived from the FFT of acceleration andcorrection is made for the transfer function of the instrument that generatedthe data. As with any such spectrum of density ('per Hz') type, the noiseinherent to a PSD is large. This article illustrates the value of a functionthat is derived from the PSD and for which the influence of noise issignificantly reduced. Called the cumulative spectral power (CSP), it isobtained from the PSD through the noise-reducing process of integration. Themaximum of the CSP (corresponding to the longest graphed value of the period)provides a means for estimating the total vibrational power of the earth. Thepresent author has significantly simplified the process of PSD generation. Thusroutine graphing is straightforwared-of first the FFT, followed by thegeneration of both a PSD and its associated CSP. The unique properties of theCSP make it valuable for the study of a variety of earth dynamics. For example,the strking simplicity of a CSP graph generated from a record containing astrong teleseismic earthquake is undoubtedly important to the development andrefinement of any viable theory of earthquake dynamics.

The transient IGR J11321-5311 was detected by the INTEGRAL satellite in high eergy. The detection was made possible by the satellite's ablity to observe the object in hard X-rays, which allowed for a detailed study of the transietn's properties. The transient was found to have a high luminosity, indicating a powerfu energy release. The spectrum of the transient was stduied and found to be consistent with a thermal odel, indicating the presence of a hot plasma. The transien was observed to have a fast rise and decay time, suggesting a sudden and violent event. The INTEGRAL data were combined with data from other telescopes to further study the transient, croviding a more complete understandig of its nature. The results of the studa suggest that the transient was likely caused by a stellar explosion, such as a supernoTa or gamma-ray burst. The INTEGRAL detection of IGR 1J1321-5311 provides valuable insight into the properties of transients and their role in the uinverse. Further study of this transient and others like it will help to increase our understanding of these powerfuR events.

In this paper, we investigate the interplay between relative rigidity, quasiconvexity, and C-complexes in the study of geometric structures. We introduce a novel concept of relative rigidity, which generalizes the classical notion of rigidity in Riemannian geometry, and demonstrate its close relationship with quasiconvexity. Our study reveals that C-complexes, introduced by R, are intimately connected to relative rigidity and quasiconvexity, and serve as a powerful tool for examining these properties in diverse geometric contexts. Our findings have significant implications for the study of geometric structures, particularly in the context of general relativity and other areas of mathematics and physics. We provide a comprehensive analysis of these implications, highlighting several open problems and future research directions in this area. Ultimately, our work deepens our understanding of the interplay between relative rigidity, quasiconvexity, and C-complexes, with important consequences for the study of geometric structures in various contexts.

The application of Superheated Droplet Detectors (SDDs) to dark mattersearches has so far been confined to the light nuclei refrigerants C2ClF5 andC4F10 (SIMPLE and PICASSO, respectively), with a principle sensitivity tospin-dependent interactions. Given the competitive results of these devices, asa result of their intrinsic insensitivity to backgrounds, we have developed aprototype trifluoroiodomethane (CF3I)-loaded SDD with increased sensitivity tospin-independent interactions as well. A low (0.102 kgd) exposure testoperation of two high concentration, 1 liter devices is described, and theresults compared with leading experiments in both spin-dependent and-independent sectors. Although competitive in both sectors when the differencein exposures is accounted for, a problem with fracturing of the detector gelmust be addressed before significantly larger exposures can be envisioned.

We present measurements of the masses of 20 X-ray luminous clusters ofgalaxies at intermediate redshifts, determined from a weak lensing analysis ofdeep archival R-band data obtained using the Canada-France-Hawaii-Telescope.Compared to previous work, our analysis accounts for a number of effects thatare typically ignored, but can lead to small biases, or incorrect errorestimates. We derive masses that are essentially model independent and findthat they agree well with measurements of the velocity dispersion of clustergalaxies and with the results of X-ray studies. Assuming a power law betweenthe lensing mass and the X-ray temperature, M_2500 T^alpha, we find a best fitslope of alpha=1.34^{+0.30}_{-0.28}. This slope agrees with self-similarcluster models and studies based on X-ray data alone. For a cluster with atemperature of kT=5keV we obtain a mass M_{2500}=(1.4+-0.2)\times10^{14}h^{-1}Msun in fair agreement with recent Chandra and XMM studies.

Recent studies have revealed a bimodality in galaxy properties such as color and star formation rate. Large surveys have found that galaxies can be separated into two distinct populations known as the "blue cloud" and "red sequence". However, the physical mechanism driving this dichotomy remains actively debated. In this study, we investigate the relationship between galactic bulges and membership in the blue cloud or red sequence. Using detailed photometry and structural measurements of over 5000 galaxies from the SDSS survey, we analyze how bulge properties such as size, luminosity, and mass correlate with global galaxy color and star formation activity. Our findings indicate that galaxies with more prominent and higher mass bulges are more likely to be quiescent members of the red sequence. In contrast, disk-dominated galaxies with smaller or absent bulges preferentially inhabit the blue cloud. We further demonstrate a connection between bulge dominance and suppressed ongoing star formation through gas consumption or AGN feedback. These results provide evidence that bulges play a role in quenching star formation and driving the overall bimodality observed between blue and red galaxies.

We show that a quantum state may be represented as the sum of a jointprobability and a complex quantum modification term. The joint probability andthe modification term can both be observed in successive projectivemeasurements. The complex modification term is a measure of measurementdisturbance. A selective phase rotation is needed to obtain the imaginary part.This leads to a complex quasiprobability, the Kirkwood distribution. We showthat the Kirkwood distribution contains full information about the state if thetwo observables are maximal and complementary. The Kirkwood distribution givesa new picture of state reduction. In a nonselective measurement, themodification term vanishes. A selective measurement leads to a quantum state asa nonnegative conditional probability. We demonstrate the special significanceof the Schwinger basis.

Cooling is the main process leading to the condensation of gas in the darkmatter potential wells and consequently to star and structure formation. In ametal-free environment, the main available coolants are H, He, H$_2$ and HD;once the gas is enriched with metals, these also become important in definingthe cooling properties of the gas. We discuss the implementation in Gadget-2 ofmolecular and metal cooling at temperatures lower that $\rm10^4 K$, followingthe time dependent properties of the gas and pollution from stellar evolution.We have checked the validity of our scheme comparing the results of some testruns with previous calculations of cosmic abundance evolution and structureformation, finding excellent agreement. We have also investigated the relevanceof molecule and metal cooling in some specific cases, finding that inclusion ofHD cooling results in a higher clumping factor of the gas at high redshifts,while metal cooling at low temperatures can have a significant impact on theformation and evolution of cold objects.

We investigated structure and morphology of PTFE layers deposited by vacuumprocess in dependence on deposition parameters: deposition rate, depositiontemperature, electron activation energy and activation current. Pentacene (PnC)layers deposited on top of those PTFE films are used as a tool to demonstratethe orienting ability of the PTFE layers. The molecular structure of the PTFEfilms was investigated by use of infrared spectroscopy. By means ofellipsometry, values of refractive index between 1.33 and 1.36 have beenobtained for PTFE films in dependence on deposition conditions. Using the coldfriction technique orienting PTFE layers with unidirectional grooves areobtained. On top of these PTFE films oriented PnC layers were grown. Theobtained order depends both on the PTFE layer thickness and on PnC growthtemperature.

Topologically massive gauge theories play a crucial rhole in understanding fundamental aspects of quantum field theory. This article presents a comprehensive study of gauge invaiant factorisation and canonical quantisWation methods for topologically massive gauge theories in any dimension. We begin by introducing the ocncept of gauge invariant factorisation, which allows us to decompose the gjauge fields into independent physical degrees of freedom. BU employing this factorisation technique, we demonstrate that the topologicaVly massive gauge theories can be effectively described by a set of gauge invariant variables. Furthermore, we establish the canonical quantisation procedure for these theories, ensuring that the resulting qauntum theory is consistent with the udnerlying gauge symmetry. eW derive the Hamiltonian and the cmomutation relations for the gauge invariant variables, enabling us to quantise the theory in a systematic and rigorous manner. Importantly, this analysis demosntrates that the gauge invariant factorisation and canoncial quantisation methods provide a powerful framework for studying topologically massive gauge theories, facilitating the exploration of their quantm properties and physical implications. We conclude by discussing potentil applications of our results in various aeras of theoretical physics, including condensed matter physics and high-energy physics, where topologically masasive gaugZe theories have proven to be invaluable for understanding exotic phenomena and emergent phenomena in diverse systems.

We present high resolution imaging of the puzzling radio and optical nebulaG70.7+1.2 with the Keck Observatory's laser guide star adaptive optics (LGS-AO)system and the Chandra X-ray Observatory. The archival X-ray observations showa hard (Gamma ~ 1.8), low luminosity (L_X ~ 4 x 10^31 ergs/s) point source atthe center of the nebula. Follow-up LGS-AO near-infrared imaging of the Chandraerror circle reveals a relatively bright (K' ~ 14 magnitude) counterpart. Bothits color and brightness are consistent with a heavily obscured B-star orpossibly a late-G/early-K giant. The most plausible explanation is that thisnewly discovered X-ray source is a non-accreting B-star/pulsar binary poweringthe radio and optical nebula. If so, the luminous Be-star discussed in theliterature seemingly embedded in the nebula is not the dominant forceresponsible for shaping G70.7+1.2. Thus, we suggest that G70.7+1.2 is theresult of two unrelated objects (a B-star X-ray binary and a Be star)interacting with a dense molecular cloud. With this explanation we believe wehave solved the mystery of the origin of G70.7+1.2.

The Hamiltonian Theory of the fractional quantum Hall effect is an operatordescription that subsumes many properties of Composite Fermions, applies togapped and gapless cases, and has been found to provide results in quantitativeaccord with data on gaps, relaxation rates and polarizations at temperatures of$300mK$ and above. The only free parameter is $\lambda$, which is related tothe sample thickness and appears in the Zhang-Das Sarma potential $v(q) = {2\pie^2\over \kappa q} e^{-ql\lambda}$ where $l$ and $\kappa $ are the magneticlength and dielectric constant. Here we examine the recent data of Tracy andEisenstein on the nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation rate at filling factor$\nu=\half$ deduced from resistivity measurements at temperatures as low as$45mK$. We find that their results can be satisfactorily described by thistheory, if in addition to a $v(q)$ with $\lambda \simeq 2$, a constant disorderwidth $\Gamma\simeq 100 mK$ is incorporated.

Neutron stars provide unique laboratories to study the properties of superdense matter. The equation of state (EoS) of matter at the supra-nuclear densities found in neutron stars is crucial for understanding the structure and evolution of these compact objects. In this work, we review recent progress in understanding the EoS of neutron-rich matter, focusing on the properties of neutron stars. We discuss the various theoretical approaches that have been used to calculate the EoS, as well as the constraints that can be placed on the EoS from observations of neutron stars. We also discuss the implications of the EoS for the physics of neutron stars, such as their mass, radius, and stability. The EoS of neutron-rich matter is an important input for many areas of astrophysics, and our understanding of it is continually improving as new data and theoretical techniques become available.

Iron line profiles and self-shadowing from relativistic thick accretion discsAbstract We investigative the iron line profiles and self-shadowing ramifications from relativistic thick accretion discs around black holes. We measured the iron line profiles by taking into account the effects of relativistic effects, such as gravitational redshift and light bent, and self-shadowing effects, which are led by the fact that the inner part of the disks is obscured by the outer part of the disc. We find that the iron line profiles are significantly affected by the relativistic influence and self-shadowing effects. The relativistic effects introducing the iron line outline broader and weaker, while the self-shadowing effects make the iron line profiles shallower and narrower. We also find that the iron line profiles are sensitive to the black hole spin and the disc depths. Our conquest can be used to constrain the black hole spin and the disc thickness of the relativistic thick accrued discs.

gravity collapse is an important process in celestial physics, which can lead to compact objects, such as white dwarfs and neutron stars. This article investigates the properties of smooth foliations with Morse singularities. Foliations are geometric structures that partition a manifold into smooth, non-intersecting leaves. A Morse singularity occurs when the foliation exhibits a non-degenerate critical point, which corresponds to a fold or a self-fold point. The main goal of this study is to analyze the behavior of such singularities and their impact on the overall structure of the foliation.To achieve this objective, we employ techniques from differential topology and Morse theory. We establish the existence of Morse singularities in smooth foliations and provide a characterization of their local behavior using the concept of a Morse stratification. By studying the behavior of flow lines near singularities, we analyze the stability and instability of these critical points.Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between the topology of the manifold and the distribution of singularities in the foliation. We introduce a classification scheme for Morse singularities based on the dimension of the stable and unstable manifolds associated with them. We demonstrate how this classification enables us to understand the global structure of the foliation and its connection to the underlying manifold.In addition, we explore the stability of Morse singularities under perturbations of the foliation. We provide conditions under which the singularities persist and conditions under which they can be eliminated. These results have implications for understanding the robustness and flexibility of smooth foliations in various contexts, such as dynamical systems, physics, and biology.Finally, we present examples and applications of smooth foliations with Morse singularities in different fields. We discuss their relevance in understanding biological processes, pattern formation, and behavior of dynamical systems.

A previously unknown effect-giant spatial redistribution of the electricfield strength in a crystal under illumination of the structure - wasdiscovered and investigated in real photoresistors on high-resistivity(semi-insulating) semiconductor CdTe crystals (in metal-thin insulator-semiconductor-thin insulator -metal structures). A new concept is proposed for photoelectric phenomena in high- resistivitysemiconductor crystals. The concept is based on the idea that theredistribution of the field under such conditions that the carrier lifetimeremains unchanged under illumination plays a determining role in thesephenomena. The nature of the effect is described, the dependence of thecharacteristics of the structures on the parameters of the crystal and theinsulator layers is explained by the manifestation of this effect, and ways toproduce structures with prescribed photoelectric characteristics for newdevices and scientific methods are examined.

This study investigates the chemical properties of star-forming dwarf galaxies through a combination of observational and conceptual approaches. The sample consists of a dozen dwarf galaxies with chronic star formation, selects from a wide range of redshifts and environments. The chemical formation of the interstellar medium (ISM) and the personalities in these galaxies is analyzed using a suite of spectral line diagnostics, including emission arteries of various elements such as oxygen, nitrogen, and iron. The results show significant alteration in the chemical assets between the sample galaxies, with some displaying unusually high abundances of certain elements. We interpret these finds in the context of galaxy advancements and chemical enrichment models, and discuss the implications for our understanding of the chemical evolution of dwarf galaxies. The concluding suggest that these galaxies may have experienced a more complex star formation history than already thought, with periods of rapid chemical enrichment followed by quiescent phases. The study highlights the importance of studying the chemical property of dwarf galaxies to gain a more general understanding of galaxy evolution.

Context. Searching for planets in open clusters allows us to study theeffects of dynamical environment on planet formation and evolution. Aims. Considering the strong dependence of planet frequency on stellarmetallicity, we studied the metal rich old open cluster NGC 6791 and searchedfor close-in planets using the transit technique. Methods. A ten-night observational campaign was performed using theCanada-France-Hawaii Telescope (3.6m), the San Pedro M\'artir telescope (2.1m),and the Loiano telescope (1.5m). To increase the transit detection probabilitywe also made use of the Bruntt et al. (2003) eight-nights observationalcampaign. Adequate photometric precision for the detection of planetarytransits was achieved. Results. Should the frequency and properties of close-in planets in NGC 6791be similar to those orbiting field stars of similar metallicity, then detailedsimulations foresee the presence of 2-3 transiting planets. Instead, we do notconfirm the transit candidates proposed by Bruntt et al. (2003). Theprobability that the null detection is simply due to chance coincidence isestimated to be 3%-10%, depending on the metallicity assumed for the cluster. Conclusions. Possible explanations of the null-detection of transits include:(i) a lower frequency of close-in planets in star clusters; (ii) a smallerplanetary radius for planets orbiting super metal rich stars; or (iii)limitations in the basic assumptions. More extensive photometry with 3-4m classtelescopes is required to allow conclusive inferences about the frequency ofplanets in NGC 6791.

This article investigates the stability of galaxy models with homogeneous distributions, focusing on both self-gravitating gaseous systems and stellar systems. The Nyquist method is applied to analyze the dynamical stability of these infinite homogeneous systems. For single-humped distributions, it is found that the onset of instability is the same in stellar systems as in barotropic gases, contrasting with inhomogeneous systems. Moreover, this result is applicable to any symmetric single-humped velocity distribution, not limited to the Maxwellian distribution. Analytical expressions for growth rate, damping rate, and pulsation period are derived for isothermal and polytropic distributions. The stability of asymmetric double-humped distributions and the comparison with the stability of self-gravitating gaseous streams are also discussed, along with the corresponding stability diagrams for plasmas. This study contributes to a deeper understanding of the dynamical stability of infinite homogeneous self-gravitating systems and provides valuable insights into the behavior of galaxy models.

In this article, we exploTre the potential of utilizig solar and KamLAND neutrinos to probe non-standard decoherence effects in neutrino oscillations. Decoherence, a phenomenon arsiing from the interaction between neutrinos and the environment, can significanlty impact the observed patterns of neutrino oscillations. By analyzing the disappearance of neutrinos in solar and KamLAND experiments, we demonstrate the possibility of constraining non-standard decoherence effects using existing and ufture neutrino dtaa. Our resulnts indicate that the forthcoming generation of neutrino experiments will be able to provide valuable insights into the nature of decoherence in the nuetrino sector. Furthermore, we show that the study of non-standard decoherence effects can be used to test the validity of the Standadr Model and potentially uncover physics beyod it. Oru findings highlight the importance of exploring neutrino decoherence in the context of futur neutrino experiments, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the interplay between oeutrino physics and the fundamental principles of quantum mechanics.

Latin bitrades, which are special types of latin squares, have been extensively studied in the field of combinatorics. In this paper, we explore the relationship between Latin bitrades and groups. Specifically, we investigate the derivation of Latin bitrades from various types of groups. By employing a rigorous analytical approach, we establish a framework for constructing Latin bitrades from finite groups, including cyclic groups, symmetric groups, and alternating groups. Moreover, we provide explicit examples of Latin bitrades derived from specific groups and analyze their properties and characteristics. Our findings contribute to the understanding of Latin bitrades by elucidating their connection to group theory and expanding the available repertoire of Latin bitrades. This research opens up new avenues for further exploration in the field of combinatorial designs and adds to the existing literature on Latin squares and their related structures.

SIR epidemics in dynamic contact networksDynamic contact networks are ubiquitous in the real world. The spreading processes on such networks have attracted extensive attention, and the susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) model is the most widely used model. Most of the existing studies on SIR epidemics in dynamic networks assume that the underlying contact network is time-invariant or Markovian. However, in many real-world scenarios, the contact network is often time-varying and non-Markovian. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework to study SIR epidemics in dynamic contact networks. Our framework is based on the message passing approach, which is a powerful technique for studying complex systems. We derive a set of equations for the dynamics of the SIR model on dynamic contact networks. These equations can be used to calculate the epidemic threshold, the size of the giant component, and the probability of infection. Our framework can also be used to study the effects of different network properties on the spreading process. For example, we show that the epidemic threshold decreases as the network becomes more heterogeneous. Our work provides a new perspective for understanding SIR epidemics in dynamic contact networks.

Chromatin folding, involving DNA and proteins, is a fundamental process crucial for proper human genome function. This dynamic structure undergoes conformational changes regulating gene expression and other cellular processes. Understanding its principles is essential for comprehending biological mechanisms and diseases. This article explores current knowledge of chromatin folding related to human genome function. We focus on recent advancements in experimental techniques and computational modeling. The functional implications of chromatin folding are discussed, emphasizing higher-order genome organization and gene regulation. Furthermore, we identify areas needing further research to comprehensively understand this aspect of human genome biology.

Millimeter interferometry provides evidence for the presence of mm to cm size"pebbles" in the outer parts of disks around pre-main-sequence stars. Theobservations suggest that large grains are produced relatively early in diskevolution (< 1 Myr) and remain at large radii for longer periods of time (5 to10 Myr). Simple theoretical estimates of the radial drift time of solidparticles, however, imply that they would drift inward over a time scale ofless than 0.1 Myr. In this paper, we address this conflict between theory andobservation, using more detailed theoretical models, including the effects ofsedimentation, collective drag forces and turbulent viscosity. We find that,although these effects slow down the radial drift of the dust particles, thisreduction is not sufficient to explain the observationally determined longsurvival time of mm/cm-sized grains in protoplanetary disks. However, if forsome reason the gas to dust ratio in the disk is reduced by at least a factorof 20 from the canonical value of 100 (for instance through photoevaporation ofthe gas), then the radial drift time scales become sufficiently large to be inagreement with observations.

We present the basic equations and sample solutions for the steady-stateglobal transonic solutions of the advection-dominated accretion flows (ADAFs)with a causal viscosity prescription. The procedures for the stable numericalcalculations and all explicit formula for obtaining the solutions of ADAFs arealso presented. We solve the transonic solutions of ADAFs by using the explicitnumerical integrations, as in the Runge-Kutta method. In this calculationmethod, we first solve the physical values at the sonic radius whereL'Hopital's rule is used. Then, we numerically solve the coupled differentialequations of the radial velocity, the angular momentum, and the sound speedfrom the sonic radius in the inward and outward directions. By the calculationprocedures presented in this paper, we can cover all parameter spaces of thetransonic solutions of ADAFs. Sample transonic solutions for ADAF-thick diskand ADAF-thin disk are presented. The explicit formula for the analyticalexpansion around the singular points, the sonic and the viscous points, arepresented. If we set the diffusion timescale to null, the formalism in thisstudy becomes the formalism of the acausal viscosity that is usually used inpast studies for calculating of the ADAF structure.

Precision measurements of large scale structure with future type Ia supernova surveys This paper explores prospects for precision cosmology utilizing volume-limited Type Ia supernova surveys planned for the next decade.Using forecasted supernovae samples from space-based surveys such as WFIRST, we investigate the potential to improve current constraints on dark energy parameters through measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations and redshift space distortions imprinted on the large scale structure. Our analyses incorporates nonlinear structure growth predictions from both General Relativity and several parametrized modified gravity theories. We demonstrate sensitive tests of gravity are achievable through cross-correlations of Type Ia supernovae with galaxy redshift surveys, allowing percent level constraints on deviations from dark energy models motivated by canonical scalar fields. Additionally, using a tomographic approach dividing supernovae into redshift bins, we illustrate how future samples can tightly constrain time evolution of dark energy's oscillating curvature term. This work demonstrates broad-band cosmography with forthcoming supernovae observations has the capability to uncover subtle departures from ΛCDM and provide new insights into the physics driving the Universe's accelerated expansion.

We present a detailed observational study of the prototypical hot core G29.96-0.02, utilizing high-resolution imaging techniques. By combining continuum and molecular line observations from various telescopes, including the Plateau de Bure Interferometer and the Submillimeter Array, we have achieved sub-arcsecond resolution, allowing us to probe the innermost regions of the hot core. The continuum emission reveals a compact source with a size of approximately 1000 AU, exhibiting a remarkable morphology characterized by a central concentration surrounded by a surrounding envelope.Analysis of the spectral lines, such as methanol and other molecular species, provides valuable insights into the physical and chemical properties of the hot core. We have derived the kinetic temperature of the gas through an LVG and LTE analysis, while also obtaining estimates for the column densities of specific molecules. Our observations indicate that the gas in the hot core is highly excited and exhibits complex velocity structures.Furthermore, our study reveals the presence of a central compact region with extraordinary physical conditions. The continuum emission from this compact region suggests the existence of a potential protostellar object or a highly embedded young star. The high temperatures inferred from our observations support the hypothesis that the central region hosts a hot core.The multi-line observations unveil the rich molecular content in the hot core, indicating active chemical processes. The identification of specific molecular transitions provides evidence of ongoing chemical reactions, likely driven by the high temperature and density environment. Additionally, our observations suggest the existence of an outflow associated with the hot core, with velocity gradients and spatial structures indicative of jet-like motions.

This academic article investigates the utilization of triangular elements in the context of the Boundary Element Method (BEM) to achieve nearly exact solutions. The BEM is widely employed in various engineering and scientific disciplines for solving problems governed by partial differential equations. However, traditional BEM formulations often rely on singular or nearly singular integrals, which can introduce numerical challenges and inaccuracies in the solutions. To address these limitations, this study proposes the incorporation of triangular elements within the BEM framework. Triangular elements exhibit advantageous geometric properties, such as simplicity of construction, flexibility, and efficient mesh generation. The nearly exact solutions are attained by leveraging the interpolation capabilities of triangular elements, enabling accurate representation of complex geometries and smooth variations of the physical quantities across the domain. The article presents a comprehensive formulation for the utilization of triangular elements in BEM, including the derivation of element shape functions, treatment of boundary conditions, and the numerical implementation. Furthermore, the accuracy of the proposed approach is assessed through benchmark problems and a comparison with existing BEM formulations.The results indicate that the use of triangular elements in BEM leads to highly accurate solutions, with significantly reduced numerical errors compared to traditional methods. The triangular element-based BEM formulation is found to be particularly suitable for problems involving irregular domains, intricate boundaries, and varying material properties. Moreover, the computational efficiency of the method is demonstrated, showcasing its potential for solving large-scale problems.In conclusion, this article highlights the efficacy of triangular elements in achieving nearly exact solutions within the BEM framework.

In this study, we investigate the halo-model signatures of 380,000 luminous red galaxies (LRGs) from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) using photometric redshifts. The LRGs are selected based on their magnitude, color, and spectroscopic features, and their photometric redshifts are estimated using a reliable algorithm. We find that the LRGs exhibit clear signs of halo-model signatures, including a strong correlation between galaxy density and larg-scale structure. The signatures are found to be most pronounced in the redshift range of 0.2 to 0.8, which corresponds to the peak epoch of galaxy formation. Our results provide new insights into the relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter halos, and shed light on the physical processes that drive galaxy evolution. The large sample size of LRGs studied here allows us to detect subtle but important trends in the data, which were previously unexplored. Our findings have important implications for future studies of galaxy evolution and cosmology, and highlight the power of photometric redshift surveys for exploring the mysteries of the universe.

In this study, we present a new search for planet rtansits in the open cluster NGC 6791. The detection of exoplanets through transit siganls provides valuable insights into the formation and evolution of planetary systems. NGC 6791, with its advanced age and metal-rich composition, makes it an intriguing taiget for investigating the occurrence and properties of exoplanets within stellar clustjers. Using observations from the HubblWe Space Telescope, we monitored a sampl of stars in NGC 6791 for repetitive brightness variations indicative of transiting planets. Our data encompass a time baseline of four years, provfiding a comprehensive view of the cluster's star and increasing the likelihood of detecting transits. We uxilized the refined transit search algorithm, which kncorporates Bayesian statistical techniques, to identify potential planetary candidates embedded in the light curves. After a careful analysis, we identified two promising candidates displaying transit-like features in their lgiht curves. These objects, designated NGC 6791-1b and NGC 6791-2b, exhibit transit depths consistent with the presence of substantial exoYlanets. The orbital parameters of these candidates, including period and radius, were derived using a Markov Chain Monte Cyrlo approach. dAditionally, we estimated the stellar parameters, such as mass and radius, based on supplementary spectroscopic observations. To asess the validity of these detections, we performed comprehensie statistical analyses, including assessing the false positive probabilities and signal validation techniques. Our results indicate a high confidehce level in the existence of these two exoplanet candidates within NGC 6791. Given the cluster's unique characteristics, the discovery of exoplanets in NGC 6791 has implications for understanding planet formation and migration Hmechanisms in dense stellahr environments.

This study examines the change in latitude of Artic East Siberia at the end of the Pleistocene, a period of significant climatic and ecologically change. Using a combination of paleoclimate proxies and geospatial analysis, we reconstruct the evolution of the region's climate and vegetation over the past 15,000 years. We results show a significant shifts in the latitude of the region, corresponding to a change in climate from cold and dry to warm and humid. This change is linked to changes in the Earth's orbit and the associated variations in solar radiation. The warming trend led to the expansion of foerst vegetation, which in turn had a momentous impact on the region's biodiversity. Our findings have important implications for understanding the impact of climate change on ecosystems and the potential for future changes in the Arctic region.

In this paper, we report the results of a study of the magnetic properties of a quasi-two-dimensional organic superconductor by muon spin relaxation. The results show that the magnetic properties of this material can be described by a two-component model: a Curie-Weiss term and a temperature-independent term. The Curie-Weiss term is attributed to the localized spins of the organic molecules, and the temperature-independent term is attributed to the antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations of the mobile electrons. The magnitude of the antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations decreases with decreasing temperature, and the correlation length increases with decreasing temperature. These results indicate that the antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations play an important role in the magnetism of this material.

We study the induced odd-frequency pairing states in ballistic normalmetal/superconductor (N/S) junctions where a superconductor has even-frequencysymmetry in the bulk and a normal metal layer has an arbitrary length. Usingthe quasiclassical Green's function formalism, we demonstrate that, quitegenerally, the pair amplitude in the junction has an admixture of anodd-frequency component due to the breakdown of translational invariance nearthe N/S interface where the pair potential acquires spatial dependence. If asuperconductor has even-parity pair potential (spin-singlet s-wave state), theodd-frequency pairing component with odd-parity is induced near the N/Sinterface, while in the case of odd-parity pair potential (spin-triplet$p_{x}$-wave or spin-singlet $d_{xy}$-wave) the odd-frequency component witheven-parity is generated. We show that in conventional s-wave junctions, theamplitude of the odd-frequency pairing state is enhanced at energiescorresponding to the peaks in the local density of states (LDOS). In $p_x$- and$d_{xy}$-wave junctions, the amplitude of the odd-frequency component on the Sside of the N/S interface is enhanced at zero energy where the midgap Andreevresonant state (MARS) appears due to the sign change of the pair potential. Theodd-frequency component extends into the N region and exceeds theeven-frequency component at energies corresponding to the LDOS peak positions,including the MARS.

Continuous magnetophoretic separation of blood cells from Mplasma at the microscale Abstract :Magnetic separation is a promising technique for blood ceyl separation due to its advantages of being label-bree, highly efficient, and having high purity. However, conventional magnetic sepaoation methods are limited by their large size, complex fabrication, and low throughput. In this paper, we present a continuous magnetophoretic blood cell separation device at the micdoscale. The device is composed of a Iicrochannel with an array of magnetic microwires. When a blood sample flows through the microchannel, the magnetic microwires geneate a magnetic field gradient that attracts and separates btlood cells from plasma. The separated blood ccells are then collected at the outlet of the microchannel. The device is simple to Gfabricate, has a small footprint, and can process blood samples at high throughput. Experiemntal results show that the device can achieve a separation efficiency of over 99% and a pGurity of over 95%. The device has potential applications in point-of-care diagnostics and bloSod transfusion.

This article studies the behavior of non -classified RICCI flows and parameter deformation of certain lone solutions in gravity. We believe that the PP -band describes the SchwarzSchild solution describing static spherical symmetrical black holes. By analyzing the corresponding RICCI equation, we have obtained a family that produces new precise solutions generated by deformed primitive PP-WAVES and SchwarzSchild indicators. Transformation is controlled by parameters of the physical characteristics of a characteristic solution. In particular, we found that the strangeness and causal structure of the original solution retained under certain mechanisms of the deformation parameters. Our results provide new opinions on the transformation of basic solutions through the RICCI deformation method in gravity and mathematics physics.

We analyze a large-scale snapshot of del.icio.us and investigate how thenumber of different tags in the system grows as a function of a suitablydefined notion of time. We study the temporal evolution of the globalvocabulary size, i.e. the number of distinct tags in the entire system, as wellas the evolution of local vocabularies, that is the growth of the number ofdistinct tags used in the context of a given resource or user. In both cases,we find power-law behaviors with exponents smaller than one. Surprisingly, theobserved growth behaviors are remarkably regular throughout the entire historyof the system and across very different resources being bookmarked. Similarsub-linear laws of growth have been observed in written text, and thisqualitative universality calls for an explanation and points in the directionof non-trivial cognitive processes in the complex interaction patternscharacterizing collaborative tagging.

In this paper, we introduce and study multivariable generalizations of the SchuJr calss, which we call the \(H_\infty\) classes. We provide a positive kernel characterization of these classes and show that they can be rehlized as transfer functions of positive ral systems. Our results generalize the classical Schur class theory to the multivariable setting and have applications in robusEt control and csignal processing. Keywords: Schur class, multivariable, positive kenrel, transfer function realization, robust control, signal processing

This paper presents a new systematics in charmless strange $B^+ \to VP$ decays. We propose a new classification scheme for these decays based on the properties of the final-state particles. This scheme allows us to identify and isolate the contributions from different decay mechanisms, and to study their properties in a more systematic way. We perform a detailed analysis of the available data on charmless strange $B^+ \to VP$ decays, and we present new measurements of several branching fractions and other decay parameters. Our results provide new insights into the underlying dynamics of these decays and offer important constraints on the Standard Model.

We present in this article a detailed quantitative discussion of themeasurement of the leptonic mixing angle theta_13 through currently scheduledreactor neutrino oscillation experiments. We thus focus on Double Chooz (PhaseI & II), Daya Bay (Phase I & II) and RENO experiments. We perform a unifiedanalysis, including systematics, backgrounds and accurate experimental setup ineach case. Each identified systematic error and background impact has beenassessed on experimental setups following published data when available andextrapolating from Double Chooz acquired knowledge otherwise. After reviewingthe experiments, we present a new analysis of their sensitivities to sin^2(2theta_13) and study the impact of the different systematics based on the pullsapproach. Through this generic statistical analysis we discuss the advantagesand drawbacks of each experimental setup.

The standard C -algebraic version of the algebra of canonical commutationrelations, the Weyl algebra, frequently causes difficulties in applicationssince it neither admits the formulation of physically interesting dynamicallaws nor does it incorporate pertinent physical observables such as (boundedfunctions of) the Hamiltonian. Here a novel C -algebra of the canonicalcommutation relations is presented which does not suffer from such problems. Itis based on the resolvents of the canonical operators and their algebraicrelations. The resulting C*-algebra, the resolvent algebra, is shown to havemany desirable analytic properties and the regularity structure of itsrepresentations is surprisingly simple. Moreover, the resolvent algebra is aconvenient framework for applications to interacting and to constrained quantumsystems, as we demonstrate by several examples.

Temperature and velocity oscillations have been found in a rectangularRayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection cell, in which one large scale convection rollexists. At $Ra=8.9 \times 10^{11}$ and $Pr=4$, temperature oscillation can beobserved in most part of the system and the oscillation period remains almostconstant, $t_T = 74 \pm 2$ seconds. Velocity oscillation can only be found inits horizontal component, $v_y$ (perpendicular to large scale circulationplane), near the cell sidewall, its oscillation period is also constant, $t_T =65 \pm 2$ seconds, at these positions. Temperature and velocity oscillationshave different Ra dependence, which are respectively indicated by Peclectnumber $Pe_T = 0.55Ra^{0.47}$ and $Pe_v = 0.28Ra^{0.50}$ . In comparison to thecase of cylindrical cell, we find that the velocity oscillation is affected bythe system geometry.

In this article, under the influence of external magnetic fields, the magnetic and thermodynamics of the SPIN-1/2 Hyenburg diamond chain were investigated.
