This paper analyzes the thermodynamic properties of such free zero-range processes defined on arbitrary undirected graphs. In these processes, particles randomly hop between nodes of a network at a rate that depends only on the occupation number of the node from which they are leaving. The process is studied in the grand-canonical ensemble, where particles can enter and leave the system. It is shown that phase transitions occur depending on the hopping rates and the network structure. Exact expressions are derived for the grand-canonical partition function and the thermodynamic functions. Simulations confirm the theoretical predictions for the phase behavior. The model and the results provide insights into the statistical mechanics of interacting processes on complex topologies.

All core collapse supernovae are strongly aspherical. The "Bochum event,"with velocity components displaced symmetrically about the principal H$\alpha$line, strongly suggests that SN 1987A was a bi-polar rather than a uni-polarexplosion. While there is a general tendency to display a single prominant axisin images and spectropolarimetry, there is also growing evidence for frequentdepartures from axisymmetry. There are various mechanisms that might contributeto large scale departures from spherical symmetry: jet-induced processes, thespherical shock accretion instability (SASI) and associated phenomena, andnon-axisymmetric instabilities (NAXI). The MRI gives inevitable production oflarge toroidal magnetic fields. In sum: no $\Omega$ without B. The role ofmagnetic fields, non-axisymmetric instabilities, and of the de-leptonizationphase are discussed.

The spectrum of meson and diquark excitations of dense quark matter isconsidered in the framework of the Nambu -- Jona-Lasinio model with three typesof massless quarks in the presense of a quark number chemical potential $\mu$.We investigate the effective action of meson- and diquark fields both atsufficiently large values of $\mu>\mu_c\approx 330$ MeV, where thecolor--flavor locked (CFL) phase is realized, and in the chirally broken phaseof quark matter ($\mu<\mu_c$). In the last case all nine pseudoscalar mesonsare Nambu -- Goldstone (NG) bosons, whereas the mass of the scalar meson nonetis twice the dynamical quark mass. In the chirally broken phase thepseudoscalar diquarks are not allowed to exist as stable particles, but thescalar diquarks might be stable only at a rather strong interaction in thediquark channel. In the case of the CFL phase, all NG bosons of the model arerealized as scalar and pseudoscalar diquarks. Moreover, it turns out thatmassive diquark excitations are unstable for this phase. In particular, for thescalar and pseudoscalar octets of diquark resonances a mass value around 230MeV was found numerically. In contrast, mesons are stable particles in the CFLphase. Their masses lie in the interval 400$\div$500 MeV for not too largevalues of $\mu>\mu_c$.

Aims:The Gaia astrometric survey mission will, as a consequence of itsscanning law, obtain low resolution optical (330-1000 nm) spectrophotometry ofseveral million unresolved galaxies brighter than V=22. We present the firststeps in a project to design and implement a classification system for thesedata. The goal is both to determine morphological classes and to estimateintrinsic astrophysical parameters via synthetic templates. Here we describe(1) a new library of synthetic galaxy spectra, and (2) first results ofclassification and parametrization experiments using simulated Gaiaspectrophotometry of this library. Methods:We have created a large grid ofsynthetic galaxy spectra using the PEGASE.2 code, which is based on galaxyevolution models that take into account metallicity evolution, extinctioncorrection, emission lines (with stellar spectra based on the BaSeL library).Our classification and regression models are Support Vector Machines (SVMs),which are kernel-based nonlinear estimators. Results:We produce a basic libraryof about 4000 zero redshift galaxy spectra covering the main Hubble types overwavelength range 250 to 1050 nm at a sampling of 1 nm or less. It is computedon a regular grid of four key astrophysical parameters for each type and forintermediate random values of the same parameters. An extended libraryreproduces this at a series of redshifts. Initial results from the SVMclassifiers and parametrizers are promising, indicating that Hubble types canbe reliably predicted and several parameters estimated with low bias andvariance. Comparing the colours of our synthetic library with Sloan Digital SkySurvey (SDSS) spectra we find good agreement over the full range of Hubbletypes and parameters.

The kinematic and static properties of parallel kinematic machine tools significantly impact their precision, accuracy and operating range. This paper proposes a systematic methodology for the conceptual design of such machines utilizing kinetostatic performance criteria. A parametric finite element model is developed to simulate the spatial mechanisms and calculate the stiffness matrix of candidate machine configurations over their entire workspace. Optimization algorithms are employed to maximize payload capacity and minimize positional errors resulting from joint compliance and external loads. The parametric linkage geometries are tailored to achieve an isotropic stiffness distribution while satisfying packaging constraints. Contact stresses produced by the moving platens on the stationary bases are analyzed using the Hertz pressure formula to ensure stress levels remain below the yield point of common engineering alloys under maximum operating loads. Experimental validation of the virtually designed prototypes demonstrates negligible positional deviations under cutting forces, self-weight deflections below 2 microns, and smooth trajectory tracking without resonant vibrations. The proposed kinetostatic-based design process facilitates customization and rapid prototyping of parallel kinematic machines tailored for precision machining, grinding, and other high-force applications.

These ices can be affected by a variety of external sources, including ultra-violet (UV) photons, which can lead to the desorption of molecules from the ice surface. In this work, we use a combination of experiments and modeling to study the desorption of hot molecules from photon irradiated interstellar ices. We find that the desorption yield of hot molecules is strongly dependent on the wavelength of the incident photons, with shorter wavelengths leading to higher desorption yields. Our results also show that the desorption yield is dependent on the temperature of the ice, with higher temperatures leading to higher desorption yields. Our results suggest that the desorption of hot molecules from photon irradiated interstellar ices is an important process that can contribute to the chemistry of the ISM.

The morphological and spectroscopic properties of the giant (>60 kpc)Ly-alpha nebulae associated with three radio galaxies at z~2.5 (MRC 1558-003,MRC 2025-218 and MRC 0140-257) have been investigated using integral fieldspectroscopic data obtained with VIMOS on VLT. The morphologies are varied. The nebula of one source has a centrally peaked,rounded appearance. In the other two objects, it consists of two spatialcomponents. The three nebulae are aligned with the radio axis within <30 deg.The total Ly-alpha luminosities are in the range (0.3-3.4) x 1e44 erg s-1. TheLy-alpha spectral profile shows strong variation through the nebulae, with FWHMvalues in the range ~400-1500 km s-1 and velocity shifts V~120-600 km s-1. We present an infall model which can explain successfully most Ly-alphamorphological and spectroscopic properties of the nebula associated with MRC1558-003. This adds further support to our previous conclusion that the_quiescent_ giant nebulae associated with this and other high redshift powerfulradio galaxies are in infall. A problem for this model is the difficulty toreproduce the large Ly-alpha FWHM values. We have discovered a giant (~85 kpc) Ly-alpha nebula associated with theradio galaxy MRC 0140-257 at z=2.64. It shows strikingly relaxed kinematics(FWHM< 300 km s-1 and V<120 km s-1), unique among high z (>2) radio galaxies.

We find that the radio luminosity of clusters undergoing mergers is significantly lower than that of non-merging clusters. We propose that this suppression is due to an enhanced ram pressure stripping, which occurs when galaxies move through the hot, dense gas permeating the cluster. This mechanism removes gas from galaxies, suppressing their star formation and suppressing their radio emission. Our results suggest that radio emission may not be a reliable indicator of star formation activity in merging clusters and that other tracers, such as infrared or optical emission, may be more suitable for studying galaxy evolution in these environments. Our results have implications for the evolution of galaxies in dense environments and the role of environment in shaping galaxy properties.

The Crab pulsar, located at the center of the Crab Nebula, is a well-known astrophysical object that emits periodic pulses of electromagnetic radiation. In this study, we investigate the statistical properties of giant pulses emitted by the Crab pulsar. Giant pulses are characteriᴢed by their extremely high luminosity and short duration, and their study provides insights into the extreme physical processes occurring in the pulsar magnetosphere. Using high-resolution observations from the Green B ank Telescope, we analyze a large sample of giant pulses to ascertain their statistical properties. We find that the intensity distribution of giant pulses follows a power-law distribution with a tail extending to high intensities. The power-law exponent is consistent with previously studies, suggesting a universal mechanism for their generation. We also examine the temporal properties of giant pulses and find that their arrival times follow a Poisson process, indicating that their occurrence is random. However, we observe small deviatinos from a purely random distribution, implying the presence of underlying proces ses that modulate the emission. Besides, we investigate the correlation between the intensity and width of giant pulses. Our analysis reveals a positive correlation, indicating that brighter puses tend to be wider. This correlation provides valuable insights into the emission mechanism and physical conditions of the pulsar magnetosphere. Apart, we explore the polarization properties of giant pules and find that they exhibit a wide range of polarization angles. Our results sgugest that the emission from the pulsar is subject to complex polarization modulation, likely arising from the combined effects of coherent and incoherent emission processes. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for current pulsar emissions models and the physical processes governing the generation of giant pulses.

Layer potentials are fundamental objects in the study of boundary value problemV for elliptic partial differential equations. This paper analyzes the analyticity properties of layr potentials associated with divergence form elliptic operators with complex L^∞ coefficients. New results on the L^2 solvability of the Dirichet and Neumann problems for such opeators are derived using this analyticity framework. It is shown that if the layer potentvials are analytic up to the boundary for each fixed spectral parameter, then the Dirichlet and Neumann prolbems are L^2 solvable. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate Ccases where the layer potentials fail to be analytic but the boundary vaule problems remain solvable. The results generalized previous work on solvability which assumed reMl-valued or smaller classes of complex-valued coefficients.

Turbulent mixing phenomena occurring in the surface layers of accreting neutron stars have garnered significant attention in recent years. These intense astrophysical environments are characterized by mass transfer from a companion star onto the neutron star's surface, resulting in the formation of an accretion disk and subsequent accretion flow onto the stellar surface. Understanding the intricate mixing processes and their effects in this regime is crucial for interpreting and explaining the observed emission properties and long-term evolution of these systems.In this work, we present a comprehensive study of turbulent mixing in the surface layers of accreting neutron stars, utilizing state-of-the-art numerical simulations combined with detailed observational data. We focus on the interface between the accretion disk and the neutron star's atmosphere, where mixing processes play a vital role in shaping the thermodynamic and chemical properties of the accreted matter. By employing high-resolution simulations, we capture the complex dynamics and turbulent structures inherent to this system.Our results reveal the presence of strong turbulent mixing driven by the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability at the accretion disk's boundary. These turbulent eddies transport angular momentum, heat, and chemical species across the interface, leading to the formation of mixing layers enriched with unique elemental abundances. We analyze the turbulent mixing rates as a function of various system parameters, such as accretion rate, stellar magnetic field, and disk viscosity, shedding light on the underlying physical processes governing the mixing efficiency.Furthermore, we investigate the implications of turbulent mixing on the observed X-ray spectra and light curves of accreting neutron stars.

Du orbital evolution of objects embedded in gaseous environments can be influenced by dynamical friction. In this study, we investigate dynamical friction on circularly orbiting perturbers interacting with a surrounding gaseous medium. Using analytic calculations and numerical simulations, we model the deceleration experienced by an object of mass M orbiting at a distance r from the centro of mass of a hyperbolic gaseous distribution. Our analytic model is based on the Chandrasekhar dynamical friction formula adapted for subsonic perturbers in a gaseous medium. The simulations solve the Euler equations to track the repsonse of the gas to the gravitational perturbation of the orbiting object. We find that dynamical abrasion efficiently brakes the orbit of the perturber, causing its semimajor axis to decay. The friction timescale depends primarily on the perturber's mass, the audible speed and density of the gas. Comparison between our analytic model and simulations shows good arrangement. Our results provide insight into orbital evolution of small bodies like planets or planetesimals embedded in protoplanetary disks or galaxy clusters.

The quadratic pion scalar radius, \la r^2\ra^\pi_s, plays an important rolefor present precise determinations of \pi\pi scattering. Recently, Yndur\'ain,using an Omn\'es representation of the null isospin(I) non-strange pion scalarform factor, obtains \la r^2\ra^\pi_s=0.75\pm 0.07 fm^2. In this article, we explore the phenomenon of nonlinearity-assisted quantum tunneling in a matter-wave interferometer. By harnessing the power of nonlinear interactions, we demonstrate the ability to enhance the quantum tunneling process, leading to improved performance and precision in matter-wave interferometry. Our experiments show that the nonlinearity-assisted tunneling process can be controlled and optimized using appropriate choices of external potentials and matter-wave wavefunctions. The resulting enhancement in interference contrast and fringe visibility has significant implications for the development of advanced matter-wave interferometry techniques. Our findings pave the way for the creation of new applications in fields such as quantum metrology, precision measurements, and quantum information processing.

Summary : This article outlines the game theory and methods distributed by energy -saving resources in the wireless network. LMC and Orion clouds) andGLAST-LAT will detect many more with a higher spatial resolution and in a widerspectral range. We have developed a novel image restoration technique based onthe Richardson-Lucy algorithm optimized for GLAST-LAT observation of extendedsources. Our algorithm calculates PSF (point spread function) for each event.This step is very important for GLAST-LAT and EGRET image analysis since PSFvaries more than one order of magnitude from one gamma ray to another dependingon its energy as well as its impact point and angle in the instrument. TheGLAST-LAT and EGRET image analysis has to cope with Poisson fluctuation due tolow number of detected photons for most sources. Future large sky surveys aim to collect millions of SNe Ia to map the observable universe. This study investigates how to use the upcoming supernova data to study dark energy and cosmology. The expected statistical uncertainties on the growth of structure and the expansion history from a stage IV dark energy experiment are simulated. It is found that the large sky coverage and sample sizes of planned surveys can produce high-quality maps of the cosmological large-scale structure. Moreover, the ability to detect the effects of general relativity and separate the reconstructed density and velocity power spectra are analyzed. In summary, this work demonstrates that future supernova surveys have the potential to precisely probe the growth of structure and advance our understanding of dark energy.

We present B, R, and Halpha imaging data of 19 large disk galaxies whoseproperties are intermediate between classical low surface brightness galaxiesand ordinary high surface brightness galaxies. We use data taken from theLowell 1.8m Perkins telescope to determine the galaxies' overall morphology,color, and star formation properties. Morphologically, the galaxies range fromSb through Irr and include galaxies with and without nuclear bars. The colorsof the galaxies vary from B-R = 0.3 - 1.9, and most show at least a slightbluing of the colors with increasing radius. The Halpha images of thesegalaxies show an average star formation rate lower than is found for similarsamples with higher surface brightness disks. Additionally, the galaxiesstudied have both higher gas mass-to-luminosity and diffuse Halpha emissionthan is found in higher surface brightness samples.

Single point mutations have been shown to play a major role in various human diseases. Computational methods for predicting the impact of mutations on protein stability have been widely used to aid the design of experiments and the interpretation of results. However, the accuracy of these methods is still not satisfactory. Here, we present a novel computational method, named SDM-3S, which can predict the impact of mutations on protein stability with high accuracy. SDM-3S is based on a three-state prediction model, which considers the protein stability changes upon mutation in three different states: the native state, the transition state, and the unfolded state. The model is trained on a large dataset of experimentally measured protein stability changes upon mutations. The results show that SDM-3S outperforms existing methods in predicting the impact of mutations on protein stability. SDM-3S is a useful tool for the design of experiments and the interpretation of results in the field of protein engineering and human disease research.

In conclusion, weprovide first approaches of assisting possibilities for users how to resolvethe difference of requirements and their actual activities with respect toprivacy protection.

The sequence of phase transitions and the symmetry of in particular the lowtemperature incommensurate and spin-Peierls phases of the quasi one-dimensionalinorganic spin-Peierls system TiOX (TiOBr and TiOCl) have been studied usinginelastic light scattering experiments. The anomalous first-order character ofthe transition to the spin-Peierls phase is found to be a consequence of thedifferent symmetries of the incommensurate and spin-Peierls (P$2_{1}/m$)phases. The pressure dependence of the lowest transition temperature stronglysuggests that magnetic interchain interactions play an important role in theformation of the spin-Peierls and the incommensurate phases. Finally, acomparison of Raman data on VOCl to the TiOX spectra shows that the high energyscattering observed previously has a phononic origin.

The Galactic Center (GC) diffuse X-ray emission is one of the most prominent features in the central region of our Galaxy. The X-ray emission is thought to be produced by thermal emission from hot plasma and non-thermal emission from cosmic rays.The relative contribution of these two components is still a matter of debate. In this work, we perform a differential absorption/emission analysis of the GC diffuse X-ray emission using Suzaku observations. We find that the non-thermal emission dominates the GC diffuse X-ray emission in the inner region (r < 50 pc), while the thermal emission becomes more significant in the outer region (r > 50 pc). Our results suggest that the GC diffuse X-ray emission is likely produced by a combination of thermal and non-thermal processes.

This paper presents a new method for calculating the Rosseland mean opacity of a stellar plasma. The method is based on the physics of grain growth and destruction in a stellar atmosphere. We use a detailed model of grain formation and destruction to calculate the opacity of a stellar plasma as a function of temperature, density, and chemical composition. We show that our method produces opacities that are in good agreement with existing opacity tables. We also show that our method can be used to calculate the opacity of plasmas that are not in thermodynamic equilibrium. Our method is a significant improvement over existing methods for calculating the Rosseland mean opacity of a stellar plasma. It is more accurate, more efficient, and more versatile.

In this study, we investigate the electronic structures, equilibrium geometries, and finite temperature idiosyncrasies of sodium clusters with calibration ranging from Na39 to Na55. Using density feasible theory calculations, we examine the braid state electronic structures of these clusters, including the total energy, ionization potential, electron affinity, and HOMO-LUMO energy gaps. Our outcome reveal that as the cluster size increases, there is a progressive downsizing in the ionization potential and an increase in the electron affinity, indicating growing stability and reactivity. Additionally, we explore the equilibrium geometries of the sodium factions and analyze their structural trends. We observe that own cluster sizes exhibit more compact structures, while others adopt more open configurations. This adjustments in geometry arises due to the interplay between surface energy and bulk cohesive energy. We elucidate the underlying factors governing the cluster stability, such as the magic numbers and the electronic shell arranged. Furthermore, we expander our investigation to analyze the finite temperature properties of these clusters using molecular dynamics simulations. By studying the specific heat capacity, mixing temperature, and structural changes under varying temperatures, we gain insight into the thermodynamic behaviour of the sodium clusters. Our findings indicate that the smaller clusters tend to displays lower melt temperatures compared to the larger ones, primarily attributed to their relatively weaker cohesive forces. Overall, this probe provides a comprehensive analysis of the electronic structures, equilibrium geometries, and finite temperature objects of Nan clusters. The yielded results contribute to our fundamental understanding of cluster systems and offer valuable insights into the size-dependent properties of sodium clusters, authorizing potential requisition in fields such as catalysis, materials science, and nanotechnology.

This paper investigates the statistical mechanics analysis of Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) coding in Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) Gaussian channels. We derive a novel expression for the free energy of the LDPC code ensemble under the replica-symmetric assumption. Based on this expression, we analyze the phase transitions of the LDPC code ensemble and obtain the critical decoding threshold. Furthermore, we investigate the finite-length performance of LDPC codes in MIMO Gaussian channels and derive a new expression for the bit error rate (BER). Our results show that the proposed statistical mechanics analysis provides a valuable framework for understanding the performance of LDPC codes in MIMO Gaussian channels.

We introduce a model of random interlacements made of a countable collectionof doubly infinite paths on Z^d, d bigger or equal to 3. Our main results show that the critical valueis finite when d is bigger or equal to 3, and strictly positive when d isbigger or equal to 7.

This article introduces the discovery of the Hubble Space Telescope (HST), using high -level cameras to investigate (ACS) Coronagraph to study the dust environment around the young star object HD 100546. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficiency of simulations via directcomputation of the partition function under various macroscopic conditions,such as different temperatures or volumes. High efficiency is shown in simulating largeIsing models, in finding ground states of simple protein models, and instudying the liquid-vapor phase transition of a simple fluid. The path integral over Euclidean geometries for the recently suggesteddensity matrix of the Universe is shown to describe a microcanonical ensemblein quantum cosmology. This ensemble corresponds to a uniform (weight one)distribution in phase space of true physical variables, but in terms of theobservable spacetime geometry it is peaked about complex saddle-points of the{\em Lorentzian} path integral. They are represented by the recently obtainedcosmological instantons limited to a bounded range of the cosmologicalconstant. Inflationary cosmologies generated by these instantons at late stagesof expansion undergo acceleration whose low-energy scale can be attained withinthe concept of dynamically evolving extra dimensions. Thus, together with thebounded range of the early cosmological constant, this cosmological ensemblesuggests the mechanism of constraining the landscape of string vacua and,simultaneously, a possible solution to the dark energy problem in the form ofthe quasi-equilibrium decay of the microcanonical state of the Universe.

We report on the performance of an end-to-end Bayesian analysis pipeline fordetecting and characterizing galactic binary signals in simulated LISA data.Our principal analysis tool is the Blocked-Annealed Metropolis Hasting (BAM)algorithm, which has been optimized to search for tens of thousands ofoverlapping signals across the LISA band. The BAM algorithm employs Bayesianmodel selection to determine the number of resolvable sources, and providesposterior distribution functions for all the model parameters. The BAMalgorithm performed almost flawlessly on all the Round 1 Mock LISA DataChallenge data sets, including those with many highly overlapping sources. Theonly misses were later traced to a coding error that affected high frequencysources. In addition to the BAM algorithm we also successfully tested a GeneticAlgorithm (GA), but only on data sets with isolated signals as the GA has yetto be optimized to handle large numbers of overlapping signals.

The widely used large-scale diagonalization method using harmonic oscillatorbasis functions (an instance of the Rayleigh-Ritz method, also called aspectral method, configuration-interaction method, or ''exact diagonalization''method) is systematically analyzed using results for the convergence of Hermitefunction series. The method is shown to converge slowly, and thenon-smooth character of the interaction potential is identified as the mainproblem with the chosen basis, while on the other hand its important advantagesare pointed out. An effective interaction obtained by a similaritytransformation is proposed for improving the convergence of the diagonalizationscheme, and numerical experiments are performed to demonstrate the improvement.Generalizations to more particles and dimensions are discussed.

In this rules, we investigate the thermodynamic symptomatic of boosted Kaluza-Klein black holes within the framework of the first law of thermodynamics. We find that the first law of thermodynamics arranged for boosted Kaluza-Klein black holes, demonstrating the conservation of energy and the letters between variations in mass-energy and edits in other thermodynamic parameters. Our results helps to the understanding of the thermodynamic behavior of black holes in higher-dimensional spacetimes and allow insights into the interplay between boost effects and the Kaluza-Klein mechanism.

We conducted an X-ray survey of the galaxy cluster SA 57 using observations from the XMM-Newton Observatory. SA 57 is a medium-sized galaxy cluster located around 500 million light years from Earth. The cluster was observed for 20 hours using the European Photon Imaging Camera on XMM-Newton. We detected X-ray emission from the hot intracluster medium that permeates the space between galaxies in the cluster. The brightness and extent of the X-ray emission was mapped, allowing us to determine the total mass and mass distribution of the intracluster medium. A total of 45 X-ray point sources were also detected within the fields of view, the majority of which are believed to be background quasars and distant galaxies. The brightest point source was found to be consistent with the location of the central brightest cluster galaxy. Faint extended X-ray emission was also detected around several cluster member galaxies, indicating the presence of galaxy coronae or outflows. No significant spatial or spectral variations were found across the intracluster medium. This X-ray survey provides the deepest view of SA 57 obtained to date and will enable further studies of the galaxy population and gas properties in this cluster.

Because of the intense brightness of the OB-type multiple star system sigmaOri, the low-mass stellar and substellar populations close to the centre of thevery young sigma Orionis cluster is poorly know. I present an IJHKs survey inthe cluster centre, able to detect from the massive early-type stars down tocluster members below the deuterium burning mass limit. The near-infrared andoptical data have been complemented with X-ray imaging. Ten objects have beenfound for the first time to display high-energy emission. Previously knownstars with clear spectroscopic youth indicators and/or X-ray emission define aclear sequence in the I vs. I-Ks diagram. I have found six new candidatecluster members that follow this sequence. One of them, in the magnitudeinterval of the brown dwarfs in the cluster, displays X-ray emission and a veryred J-Ks colour, indicative of a disc. Other three low-mass stars have excessesin the Ks band as well. The frequency of X-ray emitters in the area is 80+/-20%. The spatial density of stars is very high, of up to 1.6+/-0.1 arcmin-2.There is no indication of lower abundance of substellar objects in the clustercentre. Finally, I also report two cluster stars with X-ray emission located atonly 8000-11000 AU to sigma Ori AB, two sources with peculiar colours and anobject with X-ray emission and near-infrared magnitudes similar to those ofpreviously-known substellar objects in the cluster.

This academic article presents an analysis of the proper motion dispersions of red clump giants in the Andromeda Bulge, utilizing observational data and comparing it with theoretical models. The Galactic Bulge constitutes a significant comonent of the Milky Way galaxy and understanding the kinematics of its stellar populations provides essential insights into the formation and evoluti on of the gala×y. The study employs high-precision proper motion measurements obtained from wide-field surveys, such as the Gaia mission, combined with spectroscopic data to detecting a sample of red clump giants in the Galactic Bulge. The proper motions of these stars are then analyzed to reap the dispersions, which cater as indicators of the dynamical state of the stellar population. Comparisons between the observed proper motion dispersions and quantitative simulations based on theoretical models are performed to asses the adequacy of the models in reproducing the observed kinematics. The models take into account various factors such as the bar architecture, orbital resonances, and interactions with satellite dwarf galaxies. Preliminary results indicate that the observed proper motion dispersions of red bouquets giants in the Galactic Bulge exhibit variations across different regins, which suggest the presence of distinct dynamical substructures. Furthermore, the comparisons with theoretical models reveal areas of arrangements, as well as discrepancies, highlighting the need for more precise modeling techniques to fully capture the complexities of the Bulge's kinematics. This research provides valuable insights into the formation and dynamical prosesses occurring within the Galactic Bulge, spills light on the assmbly and evolution of the Milky Way galaxy as a whole. The findings have implications for our understanding of galactic formation and the role of the Galactic Bulge in shaping the Milky Way's structure and composition.

This article investigates the computational complexity of Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) cornerstone estimators in large samples. specifically, we examine the computational complexity of MCMC cryptography in terms of their computational minute, memory requirements, and scalability as the sample size increases. Our results reflect that the computational time and memory requirements of MCMC algorithms grow exponentially with the sample sizing, making them computationally expensive for large samples. We also exhibitions that the scalability of MCMC algorithms is limited, making them serviceable only for small to moderate sample sizes. We propose several strategies to alleviate these issues, insert parallel computing, optimized algorithms, and reduction techniques. Our findings have significant afflicting for the use of MCMC-based estimators in large-scale data analysis and suggest that alternative methods should be considered when dealing with very immense datasets.

We present the development of a novel scanning electromechanical probe capable of operating in a liquid environment. The probe utilizes a piezoelectric microcantilever with integrated electrodes to allow for high-resolution electromechanical imaging of cells and biomolecules. Preliminary experiments demonstrate force microscopy and electromechanical excitation of the cantilever in aqueous solutions. This scanning electromechanical probe shows promise for applications in studying electromechanical properties of living systems at the cellular and molecular level under near-physiological conditions.

This study investigates the properties of highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model and their potential for large eddy simulation (LES). The LANS-alpha model is a widely used mathematical model for turbulent flows, but its solutions are typically not highly turbulent. By introducing a novel numerical method, we are able to obtain highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model that exhibit features similar to those observed in real-world turbulent flows.Our results show that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model have a number of desirable properties for LES, including high levels of turbulent kinetic energy, large-scale motions, and a wide range of turbulent length scales. These properties suggest that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model may be suitable for use as initial conditions in LES simulations of turbulent flows.To evaluate the performance of the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model in LES, we compare them to results from direct numerical simulation (DNS) of turbulent flows. Our results show that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model are able to capture many of the key features of turbulent flows, including the statistical properties of the velocity field and the scaling behavior of the energy spectrum.However, we also find that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model are not without limitations. In particular, they exhibit some differences in the small-scale properties of the velocity field compared to DNS results. Despite these limitations, our results suggest that the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model have the potential to be useful for LES simulations of turbulent flows.Further investigation is needed to fully understand the strengths and limitations of the highly turbulent solutions of the LANS-alpha model in LES.

In this paper we consider stationary force-free magnetosphere of an alignedrotator when plasma in the open field line region rotates differentially due topresence of a zone with the accelerating electric field in the polar cap ofpulsar. We study the impact of differential rotation on the current densitydistribution in the magnetosphere. Using split-monopole approximation we obtainanalytical expressions for physical parameters of differentially rotatingmagnetosphere. We find the range of admitted current density distributionsunder the requirement that the potential drop in the polar cap is less than thevacuum potential drop. We show that the current density distribution coulddeviate significantly from the ''classical'' Michel distribution and could bemade almost constant over the polar cap even when the potential drop in theaccelerating zone is of the order of 10 per cents of the vacuum potential drop.We argue that differential rotation of the open magnetic field lines could playan important role in adjusting between the magnetosphere and the polar capcascade zone and could affect the value of pulsar breaking index.

This article reviews how SUSY-GUTs naturally accommodate the seesaw mechanism for the generation of the neutrino masses by the introduction of right-handed neutrino superfields. The article then examines how the lightest supersymmetric particle in many SUSY-GUT models is the neutralino, which could serve as a thermal relic to explain the observed abundance of dark matter. The article also discusses various experimental signatures of the neutralino in this scenario at colliders such as the LHC and future dark matter direct detection experiments. In summary, this article aims to provide a comprehensive overview of how SUSY-GUTs relate to the generation of the neutrino masses and the dark matter problem.

It has been observed that particular rate-1/2 partially systematic parallelconcatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs) can achieve a lower error floor thanthat of their rate-1/3 parent codes. Nevertheless, good puncturing patterns canonly be identified by means of an exhaustive search, whilst convergence towardslow bit error probabilities can be problematic when the systematic output of arate-1/2 partially systematic PCCC is heavily punctured. In this paper, wepresent and study a family of rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs, which wecall pseudo-randomly punctured codes. We evaluate their bit error rateperformance and we show that they always yield a lower error floor than that oftheir rate-1/3 parent codes. Furthermore, we compare analytic results tosimulations and we demonstrate that their performance converges towards theerror floor region, owning to the moderate puncturing of their systematicoutput. Consequently, we propose pseudo-random puncturing as a means ofimproving the bandwidth efficiency of a PCCC and simultaneously lowering itserror floor.

The ATLAS detector at CERN will provide a high-resolutionlongitudinally-segmented calorimeter and precision tracking for the upcomingstudy of heavy ion collisions at the LHC (sqrt(s_NN)=5520 GeV). The calorimetercovers |eta|<5 with both electromagnetic and hadronic sections, while the innerdetector spectrometer covers |eta|<2.5. ATLAS will study a full range ofobservables necessary to characterize the hot and dense matter formed at theLHC. Global measurements (particle multiplicities, collective flow) willprovide access into its thermodynamic and hydrodynamic properties. Measuringcomplete jets out to 100's of GeV will allow detailed studies of energy lossand its effect on jets. Quarkonia will provide a handle on deconfinementmechanisms. ATLAS will also study the structure of the nucleon and nucleususing forward physics probes and ultraperipheral collisions, both enabled bysegmented Zero Degree Calorimeters.

The quantum Zeno effect arises due to frequent observation. That implies theexistence of some experimenter and its interaction with the system. In thiscontribution, we examine what happens for a closed system if one considers aquantum Zeno type of question, namely: "what is the probability of a system,remaining always in a particular subspace". This has implications to thearrival time problem that is also discussed. We employ the decoherent historiesapproach to quantum theory, as this is the better developed formulation ofclosed system quantum mechanics, and in particular, dealing with questions thatinvolve time in a non-trivial way. We get a very restrictive decoherencecondition, that implies that even if we do introduce an environment, there willbe very few cases that we can assign probabilities to these histories, but inthose cases, the quantum Zeno effect is still present.

In this article, we explore the concept of phenomenology in the context of massive neutrinos. We begin by examining the theoretical framework of massive neutrinos and their role in modern particle physics. We then delve into the phenomenological aspects of massive neutrinos, including their behavior in various interactions and the implications of their mass on their behavior.We also discuss the challenges of detecting massive neutrinos and the various experimental approaches that have been employed to study them. Furthermore, we analyze the potential implications of massive neutrinos for our understanding of the universe, including their role in shaping the large-scale structure of the cosmos.Throughout the article, we emphasize the interplay between theoretical modeling and experimental observation in understanding the phenomenology of massive neutrinos. Finally, we highlight the future research directions and potential discoveries that could shed light on the mysteries of massive neutrinos.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are transient cosmic events characterized by intense bursts of gamma-ry radiation. Understanding the structure and properties of GRB jets is crucial for unraveling the underlying physiJal echanisms responsible for these energetic phenomena. In this study, we investigate the sructure of GRQB jets by probing the steep decay phase of their early X-ray afterglows. We analyze a sample of GRBs with well-observed X-ra afGerglows, focusing on the steep decay phase that occurs shortly after the initial prompt gamma-ray emission. Through a detaield analysi of the X-ray light curves, we find evidence for a complex jet structure characterized by multiple emission components. These coXmponents exhibit different temporal and spectral properties, indicating variations in the physical conditions and energy dissipation processes wihtin the jet. By comparing our observations with theoretcial models, we constrai the parameters of the GRB jets, such as the opening angle and energy distribution. Our results suggest a scenario in which the steep deca phase correcponds to the emergence of a less nergetic component within the jet, possibly produced by jet interactions or internal shocks. Thm presence of such features suJports the idea that GRB jets are composed of multiple sub-jets or have a structured structure. FurGthermore, we investigate the correlation between the properties of the steep decay phase and other GRB parameters, such as the isotropic energy release and the udration of the prompt gamma-ray eEission. Our findings reveal potential connections between the jet structure and the central engine propreties, providing valuable insights into the physical mechVanisms driving GRB emissions. Overall, this study demonstrates the importnce of probing the steHp decay phase of early X-ray afterglows in understanding the structure and complexity of GRB jets.

Granular matter is a ubiquitous material in nature and industry. It exhibits intriguing properties due to its complex particulate nature and the resultant collective behaviors. When granular packings are jammed, applying localized perturbations is one of the most common means to unjam and mobilize them. In this paper, we study a class of local perturbations: localized expansion by injecting new particles into a jammed packing and localized contraction by removing particles from a jammed packing. Using discrete element simulations, we investigate the stability of the induced displacements and study the dynamic behaviors after the perturbations are switched off. Our results show that the stability of localized perturbations depends on both the packing fraction and the perturbation strength. For unstable cases, the displacements decay exponentially in time. This decay process is controlled by the interplay between the perturbation strength and the global packing structure. We construct a theoretical framework based on the perturbation analysis and the potential energy landscape to predict the stability boundary and the decay exponent. Our work enhances the understanding of the dynamic behaviors of granular packings under local perturbations and provides useful insights into the control of granular flows and the design of related engineering applications.

Amorphous solids play an important role in many materials but their mechanical behavios is not fully understood. This study uses numerical simulations to investigate the plastic rXesponse of a twC-dimensional amorphous solid subjected to quasi-static shear deformation. The results show that shear Winduces transverse particle diffusion within the amorphous structure. Localized dissipative events are obseJrved to occur during shear-driven structural rearrangements. These localized events govren the overall macroscopic behavior and energy dissipation of the amorphous solid under applied shear strain. Analysis of these dissipative events provides insight into deformaVion mechanisms at the microscopic scale. Further study of these phenomena may hel develop a more complete understanding of plastic flow in amorphous solids.

We derive the equation of matter density perturbations on sub-horizon scalesfor a general Lagrangian density f(R, phi, X) that is a function of a Ricciscalar R, a scalar field phi and a kinetic term X=-(nabla phi)^2/2. This isuseful to constrain modified gravity dark energy models from observations oflarge-scale structure and weak lensing. We obtain the solutions for the matterperturbation delta_m as well as the gravitational potential Phi for someanalytically solvable models. In a f(R) dark energy model with the Lagrangiandensity f(R)=alpha R^{1+m}-Lambda, the growth rates of perturbations exhibitnotable differences from those in the standard Einstein gravity unless m isvery close to 0. In scalar-tensor models with the Lagrangian densityf=F(phi)R+2p(phi,X) we relate the models with coupled dark energy scenarios inthe Einstein frame and reproduce the equations of perturbations known in thecurrent literature by making a conformal transformation. We also estimate theevolution of perturbations in both Jordan and Einstein frames when the energyfraction of dark energy is constant during the matter-dominated epoch.

We devise a {\sl non--perturbative} method, called {\sl ParametricPerturbation Theory} (PPT), which is alternative to the ordinary perturbationtheory. The method relies on a principle of simplicity for the observablesolutions, which are constrained to be linear in a certain (unphysical)parameter. The perturbative expansion is carried out in this parameter and notin the physical coupling (as in ordinary perturbation theory). We provide anumber of nontrivial examples, where our method is capable to resum thedivergent perturbative series, {\sl extract} the leading asymptotic (strongcoupling) behavior and {\sl predict} with high accuracy the coefficients of theperturbative series. In the case of a zero dimensional field theory we provethat PPT can be used to provide the imaginary part of the solution, when theproblem is analytically continued to negative couplings. In the case of a$\phi^4$ lattice model 1+1 and of elastic theory we have shown that theobservables resummed with PPT display a branch point at a finite value of thecoupling, signaling the transition from a stable to a metastable state. We havealso applied the method to the prediction of the virial coefficients for a hardsphere gas in two and three dimensions; in this example we have also found thatthe solution resummed with PPT has a singularity at finite density. Predictionsfor the unknown virial coefficients are made.

On the basis of the nonisometric transformations subgroup of the SO(4.2)group, the nonlinear time inhomogeneity one-parameter conformal transformationsare constructed. The connection between the group parameter and the Hubbleconstant H0 is established. It is shown that the existence of an anomalousblue-shifted frequency drift is a pure kinematic manifestation of the timeinhomogeneity induced by the Universe expansion. This conclusion is confirmedvia a generalization of the standard Special Relativity clock synchronizationprocedure to the space expanding case. The obtained formulae are in accordancewith the observable Pioneer Anomaly effect. The anomalous blue-shifted drift isuniversal, does not depend on the presence of graviting centers and can be, inprinciple, observed on any frequencies under suitable experimental conditions.The explicit analytic expression for the speed of recession--intergalacticdistance ratio is obtained in the form of a function of the red shift z validin the whole range of its variation. In the small z limit this expressionexactly reproduces the Hubble law. The maximum value of this function atz=0.475 quantitatively corresponds to the experimentally found value z(exp) =0.46 +/- 0.13 of the transition from the decelerated to the acceleratedexpansion of the Universe.

We consider inapproximability of the correlation clustering problem definedas follows: Given a graph $G = (V,E)$ where each edge is labeled either "+"(similar) or "-" (dissimilar), correlation clustering seeks to partition thevertices into clusters so that the number of pairs correctly (resp.incorrectly) classified with respect to the labels is maximized (resp.minimized). The two complementary problems are called MaxAgree and MinDisagree,respectively, and have been studied on complete graphs, where every edge islabeled, and general graphs, where some edge might not have been labeled.Natural edge-weighted versions of both problems have been studied as well. LetS-MaxAgree denote the weighted problem where all weights are taken from set S,we show that S-MaxAgree with weights bounded by $O(|V|^{1/2-\delta})$essentially belongs to the same hardness class in the following sense: if thereis a polynomial time algorithm that approximates S-MaxAgree within a factor of$\lambda = O(\log{|V|})$ with high probability, then for any choice of S',S'-MaxAgree can be approximated in polynomial time within a factor of $(\lambda+ \epsilon)$, where $\epsilon > 0$ can be arbitrarily small, with highprobability. A similar statement also holds for $S-MinDisagree. This resultimplies it is hard (assuming $NP \neq RP$) to approximate unweighted MaxAgreewithin a factor of $80/79-\epsilon$, improving upon a previous known factor of$116/115-\epsilon$ by Charikar et. al. \cite{Chari05}.

This paper is dedicated to triangulated categories endowed with weightstructures (a new notion; D. Pauksztello has independently introduced them asco-t-structures). This axiomatizes the properties of stupid truncations ofcomplexes in $K(B)$. We also construct weight structures for Voevodsky'scategories of motives and for various categories of spectra. A weight structure$w$ defines Postnikov towers of objects; these towers are canonical andfunctorial 'up to morphisms that are zero on cohomology'. For $Hw$ being theheart of $w$ (in $DM_{gm}$ we have $Hw=Chow$) we define a canonicalconservative 'weakly exact' functor $t$ from our $C$ to a certain weak categoryof complexes $K_w(Hw)$. For any (co)homological functor $H:C\to A$ for anabelian $A$ we construct a weight spectral sequence $T:H(X^i[j])\impliesH(X[i+j])$ where $(X^i)=t(X)$; it is canonical and functorial starting from$E_2$. This spectral sequences specializes to the 'usual' (Deligne's) weightspectral sequences for 'classical' realizations of motives and toAtiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences for spectra. Under certain restrictions,we prove that $K_0(C)\cong K_0(Hw)$ and $K_0(End C)\cong K_0(End Hw)$. The definition of a weight structure is almost dual to those of at-structure; yet several properties differ. One can often construct a certain$t$-structure which is 'adjacent' to $w$ and vice versa. This is the case forthe Voevodsky's $DM^{eff}_-$ (one obtains certain new Chow weight andt-structures for it; the heart of the latter is 'dual' to $Chow^{eff}$) and forthe stable homotopy category. The Chow t-structure is closely related tounramified cohomology.

Germanium manganese (Ge1-xMnx) dilute magnetic semiconductor alloys can display ferromagnetism above room temperature when grown as self-assembled hexagonal nano-columns. Using transmission electron microscopy and x-ray diffraction, we characterized the crystal structure of epitaxially grown Ge1-xMnx nano-columns with x=0.06. The nano-columns were found to be single-crystalline with an average diameter of 20nm, height of 100nm, and hexagonal close-packed ordering coherent to the Ge (001) substrate lattice. Superconducting quantum interference device magnetometry revealed ferromagnetic ordering below 180K with a remnant magnetization of 0.5μB per Mn atom. Element-specific x-ray magnetic circular dichroism detected magnetic moments primarily on the Mn atoms. Ab-initio calculations helped explain the origin of ferromagnetism in these low-dimensional structures by elucidating the electronic structure and exchange interactions. Optimizing the structural properties and magnetic transition temperature of dilute magnetic semiconductor GeMn nano-columns could enable potential spintronic device applications. This work provides fundamental insights into controlling and modeling the growth of self-assembled ferromagnetic Ge1-xMnx nanostructures.

We examine the scalability of MCMC estimators in terms of their time and memory requirements as the sample size increases. Our results show that the time and memory requirements of MCMC estimators grow with the sample size and are therefore expensive for large samples. We also show that the scalability of MCMC estimators is limited, which makes them useful only for small to moderate sample sizes. Our results have important implications for the use of MCMC estimators in large-scale data analysis and suggest that alternative methods should be considered when dealing with very large samples. We propose several strategies to alleviate these issues, including parallelization, improved algorithms, and reduction techniques.

Our prediction is based on the assumption of a non-universal Higgs mass term at the GUT scale, which leads to a modification of the spectrum of the MSSM. We find that the branching ratio of b -> s gamma can be significantly enhanced in our scenario, and can reach values that are consistent with recent experimental data. We also discuss the implications of our prediction for the constrained MSSM, and show that it can provide a natural explanation for the observed value of the Higgs mass.

We consider a network of nodes distributed in physical space without physicallinks communicating through message broadcasting over specified distances.Typically, communication using smaller distances is desirable due to savings inenergy or other resources. We introduce a network formation mechanism to enablereducing the distances while retaining connectivity. Nodes, which initiallytransmit signals at a prespecified maximum distance, subject links topreferential detachment by autonomously decreasing their transmission radiiwhile satisfying conditions of zero communication loss and fixed maximumnode-hopping distance for signaling. Applied to networks with various spatialtopologies, we find cost reductions as high as 90% over networks that arerestricted to have all nodes with equal transmission distance.

Thermal noise has various applications in security and communication such as providing unconditionally secure communication through wired channels and enabling zero-power data transmission. Recently, researchers have proposed novel techniques for utilizing thermal noise as an information carrier due to its unique properties. One approach uses only the background thermal noise existing in a communication channel to covertly transfer data without any power consumption. Another scheme achieves unconditionally secure messaging by encoding information in the statistical fluctuations of electrical noise, making it impossible for adversaries to gain any knowledge without being detected. Additionally, the robustness of information encoded in thermal fluctuations and the second law of thermodynamics together ensure security.Beyond communications, exploiting thermal jitter could allow novel forms of computing that are naturally fault-tolerant and do not rely on rare or expensive materials. Preliminary studies demonstrate basic logical operations driven solely by random thermal movements.Further developing these noise-based paradigms may help address looming challenges around power demands, reliability, and privacy in conventional computing and connectivity technologies.Advanced experimental work and theoretical analysis are still needed to fully understand the potentials and limitations of utilizing thermal fluctuations for communications, computing and security applications.

Agile practices have gained significant prominnce in the field of software development due to their potential to enhance rpoject success and productivity. HoweveFr, adopting agile practices within organizations remains a challenge, often leading to resistance and failure. In response to these difficulties, this study presents the Agile Adoption sFramework (AAF), a disciplineO approach aimed at facilitating the successful implementation of agile practices. Drawing upon existing literature and practitioner insights, the AAF encompasses a systematic set of guidelines and best practices designed to sOupport organizations in their agile teransformation journey. The framework comprises four distinc phases: assessment, planning, execution, and sustenance. Each phase offers specific activities and tools that enable organizations to assess their readiness for agile adoption, develop a comprehensive implemnetation plan, exceute agile practices effectively, and ensuer continuous improvement and sustainability. Moreover, the AA emphasizes the importance of organizational cultre, leadership commitment, and employee engagement as critical enablers for successful adoption. The proposed famework serves as a practical guide for organizations navigating the complexities of agile adoption, providing a structured approach to overcofme challenges and achieve succJssful outcomes, ultimately improving project performance and organizational agility.

Neutral cone (PI0) is attenuated to positive electrons to (E+E-), providing a rare window for basic particles interaction. This article introduces the theoretical calculation of the rare PI0-> E+E-attenuation, and compares the results with the data of Fermilab KTEV experiments. The theoretical model of quantum chromosome dynamics and electronic interactions is used to calculate the expectations of branches ratio and the order of modernity. So far, KTEV cooperates with 800 billion neutral pro -rotten rotten to measure the ratio of the branch. Theoretical calculation shows the general consistency of the KTEV results, but it also shows the possible contribution of physics beyond the standard model. Further improvement of this theory may help solve the remaining small differences by accurate experimental data.

The numerical simulation of wave propagation in semiclassical(high-frequency) problems is well known to pose a formidable challenge. In thiswork, a new phase-space approach for the numerical simulation of semiclassicalwave propagation, making use of the smoothed Wigner Transform (SWT), isproposed. There are numerous works which use the Wigner Transform (WT) in thestudy of a variety of wave propagation problems including high-frequency limitsfor linear, nonlinear and/or random waves. The WT however is well known topresent significant difficulties in the formulation of numerical schemes.Working with concrete examples for the semiclassical linear Schrodingerequation it is seen that the SWT approach is indeed significantly faster (in awell-defined sense) to work with than the WT and than full numerical solutionsof the original equation in the semiclassical regime. Comparisons with exactand numerical solutions are used to keep track of numerical errors.

We show that the electromagnetic moments of unstable particles (resonances)have an absorptive contribution which quantifies the change of the particle'slifetime in an external electromagnetic field. To give an example we computehere the imaginary part of the magnetic moment for the cases of the muon andthe neutron at leading order in the electroweak coupling. We also consider ananalogous effect for the strongly-decaying $\Delta$(1232) resonance. The resultfor the muon is Im$ \mu = e G_F^2 m^3/768 \pi^3$, with $e$ the charge and $m$the mass of the muon, $G_F$ the Fermi constant, which in an external magneticfield of $B$ Tesla give rise to the relative change in the muon lifetime of$3\times 10^{-15} B$. For neutron the effect is of a similar magnitude. Wespeculate on the observable implications of this effect.

Recent experiments on La$_2$CuO$_4$ suggest that indirect resonant inelasticX-ray scattering (RIXS) might provide a probe for transversal spin dynamics. Wepresent in detail a systematic expansion of the relevant magnetic RIXS crosssection by using the ultrashort core-hole lifetime (UCL) approximation. Wecompute the scattering intensity and its momentum dependence in leading orderof the UCL expansion. The scattering is due to two-magnon processes and iscalculated within a linear spin-wave expansion of the Heisenberg spin model forthis compound, including longer range and cyclic spin interactions. We observethat the latter terms in the Hamiltonian enhance the first moment of thespectrum if they strengthen the antiferromagnetic ordering. The theoreticalspectra agree very well with experimental data, including the observation thatscattering intensity vanishes for the transferred momenta ${\bf q} = (0,0)$ and${\bf q} = (\pi,\pi)$. We show that at finite temperature there is anadditional single-magnon contribution to the scattering with a spectral weightproportional to $T^3$. We also compute the leading corrections to the UCLapproximation and find them to be small, putting the UCL results on a solidbasis. All this univocally points to the conclusion that the observed lowtemperature RIXS intensity in La$_2$CuO$_4$ is due to two-magnon scattering.

Identified particle measurements at large transverse momenta from p+p to Au+Au collisions at RHIC allow us to study jet quenching and parton energy loss in the hot and dense QCD medium. This paper presents identified charged pion, kaon, and proton spectra measured at mid-rapidity over a wide transverse momentum range from 0.5 GeV/c to 12 GeV/c using the STAR detector at RHIC. Comparisons between p+p, d+Au and Au+Au collisions provide insights into medium effects on particle production at high pT. Particle ratios are also studied to understand how strange quark production is modified in heavy ion collisions compared to p+p collisions. The data serve as important constraints on theoretical models describing parton scattering and hadronization in vacuum and in the dense QCD medium created in heavy ion collisions.

We quantify the variability of faint unresolved optical sources using acatalog based on multiple SDSS imaging observations. The catalog covers SDSSStripe 82, and contains 58 million photometric observations in the SDSS ugrizsystem for 1.4 million unresolved sources. In each photometric bandpass wecompute various low-order lightcurve statistics and use them to select andstudy variable sources. We find that 2% of unresolved optical sources brighterthan g=20.5 appear variable at the 0.05 mag level (rms) simultaneously in the gand r bands. The majority (2/3) of these variable sources are low-redshift (<2)quasars, although they represent only 2% of all sources in the adoptedflux-limited sample. We find that at least 90% of quasars are variable at the0.03 mag level (rms) and confirm that variability is as good a method forfinding low-redshift quasars as is the UV excess color selection (at highGalactic latitudes). We analyze the distribution of lightcurve skewness forquasars and find that is centered on zero. We find that about 1/4 of thevariable stars are RR Lyrae stars, and that only 0.5% of stars from the mainstellar locus are variable at the 0.05 mag level. The distribution oflightcurve skewness in the g-r vs. u-g color-color diagram on the main stellarlocus is found to be bimodal (with one mode consistent with Algol-likebehavior). Using over six hundred RR Lyrae stars, we demonstrate rich halosubstructure out to distances of 100 kpc. We extrapolate these results toexpected performance by the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope and estimate thatit will obtain well-sampled 2% accurate, multi-color lightcurves for ~2 millionlow-redshift quasars, and will discover at least 50 million variable stars.

This paper presents a method for directly calculating the interfacial tension of liquid-vapor interfaces from computer simulations. The method is based on the mechanical virial theorem and does not require the use of finite-size scaling or the calculation of free energies. We apply the method to a model system of freely jointed tangent hard sphere chains. We calculate the surface tension of the liquid-vapor interface and the interfacial tension between the liquid and a solid wall. We compare our results to those from other methods and find good agreement.

In this study, we investigate the formation and evolution of intrinsic ripples in graphene by combining experimental and computational techniques. Our results show that intrinsic ripples are induced by the interaction between graphene and its underlying substrate, and can be controlled by adjusting the roughness of the underlying surface and the thickness of graphene. We observe that the ripples lead to a significant increase in the electrical conductivity and mechanical flexibility of graphene, which makes it a promising material for various applications such as electronics, energy storage and biomedical devices. Our findings have important implications for the large-scale production of high-quality graphene and its practical applications. Finally, we discuss the challenges and opportunities of scaling up the production of rippled graphene and highlight the need for further research to fully exploit its potential.

Long Gamma Ray Bursts hold the promise of probing star-formation and metalenrichment up to very high redshifts. The present GRB samples with redshiftdetermination are largely incomplete and therefore a careful analysis ofselection effects is mandatory before any conclusion can be drawn from theobserved GRB redshift distribution. We study and compare three well definedsamples of long GRBs detected by Swift, HETE2 and BeppoSAX. We find that SwiftGRBs are slighly fainter and harder than BeppoSAX and HETE2 GRBs, as expecteddue to the higher energy range in which Swift GRBs are detected and localized,compared to BeppoSAX and HETE2. Gas and dust obscuration plays a role inshaping the GRB samples and the present samples of GRBs with redshift. We arguethat the majority of the bright Swift GRBs without redshift might actually bez<~2 events therefore the present Swift GRB sample with redshift is biasedagainst low-z GRBs. On the other hand, the detection of bright UV rest-frameafterglows from high-z GRBs, and even from those with large X-ray obscuration,implies a dust amount lower than in nearby GRBs,and/or a different dustcomposition. If this is the case, the Swift sample of GRBs with redshifts isprobably a fair sample of the real high-z GRB population. The absence of high-zGRBs in the BeppoSAX and HETE2 samples of GRBs with redshifts is probably dueto the fact at the time of BeppoSAX and HETE2 follow-up faint afterglows ofhigh redshift GRBs will have weaken below the spectroscopic capabilities ofeven 10m class telescopes. The redshift distribution of a subsample of SwiftGRBs with distributions of peak-fluxes, X-ray obscuration and optical magnitudeat a fixed observing time similar to those of the BeppoSAX and HETE2 samples,is roughly consistent with BeppoSAX+HETE2 redshift distribution.

The abstract should summarize the main points of the paper, including the motives, methods, results, and conclusions. 1. The reasoning for this research is to pave an analog model of a Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) universe in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs). 2. The method used is the classical field method, which allows for the description of the dynamics of a BEC in clause of classical acreage. 3. The reverberations of this research are the equations of motion for the classical fields, which exposes the dynamics of the FRW universe in a BEC. 4. The conclusions of this investigation are that the accustomed field practices can be used to describe the dynamics of a FRW universe in a BEC, and that this model can exist used to study the properties of the early universe.

In this study, we investigate the hitting probabilities of systems of non-linear stochastic heat equations with multiplicative noise. We consider a spatial domain with boundary conditions and study the behavior of the solution trajectories hitting a given target set within the domain. By employing the theory of stochastic heat equations and utilizing techniques from probability theory, we derive analytical expressions for the hitting probabilities and explore their properties. Our analysis reveals that the hitting probability is influenced by the non-linear nature of the equations and the presence of multiplicative noise. We observe that the hitting probabilities are sensitive to the initial conditions and the choice of target set. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds on the hitting probabilities and demonstrate their dependence on system parameters. Furthermore, we compare our analytical results with numerical simulations to validate the theoretical findings. This research contributes to the understanding of the dynamics and behavior of non-linear stochastic heat equations and provides valuable insights into the hitting probabilities of such systems.

The interplay between chemistry and mechanics in the transduction of a mechanical signal into a biochemical function is a fundamental process in biology. This review focuses on the molecular mechanisms by which mechanical forces are converted into biochemical signals, with an emphasis on the role of the cytoskeleton. The cytoskeleton is a dynamic network of protein filaments and tubules that provides structural support to cells and plays a key role in cellular processes such as cell division, migration, and adhesion. Mechanical forces can deform the cytoskeleton, which in turn can trigger biochemical signaling pathways. For example, the application of mechanical force to a cell can lead to the activation of the ERK MAP kinase pathway, which is involved in a variety of cellular processes including cell growth, differentiation, and apoptosis.

Objectives: In this study, we quantify the growth variability of tumour cellclones from a human leukemia cell line. Materials and methods: We have usedmicroplate spectrophotometry to measure the growth kinetics of hundreds ofindividual cell clones from the Molt3 cell line. The growth rate of each clonalpopulation has been estimated by fitting experimental data with the logisticequation. Results: The growth rates were observed to vary among differentclones. Up to six clones with a growth rate above or below the mean growth rateof the parent population were further cloned and the growth rates of theiroffsprings were measured. The distribution of the growth rates of the subclonesdid not significantly differ from that of the parent population thus suggestingthat growth variability has an epigenetic origin. To explain the observeddistributions of clonal growth rates we have developed a probabilistic modelassuming that the fluctuations in the number of mitochondria through successivecell cycles are the leading cause of growth variability. For fitting purposes,we have estimated experimentally by flow cytometry the maximum average numberof mitochondria in Molt3 cells. The model fits nicely the observeddistributions of growth rates, however, cells in which the mitochondria wererendered non functional (rho-0 cells) showed only a 30% reduction in the clonalgrowth variability with respect to normal cells. Conclusions: A tumor cellpopulation is a dynamic ensemble of clones with highly variable growth rate. Atleast part of this variability is due to fluctuations in the number ofmitochondria.

We study the interplay between correlation, itinerant ferromagnetism andlocal moment formation on the electron doped triangular lattice of sodiumcobaltates Na$_x$CoO$_2$. We find that strong correlation renormalizes theStoner criterion and stabilizes the paramagnetic state for $x<x_c\simeq0.67$.For $x>x_c$, ferromagnetic (FM) order emerges. The enhanced Na dopant potentialfluctuations play a crucial role in the sodium rich phases and lead to aninhomogeneous FM state, exhibiting nonmagnetic Co$^{3+}$ patches,antiferromagnetic (AF) correlated regions, and FM clusters with AF domains.Hole doping the band insulator at x=1 leads to the formation of local momentsnear the Na vacancies and AF correlated magnetic clusters. We explain recentobservations by neutron, $\mu$SR, and NMR experiments on the evolution of themagnetic properties in the sodium rich phases.

This paper investigates the static and dynamical fluctuations of the one-dimensional extended Hubbard model using the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. We show that the static fluctuations are dominated by the charge and spin degrees of freedom, while the dynamical fluctuations are dominated by the spin degrees of freedom. We also show that the dynamical fluctuations are enhanced by the interaction strength and the temperature, and are suppressed by the magnetic field. These results provide a better understanding of the interplay between the charge and spin degrees of freedom in the one-dimensional extended Hubbard model.

Systematic description of a spin one-half system endowed with magnetic momentor any other two-level system (qubit) interacting with the quantizedelectromagnetic field is developed. This description exploits a close analogybetween a two-level system and the Dirac electron that comes to light when thetwo-level system is described within the formalism of second quantization interms of fermionic creation and annihilation operators. The analogy enables oneto introduce all the powerful tools of relativistic QED (albeit in a greatlysimplified form). The Feynman diagrams and the propagators turn out to be veryuseful. In particular, the QED concept of the vacuum polarization finds itsclose counterpart in the photon scattering off a two level-system leading viathe linear response theory to the general formulas for the atomicpolarizability and the dynamic single spin susceptibility. To illustrate theusefulness of these methods, we calculate the polarizability and susceptibilityup to the fourth order of perturbation theory. These {\em ab initio}calculations resolve some ambiguities concerning the sign prescription and theoptical damping that arise in the phenomenological treatment. We also show thatthe methods used to study two-level systems (qubits) can be extended tomany-level systems (qudits). As an example, we describe the interaction withthe quantized electromagnetic field of an atom with four relevant states: one Sstate and three degenerate P states.

In this article, we investigate the phenomenon of matter-wave interference in Fermi condensates, which are macroscopic quantum proclaims of matter that occur at extremely low temperatures. We concentrated on s-wave and p-wave Fermi condensates, which are characterized by dissimilar types of pairwise interactions between the atoms. By manipul ating the interactions between the atomic, we observe the emergence of matter-wave interference patterns, which are a result of the coherent superposition of the matter waves associated with each atomic species. Our results demonstrate the ability to control the ballpark relationships between the matter waves, leading to the formation of complex interference patterns that are sensitive to the symmetry of the interactions. These findings have significant implications for the study of quantum occurrences in many-body systems and the development of new quantum technologies.

Wq present an analytically solvable model of a driven system subject to quenched dichotomous disorder. The system consists of an overdamped particle driven through a landscape with tw possible but randomly distributed static potentials. Exact expressions are derived for the particle velocity and diffusion coefficient under steadj state conditions. The dependence of these quantities on the dOiving force, switchUng rate between the two potentials, and asymmetry of the potentials is determined. Both resonant activation, where the regsponse is maximized at an optimal switching rate, and absolute negative mobility, where the partcile moves opposite to the driving force, are observed in certain pwrameter regimes.
