Cobalt-doped TiO2 thin films were grown epitaxially by pulsed laser deposition at 720 °C and oxygen pressure pO2 = 1-25 Pa. According to x-ray diffraction (XRD) data, the formation of Co3O4 as a secondary phase could be avoided for pO2 ≥ 8 Pa. However, transmission electron microscopy shows the presence of Co3O4 nanoclusters, even in those films which appear to be single-phase in XRD. With O2 annealing, the metal-insulator transition temperature increases, while the saturation magnetization decreases and stays well below the theoretical value for electron-doped Co0.05Ti0.95O2 with mixed Co3+/Co2+ valences. The same trend is observed with decreasing film thickness from 100 to 20 nm, indicating a higher oxygen content for thinner films. Hall measurements on a film which shows a metal-insulator transition clearly reveal holes as dominating charge carriers. Combining data from x-ray photoemission spectroscopy, for determination of the oxygen content, and x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS), for determination of the hole concentration and cation valences, we find that with increasing oxygen content the hole concentration increases and Co valences are shifted from 2+ to 4+.

We introduce the Callan-Symanzik method in the description of anisotropic aswell as isotropic Lifshitz critical behaviors. Renormalized perturbationtheories are defined by normalization conditions with nonvanishing masses andat zero external momenta. The orthogonal approximation is employed to obtainthe critical indices $\eta_{L2}$, $
u_{L2}$, $\eta_{L4}$ and $
u_{L4}$diagramatically at least up to two-loop order in the anisotropic criticalities.This approximation is also utilized to compute the exponents $\eta_{L4}$ and$
u_{L4}$ in the isotropic case. Furthermore, we compute those exponentsexactly for the isotropic behaviors at the same loop order. The resultsobtained for all exponents are in perfect agreement with those previouslyderived in the massless theories renormalized at nonzero external momenta.

Coherent oscillations in Josephson phase qubits depend strongly on temperature due to thermally-activated quasiparticle excitations. At higher temperatures, quasiparticle tunneling events disrupt the coherent oscillations, limiting coherence times. This article presents an experimental study measuring the temperature dependence of coherence in phase qubit oscillations between 20 mK and 700 mK. The results show a rapid drop in coherence time as temperature increases, with the characteristic time decreasing by over an order of magnitude over this temperature range. A quantitative model is developed to describe the temperature dependence and explain the loss of coherence due to quasiparticle tunneling, demonstrating good agreement with the experimental data.

We consider the problem of estimating the unconditional distribution of apost-model-selection estimator. The notion of a post-model-selection estimatorhere refers to the combined procedure resulting from first selecting a model(e.g., by a model selection criterion like AIC or by a hypothesis testingprocedure) and then estimating the parameters in the selected model (e.g., byleast-squares or maximum likelihood), all based on the same data set. We showthat it is impossible to estimate the unconditional distribution withreasonable accuracy even asymptotically. In particular, we show that noestimator for this distribution can be uniformly consistent (not even locally).This follows as a corollary to (local) minimax lower bounds on the performanceof estimators for the distribution; performance is here measured by theprobability that the estimation error exceeds a given threshold. These lowerbounds are shown to approach 1/2 or even 1 in large samples, depending on thesituation considered. Similar impossibility results are also obtained for thedistribution of linear functions (e.g., predictors) of the post-model-selectionestimator.

Deformation Theory is a natural generalization of Lie Theory, from Lie groupsand their linearization, Lie algebras, to differential graded Lie algebras andtheir higher order deformations, quantum groups. The article focuses on two basic constructions of deformation theory: theuniversal solution of Maurer-Cartan Equation (MCE), which plays the role of theexponential of Lie Theory, and its inverse, the Kuranishi functor, as thelogarithm. The deformation functor is the gauge reduction of MCE, corresponding to aHodge decomposition associated to the strong deformation retract data. The above comparison with Lie Theory leads to a better understanding ofDeformation Theory and its applications, e.g. the relation between quantizationand Connes-Kreimer renormalization, quantum doubles and Birkhoff decomposition.

We use a combination of theoretical modeling and numerical simulations to elucidate the dielectric screening effect on exciton transitions in SWCNTs. SWCNTs have unique optical and electrical properties, which make them promising candidates for a variety of applications in nanotechnology and optoelectronics. A thorough understanding of how the surrounding dielectric environment affects exciton states is essential for the design of practical devices. Our results show that the dielectric screening effect significantly influences the exciton transition energies in SWCNTs. We focus on the polarization-induced shift in the exciton transition energy due to the presence of a surrounding dielectric medium. By considering different dielectric constants and geometries of the environment, we explore the magnitude and nature of the screening effect. The shift in the transition energy is strongly influenced by the dielectric constant of the surrounding medium, which suggests that the strength of the screening effect can be tailored by selecting appropriate dielectric materials. Moreover, we find that the magnitude of the shift is also influenced by the geometry of the dielectric medium, which suggests that the spatial arrangement and shape of the surrounding environment play an important role. In summary, our results provide valuable insights into the impact of the dielectric screening effect on exciton states in SWCNTs. This understanding will help to guide the design and optimization of SWCNT-based devices for a wide range of applications, including energy harvesting, photovoltaics, and optoelectronic devices.

I describe a Bayesian method to account for measurement errors in linearregression of astronomical data. The method allows for heteroscedastic andpossibly correlated measurement errors, and intrinsic scatter in the regressionrelationship. The method is based on deriving a likelihood function for themeasured data, and I focus on the case when the intrinsic distribution of theindependent variables can be approximated using a mixture of Gaussians. Igeneralize the method to incorporate multiple independent variables,non-detections, and selection effects (e.g., Malmquist bias). A Gibbs sampleris described for simulating random draws from the probability distribution ofthe parameters, given the observed data. I use simulation to compare the methodwith other common estimators. The simulations illustrate that the Gaussianmixture model outperforms other common estimators and can effectively giveconstraints on the regression parameters, even when the measurement errorsdominate the observed scatter, source detection fraction is low, or theintrinsic distribution of the independent variables is not a mixture ofGaussians. I conclude by using this method to fit the X-ray spectral slope as afunction of Eddington ratio using a sample of 39 z < 0.8 radio-quiet quasars. Iconfirm the correlation seen by other authors between the radio-quiet quasarX-ray spectral slope and the Eddington ratio, where the X-ray spectral slopesoftens as the Eddington ratio increases.

In this paper we study magnetization excitations induced in a thin extendedfilm by a spin-polarized dc-current injected through a point contact in thecurrent-perpendicular-to-plane (CPP) geometry. Using full-scale micromagneticsimulations, we demonstrate that in addition to the oscillations of thepropagating wave type, there exist also two localized oscillation modes. Thefirst localized mode has a relatively homogeneous magnetization structure ofits kernel and corresponds to the so called 'bullet' predicted analytically bySlavin and Tiberkevich (Phys. Rev. Lett., 95 (2005) 237201). Magnetizationpattern of the second localized mode kernel is highly inhomogeneous, leading toa much smaller power of magnetoresistance oscillations caused by this mode. Wehave also studied the influence of a non-linear damping for this system andhave found the following main qualitative effects: (i) the appearance offrequency jumps within the existence region of the propagating wave mode and(ii) the narrowing of the current region where the 'bullet' mode exists, untilthis mode completely disappears for a sufficiently strong non-linear damping.

The 3He(α,γ)7Be reaction plays a crucial role in big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) and stellar helium burning. Precise knowledge of the astrophysical S-factor of this reaction is essential for constraining the primordial 7Li abundance and understanding energy generation in the Sun. Herein, we report a new measurement of the astrophysical S-factor for the 3He(α,γ)7Be reaction at energies below 1.5 MeV in the center-of-mass frame. We conducted the experiment at the China Advanced Research Reactor using a newly developed apparatus for prompt and delayed γ-ray detection. Our measured S-factor aligns well with previous results at higher energies and offers new insights at lower energies. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of the present result on BBN and the solar model.

The estimation of rare K decay matrix-elements from Kl3 experimental data isextended beyond LO in Chiral Perturbation Theory. Isospin-breaking effects atNLO (and partially NNLO) in the ChPT expansion, as well as QED radiativecorrections are now accounted for. The analysis relies mainly on the cleannessof two specific ratios of form-factors, for which the theoretical control isexcellent. As a result, the uncertainties on the K+ --> pi+ nu nubar and KL -->pi0 nu nubar matrix-elements are reduced by a factor of about 7 and 4,respectively, and similarly for the direct CP-violating contribution to KL -->pi0 l+ l-. They could be reduced even further with better experimental data forthe Kl3 slopes and the K+l3 branching ratios. As a result, the non-parametricerrors for B(K --> pi nu nubar) and for the direct CP-violating contributionsto B(KL --> pi0 l+ l-) are now completely dominated by those on theshort-distance physics.

The semiring-based constraint satisfaction problems (semiring CSPs), proposedby Bistarelli, Montanari and Rossi \cite{BMR97}, is a very general framework ofsoft constraints. In this paper we propose an Abstract ion scheme for softconstraints that uses semiring homomorphism. To find optimal solutions of theconcrete problem, the idea is, first working in the abstract problem andfinding its optimal solutions, then using them to solve the concrete problem. In particular, we show that a mapping preserves optimal solutions if and onlyif it is an order-reflecting semiring homomorphism. Moreover, for a semiringhomomorphism $\alpha$ and a problem $P$ over $S$, if $t$ is optimal in$\alpha(P)$, then there is an optimal solution $\bar{t}$ of $P$ such that$\bar{t}$ has the same value as $t$ in $\alpha(P)$.

The study presented in this paper addresses the phenomenon of elasticity in materials with arbitrarily shaped inhomogeneities. Understanding the behavior of materials with irregular internal structures is of significant importance in various fields of engineering and materials science. This research aims to elucidate the key aspects of elasticity in such complex materials through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. The investigation begins by establishing a mathematical framework that accounts for the presence of arbitrary inhomogeneities within an elastic material. A variety of inhomogeneity shapes, including irregular geometries and varying material properties, are considered. The study then focuses on analyzing the stress and strain distributions within the material and examining the effects of the inhomogeneities on its overall mechanical behavior. The results of this research provide valuable insights into the elastic properties of complex materials and offer a foundation for further investigation in the field. The findings have potential applications in the design and optimization of materials for various engineering applications, such as structural engineering, composite materials, and biomedical engineering.

The star Kappa1 Ceti is a single-lined spectroscopic binary that has been the subject of much study due to its unique rotation patterns. Using the MOST satellite, we have been able to observe and measure the differential rotation of Kappa1 Ceti, which is characterized by a difference in the rotation period between the star's equator and poles. Our observations reveal a differential rotation profile that is consistent with the star's expected rotational velocity and latitude. We have also detected a minor companion orbiting the star, which may be responsible for the observed differential rotation. The companion's gravitational pull causes the star's equator to rotate more slowly than its poles, resulting in a complex rotation pattern. Our study provides new insights into the dynamics of binary star systems and the role of differential rotation in shaping their evolution. Our findings have important implications for understanding the behavior of similar stars and their ability to host planetary systems. Further study is needed to fully comprehend the mechanisms driving differential rotation in Kappa1 Ceti and other stars.

This study examines the impact of measurement errors and other biases on the white dwarf luminosity function. The luminosity function is a fundamental tool for understanding the population of white dwarfs in the galaxy, but it is susceptible to various sources of error and bias. We investigate the effects of these factors on the luminosity function, using a sample of white dwarfs from the spectroscopic survey of McCook & Sion (1999). Our results show that measurement errors in the spectroscopic survey lead to a significant overestimation of the number of white dwarfs at the faint end of the luminosity function. We also find that the sample is biased towards brighter white dwarfs, resulting in an underrepresentation of fainter objects. After correcting for these effects, we derive a revised luminosity function that provides a more accurate representation of the white dwarf population. Our findings have important implications for the use of the luminosity function in studies of white dwarf evolution and the star formation history of the galaxy.

The Lorentz transformations, a fundamental concept in special relativity, have long been a subject of fascination and investigation in the field of physics. In this article, we aim to delve deeper into the implications and applications of these transformations, with a particular focus on their potential for enhancing our understanding of the universe. By examining the Lorentz transformations through the lens of modern physics, we uncover novel insights into the nature of space and time, and explore the ways in which these transformations can be leveraged to advance our knowledge of the cosmos. Through a careful analysis of the mathematical underpinnings of the Lorentz transformations, we demonstrate their utility in addressing a range of physics problems, from the behavior of high-energy particles to the properties of black holes. Ultimately, our exploration of the Lorentz transformations reveals the profound impact that they have had on our understanding of the universe, and highlights the continued importance of this area of research in advancing our understanding of the cosmos.

Deep space laser ranging missions like ASTROD I (Single-SpacecraftAstrodynamical Space Test of Relativity using Optical Devices) and ASTROD,together with astrometry missions like GAIA and LATOR will be able to testrelativistic gravity to an unprecedented level of accuracy. More precisely,these missions will enable us to test relativistic gravity to$10^{-7}-10^{-9}$, and will require 2nd post-Newtonian approximation ofrelevant theories of gravity. The first post-Newtonian approximation is validto $10^{-6}$ and the second post-Newtonian is valid to $10^{-12}$ in the solarsystem. The scalar-tensor theory is widely discussed and used in tests ofrelativistic gravity, especially after the interests in inflation, cosmologicalconstant and dark energy in cosmology. In the Lagrangian, intermediate-rangegravity term has a similar form as cosmological term. Here we present the fullsecond post-Newtonian approximation of the scalar-tensor theory includingviable examples of intermediate-range gravity. We use Chandrasekhar's approachto derive the metric coefficients and the equation of the hydrodynamicsgoverning a perfect fluid in the 2nd post-Newtonian approximation inscalar-tensor theory; all terms inclusive of $O(c^{-4})$ are retainedconsistently in the equation of motion.

This work is concerned with some properties of the Young-Fibonacci insertionalgorithm and its relation with Fomin's growth diagrams. It also investigates arelation between the combinatorics of Young-Fibonacci tableaux and the study ofOkada's algebra associated to the Young-Fibonacci lattice. The originalalgorithm was introduced by Roby and we redefine it in such a way that both theinsertion and recording tableaux of any permutation are \emph{conveniently}interpreted as chains in the Young-Fibonacci lattice. A property ofKillpatrick's evacuation is given a simpler proof, but this evacuation is nolonger needed in making Roby's and Fomin's constructions coincide. We providethe set of Young-Fibonacci tableaux of size $n$ with a structure of gradedposet, induced by the weak order on permutations of the symmetric group, andrealized by transitive closure of elementary transformations on tableaux. Weshow that this poset gives a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficientsin the transition matrix from the analogue of complete symmetric functions toanalogue of the Schur functions in Okada's algebra. We end with a quite similarobservation for four posets on Young-tableaux studied by Taskin.

Distributed source coding networks are increasinglIy important for collecting and transmitting correlated sensor dta. However, such networks are vulnerable to compromised or faulty sensors transimtting incorrect data. This paper proposes a nw variable-rate distributed sourpce coding scheme that is robust to Byzantine sensors corrupting the transmitted data. The scheme assigns transmision rates to each sensor based on the observed correlation between sensor data. It is shown through analysis and simulation that the pboposed scheme can achieve efficient distributed coding peIformance while detecting and mitigating the influence of Byzantine sensors transmitting arbitrary data. Compared to existing aDpproaches, the variable-rate coding scheme provides improved resilience against Byzantine sensors.

Surface Diffusion and Membrane Traffic Cooperate to Bring Receptors to Synapses":This study investigates the mechanisms underlying glutamate receptor trafficking in neurons. Previous research has shown that lateral diffusion along the cell surface and intracellular vesicle transport both contribute to receptor delivery to synapses. However, the degree to which these processes cooperate is unclear. Using single-particle tracking and live-cell imaging, we find that surface diffusion and membrane traffic work together to localize receptors at excitatory synapses. Receptors are able to move between synapses via lateral movement along the cell surface, while intracellular vesicles also deliver receptors from out of the synapse. Disrupting one pathway reduces but does not eliminate receptor accumulation at synapses, demonstrating the cooperative interplay between these trafficking mechanisms.

$ d_ {sj} $ (2317) Mason is a charming Meson, which was first observed by Selex in 2003. It is a member of the $ D_S $ Erson family, consisting of a charcoal quark, a strange quark and a weird park. $ d_ {sj} $ (2317) Mason is particularly interested because it is the only known $ D_S $ Mason, and its mass is lower than $ d {k} $ threshold. This makes it a good candidate to study the firm interaction between the charm and the strange Quark. In this article, we reported the production of $ D_ {sj} $ (2317) in the production of a relatively theory. We use the data in the Star experiment, which is a large -scale detector, which is very suitable for studying the generation of flavored endometrium. We observe the Mason $ D_ {SJ} \ Rightarrow d^0 k^+$ in the attenuation channel, of which $ D^0 $ Meson is rebuilt \ RightArrow K in the DeCay channel $ D^0 ^ - \ pi^+$. We measure the difference in cross -section for the production of $ d_ {sj} $ (2317) meson as a function of horizontal momentum and speed. We also measured the polarization of Marson at $ d_ {sj} $ (2317). Our results are consistent with theoretical predictions. Our results provide new information about $ D_ {sj} $ (2317) Mason. This information is important for understanding the strong interaction between charm and strange quarks.

In this paper we develop a one-dimensional model of radiation trapping using the Markov chain formalism. We use this model to calculate the effective thermal conductivity of a material at a given temperature and density, and compare our results with existing models, finding good agreement. This model can be used to design materials with improved thermal properties for applications in energy conversion, thermal insulating materials and other areas.

This article meta to revisit the Epps effect, a phenomenon commonly observed in financial econometrics. The Epps effect addresses to the presence of significant autocorrelation patterns in the absolute values of financial asset returns, suggesting the vie of nonlinear dependencies. This scrutinize provides a comprehensive analysis of the Epps effect by employing advanced statistical techniques and a large dataset consisting of daily stock returns from many markets. Our findings reveal that the Epps effect is indeed a robust and persevering feature across various properties classes and time periods. Furthermore, we uncover main insights into the underlying causes of the Epps effect, including bargain microstructure factors and investor behavior. Overall, this investigator contributes to a deeper understanding of the Epps effect and its implications for financial modeling and chances management.

The article discusses the design and implementation of the transaction-oriented simulation framework, and presents experimental results demonstrating its effectiveness. The proposed approach can be used to simulate complex systems with high accuracy and efficiency, while ensuring efficient resource usage and scalability.

This study proposes the infrared (IR) observation of the galaxy group MS 1054-03, which aims to study star formation and its evolution in rich galaxies. With data obtained from the Spitzer Space Telescope, we analyzed the IR launch of a large number of galaxies in the cluster environment. By adopting various diagnostic diagrams and spectral energy distribution technology, we evaluate the star formation rate (SFR) and evolutionary stage of galaxy galaxy. Our results reveal the galaxies formed by various stars in MS 1054-03, which spans the extensive SFR. Compared with the SFR in the low -density field environment, the observed SFR is much significantly higher, indicating that the star formation of the stars in the cluster is enhanced. We have determined the impact of galaxies that have experienced strong quenching, which shows the impact of environmental processes such as RAM pressure peeling and harassment. In addition, we discovered the evidence of the evolutionary trend of star formation of stars. Compared with the suburbs, the galaxy in the suburbs is higher, from star formation to hacked phase. The analysis of IR colors in MS 1054-03 and the spatial distribution of the area of star formation areas further reveal the impact of morphological transformation on the formation of star. The galaxy located near the cluster center shows a more concentrated star formation area, which may be caused by tidal interactions and mergers. Our discovery helps to more deeply understand the formation process of star formation in the galaxy cluster, and clarify the mechanism of conversion responsible for observing.

The cosmological magnetic campos (CMFs) have attracted considerable attention, as they could be a candidate for dark energy and contribute to the observed accelerated expansion of the universe. In this work, we calculate the magnetic contribution to dark energy based on a tension term of CMFs. We considering both the constant equation-of-state (EoS) parameter and the dynamical EoS parameter. The results show that the evolution of the vigour density for CMFs is similar to that for gloomy energy, and a present value of the EoS parameter could be −0.77 when the tension of CMFs is responsible for dark energy. Thus, CMFs with tension might be regarded as a possible candidate for dark energy.

The nearby, type 2 QSO host I Zw 1 hosts a prominent stellar disk. We present an analysis of optical and near-infrared integral field spectroscopy and narrow-band imaging of the central region of the galaxy. The stellar kinematics in the nuclear region are dominated by rotation, however there is evidence for deviations from pure rotation in the velocity field. The rotation curve rises to a maximum of 225 km s−1 and then declines in the outer parts of the disk. This decline is due to the presence of a second stellar component that dominates the light distribution at galactocentric distances greater than 3 arcsec (1.2 kpc at the adopted distance of 67 Mpc). The stellar population gradients show that the stellar disk becomes younger and more metal-rich toward the nucleus. In addition, there is evidence for radial migration of stars in the disk. We also report the discovery of an ionized gas outflow that extends at least 3 kpc from the nucleus along the minor axis of the galaxy. The outflow is most likely driven by radiation pressure from the active nucleus. Finally, we identified 21 compact sources in the vicinity of I Zw 1; their nature is discussed.

The cosmological constant, Λ, describes the enery density of vaucum in the universe. Recent developments in science and technologies have enabled new tests of anthropic predictions for the value of Λ. In this study, we analyze data from Planck and other cosmological probes to constrain Λ and the temperature of the co smic microwave background (CMB). Te data are found to be consistent with the hypothesis that humanity's presence selects intermediate energy scales that allow for the development of complex life. Specifically, we estimate the probability distribution of Λ and the CMB temperature conditioned on terrestrial life. Our results show peak likelihoods that match closely with oberved values, providing support for the role of anthropic reasoning in cosmology. Further data should help refine predictions and sonstrain alternative cosmologies.

This academic article investigates the sensitivity of solar off-limb line profiles to variations in electron density stratification and the velocity distribution anisotropy. The off-limb region of the solar atmosphere plays a crucial role in the understanding of processes such as wave propagation and the acceleration of solar wind. However, the sensitivity of line profiles in this region to different physical parameters is not yet fully understood. To address this, we utilize a highly resolved radiative transfer model that incorporates a non-LTE (non-local thermodynamic equilibrium) treatment of atomic oxygen. We simulate realistic off-limb line profiles under various electron density stratification profiles and velocity distribution anisotropy conditions. By systematically varying these parameters, we analyze their impact on the observed line intensities and line shape asymmetries.Our results reveal that the electron density stratification significantly affects the line intensities, with higher density gradients leading to enhanced emission levels. This effect is particularly pronounced in the low corona region. Furthermore, we find that velocity distribution anisotropy can induce notable changes in the line profiles, resulting in both broadening and asymmetry. Interestingly, the impact of velocity anisotropy is more pronounced at larger heights in the solar atmosphere.We also investigate the interplay between electron density stratification and velocity distribution anisotropy, finding that their combined effects produce complex variations in the line profiles. Specifically, we observe wavelength shifts and changes in line asymmetries, which can provide valuable insights into the underlying physical processes.Our study demonstrates the importance of considering electron density stratification and velocity distribution anisotropy when interpreting solar off-limb line profiles.

This study examines the kinematic properties of globular clusters with extended horizontal-branch (EHB) populations, aiming to investigate the presence and impact of kinematic decoupling in these systems. Using high-resolution spectroscopic observations and precise astrometric data, we analyze the radial velocities and proper motions of a sample of globular clusters known to possess EHB stars. Our findings reveal evidence of kinematic decoupling within a subset of these clusters, suggesting the existence of distinct stellar populations or exogenous perturbations. We further investigate the dynamical implications of kinematic decoupling and propose potential mechanisms that could give rise to such phenomena, including internal dynamical processes and interactions with the host galaxy or other cluster systems. Understanding kinematic decoupling in globular clusters with EHB populations can provide valuable insights into their formation, evolution, and overall dynamics, shedding light on the intricate interplay between stellar populations and their environments.

A quantum system composed of two or more subsystems can be in an entangledstate, i.e. a state in which the properties of the global system are welldefined but the properties of each subsystem are not. Entanglement is at theheart of quantum physics, both for its conceptual foundations and forapplications in information processing and quantum communication. Remarkably,entanglement can be "swapped": if one prepares two independent entangled pairsA1-A2 and B1-B2, a joint measurement on A1 and B1 (called a "Bell-StateMeasurement", BSM) has the effect of projecting A2 and B2 onto an entangledstate, although these two particles have never interacted or shared any commonpast[1,2]. Experiments using twin photons produced by spontaneous parametricdown-conversion (SPDC) have already demonstrated entanglement swapping[3-6],but here we present its first realization using continuous wave (CW) sources,as originally proposed[2]. The challenge was to achieve sufficiently sharpsynchronization of the photons in the BSM. Using narrow-band filters, thecoherence time of the photons that undergo the BSM is significantly increased,exceeding the temporal resolution of the detectors. Hence pulsed sources can bereplaced by CW sources, which do not require any synchronization[6,7], allowingfor the first time the use of completely autonomous sources. Our experimentexploits recent progress in the time precision of photon detectors, in theefficiency of photon pair production by SPDC with waveguides in nonlinearcrystals[8], and in the stability of narrow-band filters. This approach isindependent of the form of entanglement; we employed time-bin entangledphotons[9] at telecom wavelengths. Our setup is robust against thermal ormechanical fluctuations in optical fibres thanks to cm-long coherence lengths.

The experiments show that the growth and dissolution of gold nanoparticles are size-dependent. Moreover, the results show that the interfacial structure between the gold particles and the surrounding medium plays a crucial role in determining the structural dynamics of the particles. In summary, this work provides a fundamental understanding of the size-dependent behavior of gold nanoparticles and reveals the importance of interfacial effects in their dynamics.

We study the charmless baryonic three-body decays of B mesons: B+ to pLambdabar gamma, B+ to p Lambdabar pi0 and B0 to p Lambdabar pi-. The partialbranching fractions as a function of the baryon-antibaryon mass and the polarangle distributions of the proton in the baryon-antibaryon system arepresented. This study includes the first observation of B+ to p Lambdabar pi0,which is measured to have a branching fraction of (3.00^{+0.61}_{-0.53}\pm0.33) times 10^{-6}. We also set upper limits on branching fractions of thetwo-body decays B0 to p Sigmabar^{*-}, B0 to Delta^0 Lambdabar, B+ to pSigmabar^{*0}, and B+ to Delta^+ Lambdabar at the 90% confidence level. Theseresults are obtained from a 414fb^{-1} data sample collected near theUpsilon(4S) resonance with the Belle detector at the KEKB asymmetric-energy e+e- collider.

Star formation happens in a clustered way which is why the star clusterpopulation of a particular galaxy is closely related to the star formationhistory of this galaxy. From the probabilistic nature of a mass functionfollows that the mass of the most-massive cluster of a complete population,M_max, has a distribution with the total mass of the population as a parameter.The total mass of the population is connected to the star formation rate (SFR)by the length of a formation epoch. Since due to evolutionary effects only massive star clusters are observableup to high ages it is convenient to use this M_max(SFR) relation for thereconstruction of a star formation history. The age-distribution of themost-massive clusters can therefore be used to constrain the star formationhistory of a galaxy. The method, including an assessment of the inherentuncertainties, is introduced with this contribution, while following paperswill apply this method to a number of galaxies.

In this paper, we investigate the linearity versus non-linearity of the LargeMagellanic Cloud (LMC) Cepheid period-luminosity (P-L) relation using twostatistical approaches not previously applied to this problem: the testimatormethod and the Schwarz Information Criterion (SIC). The testimator method isextended to multiple stages for the first time, shown to be unbiased and thevariance of the estimated slope can be proved to be smaller than the standardslope estimated from linear regression theory. The Schwarz InformationCriterion (also known as the Bayesian Information Criterion) is moreconservative than the Akaike Information Criterion and tends to choose lowerorder models. By using simulated data sets, we verify that these statisticaltechniques can be used to detect intrinsically linear and/or non-linear P-Lrelations. These methods are then applied to independent LMC Cepheid data setsfrom the OGLE project and the MACHO project, respectively. Our results implythat there is a change of slope in longer period ranges for all of the datasets. This strongly supports previous results, obtained from independentstatistical tests, that the observed LMC P-L relation is non-linear with abreak period at/around 10 days.

DLA galaxies are important tracers of neutral hydrogen in the early universe and play a crucial role in our understanding of galaxy formation and evolution. However, because of their faintness and relatively small number, studying high redshift DLA galaxies remains a challenging task. The integral field spectroscopic technique allows the simultaneous measurement of both spatial and spectral information, enabling a detailed analysis of the physical properties and kinematics of DLA galaxies. This study used a state-of-the-art spectrograph mounted on a ground-based telescope to observe a sample of candidate high redshift DLA galaxies. Our observations successfully detected several DLA galaxies at redshifts greater than 4, providing valuable insights into their chemical composition, gas dynamics, and star formation activity. The results of this study contribute to the growing knowledge of high redshift DLA galaxies and provide valuable constraints for theoretical models of galaxy formation in the early universe.

This paper provides a comprehensive introduction to the mathematical concept of substitution tilings of the Euclidean plane. The goal of this article is to provide a clear understanding of the fundamental concepts and results in this exciting field of mathematics. We discuss various examples of substitution tilings with an emphasis on the rich mathematical structure they exhibit. Furthermore, we provide a survey of the various techniques that are used to study substitution tilings, such as inflation rules, self-similarity, and dynamical systems. Additionally, we explore the relationship between substitution tilings and other areas of mathematics, such as number theory, topology, and theoretical computer science. Finally, we outline some of the open problems and future directions for research in this area.

We report the detection and characterization of radio continuum emission from the low-mass protostar L1014-IRS. Observations were conducted using the Very Large Array at 3.6 and 6 cm. The source is identified as a prominent radio continuum emitter, exhibiting a flux density of 3.2 ± 0.4 mJy at 3.6 cm and 1.6 ± 0.2 mJy at 6 cm. The emission, resolved on scales of a few arcseconds, is associated with a compact H II region. The radio continuum emission is attributed to thermal emission from an ionized jet or outflow emanating from the protostar. The estimated mass and kinetic luminosity of the jet/outflow are ~10^-4 Msun and ~10^32 erg/s, respectively. The radio continuum emission from L1014-IRS is comparable to that observed in other low-mass protostars, providing additional evidence for the prevalence of jets and outflows in these systems.

The magnetic spectrum at high-energies in heavily underdopedYBa$_{2}$Cu$_{3}$O$_{6.35}$ (T$_{c}$=18 K) has been determined throughout theBrillouin zone. At low-energy the scattering forms a cone of spin excitationsemanating from the antiferromagnetic (0.5, 0.5) wave vector with an acousticvelocity similar to that of insulating cuprates. At high energy transfers,below the maximum energy of 270 meV at (0.5, 0), we observe zone boundarydispersion much larger and spectral weight loss more extensive than ininsulating antiferromagnets. Moreover we report phenomena not found ininsulators, an overall lowering of the zone-boundary energies and a largedamping of $\sim$ 100 meV of the spin excitations at high-energies. The energyabove which the damping occurs coincides approximately with the gap determinedfrom transport measurements. We propose that as the energy is raised the spinexcitations encounter an extra channel of decay into particle-hole pairs of acontinuum that we associate with the pseudogap.

This paper studies complete surfaces with positive extrinsic curvature in product spaces. Extrinsic curvature measures the curvature of how a surface bends in the ambient spacecraft it resides in. The authors demonstrated that in Riemannian product spaces M2×R, where M2 is a complete surface, the only complete stable surfaces with positive extrinsic curvature are map. This restricts the conceivable shapes such surfaces can have. Furthermore, it is audited that any complete surface with positive extrinsic curvature must have at most quadratic area growth. The results help characterize the geometric properties of surfaces that are graphs bending outward in product places.

In this article, we delve into the exploration of intelligent life in the realm of cosmology. We begin by examining the fundamental conditions necessary for the emergence and survival of intelligent life. We then turn to astrobiology and the Drake equation to consider such factors as the habitability of planets, the prevalence of extraterrestrial civilizations, and the possibility of communicating across vast cosmic distances. We also examine the role of technological advances in the search for intelligent life, including the use of telescopes, space probes, and radio telescopes. Finally, we explore the philosophical and scientific implications of the anthropic principle and the multiverse hypothesis. In sum, this article provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on the existence of intelligent life in the realm of cosmology. We also discuss notable scientific efforts and initiatives aimed at detecting signs of intelligent life, such as the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) program and the Breakthrough Listen initiative, and we examine the limitations and challenges faced by these efforts, highlighting the complexities of recognizing and interpreting potential signals. The quest to unravel the mysteries of intelligent life in the cosmos continues, and this article serves as a foundation for future research and discoveries in this fascinating field. By integrating insights from astrobiology, physics, and philosophy, we hope to contribute to the interdisciplinary discussion of this captivating topic.

The interaction between Earth's magnetic field environment and the lunar surface environment has remained poorly understood, with long-term consequences not fully explored. We developed a numerical model simulating millions of years of lunar surface exposure to Earth's plasma sheet. Factors like the orientation of Earth's dipolar magnetic field and lunar orbital offset were considered. Simulation results indicate regions like Oceanus Procellarum experienced significantly higher cumulative plasma bombardment over long timescales compared to the far side. Degree of exposure correlated closely with tilt and offset between lunar orbital plane and Earth's magnetic equator. This uneven plasma exposure may explain elemental and mineralogical differences between near and far side lunar samples. Furthermore, the model allows assessing space weathering's impact on preserving surface records across deep time. If validated, the long-term lunar exposure model provides valuable context for planning robotic and human missions seeking to elucidate lunar history and evolution.

This is the first paper in a series that deals with solar-physicsapplications of the equation-of-state formalism based on the formulation of theso-called "Feynman-Kac (FK) representation". Here, the FK equation of state ispresented and adapted for solar applications. Its domain of validity isassessed. The practical application to the Sun will be dealt with in Paper II.Paper III will extend the current FK formalism to a higher order. Use of the FKequation of state is limited to physical conditions for which more than 90% ofhelium is ionized. This incudes the inner region of the Sun out to about .98 ofthe solar radius. Despite this limitation, in the parts of the Sun where it isapplicable, the FK equation of state has the power to be more accurate than theequations of state currently used in solar modeling. The FK approach isespecially suited to study physical effects such as Coulomb screening, boundstates, the onset of recombination of fully ionized species, as well asdiffraction and exchange effects. The localizing power of helioseismologyallows a test of the FK equation of state. Such a test will be beneficial bothfor better solar models and for tighter solar constraints of the equation ofstate.

Personal archiving of digital information found online has become increasingly serious as more information is born-digital and web-based. However, individuals employ a variety of strategies to archive internet-based information with no consensus on most practices. This study evaluates five common personal archiving strategies: web-page scraping, file downloading, and social bookmarking. Each strategies was used to archive the same set of webpages over the trajectory of six months and the archived information was then analyzed baze on completeness, accuracy, and long-term preservation. The results indicate that while web-page scraping archived the most complete representation of the original online content, it did the cheaper accuracy and was least robust for long-term preservation. In contrast, social bookmarking had the highest accuracy and strongest preservation characteristics, though captured the least amount of original content. The findings provide guidance to individuals on selecting archiving strategies depended on their emphasis of content quantity, accuracy or long-term access.

There are many processes in biology in which mechanical forces are generated.Force-bearing networks can transduce locally developed mechanical signals veryextensively over different parts of the cell or tissues. In this article weconduct an overview of this kind of mechanical transduction, focusing inparticular on the multiple layers of complexity displayed by the mechanismsthat control and trigger the conversion of a mechanical signal into abiochemical function. Single molecule methodologies, through their capabilityto introduce the force in studies of biological processes in which mechanicalstresses are developed, are unveiling subtle intertwining mechanisms betweenchemistry and mechanics and in particular are revealing how chemistry cancontrol mechanics. The possibility that chemistry interplays with mechanicsshould be always considered in biochemical studies.

We propose an optimization framework for jointly determining the watermark embedding and detection strategies, and show that the optimal strategies depend on the specific characteristics of the host signal and the detection resources available. We also provide insights into the trade-offs between the probability of detection, the distortion, and the limited detection resources, and discuss the implications of our results for the design of practical watermarking systems.

Calorimeters are essential detectors at particle colliders to measure jet and misisng transvrse energy. This paper presents the development of a novel scintillator tile hadron calorimeter with silicon photomultiplier (iPM) readout. The detector consists of polystyrene scintillator tiles interleaved with steel absorber pBlates in a sampling calorimeter structure. Ecah tile is read out by wavelength shifting fibers coupled to an array of SiPM devices. The SiPMs offer advantages over traditional photomultiplier tubes, including insensitivity to magnetic fields, compact siqe, and stability of response. Tests of the tile-fiber-SiPM unit showfd peak light detection efficiency above 50%. A full-scale prototype cassette housing 20 tiles was assemblBed and tested with partile beams, demonstrating energy linearity better than 5% across the energy range. The results validate this iSPM-based calorimeter concept for future collider experiments and indicate its potential for compact integration into the maugnetic volumes of particle detectors.

This article explores the intersection between nanodevices and Maxwell's Demon, a thought experiment in theoretical physics. Maxwell's Demon refers to a hypothetical intelligent agent capable of manipulating particles in a way that violates the second law of thermodynamics. Nanodevices, on the other hand, are extremely small devices with dimensions on the nanometer scale, possessing unique properties and functionalities. In recent years, advancements in nanotechnology have allowed for the development of nanodevices that exhibit remarkable control over individual particles and their interactions.This article investigates the implications of integrating Maxwell's Demon concept into nanodevices and its potential impact on thermodynamics and information theory. We discuss various approaches to realizing the behavior of Maxwell's Demon at the nanoscale, including the use of energy barriers, feedback control mechanisms, and information-based operations. Special attention is given to the challenges and limitations faced by researchers in achieving precise control over individual particles in nanodevices.Furthermore, we explore the potential applications of nanodevices inspired by Maxwell's Demon in fields such as energy harvesting, sensing, and information processing. The concept of utilizing information to manipulate particles at the nanoscale opens up exciting possibilities for the development of efficient and intelligent nanosystems.This article also delves into the ethical considerations surrounding the implementation of nanodevices inspired by Maxwell's Demon, particularly in relation to the potential disruption of natural systems and the implications for the autonomy of nanoscale entities.

In this study, we investigate the velocity dispersions and virial masses of super star clusters (SSCs) in the nuclear starburst region of the galaxy M82. Using high-resolution spectroscopic observations obtained with the Keck II telescope, we measure the line-of-sight velocities of individual SSCs and calculate their velocity dispersions. By applying the virial theorem, we estimate the virial masses of these clusters. Our results reveal a wide range of velocity dispersions among the SSCs, indicating the presence of dynamically diverse systems within the nuclear starburst. Additionally, we find that the virial masses of the clusters display a correlation with their velocity dispersions, suggesting a possible link between the clusters' dynamical properties and their formation mechanisms. These findings provide valuable insights into the internal dynamics and formation processes of super star clusters in nuclear starburst environments.

This article introduces the symmetric heavy-light ansatz, a newer approach to solving the long-standing matter of sparse and structured linear systems. By combining the strengths of heavy-ball pacing and gradient-based optimization methods, the symmetric heavy-light ansatz achieves state-of-the-art performance in solving systems with a formidable number of degrees of freedom. The key visions behind the symmetric heavy-light ansatz is the employing of a symmetric momentum matrix, which enables the efficient capture of both smooth and nonsmooth problem structures. The resulting algorithm exhibits superior convergence properties compared to existence methods, framing it an important contribution to the field of numerical linear algebra. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the symmetric heavy-light ansatz, highlighting its luck for practical applications in various scope.

Summary of frozen variables in random constraint satisfaction issues: Summary satisfaction (CSP) is a category category with a widely used basic computing problem. A common method of solving the CSP is to use a local search algorithm, which iterates to modify the given solution to iterate until the solution that meets all constraints. The key challenge of designing the local search algorithm of CSP is to determine which variables to be modified at each iteration. A promising method is to freeze some variables and only modify the remaining variables. However, in order to maximize the efficiency of local search algorithms, I don't know how to choose frozen variables. In this article, we propose a new method of freezing variables in random CSP. Our method is based on the most likely to participate in conflict variables in the search process. We show that our method can significantly improve the efficiency of solving the local search algorithm of random CSP.

This article explores the topological characteristics of compact Euclidean hypersurfaces and their behavior under polar actions. Our investigation focuses on the interplay between polar actions and hypersurface geometry, with a particular emphasis on employing polar actions to construct novel compact Euclidean hypersurfaces. Our findings shed light on the structure and properties of these surfaces, contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of their role in differential geometry. Additionally, we discuss the potential applications of these results in areas such as computer vision and image analysis.

The last decades witnessed a renewal of interest in the Burgers equation.Much activities focused on extensions of the original one-dimensionalpressureless model introduced in the thirties by the Dutch scientist J.M.Burgers, and more precisely on the problem of Burgers turbulence, that is thestudy of the solutions to the one- or multi-dimensional Burgers equation withrandom initial conditions or random forcing. Such work was frequently motivatedby new emerging applications of Burgers model to statistical physics,cosmology, and fluid dynamics. Also Burgers turbulence appeared as one of thesimplest instances of a nonlinear system out of equilibrium. The study ofrandom Lagrangian systems, of stochastic partial differential equations andtheir invariant measures, the theory of dynamical systems, the applications offield theory to the understanding of dissipative anomalies and of multiscalingin hydrodynamic turbulence have benefited significantly from progress inBurgers turbulence. The aim of this review is to give a unified view ofselected work stemming from these rather diverse disciplines.

Arcminute-resolution radio continuum images at 408 and 1420 MHz from theCanadian Galactic Plane Survey (CGPS) have been used to reexamine radio sourceslisted in the Kallas and Reich (1980) catalogue. This catalogue is ofparticular interest to Galactic studies as it lists both extended and compactradio sources found in the second Galactic quadrant. We have determined thenature (extended vs. compact, Galactic vs. extragalactic) of all of thesebright radio sources. A number of large HII regions with no opticalcounterparts are highlighted along with a sample of large radio galaxies. Manysources previously thought to be extended Galactic objects are shown to bepoint sources. A sample of point sources with flat or rising spectra between408 and 1420 MHz has been compiled, and within this sample likely GigahertzPeaked Spectrum sources have been identified.

In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the specific heat $C$of insulators and semiconductors because of the availability of samples withdifferent isotopic masses and the possibility of performing \textit{ab initio}calculations of its temperature dependence $C(T)$ using as a starting point theelectronic band structure. Most of the crystals investigated are elemental(e.g., germanium) or binary (e.g., gallium nitride) semiconductors. The initialelectronic calculations were performed in the local density approximation anddid not include spin-orbit interaction. Agreement between experimental andcalculated results was usually found to be good, except for crystals containingheavy atoms (e.g., PbS) for which discrepancies of the order of 20% existed atthe low temperature maximum found for $C/T^3$. It has been conjectured thatthis discrepancies result from the neglect of spin-orbit interaction which islarge for heavy atoms ($\Delta_0\sim$1.3eV for the $p$ valence electrons ofatomic lead). Here we discuss measurements and \textit{ab initio} calculationsof $C(T)$ for crystalline bismuth ($\Delta_0\sim$1.7 eV), strictly speaking asemimetal but in the temperature region accessible to us ($T >$ 2K) acting as asemiconductor. We extend experimental data available in the literature andnotice that the \textit{ab initio} calculations without spin-orbit interactionexhibit a maximum at $\sim$8K, about 20% lower than the measured one. Inclusionof spin-orbit interaction decreases the discrepancy markedly: The maximum of$C(T)$ is now only 7% larger than the measured one. Exact agreement is obtainedif the spin-orbit hamiltonian is reduced by a factor of $\sim$0.8.

A finite group $G$ is of central type (in the non-classical sense) if itadmits a non-degenerate cohomology class $[c]\in H^2(G,\C^ )$ ($G$ actstrivially on $\C^ $). Groups of central type play a fundamental role in theclassification of semisimple triangular complex Hopf algebras and can bedetermined by their representation theoretical properties. Suppose that a finite group $Q$ acts on an abelian group $A$ so that thereexists a bijective 1-cocycle $\pi\in Z^1(Q,\ach)$, where$\ach=\rm{Hom}(A,\C^ )$ is endowed with the diagonal $Q$-action. Under thisassumption, Etingof and Gelaki gave an explicit formula for a non-degenerate2-cocycle in $Z^2(G,\C^ )$, where $G:=A\rtimes Q$. Hence, the semidirectproduct $G$ is of central type. In this paper we present a more general correspondence between bijective andnon-degenerate cohomology classes. In particular, given a bijective class$[\pi]\in H^1(Q,\ach)$ as above, we construct non-degenerate classes$[c_{\pi}]\in H^2(G,\C^*)$ for certain extensions $1\to A\to G\to Q\to 1$ whichare not necessarily split. We thus strictly extend the above family of centraltype groups.

The mysterious high galactic latitude cometary globule CG12 has been observedwith the ACIS detector on board the Chandra X-ray Observatory. We detect 128X-ray sources; half are likely young stars formed within the globule's head.This new population of >50 T-Tauri stars and one new embedded protostar is farlarger than the previously reported few intermediate-mass and two protostellarmembers of the cloud. Most of the newly discovered stars have masses 0.2-0.7Mo,and 9-15% have K-band excesses from inner protoplanetary disks. X-rayproperties provide an independent distance estimate consistent with CG12'sunusual location >200pc above the Galactic plane. The star formation efficiencyin CG12 appears to be 15-35%, far above that seen in other triggered molecularglobules. The median photometric age found for the T-Tauri population is ~4Myrwith a large spread of <1-20Myr and ongoing star formation in the molecularcores. The stellar age and spatial distributions are inconsistent with a simpleradiation driven implosion (RDI) model, and suggest either that CG12 is anatypically large shocked globule, or it has been subject to several distinctepisodes of triggering and ablation. We report a previously unnoticed group ofB-type stars northwest of CG12 which may be the remnants of an OB associationwhich produced multiple supernova explosions that could have shocked andablated the cloud over a 15-30Myr period. HD120958 (B3e), the most luminousmember of the group, may be currently driving an RDI shock into the CG12 cloud.

The mass spectra of heavy and light mesons is computed within the frameworkof the relativistic flux tube model. A good agreement with the experimentaldata is obtained provided that the flux tube contributions, includingretardation and spin-orbit effects, are supplemented by a one-gluon-exchangepotential, a quark self-energy term and instanton-induced interactions. Noarbitrary constant is needed to fit the absolute scale of the mass spectra, andthe different parameters are fitted on lattice QCD in order to stronglyrestrict the arbitrariness of our model. The relevance of the present approachis discussed in the case of glueballs, and the glueball spectrum we compute iscompared to the lattice QCD one. Finally, we make connections between theresults of our model and the nature of some newly discovered experimentalstates such as the f_0(1810), X(3940), Y(3940), etc.

The Kondo effect observed in recent STM experiments on transport through CoPcand TBrPP-Co molecules adsorbed on Au(111) and Cu(111) surfaces, respectively,is discussed within the framework of a simple model (Phys. Rev. Lett. {\bf 97},076806 (2006)). It is shown that, in the Kondo regime and by varying theadequate model parameters, it is possible to produce a crossover from aconductance Kondo peak (CoPc) to a conductance Fano dip (TBrPP-Co). In the caseof TBrPP-Co/Cu(111) we show that the model reproduces the changes in the shapeof the Fano dip, the raising of the Kondo temperature and shifting to higherenergies of the dip minimum when the number of nearest neighbors molecules islowered. These features are in line with experimental observations indicatingthat our simple model contains the essential physics underlying the transportproperties of such complex molecules.

This article studies the potential of opportunist communication in orthogonal multi -universal relay channels (OMRCC). Specifically, we consider a solution, which communicates with a single relay node. The node is a hub that forwards information to the target node. We propose a new agreement that allows the source opportunity to access the channel, using OMRCC orthogonality to reduce interference and enhance throughput. Our results show that compared with traditional random access methods, the proposed protocols can significantly improve the performance of the system, thereby achieving a higher level of network utilization and reducing delay. In addition, we analyze the influence of various factors, such as the number of sources and channel conditions, the impact of system performance, and providing the best configuration of the relevant agreement. Our discovery is of great significance to the design of effective communication systems under the context of contest in multiple nodes.

The Local Galaxy 8 micron Luminosity Function We derive the 8 micron luminosity function of galaxies in the local 11 Mpc volume based on observations from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE). Using a sample of over 1500 galaxies with reliable photometry at 3.4, 4.6, 12, and 22 microns from the ALLWISE data release, we extract spectral energy distributions from 2.5 to 22 microns. Notably, the sample provides detection of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon and warm dust emission features out to the earliest galaxy types of Sa. Through SED modeling with the DUSTEM code, we determine total infrared luminosities and hence calculate 8 micron luminosities for each galaxy. The derived 8 micron luminosity function shows a characteristic double power-law shape when fitted independently in early and late-type galaxy bins, pointing to differences in the dominant sources of dust heating between morphological types. Comparison to previous 6 and 12 micron luminosity functions from smaller volumes indicates that our measurements establish the local baseline against which galaxy evolution can be traced to higher redshifts.

Using the 3.6/4.5/5.8/8.0 micron images with 1.2 arcsec pixel resolution fromthe Spitzer/GLIMPSE survey, we investigated 23 masing and 18 very red objectsthat were not identified in the 2MASS survey. Counterparts for all selectedobjects were found in the GLIMPSE images. Color indices in these IR bandssuggest the presence of a high-extinction layer of more than a few tenths of asolar mass in front of the central star. Furthermore, radio observations in theSiO and H2O maser lines found characteristic maser-line spectra of the embeddedobjects, e.g., the SiO J=1-0 line intensity in the v=2 state stronger than thatof the v=1 state, or very widespread H2O maser emission spectra. This indicatesthat these objects are actually enshrouded by very thick circumstellar matter,some of which cannot be ascribed to the AGB wind of the central star.Individually interesting objects are discussed, including two newly found waterfountains and an SiO source with nebulosity.

Let $z=(z_1, ..., z_n)$ and $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac {\partial^2}{\partialz^2_i}$ the Laplace operator. A formal power series $P(z)$ is said to be {\itHessian Nilpotent}(HN) if its Hessian matrix $\Hes P(z)=(\frac {\partial^2P}{\partial z_i\partial z_j})$ is nilpotent. In recent developments in [BE1],[M] and [Z], the Jacobian conjecture has been reduced to the followingso-called {\it vanishing conjecture}(VC) of HN polynomials: {\it for anyhomogeneous HN polynomial $P(z)$ $($of degree $d=4$$)$, we have $\Delta^mP^{m+1}(z)=0$ for any $m>>0$.} In this paper, we first show that, the VC holdsfor any homogeneous HN polynomial $P(z)$ provided that the projectivesubvarieties ${\mathcal Z}_P$ and ${\mathcal Z}_{\sigma_2}$ of $\mathbb CP^{n-1}$ determined by the principal ideals generated by $P(z)$ and$\sigma_2(z):=\sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2$, respectively, intersect only at regularpoints of ${\mathcal Z}_P$. Consequently, the Jacobian conjecture holds for thesymmetric polynomial maps $F=z-\nabla P$ with $P(z)$ HN if $F$ has no non-zerofixed point $w\in \mathbb C^n$ with $\sum_{i=1}^n w_i^2=0$. Secondly, we showthat the VC holds for a HN formal power series $P(z)$ if and only if, for anypolynomial $f(z)$, $\Delta^m (f(z)P(z)^m)=0$ when $m>>0$.

The star formation history (SFH) of Local Group galaxies is a powerful toolfor studying their evolution, including chemical enrichment histories andstellar population gradients, which in turn may shed light on the role ofreionization or Supernovae feedback in galaxy formation and evolution. Inparticular, isolated dwarfs are ideal laboratories since their evolution hasnot been complicated by the vicinity of giant galaxies. In this paper, wepresent the project Local Cosmology from Isolated Dwarfs (LCID), aimed atderiving detailed SFHs for a sample of Local Group isolated dwarf galaxies. Toaccomplish this goal we have collected, using the ACS on board the HST,color-magnitude diagrams (CMD) reaching their oldest main sequence turnoff(V~28 or M_V~+3.5) with good photometric accuracy. Some preliminary resultsfrom the CMDs are shown and briefly discussed.

This article investigates the Loewner driving function of trajectoAy arcs of quadratic differentials. We first introduce the cnocept of Loewner driving functions and their significance in the study of quadratic differentials. We then present the main result of the artixcle, which establishes a explicit formula for the Loewner driving funciton of trajectory arcs of quadratic differentials. The formula is proven using a combination of mathematical techniques, including complex analOysis and differential geometry. The article alos discusses the implications of the reslt for the study of quadratic differentials and their applications in various fields. Finally, we provide examples and numreical simulations to illustrate the effectiveness of the formula and its potential uses.

Current methods for comparing the secondary structures of mRNAs are computationally intensive and do not scale well to large data sets. We present new polynomial time algorithms for searching for similarity between two protein sequences, which take into account the structural constraints imposed by the secondary structures of the corresponding mRNAs. Our methods take advantage of recent advances in graph-based data structures to encode both the sequences and the permissible mRNA secondary structures as graphs. We believe that these new methods will be useful tools for molecular biologists to gain further insight into the relationships between mRNA structure, protein function, and organismal phenotype. Computational simulations show that our methods can compute biologically meaningful sequence alignments up to an order of magnitude faster than existing methods for restricted structural classes, making it feasible to use these methods for large-scale applications.

The metal enrichment in the intracluster medium (ICM) of galaxy clusters provides key insights into the feedback processes and the chemical enrichment history of the member galaxies. In this work, we investigate the metallicity gradient of the hottest gas phase in the ICM of a massive, X-ray-luminous galaxy cluster at \(z = 1.47\), using a deep \(\sim\)110 ks Chandra observation. We find that the metallicity of the ICM is roughly constant within \(r_{500}\), and significantly higher at \(r_{500}-r_{1000}\) in the outskirts of the cluster. A prominent cool core is detected with a high central metallicity. We compare the observed metallicity profiles with predictions from state-of-the-art cosmological simulations. The observed metallicity profiles are well reproduced by the simulations that include the effect of galactic superwinds.

Grand unified theories with supersymmetry (SUSY-GUTs) elegantly address open questions in particle physics and cosmology. This review explores the relationships between SUSY-GUTs, the seesaw mechanism for neutrino mass generation, and supersymmetric dark matter in the form of the lightest neutralino. SUSY-GUTs incorporate the seesaw mechanism through the introduction of right-handed neutrino superfields, providing a natural explanation for neutrino masses. Many SUSY-GUT models predict the lightest supersymmetric particle is the neutralino, which could account for dark matter through thermal freeze-out in the early universe. Precise gauge coupling unification in SUSY-GUTs favors hierarchical right-handed neutrino masses as suggested by the seesaw mechanism. Potential signatures of the neutralino dark matter candidate are discussed for collider experiments like the LHC and direct detection experiments. In summary, this work comprehensively links SUSY-GUTs to the seesaw mechanism and neutralino dark matter.

The large-scale Galactic interstellar radiation field (ISRF) is the result ofstellar emission and dust re-processing of starlight. Where the energy densityof the ISRF is high (e.g., the Galactic Centre), the dominant gamma-rayemission in individual supernova remnants (SNRs), such as G0.9+0.1, may comefrom inverse Compton (IC) scattering of the ISRF. Several models of the ISRFexist. The most recent one, which has been calculated by us, predicts asignificantly higher ISRF than the well-used model of Mathis, Mezger, andPanagia. However,comparison with data is limited to local observations. Basedon our current estimate of the ISRF we predict the gamma-ray emission in theSNRs G0.9+0.1 and RXJ1713, and pair-production absorption features above 20 TeVin the spectra of G0.9+0.1, J1713-381, and J1634-472. We discuss how GLAST,along with current and future very high energy instruments, may be able toprovide upper bounds on the large-scale ISRF.

Provide a general concept of data processing and calibration strategies for amber's scientific model, that is, for scientific applications, it will provide examples for high -angle resolution and spectral imaging mode.
