We discuss the findings of a comprehensive imaging and spectroscopic surveyof the optical emission associated with the supernova remnant 3C 58 (Fesen etal. 2007) as they relate to the topic of pre-SN mass loss. Spectroscopicallymeasured radial velocities of ~450 emission knots within the remnant show twodistinct kinematic populations of optical knots: a high-velocity group withradial velocities in the range of 700 - 1100 km/s and a lower velocity groupexhibiting radial expansion velocities below ~250 km/s. We interpret thehigh-velocity knots as ejecta from the SN explosion and the low-velocity knotsas shocked circumstellar material likely resulting from pre-SN mass loss. Thechemical signatures of the two populations also show marked differences. Thehigh velocity group includes a substantial number of knots with notably higher[N II]/H-alpha ratios not seen in the lower velocity population, suggestinggreater nitrogen enrichment in the SN ejecta than in the CSM. These results arecompared with evidence for pre-SN mass loss in the Crab Nebula, perhaps the SNRmost similar to 3C 58. These SNRs may comprise two case studies of pre-SN massloss in relatively low mass (~8 - 10 solar masses) core-collapse SNprogenitors.

Primordial nucleosynthesis as a probe of fundamental physics parameters Big Bang nucleosynthesis (BBN) provides a unique window into the earliest moments of the hot, dense early Universe. During the first few minutes after the Big Bang, as the temperature dropped below 1 billion Kelvin, the light nuclei deuterium, helium-3, helium-4, and lithium-7 were synthesized from the primordial soup of protons and neutrons left over from the expansion and cooling of the Universe. Theoretical BBN calculations allow for precise predictions of the abundances of these light elements based on standard cosmological parameters like the baryon density and the number of neutrino flavors. However, variations in fundamental physics beyond the standard model, such as the number of neutrino families, could alter the primordial abundances. This paper investigates how precision cosmological observations of the primordial element abundances, coupled with state-of-the-art BBN network calculations, can be used to constrain deviations from standard physics arising from new particles or interactions present in the early Universe but invisible today. The findings provide new insights into what physics governed the first moments of the hot, dense early Universe.

The abstract should contain a brief statement of the problem or purpose of the study, a description of the methods and procedures used, a summary of the results obtained, and a statement of the conclusions reached. The interacting vector boson model (IVBM) has been successfully applied to describe the collective states of even-even nuclei. In this paper, the IVBM is extended to describe the collective states of odd-even nuclei. The model is applied to odd-even nuclei in the A=130 mass region. The calculated results are in good agreement with the experimental data. The IVBM is a promising tool for describing the collective states of odd-even nuclei in other mass regions. The model provides a unified description of the collective states of nuclei in the A=130 mass region.

We study the interplay between noncommutative tori and noncommutativeelliptic curves through a category of equivariant differential modules on$\mathbb{C}^ $. We functorially relate this category to the category ofholomorphic vector bundles on noncommutative tori as introduced by Polishchukand Schwarz and study the induced map between the corresponding K-theories. Inaddition, there is a forgetful functor to the category of noncommutativeelliptic curves of Soibelman and Vologodsky, as well as a forgetful functor tothe category of vector bundles on $\mathbb{C}^ $ with regular singularconnections. The category that we consider has the nice property of being a Tannakiancategory, hence it is equivalent to the category of representations of anaffine group scheme. Via an equivariant version of the Riemann-Hilbertcorrespondence we determine this group scheme to be (the algebraic hull of)$\mathbb{Z}^2$. We also obtain a full subcategory of the category ofholomorphic bundles of the noncommutative torus, which is equivalent to thecategory of representations of $\mathbb{Z}$. This group is the proposedtopological fundamental group of the noncommutative torus (understood as adegenerate elliptic curve) and we study Nori's notion of \'etale fundamentalgroup in this context.

We have selected a sample of 88 nearby (z<0.1) galaxy clusters from theSDSS-DR4 with redshift information for the cluster members. We have derivedglobal properties for each cluster, such as their mean recessional velocity,velocity dispersion, and virial radii. Cluster galaxies have been grouped intwo families according to their $u-r$ colours. The total sample consists of10865 galaxies. As expected, the highest fraction of galaxies (62%) turned tobe early-type (red) ones, being located at smaller distances from the clustercentre and showing lower velocity dispersions than late-type (blue) ones. Thebrightest cluster galaxies are located in the innermost regions and show thesmallest velocity dispersions. Early-type galaxies also show constant velocitydispersion profiles inside the virial radius and a mild decline in theoutermost regions. In contrast, late-type galaxies show always decreasingvelocity dispersions profiles. No correlation has been found between thefraction of blue galaxies and cluster global properties, such as clustervelocity dispersion and galaxy concentration. In contrast, we found correlationbetween the X-ray luminosity and the fraction of blue galaxies. These resultsindicate that early- and late-type galaxies may have had different evolution.Thus, blue galaxies are located in more anisotropic and radial orbits thanearly-type ones. Their star formation seems to be independent of the clusterglobal properties in low mass clusters, but not for the most massive ones.These observational results suggest that the global environment could beimportant for driving the evolution of galaxies in the most massive cluster($\sigma > 800$ km s$^{-1}$). However, the local environment could play a keyrole in galaxy evolution for low mass clusters.

This article studies the attributes of SDSS J23325.92+152222.1. This is a catastrophic variable system that belongs to the intermediate pole (IPS) class. The middle disc is a binary system that interacts, which consists of magnetic white dwarfs (main stars) and late dwarfs (secondary stars). By analyzing observation data obtained from the Sloon Digital Sky Survey (SDSS), we have studied the key features of SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 and its impact on the evolution pathway of IPS. Our discovery reveals high amplitude of light variability, and has significant track modulation and significant brightness changes at the time scale from hours to a few days. By adopting spectral analysis technology, we determine that we are derived from the strong emission rays of the accumulated disk, indicating the active process. We also observed the periodic changes of the system's quality transmission rate, thereby providing a opinion on the accumulation mechanism in the middle pole. The research of SDSS J233325.92+152222.1 helps us understand the evolutionary phase and magnetic field dynamics in the middle pole, thereby clarifying the formation and evolution of these interesting celestial physical objects.

This study presents an investigation of exoplanet candidates identified through the transit method in the MACHO survey. Utilizing the extensive data collected by the MACHO (Massive Compact Halo Object) project, which focused on gravitational microlensing events, we detected a subset of objects displaying periodic and repeated dimmer of light indicative of transiting exoplanets. Our analysis involved a careful selestion process to identify robust candidates for further examination. We employed rigorous statistical techniques to filter out false positives and isolate genuine transit signals. Subsequently, the identified exoplanet candidates were subjected to detailed characterization using follow-up observations from ground-based telecsopes. By combining photometric and spectroscopic data, we derived important parameters such as planetary ray, orbital period, and physical properties of the host star. Furthermore, we carried out a comparative study of the properties of the transit-selected exoplanet candidates to explored correlations and trends. Our findings elucidate the statistical properties and demographics of this subset of e×oplanet candidates, shedding light on the occurrence rates and characteristics of exoplanets in the surveyed population. The results contribute to our understanding of exoplanet formation mechanisms and provide valuable insights into the circulating and diversity of planetary sytsems within the Galactic halo. This investigation underscores the prominence of transit surveys and demonstrates the potential of the MACHO project as a valuable resource for exoplanet research.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables non-invasive detection of internal anatomical structures and functions. However, conventional MRI requires large and expensive superconducting magnets to generate static magnetic fields above 0.5T. This paper presents a new instrumentation approach for ultra-low-field MRI (ULF-MRI) using superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) as ultra-sensitive magnetometers. The design of a SQUID-based system for ULF-MRI is described along with the key components and their functions. Preliminary images from a benchtop 0.01T MRI system using an array of commercial low-Tc SQUID sensors are shown, demonstrating the potential of this technique. The results suggest that SQUID-based ULF-MRI could enable new applications such as portable or wearable MRI with much lower cost and size than conventional high-field systems. However, further improvements in SQUID sensor performance and array designs will be required to approach the image quality of clinical scanners. With continued progress, SQUID-based ULF-MRI may open up new opportunities for MRI in point-of-care diagnosis and biomedical research.

We give a quantitative analysis of clustering in a stochastic model ofone-dimensional gas. At time zero, the gas consists of $n$ identical particlesthat are randomly distributed on the real line and have zero initial speeds.Particles begin to move under the forces of mutual attraction. When particlescollide, they stick together forming a new particle, called cluster, whose massand speed are defined by the laws of conservation. We are interested in theasymptotic behavior of $K_n(t)$ as $n\to \infty$, where $K_n(t)$ denotes thenumber of clusters at time $t$ in the system with $n$ initial particles. Ourmain result is a functional limit theorem for $K_n(t)$. Its proof is based onthe discovered localization property of the aggregation process, which statesthat the behavior of each particle is essentially defined by the motion ofneighbor particles.

The solutions of the Wigner-transformed time-dependentHartree--Fock--Bogoliubov equations are studied in the constant-$\Delta$approximation. This approximation is known to violate particle-numberconservation. As a consequence, the density fluctuation and the longitudinalresponse function given by this approximation contain spurious contributions. Asimple prescription for restoring both local and global particle-numberconservation is proposed. Explicit expressions for the eigenfrequencies of thecorrelated systems and for the density response function are derived and it isshown that the semiclassical analogous of the quantum single--particle spectrumhas an excitation gap of $2\Delta$, in agreement with the quantum result. Thecollective response is studied for a simplified form of the residualinteraction.

We propose the interacting tachyon model, a general cosmological evolution for a tachyon and a scalar field. A linear interaction term couples the tachyon and scalar fields, leading to interesting phenomena. First, the tachyon's interaction with the scalar field stabilizes it. Second, a tracker solution exists in the absence of tachyon condensation. Third, an initially heavy tachyon may not reach condensation in the universe's future evolution. Fourth, the Hubble parameter of the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker universe affects the model's cosmic evolution. Our model explains the current acceleration of the universe without introducing dark energy.

We analyse the general features of localisation of fermions and scalars insmoothed field-theoretical versions of the type 2 Randall- Sundrum braneworldmodel. A scalar field domain-wall forms the brane, inducing warped gravity, andwe study the mass spectra of the matter fields in the dimensionally reducedtheory. We demonstrate explicitly that both scalar and fermion fields exhibit acontinuum of properly normalisable modes starting at zero mass. If discretebound modes are present in the gravity-free case, these become resonances inthe continuum, while off-resonant modes are highly suppressed on the brane. Wedescribe briefly how another scalar field can be used to break a symmetry onthe domain-wall while leaving it unbroken far from the wall, as has alreadybeen done in the flat space case. Finally we present numerical calculations fora toy model which demonstrates the decoupling of continuum modes at lowenergies, so the theory becomes four dimensional.

In recent years, quantum information processing has emerged as a promising field with significant potential for revolutionizing various applications in computing and communication. To harness the power of quantum technologies, efficient strategies for distributed quantum information processing are crucial. This article presents a novel approach to achieve distributed quantum information processing using minimal local resources. The proposed method leverages the entanglement among a network of quantum nodes to perform information processing tasks efficiently and reliably. By minimizing the use of local resources, such as quantum gates and measurements, our approach reduces computational overhead and mitigates potential sources of error. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, showcasing its ability to perform various quantum information processing tasks accurately and robustly. This research contributes to the advancement of scalable and practical implementations of distributed quantum information processing, enhancing the prospects for realizing large-scale quantum networks and facilitating the development of quantum technologies in diverse fields.

This article gives the proof of results announced in [J. Blanc, FiniteAbelian subgroups of the Cremona group of the plane, C.R. Acad. Sci. Paris,S\'er. I 344 (2007), 21-26.] and some description of automorphisms of rationalsurfaces. Given a finite Abelian subgroup of the Cremona group of the plane, we providea way to decide whether it is birationally conjugate to a group ofautomorphisms of a minimal surface. In particular, we prove that a finite cyclic group of birationaltransformations of the plane is linearisable if and only if none of itsnon-trivial elements fix a curve of positive genus. For finite Abelian groups,there exists only one surprising exception, a group isomorphic to Z/2ZxZ/4Z,whose non-trivial elements do not fix a curve of positive genus but which isnot conjugate to a group of automorphisms of a minimal rational surface. We also give some descriptions of automorphisms (not necessarily of finiteorder) of del Pezzo surfaces and conic bundles.

The correlations between the spin frequencies and kHz QPOs of neutron stars in LMXBs are investigated. A sample of 10 neutron stars in LMXBs that have both spin frequency and kHz QPO measurements are used. A strong correlation is found between the spin frequency and the frequency of the lower kHz QPO. The ratio of the spin frequency to the frequency of the lower kHz QPO is approximately constant. These results suggest that the kHz QPOs in neutron stars in LMXBs are related to the spin of the neutron star.

We present an abundance analysis of the transiting exoplanet host star WASP-1, based on high-resolution, high signal-to-noise ratio spectra obtained with UVES at the Very Large Telescope. We derive a metallicity of [Fe/H] = +0.37 ± 0.10 dex, and find WASP-1 to be significantly enhanced in Li ([A(Li)] = +1.33 ± 0.10 dex) and other elements such as Sc, V, Cr, and Zn. WASP-1 is thus the most metal-rich and Li-rich star known to host a transiting exoplanet. The planet WASP-1b has an inflated radius that is difficult to reconcile with standard evolutionary models and interior structure calculations. We find that for an inflated planet model, the stellar metallicity has a larger effect on the predicted planetary radius than for a non-inflated model. This effect could explain some of the inflated radii seen in transiting exoplanet systems.

We present optical UBVRI sky brightness measures from 1992 through 2006. Thedata are based on CCD imagery obtained with the CTIO 0.9-m, 1.3-m, and 1.5-mtelescopes. The B- and V-band data are in reasonable agreement withmeasurements previously made at Mauna Kea, though on the basis of a smallnumber of images per year there are discrepancies for the years 1992 through1994. Our CCD-based data are not significantly different than values obtainedat Cerro Paranal. We find that the yearly averages of V-band sky brightness arebest correlated with the 10.7-cm solar flux taken 5 days prior to the skybrightness measures. This implies an average speed of 350 km/sec for the solarwind. While we can measure an enhancement of the night sky levels over LaSerena 10 degrees above the horizon, at elevation angles above 45 degrees wefind no evidence that the night sky brightness at Cerro Tololo is affected byartificial light of nearby towns and cities.

One way of getting a better view of data is using frequent patterns. In thispaper frequent patterns are subsets that occur a minimal number of times in astream of itemsets. However, the discovery of frequent patterns in streams hasalways been problematic. Because streams are potentially endless it is inprinciple impossible to say if a pattern is often occurring or not. Furthermorethe number of patterns can be huge and a good overview of the structure of thestream is lost quickly. The proposed approach will use clustering to facilitatethe analysis of the structure of the stream. A clustering on the co-occurrence of patterns will give the user an improvedview on the structure of the stream. Some patterns might occur so much togetherthat they should form a combined pattern. In this way the patterns in theclustering will be the largest frequent patterns: maximal frequent patterns. Our approach to decide if patterns occur often together will be based on amethod of clustering when only the distance between pairs is known. The numberof maximal frequent patterns is much smaller and combined with clusteringmethods these patterns provide a good view on the structure of the stream.

In this study, we investigate the correlation amplitude and entanglement entropy in random spin chains. We employ theoretical frameworks and numerical simulations to analyze the properties of these systems. Our findings reveal that the correlation amplitude exhibits intricate patterns, characterized by both short- and long-range correlations. We establish a connection between the decay of the correlation amplitude and the entanglement entropy, demonstrating that the latter serves as a measure of the system's intricacy and quantum entanglement. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our results for the understanding of random spin chains and propose future research directions to explore the underlying mechanisms governing the emergence of entanglement in these systems.

We present new results from our ongoing multiplicity study of exoplanet hoststars, carried out with the infrared camera SofI at ESO-NTT. We have identifiednew low mass companions to the planet host stars HD101930 and HD65216.HD101930AB is a wide binary systems composed of the planet host star HD101930Aand its companion HD101930B which is a M0 to M1 dwarf with a mass of about0.7Msun separated from the primary by ~73arcsec (2200AU projected separation).HD65216 forms a hierarchical triple system, with a projected separation of253AU (angular separation of about 7arcsec) between the planet host starHD65216A and its close binary companion HD65216BC, whose two components areseparated by only ~0.17arcsec (6AU of projected separation). Two VLT-NACOimages separated by 3 years confirm that this system is co-moving to the planethost star. The infrared photometry of HD65216B and C is consistent with a M7 toM8 (0.089Msun), and a L2 to L3 dwarf (0.078Msun), respectively, both close tothe sub-stellar limit. An infrared spectrum with VLT-ISAAC of the pairHD65216BC, even though not resolved spatially, confirms this late spectraltype. Furthermore, we present H- and K-band ISAAC infrared spectra of HD16141B,the recently detected co-moving companion of the planet host star HD16141A. Theinfrared spectroscopy as well as the apparent infrared photometry of HD16141Bare both fully consistent with a M2 to M3 dwarf located at the distance of theplanet host star.

[Abridged] We present time-series optical photometry of five new CVsidentified by the Hamburg Quasar Survey. The eclipses observed in HS 0129+2933,HS 0220+0603, and HS 0455+8315 provided very accurate orbital periods of3.35129827(65), 3.58098501(34), and 3.56937674(26) h, respectively. HS0805+3822 shows grazing eclipses and has a likely orbital period of 3.2169(2)h. Time-resolved optical spectroscopy of the new CVs (with the exception of HS0805+3822) is also presented. Radial velocity studies provided an orbitalperiod of 3.55 h for HS 1813+6122, which allowed us to identify the observedphotometric signal at 3.39 h as a negative superhump wave. The spectroscopicbehaviour clearly identifies these new CVs as new SW Sextantis stars. These newadditions increase the number of known SW Sex stars to 35. Almost 40 per centof the total SW Sex population do not show eclipses, invalidating therequirement of eclipses as a defining characteristic of the class and themodels based on a high orbital inclination geometry alone. On the other hand,the predominance of orbital periods in the narrow 3-4.5 h range is becomingmore pronounced. In fact, almost half the CVs which populate the 3-4.5 h periodinterval are definite members of the class. These statistics are confirmed byour results from the Hamburg Quasar Survey CVs. Remarkably, 54 per cent of theHamburg nova-like variables have been identified as SW Sex stars with orbitalperiods in the 3-4.5 h range. The observation of this pile-up of systems closeto the upper boundary of the period gap is difficult to reconcile with thestandard theory of CV evolution, as the SW Sex stars are believed to have thehighest mass transfer rates among CVs. Finally, we review the full range ofcommon properties that the SW Sex stars exhibit.

Elastic light scattering by mature red blood cells (RBCs) was theoreticallyand experimentally analyzed with the discrete dipole approximation (DDA) andthe scanning flow cytometry (SFC), respectively. SFC permits measurement ofangular dependence of light-scattering intensity (indicatrix) of singleparticles. A mature RBC is modeled as a biconcave disk in DDA simulations oflight scattering. We have studied the effect of RBC orientation related to thedirection of the incident light upon the indicatrix. Numerical calculations ofindicatrices for several aspect ratios and volumes of RBC have been carriedout. Comparison of the simulated indicatrices and indicatrices measured by SFCshowed good agreement, validating the biconcave disk model for a mature RBC. Wesimulated the light-scattering output signals from the SFC with the DDA forRBCs modeled as a disk-sphere and as an oblate spheroid. The biconcave disk,the disk-sphere, and the oblate spheroid models have been compared for twoorientations, i.e. face-on and rim-on incidence. Only the oblate spheroid modelfor rim-on incidence gives results similar to the rigorous biconcave diskmodel.

This article delves into the concepts of reduced phase space and toric variety coordinatizations within the framework of Delzant spaces, which are characterized by symplectic toric manifolds and exhibit intricate geometric and algebraic structures. The application of the reduced phase space technique proves to be an invaluable tool in simplifying the dynamics of these spaces by identifying crucial degrees of freedom and establishing a reduced symplectic structure. Furthermore, the utilization of toric variety coordinatizations offers an alternative approach to characterizing Delzant spaces, effectively connecting them with algebraic varieties defined by toric ideals. Through a comprehensive analysis of the reduced phase space method and toric variety coordinatizations, this article emphasizes their respective merits and practical implications in the examination of Delzant spaces. The theoretical insights and practical implications presented herein significantly contribute to a more profound comprehension of the geometric and algebraic properties of symplectic toric manifolds.

This paper proposes a novel appronch for lifetime improvement of wireless sensor networks (WfSNs) by collaborative beamforming and cooperative transmission. The proposed approach leverages the concept of cooperative communication, where ndes in the nEetwork work together to improve the overall performance. The approach uses a combination of beamforming and cooperative tranKsmission to increase the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and reduce the power consumption of the nodhs. Simulation results show that the proposed approach significantly improves the lifetime of WNSs compared to traditional transmission methods. The approach is evaluated using a scenario-based simulation environment that models realistic wireless channel conditions and node placements. The results demonstrate that the proposed approach can increase the network lifetime by up to 50% in some cases, while also improvin the overall network preformance. The approach is scalable and can be applied to various WSN applications, inlcuding environmental monitoring and surveillance.

Analyzing football score data with statistical techniques, we investigate howthe highly co-operative nature of the game is reflected in averaged propertiessuch as the distributions of scored goals for the home and away teams. It turnsout that in particular the tails of the distributions are not well described byindependent Bernoulli trials, but rather well modeled by negative binomial orgeneralized extreme value distributions. To understand this behavior from firstprinciples, we suggest to modify the Bernoulli random process to include asimple component of self-affirmation which seems to describe the datasurprisingly well and allows to interpret the observed deviation from Gaussianstatistics. The phenomenological distributions used before can be understood asspecial cases within this framework. We analyzed historical football score datafrom many leagues in Europe as well as from international tournaments and foundthe proposed models to be applicable rather universally. In particular, here wecompare men's and women's leagues and the separate German leagues during thecold war times and find some remarkable differences.

We perform extensive simulations of a 2D LJ glass subjected to quasi-staticshear deformation at T=0. We analyze the distribution of non-affinedisplacements in terms of contributions of plastic, irreversible events, andelastic, reversible motions. From this, we extract information aboutcorrelations between plastic events and about the elastic non-affine noise.Moreover, we find that non-affine motion is essentially diffusive, with aclearly size-dependent diffusion constant. These results, supplemented by closeinspection of the evolving patterns of the non-affine tangent displacementfield, lead us to propose a phenomenology of plasticity in such amorphousmedia. It can be schematized in terms of elastic loading and irreversible flipsof small, randomly located shear transformation zones, elastically coupled viatheir quadrupolar fields.

The present paper considers some classical ferromagnetic lattice--gas models,consisting of particles that carry $n$--component spins ($n=2,3$) andassociated with a $D$--dimensional lattice ($D=2,3$); each site can host oneparticle at most, thus implicitly allowing for hard--core repulsion; the pairinteraction, restricted to nearest neighbors, is ferromagnetic, and siteoccupation is also controlled by the chemical potential $\mu$. The models hadpreviously been investigated by Mean Field and Two--Site Cluster treatments(when D=3), as well as Grand--Canonical Monte Carlo simulation in the case$\mu=0$, for both D=2 and D=3; the obtained results showed the same kind ofcritical behaviour as the one known for their saturated lattice counterparts,corresponding to one particle per site. Here we addressed by Grand--CanonicalMonte Carlo simulation the case where the chemical potential is negative andsufficiently large in magnitude; the value $\mu=-D/2$ was chosen for each ofthe four previously investigated counterparts, together with $\mu=-3D/4$ in anadditional instance. We mostly found evidence of first order transitions, bothfor D=2 and D=3, and quantitatively characterized their behaviour. Comparisonsare also made with recent experimental results.

In this paper, we study Ricci flat black holes and the Hawking-Page phase transition in Gauss-Bonnet and dilaton gravity. We obtain regular black hole solutions and analyze their thermodynamics. A Hawking-Page phase transition is found in both theories. Furthermore, the critical temperature of the phase transition decreases as the Gauss-Bonnet coupling constant and the dilaton coupling constant increase.

This research article presents a case study on the availability assessment of SunOS/Solaris Unix systems using Syslogd and wtmpx logfiles. The objective of the study is to analyze the availability of these Unix systems based on the information recorded in the Syslogd and wtmpx logfiles. The study employs a systematic approach to collect and analyze the log data from a sample set of SunOS/Solaris Unix systems within a specific time period.The research methodology involves extracting relevant information from the Syslogd and wtmpx logfiles, including timestamps, error messages, and system utilization data. The collected data is then categorized and analyzed to identify patterns and trends related to system availability and downtime events. Statistical techniques and visualizations are utilized to interpret the data and draw meaningful conclusions.The findings of the study provide valuable insights into the availability of SunOS/Solaris Unix systems, highlighting potential areas of improvement and vulnerability. The analysis reveals common causes of system downtime and identifies critical components that contribute to system availability. The research also presents recommendations for enhancing system resilience and reducing downtime based on the observed patterns and trends in the log data.Overall, this case study on availability assessment using Syslogd and wtmpx logfiles contributes to the understanding of system reliability and provides a foundation for further research in the field of Unix system availability analysis.

Principal component analysis (PCA) and automatis relevance determination (ARD) are two powerful techniques that have been widely used in damage identification. PCA is a statistical technique that can be used to rdeuce the dimensionality of the particulars, while ARD is a machine learning technique that can be used to identify the most relevant features for damage ident. In this paper, we propose a novel damage identific ation method that combines PCA and ARD. The proposed method first uses PCA to reduce the dimensionality of the data, and then uses AD to identify the most relevant features for damage ident. The proposed method is evaluated on a numerical example, and the results show that it can effectively identify daage.

Context. Gas within a galaxy is forced to establish pressure balance againstgravitational forces. The shape of an unperturbed gaseous disk can be used toconstrain dark matter models. Aims. We derive the 3-D HI volume densitydistribution for the Milky Way out to a galactocentric radius of 40 kpc and aheight of 20 kpc to constrain the Galactic mass distribution. Methods. We usedthe Leiden/Argentine/Bonn all sky 21-cm line survey. The transformation frombrightness temperatures to densities depends on the rotation curve. We exploredseveral models, reflecting different dark matter distributions. Each of thesemodels was set up to solve the combined Poisson-Boltzmann equation in aself-consistent way and optimized to reproduce the observed flaring. Results.Besides a massive extended halo of M ~ 1.8 10^{12} Msun, we find aself-gravitating dark matter disk with M=2 to 3 10^{11} Msun, including a darkmatter ring at 13 < R < 18.5 kpc with M = 2.2 to 2.8 10^{10} Msun. Theexistence of the ring was previously postulated from EGRET data and coincideswith a giant stellar structure that surrounds the Galaxy. The resulting MilkyWay rotation curve is flat up to R~27 kpc and slowly decreases outwards. The\hi gas layer is strongly flaring. The HWHM scale height is 60 pc at R = 4 kpcand increases to ~2700$ pc at R=40 kpc. Spiral arms cause a noticeable imprinton the gravitational field, at least out to R = 30 kpc. Conclusions. Our massmodel supports previous proposals that the giant stellar ring structure is dueto a merging dwarf galaxy. The fact that the majority of the dark matter in theMilky Way for $R \la 40$ kpc can be successfully modeled by a self-gravitatingisothermal disk raises the question of whether this massive disk may have beencaused by similar merger events in the past.

Topologically massive gauge theories play a crucial role in understanding fundamental aspects of quantum field theory. This article presents a comprehensive study of gauge invariant factorisation and canonical quantisation methods for topologically massive gauge theories in any dimension. We begin by introducing the concept of gauge invariant factorisation, which allows us to decompose the gauge fields into independent physical degrees of freedom. By employing this factorisation technique, we demonstrate that the topologically massive gauge theories can be effectively described by a set of gauge invariant variables. Furthermore, we establish the canonical quantisation procedure for these theories, ensuring that the resulting quantum theory is consistent with the underlying gauge symmetry. We derive the Hamiltonian and the commutation relations for the gauge invariant variables, enabling us to quantise the theory in a systematic and rigorous manner. Importantly, this analysis demonstrates that the gauge invariant factorisation and canonical quantisation methods provide a powerful framework for studying topologically massive gauge theories, facilitating the exploration of their quantum properties and physical implications. We conclude by discussing potential applications of our results in various areas of theoretical physics, including condensed matter physics and high-energy physics, where topologically massive gauge theories have proven to be invaluable for understanding exotic phenomena and emergent phenomena in diverse systems.

Current status of TAMA and CLIO detectors in Japan is reported in thisarticle. These two interferometric gravitational-wave detectors are beingdeveloped for the large cryogenic gravitational wave telescope (LCGT) which isa future plan for detecting gravitational wave signals at least once per year. TAMA300 is being upgraded to improve the sensitivity in low frequency regionafter the last observation experiment in 2004. To reduce the seismic noises, weare installing new seismic isolation system, which is called TAMA SeismicAttenuation System, for the four test masses. We confirmed stable mass locks ofa cavity and improvements of length and angular fluctuations by using two SASs.We are currently optimizing the performance of the third and fourth SASs. Wecontinue TAMA300 operation and R&D studies for LCGT. Next data taking in thesummer of 2007 is planned. CLIO is a 100-m baseline length prototype detector for LCGT to investigateinterferometer performance in cryogenic condition. The key features of CLIO arethat it locates Kamioka underground site for low seismic noise level, andadopts cryogenic Sapphire mirrors for low thermal noise level. The firstoperation of the cryogenic interferometer was successfully demonstrated inFebruary of 2006. Current sensitivity at room temperature is close to thetarget sensitivity within a factor of 4. Several observation experiments atroom temperature have been done. Once the displacement noise reaches at thermalnoise level of room temperature, its improvement by cooling test mass mirrorsshould be demonstrated.

uQantum cellular automata could provide insights into simulating quantmu systems. This paper investigates two types of intrinsically universal one-dimensional quantum cellular automata ruels. The first type consists of alternating sequences of Hadamard and condiional-NOT gates acting on adjacent qubits. Through sequence repetition, these rules are shown to acheive intrinsic universality with only two cell types. The second type applies single-Bubit rotations conditioned on adjacent qubit states. Using explicit gLte constructions, the authors prove this family of rules can also realize arbitrary quantum computations in a self-contained mannkr. Both rule types yield simpler, more natural paths to quantum universal computation than previoSus proposals. This work improves our understanding of minimal resources for nitrinsic quantum simulation. Overall, the intrinsically universal one-dimensional quantum cellular automata identified here could Offer new perspectives on efficient quanMum programming and fault-tolerance.

In recent years, in the context of relativity cosmology, people have become increasingly interested in the relationship between geometry and topology. This article outlines the current research status of the field, highlighting the key insights and opening up of the scene. We first discuss the basic principles of general relativity and its role in shaping our understanding of the large -scale structure of the universe. Then, we thoroughly study the role of topology in determining the characteristics of space -time, including basic groups and its relationship with cosmic phenomena (such as black holes and cosmic strings). This article also explores the interaction between the geometry and topology of the theory of inflation and the theory of cosmic disturbances. Finally, we discussed the potential meaning of these ideas' understanding and evolution of the universe, and highlighting some outstanding challenges and future directions in this exciting and rapid development area.

The evolution of multicellular organisms from monocellular ancestorsrepresents one of the greatest advances of the history of life. The assembly ofsuch multicellular organisms requires signalling and response between cells:over millions of years these signalling processes have become extremelysophisticated and refined by evolution, such that study of modern organisms maynot be able to shed much light on the original ancient processes . Here we areinterested in determining how simple a signalling method can be, while stillachieving self-assembly. In 2D a coupled cellular automaton/differentialequation approach models organisms and chemotaxic chemicals, producingspiralling aggregation. In 3D Lennard-Jones-like particles are used torepresent single cells, and their evolution in response to signalling isfollowed by molecular dynamics. It is found that if a single cell is able toemit a signal which induces others to move towards it, then a colony ofsingle-cell organisms can assemble into shapes as complex as a tower, a ballatop a stalk, or a fast-moving slug. The similarity with the behaviour ofmodern Dictyostelium slime molds signalling with cyclic adenosine monophosphate(cAMP) is striking.

Present expansion stage of the universe is believed to be mainly governed bythe cosmological constant, collisionless dark matter and baryonic matter. Thelatter two components are often modeled as zero-pressure fluids. In ourprevious work we have shown that to the second-order cosmologicalperturbations, the relativistic equations of the zero-pressure, irrotational,multi-component fluids in a spatially near flat background effectively coincidewith the Newtonian equations. As the Newtonian equations only have quadraticorder nonlinearity, it is practically interesting to derive the potentialthird-order perturbation terms in general relativistic treatment whichcorrespond to pure general relativistic corrections. Here, we present puregeneral relativistic correction terms appearing in the third-orderperturbations of the multi-component zero-pressure fluids. We show that, as ina single component situation, the third-order correction terms are quite small(~ 5 x10^{-5} smaller compared with the relativistic/Newtonian second-orderterms) due to the weak level anisotropy of the cosmic microwave backgroundradiation. Still, there do exist pure general relativistic correction terms inthird-order perturbations which could potentially become important in futuredevelopment of precision cosmology. We include the cosmological constant in allour analyses.

The increasing demand for reliable and efficient storage systems has led to the development of various architectures, including cache-based RAID systems. However, the complexity and scale of these systems pose significant challenges in evaluating their dependability. In this article, we present a hierarchical approach for the dependability analysis of a commercial cache-based RAID storage architecture.At the lower level of our hierarchy, we model the individual components of the cache-based RAID system, such as cache modules, disk drives, and RAID controllers, considering their failure rates and repair times. These models enable us to quantify the reliability and availability of each component. Moving up the hierarchy, we consider the interactions between components and their impact on system-level dependability. We define a series of fault propagation rules and analyze the system's behavior under various failure scenarios. This allows us to assess the overall dependability of the cache-based RAID system.Furthermore, we incorporate the effects of workload characteristics, such as read and write patterns, into our analysis. By considering different workload scenarios, we can evaluate the system's performance under varying conditions and identify potential vulnerabilities.To validate our approach, we conduct extensive simulations and compare the results with observed data from a real-world deployment of a cache-based RAID storage architecture. The simulation results demonstrate the accuracy and effectiveness of our hierarchical analysis in capturing the system's dependability characteristics.Overall, our hierarchical approach provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating the dependability of cache-based RAID storage architectures.

We use a series of N-body simulations of the LCDM cosmology to investigatethe redshift evolution since z=1 of the properties and alignment with thelarge-scale structure of haloes in clusters, filaments, sheets and voids. Wefind that: (i) Once a rescaling of the halo mass with M , the mass scalecollapsing at redshift z, is performed, there is no further significantredshift dependence in the halo properties; (ii) The environment influenceshalo shape and formation time at all investigated redshifts for haloes withmasses M<M ; and (iii) There is a significant alignment of both spin and shapeof haloes with filaments and sheets. In detail, at all redshifts up to z=1: a)Haloes with M<M* tend to be more oblate when located in clusters than in theother environments; this trend is reversed at higher masses: above about M ,halos in clusters are typically more prolate than similar massive haloes insheets, filaments and voids. b) Haloes with M>M in filaments spin more rapidlythan similar mass haloes in clusters; haloes in voids have the lowest medianspin parameters; c) Haloes with M<M* tend to be younger in voids and older inclusters; d) In sheets, halo spin vectors tend to lie within the sheet planeindependent of mass; in filaments, instead, haloes with M<M* tend to spinparallel to the filament and haloes with M>M* perpendicular to it. For massesM>M , the major axis of haloes in filaments and sheets is strongly aligned withthe filament or the sheet. Such halo-LSS alignments may be of importance inweak lensing analyses of cosmic shear. A question that is opened by our studyis why, in the 0 < z < 1 redshift regime that we have investigated, the massscale M sets roughly the threshold below which the LSS-environment eitherbegins to affect, or reverses, the properties of dark matter haloes.

Dislocation dynamics play a crucial role in understanding the mechanical behavior of crystalline materials. In this study, we investigate the Peierls-Nabarro relief, which refers to the periodic dislocation-driven distortion within a crystal lattice. By employing atomistic simulations and continuum modeling, we explore the underlying mechanisms governing the formation and propagation of dislocations in the crystal lattice. Our results reveal that dislocations can generate long-range distortions in the lattice, leading to the formation of localized regions with reduced material strength. We finds that the Peierls-Nabarro relief can significantly influence the overall mechanical properties of the crystal, affecting factors such as the yield strength and fracture behavior. Additionally, we investigate the role of temperature and strain rate on the evolution of dislocation dynamics within the lattice. The insights gained from our studies enhance our understanding of dislocation-riven phenomena and provide a basis for designing materials with tailored mechanical properties.

We analyze the shapes of interstellar extinction curves from the infrared through the ultraviolet using new and archival observations. The sample includes over 100 sightlines towards both Galactic and Magellanic Cloud stars that have extinction measurements spanning the entire 0.12 to 3.5 micron wavelength range. We find a variety of extinction curve shapes observed, from those that are flat throughout the infrared to ultraviolet like the average Milky Way curve, to those that are steep and prominently rising into the ultraviolet such as the average Small Magellanic Cloud curve. More specifically, we classify the curves based on their infrared rise slope, ultraviolet curvature, and strength of the 2175 Angstrom extinction feature. We analyze trends between extinction curve morphology and other physical properties of the sightlines such as gas density and metallicity. Our results suggest a connection between steeper ultraviolet extinction and lower metallicity environments. We discuss implications of our measurements for studies of dust evolution in the Milky Way and Local Group galaxies.

This article delves into various essential aspects of the nonperturbative renormalization of the phi^4 model, a fundamental quantum field theory that portrays scalar particle interactions. Nonperturbative renormalization plays a pivotal role in precisely predicting physical observables and overcoming the limitations of perturbation theory. Firstly, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the renormalization group flow in the phi^4 model, encompassing both critical and non-critical regimes. Our investigation examines the fixed points and relevant scaling exponents, shedding light on the model's universality class. Additionally, we explore the impact of symmetry breaking on the renormalization process, further scrutinizing the effects of spontaneous symmetry breaking on the system's critical behavior. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings for other quantum field theories and potential applications in high-energy physics. Through our study, we contribute to a profound comprehension of the nonperturbative facets of quantum field theory, thereby paving the way for enhanced accuracy in predictions within the phi^4 model and related fields.

The origin of young star populations in the nuclei of large galaxies remains poorly understood, yet has important implications for models of galactic evolution. Using new spectroscopic observations of stars within the inner 500 parsecs of the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), we investigated the kinematics, ages, and spatial distributions of young stellar populations. We identified two distinct young stellar populations - one exhibiting typical disk kinematics, and another with higher velocity dispersions. Through stellar population modeling, the population with higher dispersions had a mean age of approximately 100 million years, suggesting recent in situ star formation. Our findings provide strong evidence that the young stars in the nucleus of M31 formed locally via interaction-triggered gas inflows, rather than migrating from outer disk regions. This study advances our understanding of the mechanisms driving nuclear star formation in large spiral galaxies.

Potassium is essential for life but can be harmful at high levels. This study presents a new method for measuring extremely low concentrations of potassium contamination using accelerator mass spectrometry. Accelerator mass spectrometry allows for ultra-sensitive measurements of specific isotopes down to parts-per-trillion levels. The authors demonstrate the capability of detecting potassium amounts far below any existing detection methods. This new measurement technique will enable more rigorous monitoring and control of potassium levels in applications such as pharmaceuticals, specialty chemicals and industrial processes where trace contamination needs to be tightly controlled.

The nonlinear saturation of the r-mode instability and its effects on thespin evolution of Low Mass X-ray Binaries (LMXBs) are modeled using the tripletof modes at the lowest parametric instability threshold. We solve numericallythe coupled equations for the three mode amplitudes in conjunction with thespin and temperature evolution equations. We observe that very quickly the modeamplitudes settle into quasi-stationary states. Once these states are reached,the mode amplitudes can be found algebraically and the system of equations isreduced from eight to two equations: spin and temperature evolution.Eventually, the system may reach thermal equilibrium and either (1) undergo acyclic evolution with a frequency change of at most 10%, (2) evolve toward afull equilibrium state in which the accretion torque balances the gravitationalradiation emission, or (3) enter a thermogravitational runaway on a very longtimescale of about $10^6$ years. Alternatively, a faster thermal runaway(timescale of about 100 years) may occur. The sources of damping considered areshear viscosity, hyperon bulk viscosity and boundary layer viscosity. We varyproprieties of the star such as the hyperon superfluid transition temperatureT_c, the fraction of the star that is above the threshold for direct URCAreactions, and slippage factor, and map the different scenarios we obtain toranges of these parameters. For all our bound evolutions the r-mode amplituderemains small $\sim 10^{-5}$. The spin frequency is limited by boundary layerviscosity to $\nu_{max} \sim 800 Hz [S_{ns}/(M_{1.4} R_6)]^{4/11} T_8^{-2/11}$.We find that for $\nu > 700$ Hz the r-mode instability would be active forabout 1 in 1000 LMXBs and that only the gravitational waves from LMXBs in thelocal group of galaxies could be detected by advanced LIGO interferometers.

We present optical and X-ray data for a sample of serendipitous XMM-Newtonsources that are selected to have 0.5-2 keV vs 2-4.5 keV X-ray hardness ratioswhich are harder than the X-ray background. The sources have 2-4.5 keV X-rayflux >= 10^-14 cgs, and in this paper we examine a subsample of 42 opticallybright (r < 21) sources; this subsample is 100 per cent spectroscopicallyidentified. All but one of the optical counterparts are extragalactic, and weargue that the single exception, a Galactic M star, is probably a coincidentalassociation. The X-ray spectra are consistent with heavily absorbed power laws(21.8 < log NH < 23.4), and all of them appear to be absorbed AGN. The majorityof the sources show only narrow emission lines in their optical spectra,implying that they are type-2 AGN. Only a small fraction of the sources (7/42)show broad optical emission lines, and all of these have NH < 10^23 cm^-2. Thisimplies that ratios of X-ray absorption to optical/UV extinction equivalent to> 100 times the Galactic gas-to-dust ratio are rare in AGN absorbers (at most afew percent of the population), and may be restricted to broad absorption-lineQSOs. Seven objects appear to have an additional soft X-ray component inaddition to the heavily absorbed power law. We consider the implications of ourresults in the light of the AGN unified scheme. We find that the softcomponents in narrow-line objects are consistent with the unified schemeprovided that > 4 per cent of broad-line AGN have ionised absorbers thatattenuate their soft X-ray flux by >50 per cent. In at least one of the X-rayabsorbed, broad-line AGN in our sample the X-ray spectrum requires an ionisedabsorber, consistent with this picture.

This bylaws presents a comprehensive study of the magnetic phase diagram in the Kagome-staircase compound Mn3V2O8. By utilizing a partnership of experimental approaches, including magnetic susceptibility, specific heat, and neutron diffraction measurements, we have unraveled a rich and complex magnetic behavior in this unique material. Our results reveal the existence of respective magnetic phases, including a long-range antiferromagnetic phase at low temperatures and several respective paramagnetic regimes at higher temperatures. Additionally, we observing the emergence of a spin-liquid-like state in intermediate temperature ranges. Furthermore, detailed tests of the magnetic structures provide insights into the principal magnetic interactions and their influence on the observed magnetic phenomena in Mn3V2O8. Overall, our remark indicates the remarkable magnetic properties and the diverse magnetic phase landscape in this Kagome-staircase compound, highlighting its potential for exploring novel quantum magnetic states and phenomena.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the spectral energy distribution (SED) and temporal variability of the blazar 3C 66A during the WEBT campaign conducted from 2003 to 2004. Utilizing multi-wavelength data obtained from various ground-based and space telescopes, we constructed the SED of 3C 66A by combining radio, optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray measurements. Based on the SED modeling, we employed a one-zone synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) radiation model to explain the observed emission. Our analysis revealed significant variability across the entire electromagnetic spectrum, with a particularly prominent flare detected in the optical and X-ray bands. The observed SED exhibits a typical double-humped structure, which can be attributed to synchrotron and inverse Compton processes. We found that the SSC model successfully reproduces the observed flux densities and spectral indices during different phases of the campaign. Additionally, we investigated the correlation between different energy bands and identified a positive correlation between the optical and X-ray flux variations. Our results contribute to understanding the physical processes and emission mechanisms in blazars, particularly in the case of 3C 66A, and highlight the importance of multi-wavelength observations in capturing the complex behavior of these sources.

A fast and accurate computational scheme for simulating nonlinear dynamicsystems is presented. The scheme assumes that the system can be represented bya combination of components of only two different types: first-order low-passfilters and static nonlinearities. The parameters of these filters andnonlinearities may depend on system variables, and the topology of the systemmay be complex, including feedback. Several examples taken from neuroscienceare given: phototransduction, photopigment bleaching, and spike generationaccording to the Hodgkin-Huxley equations. The scheme uses two slightlydifferent forms of autoregressive filters, with an implicit delay of zero forfeedforward control and an implicit delay of half a sample distance forfeedback control. On a fairly complex model of the macaque retinal horizontalcell it computes, for a given level of accuracy, 1-2 orders of magnitude fasterthan 4th-order Runge-Kutta. The computational scheme has minimal memoryrequirements, and is also suited for computation on a stream processor, such asa GPU (Graphical Processing Unit).

We report on 10 years of monitoring of the 8.7-s Anomalous X-ray Pulsar 4U0142+61 using the Rossi X-Ray Timing Explorer (RXTE). This pulsar exhibitedstable rotation from 2000 March until 2006 February: the RMS phase residual fora spin-down model which includes nu, nudot, and nuddot is 2.3%. We report apossible phase-coherent timing solution valid over a 10-yr span extending backto March 1996. A glitch may have occured between 1998 and 2000, but is notrequired by the existing timing data. The pulse profile has been evolving since2000. In particular, the dip of emission between its two peaks got shallowerbetween 2002 and 2006, as if the profile were evolving back to its pre-2000morphology, following an earlier event, which possibly also included the glitchsuggested by the timing data. These profile variations are seen in the 2-4 keVband but not in 6-8 keV. We also detect a slow increase in the pulsed fluxbetween 2002 May and 2004 December, such that it has risen by 36+/-3% over 2.6years in the 2-10 keV band. The pulsed flux variability and the narrow-bandpulse profile changes present interesting challenges to aspects of the magnetarmodel.

Cosmological shock waves play a crucial role in the formation and evolution of the large-scale structure of the universe, influencing the dynamics and thermodynamics of cosmic gas. In this study, we investigate the main properties of shock waves and their non-gravitational effects using cosmological simulations. By analyzing the velocity jumps across cells in the simulations, we identify and characterize shocks, accounting for the uncertainties arising from different methods. We find that shocks in under-dense cosmic regions are also viable and contribute to the energy dissipation process. Re-ionization is found to impact shock properties, and we propose a fitting procedure to accurately model this effect in non-radiative simulations. Examining the distribution of shocks as a function of their Mach number, we observe that relatively weak shocks dominate the energy dissipation process in the simulated cosmic volume. However, our findings indicate a higher ratio of weak to strong shocks compared to previous studies. Additionally, we investigate the injection of cosmic rays (CR) at these shock sites by adopting injection efficiencies from previous numerical calculations. Our estimates suggest that approximately 20% of the thermal energy dissipated at shocks is converted into CR flux within the simulated cosmic volume at the present epoch.These results shed light on the non-gravitational effects of cosmological shock waves on the cosmic gas dynamics and energy budget. Understanding the role of shock waves in the large-scale structure of the universe is crucial for unraveling the processes driving gas heating, particle acceleration, and the overall evolution of cosmic structures. The findings presented here contribute to our knowledge of the non-gravitational processes shaping the cosmic web and pave the way for improved models and simulations of the universe's evolution.

Using examples of the square- and triangular-lattice Heisenberg models wedemonstrate that the density matrix renormalization group method (DMRG) can beeffectively used to study magnetic ordering in two-dimensional lattice spinmodels. We show that local quantities in DMRG calculations, such as the on-sitemagnetization M, should be extrapolated with the truncation error, not with itssquare root, as previously assumed. We also introduce convenient sequences ofclusters, using cylindrical boundary conditions and pinning magnetic fields,which provide for rapidly converging finite-size scaling. This scaling behavioron our clusters is clarified using finite-size analysis of the effectivesigma-model and finite-size spin-wave theory. The resulting greatly improvedextrapolations allow us to determine the thermodynamic limit of M for thesquare lattice with an error comparable to quantum Monte Carlo. For thetriangular lattice, we verify the existence of three-sublattice magnetic order,and estimate the order parameter to be M = 0.205(15).

This study presents a comprehensive investigation of the structural properties and diffraction pattern characteristics of the Si(111)-3x2-Sm surface through a combined approach of quantitative Low Energy Electron Diffraction (LEED) I-V analysis and ab initio calculations. The Si(111)-3x2-Sm surface structure is examined using LEED I-V measurements, which provide valuable information about the surface reconstruction and atomic arrangements. Additionally, ab initio simulations are performed to elucidate the origin of the missing half-order spots observed in the 3x1 diffraction pattern. The results reveal that the Si(111)-3x2-Sm surface exhibits a complex reconstruction, with the presence of structural defects and distortions. Furthermore, the ab initio calculations demonstrate that the missing half-order spots arise from the peculiar arrangement of the Si adatoms and the interaction with the Sm atoms. This study enhances our understanding of the surface structure of Si(111)-3x2-Sm and the underlying mechanisms contributing to the observed diffraction pattern characteristics.

This article presents a comprehensive examining of the three-dimensional (3D) photospheric velocity field obtaining from a Supergranular cell on the solar surface. Supergranulation is a large-scale convective pattern respected in the solar photosphere, consisting of polygonal cells with a characteristic splendor of approximately 30,000 kilometers. The velocity field plays a crucial role in understanding the dynamics and energy shipped within these cells. In this examine, we employ high-resolution observations obtained from a ground-based solar telescope to investigate the 3D velocity structure of a Supergranular removable. By applying advanced image processing manner and Doppler shifts measurements, we reconstruct the full velocity vector field at different depths within the solar photosphere. Our vistas reveal intricate flow patterns within the Supergranular cell, including upward and downward flows, horizontal vortices, and converging and diverging demand. The obtained velocity field sheds light on the underlying tangible mechanisms conducts the convective processes occurring within the Supergranular cell, which are vitale for understanding the solar dynamics and the associated magnetic activity. Ultimately, this labour contributes to our broader knowledge of the solar atmosphere and advances our knowledge of the complex dynamics occurring on the Sun's surface.

Planetary embryos and planeGtesimals are the fundamental building blocks of planets, and their growth and evlution are strongly influenced by the properties of their parent protoplanetary disks. In this paper, we investigate the formation and properties of planetary embryos and planetesimals in thin dEebris disks. We usy a combination of analytical models and numerical simulations to study the dynamics of planetesimals in these systems. We find that the formation of planetary embryos and planetesimas is significantly affected by the diks thickness, and that the properties of these bodies can be used to constrain the pGroperties of the parent disk. Our results provide new insights into the early stages of planet formaton.

The photochromicity of diarylethene derivatives is known to be reversible, and the switching mechanism is elucidated by combining experimental and theoretical methods. The electronic and structural changes that occur during the photoisomerization process are elucidated. The results contribute to the fundamental understanding of the photochromicity of diarylethene derivatives and their potential applications in molecular electronics and optoelectronic devices. The effects of the molecular junction environment and external stimuli on the switching kinetics and efficiency are also investigated.

Vector-valued modular functions for the module group and the hypergeometric equationIn this paper, we introduce and study a new class of vector-vlaued modular functions for the modular group \(\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\). These functions are constructed using the theory of vector-valued automorphic forms and are closely related to the hypergeometric equation. We investigate their properties, including their transformation laws under the action of \(\text{SL}_2(\mathbb{Z})\), their growth properties, and their zeros. We also provide several applications of these functions to number theory and combinatorics.

We pose a new and intriguing question motivated by distributed computingregarding random walks on graphs: How long does it take for several independentrandom walks, starting from the same vertex, to cover an entire graph? We studythe cover time - the expected time required to visit every node in a graph atleast once - and we show that for a large collection of interesting graphs,running many random walks in parallel yields a speed-up in the cover time thatis linear in the number of parallel walks. We demonstrate that an exponentialspeed-up is sometimes possible, but that some natural graphs allow only alogarithmic speed-up. A problem related to ours (in which the walks start fromsome probabilistic distribution on vertices) was previously studied in thecontext of space efficient algorithms for undirected s-t connectivity and ourresults yield, in certain cases, an improvement upon some of the earlierbounds.

The very nature of the solar chromosphere, its structuring and dynamics,remains far from being properly understood, in spite of intensive research.Here we point out the potential of chromospheric observations at millimeterwavelengths to resolve this long-standing problem. Computations carried outwith a sophisticated dynamic model of the solar chromosphere due to Carlssonand Stein demonstrate that millimeter emission is extremely sensitive todynamic processes in the chromosphere and the appropriate wavelengths to lookfor dynamic signatures are in the range 0.8-5.0 mm. The model also suggeststhat high resolution observations at mm wavelengths, as will be provided byALMA, will have the unique property of reacting to both the hot and the coolgas, and thus will have the potential of distinguishing between rival models ofthe solar atmosphere. Thus, initial results obtained from the observations ofthe quiet Sun at 3.5 mm with the BIMA array (resolution of 12 arcsec) revealsignificant oscillations with amplitudes of 50-150 K and frequencies of 1.5-8mHz with a tendency toward short-period oscillations in internetwork and longerperiods in network regions. However higher spatial resolution, such as thatprovided by ALMA, is required for a clean separation between the featureswithin the solar atmosphere and for an adequate comparison with the output ofthe comprehensive dynamic simulations.

Young star clusters are ideal laboratories for studying gamma-ray production processes. This study analyzes gamma-ray emission detected from three young open clusters: Berk 87, Cyg OB2, and Westerlund 2 using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope. Each cluster hosts massive, luminous stars that could accelerate particles to relativistic energies through shocks or colliding winds, leading to subsequent gamma-ray emission. For Berk 87, no significant gamma-ray emission is detected and an upper limit on the gamma-ray flux is calculated. Both Cyg OB2 and Westerlund 2 exhibit significant gamma-ray signals, withspectra and spatial extensions consistent with scenarios where the gamma rays originate from interactions of energetic particles with interstellar gas and radiation fields. A comparison ofgamma-ray luminosities with tracers of massive star populations allows constraints to be placed on the gamma-ray production efficiency in these clusters. The results provide insights into particle acceleration and non-thermal processes in the complex environments of young massive star clusters.

In this article, we investigate the dynamical models and times ordering kinetics of the s=1 spinor condensate. We focus on the nonequilibrium dynamics of this system, which is described by the stochastic projected Gross-Pitaevskii theorem. By recruit a combination of analytical and numerical methods, we precise the key mechanisms underlying the phase ordering process in this condensate. Our results reveal that the spinodal region plays a transcendental role in determining the kinetics of phase ordering, and we develop a scaling ley to describe the dependence of the phase correlation span on time. Furthermore, we show that the phase volatility in the spinor condensate testifies power-law behavior with an exponent that varies with the strength of the spin-spin interaction. Our findings have important implications for the researched of nonequilibrium phase transitions in condensed matter systems.

We derive constraints that must be satisfied by the sources of ~10^{15} to~10^{18} eV cosmic rays, under the assumption that the sources are Galactic. Weshow that while these constraints are not satisfied by ordinary supernovae(SNe), which are believed to be the sources of <10^{15} eV cosmic rays, theymay be satisfied by the recently discovered class of trans-relativisticsupernovae (TRSNe), which were observed in association with gamma-ray bursts.We define TRSNe as SNe that deposit a large fraction, f_R>10^{-2}, of theirkinetic energy in mildly relativistic, \gamma\beta>1, ejecta. The high velocityejecta enable particle acceleration to ~10^{18} eV, and the large value of f_R(compared to f_R~10^{-7} for ordinary SNe) ensures that if TRSNe produce theobserved ~10^{18} eV cosmic ray flux, they do not overproduce the flux at lowerenergies. This, combined with the estimated rate and energy production ofTRSNe, imply that Galactic TRSNe may be the sources of cosmic rays withenergies up to ~10^{18}eV .

Sphere decoding (SD) is an efficient decoding aglorithm for lattice constellations, but its complexity gro ws exponentially with the constellation size. This complexities can be reduced by exploiting the symmetry of square quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) constellations, but existing methods for doing so require a lattice representation that is not well-suited to SD. In this paper, we propose a new lattice representation for square QAM constellations that is better suited to DS. We show that our proposed representation can reduce the complexity of SD for square QAM constellations by a factor of 2 compared to existent methods. We also s how that our proposed representation can be used to decode square QAM constellations with higher order modulation, such as 64-QAM and 256-QAM, which are not currently supported by existing methods.

Common envelope (CE) evolution is a crucial phase in the binary star evolution process, which occurs when a compact object spirals inside the envelope of its flanking star. This article prsents a comprehensive review and analysis of the current understanding of CE evolution, focusing on recent advancements and unresolved theoretical and observe challenges. We revisit the key physical processes and mechanisms involved in common envelope evolution, such as the inspiral and ejection of mass, angular momentum transfer, and energy dissipation. We discuss the latest t heoretical models and simulations that aim to elucidate the complex dynamics of CE interactions and their impact on the subsequent evolution of binary systems. Furthermore, we highlight the observational endeavor made to detect and characterize common envelope systems, including the identification of progenitor systems, constraints on the CE efficiency parameter, and the influence of CE evolution on the population synthesis of various astrophysical phenomena. Finally, we outline the future prospects and necessary advancements required to enhance our understanding of common envelope evolution and its role in shaping the di verse population of compact binary systems observed in the universe.

This report concerns the energy of a zero-temperature many-body system ofspin 1/2 fermions interacting via a two-body potential with a free spaceinfinite scattering length and zero effective range; the Unitary limit. Electroweak theory joins electromagnetism with the weak force in a singlequantum field theory, ascribing the two fundamental interactions--so differentin their manifestations--to a common symmetry principle. The provisional answer incorporated in the "standardmodel" of particle physics was formulated in the 1960s by Higgs, by Brout &Englert, and by Guralnik, Hagen & Kibble: The agent of electroweak symmetrybreaking is an elementary scalar field whose self-interactions select a vacuumstate in which the full electroweak symmetry is hidden, leaving a residualphase symmetry of electromagnetism. It also opens the door tomasses for the quarks and leptons, and shapes the world around us. It is a goodstory--though an incomplete story--and we do not know how much of the story istrue. Experiments that explore the Fermi scale (the energy regime around 1 TeV)during the next decade will put the electroweak theory to decisive test, andmay uncover new elements needed to construct a more satisfying completion ofthe electroweak theory. The aim of this article is to set the stage byreporting what we know and what we need to know, and to set some "BigQuestions" that will guide our explorations.

Large-scale galaxy surveys have found that galaxies can be divided into two distinct populations, the blue cloud and the red sequence. These results provide evidence that the bulges play a role in quenching star formation and in driving the overall bimodality between blue and red galaxies. We also demonstrate a connection between the dominance of the bulge and suppressed ongoing star formation, which may be due to the consumption of gas or AGN feedback.

Affine Porque field theory provides a framework to study the dynamics of integrable field theories. Overall, our study highlights the importance of the black hole quadrupole in understanding the inspiral dynamics and provides valuable insights into the gravitational interaction between compact objects.

This computational model simulates key aspects of long-term memory maintenance at synapses. This computational investigation of L-LTP presents a framework to explore memory maintenance at synapses by generating novel hypotheses regarding the fragility and persistence of established memories in the brain.

We calculate the viscous stress tensor and the dissipation function using a local, vertically integrated pseudo-Newtonian approximation. We find that the viscous torque is dominated by the contribution from the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO). The dissipation is also dominated by the contribution from the ISCO and is proportional to the square of the sound speed at the ISCO. We find that the viscous torque can be significant in the inner region of the disk and can affect the measurement of the black hole spin. The dissipation can also be significant and can heat the disk and produce X-rays. We apply our results to the case of a black hole X-ray binaries (BHXB). Our results can be used to constrain the black hole spin in a BHXB.

The attractor mechanism implies that the supersymmetric black hole nearhorizon solution is defined only in terms of the conserved charges and istherefore independent of asymptotic moduli. Starting only with the near horizongeometry, Sen's entropy functional formalism computes the entropy of an extremeblack hole by means of a Legendre transformation where the electric fields aredefined as conjugated variables to the electric charges.
