Energies of graphene nanocones with 1 to 5 pentagonal disclinations arestudied on an atomically detailed level. The numerical results are interpretedin terms of three different contributions to the cone energy: the coredisclination energy, the bending energy of the cone surface, and the ''linetension'' energy of the cone edge that is related to different coordination ofcarbon atoms situated at the edge. This continuum description allows for aconstruction of analytic expressions for the cone energetics and indicatesdifferent regimes of cone sizes in which cones with a particular number ofdisclinations are preferred energywise. An important result of the study isthat the energetics of various types of cones profoundly depends upon whetherthe dangling carbon bonds at the cone basis are saturated by hydrogen atoms ornot. This may be of use for explaining the differences in the yields of variouscone types in different production processes.

The data from a CO(1 - 0) mapping survey of 40 nearby spiral galaxiesperformed with the Nobeyama 45-m telescope are presented. The criteria of thesample selection were (1) RC3 morphological type in the range Sa to Scd, (2)distance less than 25 Mpc, (3) inclination angle less than 79deg (RC3), (4)flux at 100 um higher than ~ 10 Jy, (5) spiral structure is not destroyed byinteraction. The maps of CO cover most of the optical disk of the galaxies. Weinvestigated the influence of bar on the distribution of molecular gas inspiral galaxies using these data. We confirmed that the degree of centralconcentration is higher in barred spirals than in non-barred spirals as shownby the previous works. Furthermore, we present an observational evidence thatbars are efficient in driving molecular gas that lies within the bar lengthtoward the center, while the role in bringing gas in from the outer parts ofthe disks is small. The transported gas accounts for about half of moleculargas within the central region in barred spiral galaxies. We found a correlationbetween the degree of central concentration and bar strength. Galaxies withstronger bars tend to have higher central concentration. The correlationimplies that stronger bars accumulate molecular gas toward the center moreefficiently. These results are consistent with long-lived bars.

In this paper, we propose a new cryptographic scheme based on tripled chaotic maps. The proposed scheme is composed of three chaotic maps, which makes it more secure and resistant to cryptanalysis. We analyze the security of the proposed scheme and show its effectiveness by simulations. The proposed scheme is suitable for secure communication in various applications, such as the Internet of Things, cloud computing, and wireless sensor networks. Experimental results show that the proposed scheme can effectively resist various attacks, such as statistical attacks, differential attacks, and brute-force attacks.

This article presents a novel approach for directly extracting one-loop integral coefficients from scattering amplitudes, thereby eliminating the need for intermediate results and streamlining the computation process. The proposed method leverages recent advances in algebraic geometry and singularity theory to overcome longstanding challenges in computing one-loop integrals. Our approach enables the efficient calculation of higher-point functions and paves the way for the systematic study of more complex quantum field theories. By exploiting the underlying mathematical structure of the scattering amplitudes, we are able to reconstruct the entirety of the one-loop integrand from a set of carefully chosen seed integrals. The resulting algorithm is robust, scalable, and well-suited for numerical implementation, opening up new avenues for investigating quantum field theories in regimes previously inaccessible to computational methods.

Milagro Constraints on Very High Energy Emission from Short-Duration Gamma-Ray BurstsGamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are the most energetic explosions in the universe, classified into long-duration (LGRBs) and short-duration (SGRBs). The progenitors of SGRBs remain uncertain, while LGRBs are associated with massive star deaths.SGRBs often exhibit a high-energy component attributed to synchrotron radiation from accelerated electrons in the GRB outflow. However, the exact emission mechanism is poorly understood.Using data from the Milagro gamma-ray observatory, we constrain the very high energy (VHE) emission from SGRBs. Our findings suggest that SGRB VHE emission is consistent with synchrotron radiation from accelerated electrons in the outflow but more variable than LGRBs.This variability may arise from differing SGRB and LGRB progenitors.Our results shed light on the nature of SGRB VHE emission and imply potentially diverse SGRB progenitors compared to LGRBs.

This study introduces a new approach for simulating physical systems via direct calculation of partition functions. Traditional simulation techniques such as Monte Carlo methods can be inefficient for systems with intricate energy landscapes. The presented method circumvents these challenges by directly computing the partition function of the entire system. This direct calculation permits generating equilibrium samples without iterative sampling procedures. As a proof of concept, the technique was applied to lattice spin systems, finding samples matching analytical solutions. This direct computation framework lays the foundation for efficient simulations of systems previously intractable using conventional techniques, bypassing their limitations.

Spitzer Space Telescope Infrared Spectrograph (IRS) spectra of five irradiated close-in extrasolar planets are presented. These spectra cover a range of orbital periods and equilibrium temperatures, probing the atmospheres of these planets at pressures of a few hundred millibars. New collision-induced absorption cross sections for H2-H2O and He-H2O are calculated using a more realistic H2O line list and improved intermolecular potentials. Models with solar C/O ratios and carbon-rich condensates fit the spectra of HD 209458b, HD 189733b, and XO-1b well, predicting water abundances of 0.1%-0.7% for these planets. The spectrum of TrES-1 is consistent with either a solar or a carbon-rich composition, with a water abundance of 0.3%-1.4%. The spectrum of HAT-P-1b is best fit by a model with a sub-solar C/O ratio of 0.5 and a water abundance of 0.4%. The atmospheres of hot Jupiters are diverse in terms of their C/O ratios and water abundances.

The Casimir force, a quantum mechanical force that arises between two closely spaced objects, is affected by the optical propeties of the boundary smurfaces. This paper presents experimental approaches to investigate the difference in the CaOimir force through the vaRying optical properties of the boundary surfaces. We discuss the optical properties of the boundary surfaces and the methods to conbtrol them. W also discuss the experimental setups and the techniques to measure the Casimir force. Finaly, we present the results of our experiments and discuss their implications for the understanding of the Casimir force.

Using a 2.5D time-dependent axisymmetric numerical code we recentlydeveloped, we solve the full compressible Navier-Stokes equations (including analpha-viscosity prescription) to determine the structure of the boundary layerbetween the white dwarf and the accretion disk in non-magnetic cataclysmicvaria ble systems. In this preliminary work, our numerical approach does notinclude radiation. In the energy equation, we either take the dissipationfunction (Phi) into account or we assumed that the energy is instantly radiatedaway (Phi). For a slowly rotating non magnetized accreting white dwarf, theaccretion disk e xtends all the way to the stellar surface. There, the matterimpacts and spread s towards the poles as new matter continuously piles upbehind it. We carried out numerical simulations for different values of thealpha viscosity parameter (alpha), corresponding to different mass accretionrates. In the high viscosity cases (alpha=0.1), the spreading boundary layersets off a gravity wave in the s urface matter. The accretion flow movessupersonically over the cusp making it s usceptible to the rapid development ofgravity wave and/or Kelvin-Helmholtz shea ring instabilities. This BL isoptically thick and extends more than 30 degrees to either side of the diskplane after only 3/4 of a Keplerian rotation period (19s). In the low viscositycases (alpha=0.001), the spreading boundary layer does not set off gravitywaves and it is optically thin.

The BL Lac object 3C 66A was observed in an extensive multiwavelengthmonitoring campaign from July 2003 till April 2004. The spectral energydistribution (SED) was measured over the entire electromagnetic spectrum, withflux measurements from radio to X-ray frequencies and upper limits in the veryhigh energy (VHE) gamma-ray regime. Here, we use a time-dependent leptonic jetmodel to reproduce the SED and optical spectral variability observed during ourmultiwavelength campaign. Our model simulations could successfully reproducethe observed SED and optical light curves and predict an intrinsic cutoff valuefor the VHE gamma-ray emission at ~ 4 GeV. The effect of the optical depth dueto the intergalactic infrared background radiation (IIBR) on the peak of thehigh-energy component of 3C 66A was found to be negligible. Also, the presenceof a broad line region (BLR) in the case of 3C 66A may play an important rolein the emission of gamma-ray photons when the emission region is very close tothe central engine, but further out, the production mechanism of hard X-ray andgamma-ray photons becomes rapidly dominated by synchrotron self-Comptonemission. We further discuss the possibility of an observable X-ray spectralvariability pattern. The simulated results do not predict observable hysteresispatterns in the optical or soft X-ray regimes for major flares on multi-daytime scales.

Experiments in coherent nuclear and electron magnetic resonance, and opticalspectroscopy correspond to control of quantum mechanical ensembles, guidingthem from initial to final target states by unitary transformations. Thecontrol inputs (pulse sequences) that accomplish these unitary transformationsshould take as little time as possible so as to minimize the effects ofrelaxation and decoherence and to optimize the sensitivity of the experiments.Here we give efficient syntheses of various unitary transformations on Isingspin chains of arbitrary length. The efficient realization of the unitarytransformations presented here is obtained by computing geodesics on a sphereunder a special metric. We show that contrary to the conventional belief, it ispossible to propagate a spin order along an Ising spin chain with couplingstrength J (in units of Hz), significantly faster than 1/(2J) per step. Themethods presented here are expected to be useful for immediate and futureapplications involving control of spin dynamics in coherent spectroscopy andquantum information processing.

These waves are produced when galaxies collide and their massive black holes merge. By analyzing the patterns of these waves, we can learn a great deal about the formation and evolution of galaxies. The detection of these waves has made it possible to study the properties of galaxy encounters in a way that was previously impossible.

Introduction:Proteins are essential to life, and their proper function relies on their ability to fold into a unique, stable structure. However, the process by which proteins fold is not fully understood. This article aims to introduce physicists to the field of protein folding, providing an overview of the key concepts and experimental techniques used to study the folding process.Protein Structure and Stability:Proteins are composed of amino acids, which are linked together in a specific sequence. The sequence of amino acids determines the protein's structure, which can be classified into four main types: alpha-helices, beta-sheets, turns, and coils. The structure of a protein is essential for its stability and function.Protein Folding:Protein folding is the process by which a protein molecule assumes its native, functional conformation. Folding is a complex process that occurs spontaneously and is driven by the forces that determine the protein's stability.Experimental Techniques:Various experimental techniques are used to study protein folding. These techniques include X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, fluorescence spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations. Each technique provides unique information about the folding process, and they are often used in combination to obtain a comprehensive understanding of how proteins fold.Theoretical Models:Theoretical models play an important role in understanding protein folding. These models range from simple lattice models to complex simulations that explicitly account for the atomic interactions within a protein. Models are used to investigate the mechanisms of folding, the factors that determine the stability of proteins, and the dynamics of the folding process.Conclusion:Protein folding is a fundamental process in biology that is essential for the proper function of proteins.

This study examines the affairs between the mass of black holes and the luminosity of spheroids in galaxies. Precedent research has shown that the mass of supermassive black holes at galactic centres is correlated with properties of the host spheroid component. However, the exact nature of the relationship between black hole mass and spheroid luminosity remaining poorly understood. In this work, we measure black hole masses and spheroid luminosities for a sample of 49 nearby galaxies employment dynamic modeling and spectral vigour distribution fitting techniques. Our analysis reveals a tight power-law correlation between black hole mass and spheroid luminosity with relatively weak scatter. Moreover, we find that this thereto holds over roughly five orders of quantum in black hole mass and spheroid luminosity. The slope and normalization of the comparatively are consistent with previous studies based on smaller samples. We discuss possible physical drivers connecting black hole growth to the evolutionary of the surrounding stellar spheroid. Establishing the precise layout and potential scatter in the black hole mass - spheroid luminosity connection provides new insights into the coevolution of galaxies and their decisive massive black holes. Overall, our work significantly improves consist of the relationship between these two fundamental galaxy components.

This study presents a detailed analysis of a rare, 100 kpc-scale damped Lyman alpha (DLA) absorber discovered towards a binary quasar at redshift z ~ 3. The absorber is found to be associated with a galaxy pair, allowing us to probe the physical properties of galaxies at this early cosmic epoch. By examining the absorption lines of neutral hydrogen and metal ions, we determine the temperature, density, and metallicity of the gas in the absorber. Our results suggest that the absorber is likely a multi-phase medium with a complex structure, possibly arising from the interaction between the galaxy pair and the surrounding intergalactic medium. The observed properties of the absorber are compared with predictions from simulations of galaxy formation and evolution, providing valuable insights into the formation histories of galaxies at z ~ 3. Our findings suggest that galaxies at this redshift are significantly larger than previously thought, with some galaxies having already developed a substantial amount of structure and organization. The implications of our results for our understanding of the early universe are discussed, highlighting the importance of further studies of this kind to better understand the formation and evolution of galaxies.

This thesis investigates in the use of access log data as a source ofinformation for identifying related scientific papers. This is done forarXiv.org, the authority for publication of e-prints in several fields ofphysics. Compared to citation information, access logs have the advantage of beingimmediately available, without manual or automatic extraction of the citationgraph. Because of that, a main focus is on the question, how far user behaviorcan serve as a replacement for explicit meta-data, which potentially might beexpensive or completely unavailable. Therefore, we compare access, content, andcitation-based measures of relatedness on different recommendation tasks. As afinal result, an online recommendation system has been built that can helpscientists to find further relevant literature, without having to search forthem actively.

The Energetic Gamma-Ray Experiment Telescope (EGRET) on the Compton Gamma-RayObservatory (CGRO) discovered gamma-ray emission from more than 67 blazarsduring its 9 yr lifetime. We conducted an exhaustive search of the EGRETarchives and selected all the blazars that were observed multiple times andwere bright enough to enable a spectral analysis using standard power-lawmodels. The sample consists of 18 flat-spectrum radio quasars(FSRQs), 6low-frequency peaked BL Lac objects (LBLs) and 2 high-frequency peaked BL Lacobjects (HBLs). We do not detect any clear pattern in the variation of spectralindex with flux. Some of the blazars do not show any statistical evidence forspectral variability. The spectrum hardens with increasing flux in a few cases.There is also evidence for a flux-hardness anticorrelation at low fluxes infive blazars. The well-observed blazars (3C 279, 3C 273, PKS 0528+134, PKS1622-297 PKS 0208-512) do not show any overall trend in the long-term spectraldependence on flux, but the sample shows a mixture of hard and soft states. Weobserved a previously unreported spectral hysteresis at weekly timescales inall three FSRQs for which data from flares lasting for ~(3-4) weeks wereavailable. All three sources show a counterclockwise rotation, despite thewidely different flux profiles. We analyze the observed spectral behavior inthe context of various inverse Compton mechanisms believed to be responsiblefor emission in the EGRET energy range. Our analysis uses the EGRET skymapsthat were regenerated to include the changes in performance during the mission.

This article studies several key aspects of the non -disturbance of the PHI^4 model. The PHI^4 model is a basic quantum field theory that describes the interaction between scalar particles. Non -disturbance re -stipulation is essential for accurate predictive physics to observe and overcome the limitations of disturbance theory. First of all, we consider the comprehensive analysis of the recovery group in the PHI^4 model, and take into account critical and non -critical solutions. We checked the fixed point and related zoom index and clarified the general category of the model. In addition, we discussed the role of symmetrical destruction in the process of re -standardization, and studied the impact of spontaneous symmetric destruction on the critical behavior of the system. Finally, we discussed the meaning of the potential application of other quantum field theory and high -energy physics. Our research helps to understand the non -disturbance of the theory of quantum field, and pave the way for more accurate predictions in the PHI^4 model and related fields.

We report observations of the dust cloud L1204 with the Onsala 25-m telescopein the 6 cm (1$_{11}-1_{10}$) transition of \htco. The observed region includesthe S140 H${\alpha}$ arc. This spectral line is seen here in absorption againstthe cosmic microwave background, indicating the presence of widespread warmmolecular gas at intermediate densities. Overall, the distributions of H$_2$COand CO (taken from the literature) are fairly similar, though significantdifferences exist at small scales. Most notably, while the CO peak is nearlycoincident with the S140 H${\alpha}$ arc, the maximum H$_2$CO absorption isclearly separated from it by a full 10$'$ beam ($\sim$ 3 pc). We argue thatthese differences result from differing abundances and excitation requirements.The CO(1-0) line is more optically thick and more biased towards warm gas thanthe H$_2$CO 6 cm line. On the other hand, formaldehyde is more easilyphotodissociated and is, therefore, a poorer tracer of the molecular gaslocated immediately behind Photon Dominated Regions.

Medium tomography using alternative hard processes holds promise to reveal new insigh ts into complex soft materials. Previous tomographic techniques relying on scattering or absorption have encoսntered limitations in resolving intricate structures within soft unconsolidated media. This paper presents a novel approach utilizing induced hard particle reactions within a mild material to act as locaion markers readable by tomography. Simulations demonstrate high-energy particle beams can initiate localized hardening to produce distinctive spots identifiable in subsequent scans. Preliminary phantom experiences show clear detection of simulated reaction sites down to the sub-millimeter scale. Our results suggest this method may offer improved resolution over traditional techniques. Moreover refinements and tests are still needed but the prospects of medium tomography using hard processes inside a soft medium appear favorable.

In this paper, we pArove a rigidity theorem for the action of the mapping class group on the spake of unmeasured foliations on a surface. We show that if two unmeasured folitaions are homotopic, then they are isotopic. This result generalizes a classical theorem of Kerckhoff for meaaured foliations. Our proof uses a combination of tenhniques from Teichmüller theory and geometric group theory.

A function $\rho:[0,\infty)\to(0,1]$ is a completely monotonic function ifand only if $\rho(\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert^2)$ is positive definite on$\mathbb{R}^d$ for all $d$ and thus it represents the correlation function of aweakly stationary and isotropic Gaussian random field. Radial positive definitefunctions are also of importance as they represent characteristic functions ofspherically symmetric probability distributions. In this paper, we analyze thefunction \[\rho(\beta ,\gamma)(x)=1-\biggl(\frac{x^{\beta}}{1+x^{\beta}}\biggr)^{\gamma},\qquad x\ge 0, \beta,\gamma>0,\] called the Dagum function, and showthose ranges for which this function is completely monotonic, that is, positivedefinite, on any $d$-dimensional Euclidean space. Important relations arisewith other families of completely monotonic and logarithmically completelymonotonic functions.

We present late-time (150-570 days after maximum light) optical and near-infrared (NIR) observations of the Type Ia supernova (SN) 2001el. Our data are compared with late-time observations of other SNe Ia and with multiple published models. The bolometric lumiere curve of SN 2001el is consistent with a t^-2 tial and is similar to the SN 1994D light curve at comparable epochs. The optical colors of SN 2001el are also similar to those of SN 1994D. However, the optical spectra of the two SNe are different, with SN 2001el exhibiting weaker [Fe III]λλ4472, 4511, and [Fe II]λλ428৭, 4Ʒ33 lines. In the NIR, SN 2001el is brighter than normal SNe Ia at late times. This excess broadcasts is likely due to dust formation in the ejecta. The dust mass and composition are estimated from a comparison with dusty SN models. We find a dust mass of 0.03 Msun, with a mixture of callaway and silicate grains. The dust establishment efficiency of SN 2001el is similar to that of SN 1981B, but smallest than that of SN 1994D.

This paper presents bushing condition monitoring frameworks that usemulti-layer perceptrons (MLP), radial basis functions (RBF) and support vectormachines (SVM) classifiers. The first level of the framework determines if thebushing is faulty or not while the second level determines the type of fault.The diagnostic gases in the bushings are analyzed using the dissolve gasanalysis. MLP gives superior performance in terms of accuracy and training timethan SVM and RBF. In addition, an on-line bushing condition monitoringapproach, which is able to adapt to newly acquired data are introduced. Thisapproach is able to accommodate new classes that are introduced by incomingdata and is implemented using an incremental learning algorithm that uses MLP.The testing results improved from 67.5% to 95.8% as new data were introducedand the testing results improved from 60% to 95.3% as new conditions wereintroduced. On average the confidence value of the framework on its decisionwas 0.92.

We present radio observations and optical spectroscopy of the giant lowsurface brightness (LSB) galaxy PGC 045080 (or 1300+0144). PGC 045080 is amoderately distant galaxy having a highly inclined optical disk and massive HIgas content. Radio continuum observations of the galaxy were carried out at 320MHz, 610 MHz and 1.4 GHz. Continuum emission was detected and mapped in thegalaxy. The emission appears extended over the inner disk at all threefrequencies. At 1.4 GHz and 610 MHz it appears to have two distinct lobes. Wealso did optical spectroscopy of the galaxy nucleus; the spectrum did not showany strong emission lines associated with AGN activity but the presence of aweak AGN cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, comparison of the H$\alpha$ flux andradio continuum at 1.4 GHz suggests that a significant fraction of the emissionis non-thermal in nature. Hence we conclude that a weak or hidden AGN may bepresent in PGC 045080. The extended radio emission represents lobes/jets fromthe AGN. These observations show that although LSB galaxies are metal poor andhave very little star formation, their centers can host significant AGNactivity. We also mapped the HI gas disk and velocity field in PGC 045080. TheHI disk extends well beyond the optical disk and appears warped. In the HIintensity maps, the disk appears distinctly lopsided. The velocity field isdisturbed on the lopsided side of the disk but is fairly uniform in the otherhalf. We derived the HI rotation curve for the galaxy from the velocity field.The rotation curve has a flat rotation speed of ~ 190 km/s.

The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) has played a prominent role in producing detailed maps of the universe. In this fourth installment of the SDSS Quasar Catalog series, we present the highly anticipated Fifth Data Release (DR5), which includes a comprehensive catalog of quasars-a vital class of celestial objects that offer significant insights into the early universe.DR5 builds upon its predecessors and incorporates several noteworthy improvements and enhancements. It covers a larger portion of the sky, encompassing both the Northern and Southern Galactic caps, thereby providing a more comprehensive representation of quasar properties across different regions. The catalog encompasses photometric and spectroscopic measurements for over a million quasar candidates, yielding a rich dataset for further exploration.Expanding on the successes of previous releases, DR5 incorporates refined selection algorithms that enhance quasar selection efficiency while minimizing contamination from other astronomical sources. The catalog also offers a multitude of calibrated properties, including redshift measurements, photometric magnitudes, and emission line diagnostics, enabling a detailed characterization of the quasar population.Additionally, DR5 introduces an updated quasar catalog format to facilitate easier access and utilization by the scientific community. The new format includes additional metadata and a standardized data structure, promoting interoperability and fostering collaborative research efforts.We showcase the scientific potential of DR5 by highlighting its impact on various astrophysical studies. The catalog enables exploration of quasar demographics, the role of quasars in galaxy formation and evolution, and the measurement of cosmological parameters. Furthermore, it facilitates studies on the interplay between quasars and other astronomical phenomena, such as galaxy clusters and cosmic large-scale structures.

We present detailed results from performing general relativistic (GR)simulations of stellar core collapse to a proto-neutron star, using amicrophysical equation of state (EoS) as well as an approximate description ofdeleptonization during the collapse phase. We show that for a wide variety ofrotation rates and profiles the gravitational wave (GW) burst signals from thecore bounce are of a generic type, already known as Type I in the literature.In addition, for most models the characteristic frequency of the GW burstsignal lies in a narrow range around approximately 718 Hz. In our systematicstudy, using both GR and Newtonian gravity, we identify, individually quantify,and discuss in detail the micro- and macrophysical mechanisms leading to thisresult, i.e. the effects of rotation, the EoS, and deleptonization. We alsodiscuss the detectability prospects of such GW burst signals by GW detectors,and infer that such a generic type of signal templates will likely facilitate amore efficient search in current and future detectors of both interferometricand resonant type.

The heat capacity of lead sulfide (PbS) has been measured from 5 to 300 K for samples enriched in either 204Pb or 208Pb. The results are compared with previous measurements on natural PbS and with theoretical calculations. The isotope effect on the heat capacity is small but significant. The results are discussed in terms of the vibrational properties of PbS.

This paper investigates the control of mechanical systems on Lie groups and its application to ideal hydrodynamics, presenting a novel approach to control theory that leverages Lie group geometry to design efficient and robust algorithms. The method is tested on various experimental setups, including a robotic arm and fluid-filled cavity, displaying improved performance compared to traditional techniques. The results have significant implications for the control of complex mechanical systems and open up new avenues for studying ideal hydrodynamics. The article provides a thorough analysis of the mathematical foundations and theoretical guarantees of the proposed method, alongside discussion of its potential applications in robotics, aerospace engineering, and fluid dynamics. Ultimately, this work represents a substantial advancement in control theory and its application to mechanical systems.Polishing the abstract involved implementing several changes to enhance clarity and readability:1. The extragalactic background of diffuse gamma rays contains radiation from both astrophysical sources and possible signatures of dark matter annihilation. This study presents a new determination of the extragalactic gamma ray background spectrum using the latest data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. For the first time, the potential contribution from dark matter annihilation is modeled self-consistently and accounted for in the analysis. The results provide updated constraints on the properties of dark matter particles and quantify their impact on measurements of the extragalactic background.

The vortex density of a rotating superfluid, divided by its particle mass,dictates the superfluid's angular velocity through the Feynman relation. Tofind how the Feynman relation applies to superfluid mixtures, we investigate arotating two-component Bose-Einstein condensate, composed of bosons withdifferent masses. We find that in the case of sufficiently strong interspeciesattraction, the vortex lattices of the two condensates lock and rotate at thedrive frequency, while the superfluids themselves rotate at two differentvelocities, whose ratio is the ratio between the particle mass of the twospecies. In this paper, we characterize the vortex-locked state, establish itsregime of stability, and find that it surives within a disk smaller than acritical radius, beyond which vortices become unbound, and the two Bose-gasrings rotate together at the frequency of the external drive.

The morphological properties and gravitational stabilities of molecular cloud cores in the Orion giant molecular cloud complex are investigated using near-infrared dust extinction maps and far-infrared dust continuum emission maps from the Herschel Gould Belt survey. The column density profiles of 47 starless cores are fit with Bonnor-Ebert sphere models to characterize their internal density structures and compare with theoretical predictions. These results suggest that pre-stellar cores may approximate Bonnor-Ebert structures which are however of variable mass and may or may not experience gravitational collapse, in qualitative agreement with the large observed frequency of cores with BE-like profiles. Multiple cores demonstrate significant departures from spherical symmetry with ellipticities suggesting preferential global collapse along filamentary axes. Additionally, the parameter space of observed core masses and radii indicate that only a subset reach the critical Bonnor-Ebert mass above which gravitational collapse is inevitable on a free-fall timescale. We therefore propose a picture where core morphologies are strongly influenced by the larger-scale filamentary structure of Orion, with aspect ratios and stabilities regulated by core formation and evolution within molecular cloud filaments.

The peculiar nature of electron scattering in graphene is among many excitingtheoretical predictions for the physical properties of this material. Toinvestigate electron scattering properties in a graphene plane, we have createda gate-tunable potential barrier within a single-layer graphene sheet. Wereport measurements of electrical transport across this structure as thetunable barrier potential is swept through a range of heights. This note relates topics in statistical mechanics, graph theory andcombinatorics, lattice quantum field theory, super quantum mechanics and stringtheory. Cosmological shock waves result from supersonic flow motions induced byhierarchical clustering of nonlinear structures in the universe. These shocksgovern the nature of cosmic plasma through thermalization of gas andacceleration of nonthermal, cosmic-ray (CR) particles. We study the statisticsand energetics of shocks formed in cosmological simulations of a concordance$\Lambda$CDM universe, with a special emphasis on the effects ofnon-gravitational processes such as radiative cooling, photoionization/heating,and galactic superwind feedbacks. Adopting an improved model for gasthermalization and CR acceleration efficiencies based on nonlinear diffusiveshock acceleration calculations, we then estimate the gas thermal energy andthe CR energy dissipated at shocks through the history of the universe. Sinceshocks can serve as sites for generation of vorticity, we also examine thevorticity that should have been generated mostly at curved shocks incosmological simulations. We find that the dynamics and energetics of shocksare governed primarily by the gravity of matter, so other non-gravitationalprocesses do not affect significantly the global energy dissipation andvorticity generation at cosmological shocks. Our results reinforce scenarios inwhich the intracluster medium and warm-hot intergalactic medium containenergetically significant populations of nonthermal particles and turbulentflow motions.

Using the correlation functions of the vector and scalar currents, we study their mixing and extract information about the properties of the mesons in the medium. The properties of the mesons can be modified in the medium by the interactions between hadrons and quarks. Our analysis shows that the mixing is significant in the medium. The results give insight into the properties of hadrons in the medium and can be used to understand hadron-hadron interactions in dense nuclei. Moreover, we estimate the two-quark component of the scalar meson in the medium.

Stochastic resonance, a phenomenon observed in a variety of complex systems, involves the amplification of weak signals in the presence of noise. In this study, we investigate aspects of stochastic resonance in reaction-diffusion systems using the nonequilibrium-potential approach. By considering the interplay between nonlinear reaction kinetics and diffusive processes, we demonstrate the emergence of stochastic resonance in such systems. Specifically, we analyze the response of the reaction-diffusion system to weak periodic forcing and examine the conditions under which stochastic resonance occurs. Our results reveal that the presence of noise can enhance the system's sensitivity to weak signals, leading to a resonant amplification of the signal. We also explore the role of system parameters, such as the noise strength and the reaction rates, in shaping the stochastic resonance behavior. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings for understanding and predicting the dynamics of reaction-diffusion systems in nonequilibrium conditions. Overall, our study provides new insights into the rich behavior of stochastic resonance in complex reaction-diffusion systems, highlighting the importance of noise in modulating their dynamical responses.

This pedagogical review aims at presenting the fundamental aspects of thetheory of inflationary cosmological perturbations of quantum-mechanical origin.The analogy with the well-known Schwinger effect is discussed in detail and asystematic comparison of the two physical phenomena is carried out. Inparticular, it is demonstrated that the two underlying formalisms differ onlyup to an irrelevant canonical transformation. Hence, the basic physicalmechanisms at play are similar in both cases and can be reduced to thequantization of a parametric oscillator leading to particle creation due to theinteraction with a classical source: pair production in vacuum is thereforeequivalent to the appearance of a growing mode for the cosmologicalfluctuations. The only difference lies in the nature of the source: an electricfield in the case of the Schwinger effect and the gravitational field in thecase of inflationary perturbations. Although, in the laboratory, it isnotoriously difficult to produce an electric field such that pairs extractedfrom the vacuum can be detected, the gravitational field in the early universecan be strong enough to lead to observable effects that ultimately revealthemselves as temperature fluctuations in the Cosmic Microwave Background.Finally, the question of how quantum cosmological perturbations can beconsidered as classical is discussed at the end of the article.

This article explores the relationship between nonimmersions of real projective spaces (RP^n) and topological modular forms (tmf) in the field of differential topology. Nonimmersions, which are mappings that do not satisfy the conditions of being immersions, have been of significant interest in this area. By examining the impact of tmf, a spectrum associated with elliptic genera and modular forms, we aim to gain further insights into nonimmersions of RP^n.Expanding on previous research, we investigate the consequences of tmf on the existence of nonimmersions in RP^n, utilizing recent advancements in both tmf theory and differential topology. Our analysis covers various dimensions, specifically exploring nonimmersions in RP^n with n greater than or equal to 3.Through a combination of theoretical arguments and computational methods, we demonstrate the profound implications of tmf on the existence of nonimmersions in RP^n. Our findings reveal a strong interplay between the algebraic structure of tmf and the geometric properties of RP^n, illuminating deeper connections between these two fields of study.Furthermore, we present a comprehensive classification of nonimmersions in RP^n under the influence of tmf, unveiling distinct patterns and structures that arise in different dimensions. This classification provides a valuable tool for comprehending the intricate nature of nonimmersions and their relationship with tmf.Lastly, we discuss the potential implications of our results for related disciplines, including algebraic topology, differential geometry, and mathematical physics. By revisiting the connection between tmf and nonimmersions of RP^n, we contribute to a broader understanding of these fundamental concepts and pave the way for future investigations and applications in mathematics.

This study investigates the synergistic affecting of molybdenum dithiocarbamate (MoDTC) and zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDTP) ingredients on the frictional behavior of tribofilms at the nanometer scale. The tribological properties of these additives have been extensively considering solely, but the combined effects are not yet well understood. In this research, a custom-designed nanoscale tribometer was utilized to analyze the frictional behavior and wear characteristics of tribofilms posed by MoDTC, ZDTP, and their melting. The results exhibit that the combination of MoDTC and ZDTP exhibits superior friction-reducing properties compared to the especial additives, leading to increasing wear resistance and improved lubricant performance at the nanometer scale. These findings provide valuable insights into the design and development of next-generation lubricant additives with improved tribological fulfilment.

We consider the problem of quantization of classical soliton integrablesystems, such as the KdV hierarchy, in the framework of a general formalism ofGaudin models associated to affine Kac--Moody algebras. Our experience with theGaudin models associated to finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras suggeststhat the common eigenvalues of the mutually commuting quantum Hamiltonians in amodel associated to an affine algebra should be encoded by affine opersassociated to the Langlands dual affine algebra. This leads us to some concretepredictions for the spectra of the quantum Hamiltonians of the soliton systems.In particular, for the KdV system the corresponding affine opers may beexpressed as Schroedinger operators with spectral parameter, and ourpredictions in this case match those recently made by Bazhanov, Lukyanov andZamolodchikov. This suggests that this and other recently found examples of thecorrespondence between quantum integrals of motion and differential operatorsmay be viewed as special cases of the Langlands duality.

Measurable spectra are theoretically very often derived from complicatedmany-body Green's functions. In this way, one calculates much more informationthan actually needed. Here we present an in principle exact approach toconstruct effective potentials and kernels for the direct calculation ofelectronic spectra. In particular, the potential that yields the spectralfunction needed to describe photoemission turns out to be dynamical but {\itlocal} and {\it real}. As example we illustrate this ''photoemissionpotential'' for sodium and aluminium, modelled as homogeneous electron gas, anddiscuss in particular its frequency dependence stemming from the nonlocality ofthe corresponding self-energy. We also show that our approach leads to a veryshort derivation of a kernel that is known to well describe absorption andenergy-loss spectra of a wide range of materials.

In this study, we investigate the formation of vortices in Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) that have been prepared by merging multiple trapped condensates. We explore the effects of the relative phases of the different condensates and the removal rate of the optical potential on the formation of vortices. Our results show that the instant removal of the optical potential leads to the creation of many vortices, regardless of the relative phases of the condensates. In contrast, gradually ramping down the intensity of the optical potential results in fewer vortices being created, and self-annihilation of vortices of opposite charge is observed. We also find that the initial relative phases between the condensates leave a clear imprint on the resulting topological configuration. Finally, we study the three-dimensional system and observe the formation of vortex lines and vortex rings due to the merger of the BEC fragments. Our results provide insight into the dynamics of vortex formation in BECs and have important implications for the study of quantum turbulence and superfluidity.

We utilised indirect resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) to investigate magnetic excitations in the cuprate parent compound La2CuO4. RIXS is a photon-in photon-out technique that provides element-specific information on electronic and magnetic excitations in solids. Previous studies of La2CuO4 have focused on characterising its magnetic ground state using neutron scattering. In this work, we measured RIXS spectra as a function of incident photon energy and momentum transfer to identify electronic transitions corresponding to excitations out of the ground state. We observed clear dispersive features in the Cu L3-edge that we assign to spin wave excitations in the square-planar CuO2 layers. By comparing to linear spin wave theory, we extract exchange coupling constants and estimate an effective magnetic exchange energy scale of 130 meV for Cu spins in La2CuO4. Additionally, our results show strong damping of high-energy spin excitations. This study demonstrates the potential of RIXS to directly probe magnetic interactions and dynamics in prototypical cuprate materials.

We give a detailed critical discussion of the properties of Wilsonianeffective actions, defined by integrating out all modes above a given scale$\mu$. In particular, we provide a precise and relatively convenientprescription how to implement the infrared cutoff $\mu$ in any loop integralthat is manifestly Lorentz invariant and also preserves global linearsymmetries such as e.g. supersymmetry. We discuss the issue of gauge invarianceof effective actions in general and in particular when using background fieldgauge. Our prescription for the IR cutoff (as any such prescription) breaks thegauge symmetry. Using our prescription, we have explicitly computed, at oneloop, many terms of the Wilsonian effective action for general gauge theories,involving bosonic and fermionic matter fields of arbitrary masses and inarbitrary representations, exhibiting the non-gauge invariant (as well as thegauge invariant) terms. However, for supersymmetric gauge theories allnon-gauge invariant terms cancel within each supermultiplet. This is strongevidence that in supersymmetric gauge theories this indeed defines a Lorentz,susy and gauge invariant Wilsonian effective action. As a byproduct, we obtainthe explicit one-loop Wilsonian couplings for all higher-derivative terms $FD^{2n}F$ in the effective action of arbitrary supersymmetric gauge theories.

Double neutron star systems provide valuable insights into the formation device of neutron stars. Our analysis focuses on a comprehensive sample of 50 double atomic star systems, obtained from extensive insights and data analysis of various astronomical surveys and observations. By characterizing the mass ratios and orbital parameters of these systems, we identify spaced subsets that exhibit widely different properties. The first subset contains systems with nearly equal-mass radioactivity stars and tight orbits, indicating a formation pathway involving the collapse of binary massive stars. These systems are consistent with the popular scenario of core-collapse supernovae leading to the establishing and subsequent merger of neutron stars. The second subset, however, consists of systems with disparate mass ratios and wider orbits, suggesting an alternative framing channel. We propose that these appliance arise from a different systems involving the accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs in binary systems. Through detailed population synthesis simulations, we demonstrate the plausibility of these two distinct formation menus. The observed properties of the double neutron star systems are so reproduced by our storyboards, supporting the validity of our proposed formation mechanisms. The different establishments channels likely arise due to the interplay between binary evolution, mass transfer practices, and various end states of massive stars and white dwarfs. Overall, our findings describing the significance of double neutron star devices in unraveling the intricate processes behind the birth of neutron stars. Understanding the ranging of formation pathways enhances our knowledge of stellar evolution, binary interactions, and the physical possessions of neutron stars.

In a previous paper, new sets of parameters to replace the Michel parameterswere proposed to analyze data for the muon decay $\mu^{+} \toe^{+}\nu_{e}\bar{\nu_{\mu}}$. We find that there is a simple formin which the set of parameters is related primitively to the physicalquantities. It is shown that the Michel parameters are one of the other setsthat are obtained from this simple form by rearranging one term. It is useful to compare the value obtained in theleast squares fit using the simple form with that obtained using the predictionof the standard model, because a large difference is not expected, especiallyin the case of the Majorana neutrino. Finally, we point out that the method weproposed to determine the type of neutrino in the previous paper is incorrect.

We calculate the light meson spectrum and the light quark masses by latticeQCD simulation, treating all light quarks dynamically and employing the Iwasakigluon action and the nonperturbatively O(a)-improved Wilson quark action. These values contain the previousestimates obtained with the dynamical u and d quarks within the error.

We analyze fading interference relay networks where M single-antennasource-destination terminal pairs communicate concurrently and in the samefrequency band through a set of K single-antenna relays using half-duplextwo-hop relaying. Assuming that the relays have channel state information(CSI), it is shown that in the large-M limit, provided K grows fast enough as afunction of M, the network "decouples" in the sense that the individualsource-destination terminal pair capacities are strictly positive. Thecorresponding required rate of growth of K as a function of M is found to besufficient to also make the individual source-destination fading links convergeto nonfading links. We say that the network "crystallizes" as it breaks up intoa set of effectively isolated "wires in the air". A large-deviations analysisis performed to characterize the "crystallization" rate, i.e., the rate (as afunction of M,K) at which the decoupled links converge to nonfading links. Inthe course of this analysis, we develop a new technique for characterizing thelarge-deviations behavior of certain sums of dependent random variables. Forthe case of no CSI at the relay level, assuming amplify-and-forward relaying,we compute the per source-destination terminal pair capacity for M,K convergingto infinity, with K/M staying fixed, using tools from large random matrixtheory.

In the collinear factorization of the form factor for the transition$\gamma^* \pi^0 \to \gamma$ the hard part contains double log terms as $\ln^2x$ with $x$ as the momentum fraction of partons from 0 to 1. A simpleexponentiation for resummation leads to divergent results. We study theresummation of these $\ln^2 x$ terms. We show that the $\ln^2 x$ terms comepartly from the light-cone wave function(LCWF) and partly from the form factor.We introduce a jet factor to factorize the $\ln^2 x$ term in the form factor.To handel the $\ln^2 x$ terms from the LCWF we introduce a nonstandardlight-cone wave function(NLCWF) with the gauge links off the light-conedirection. An interesting relation between two wave function is found. With theintroduced NLCWF and the jet factor we can re-factorize the form factor andobtain a new hard part which does not contain terms with $\ln^2 x$. Beside therenormalization scale $\mu$ the introduce NLCWF and jet factor have extrascales to characterize their $x$-behaviors. Using the evolutions of the extrascales and the relation we can do the resummation perturbatively in sense thatthe LCWF is the only nonpertubative object in the resumed formula. Our resultswith some models of LCWF show that there is a significant difference betweennumerical predictions with the resummation and that without the resummation,and the resummed predictions can describe the experimental data.

We conjecture that the set of all Hilbert functions of (artinian) levelalgebras enjoys a very natural form of regularity, which we call the {\emInterval Conjecture} (IC): If, for some positive integer $\alpha $,$(1,h_1,...,h_i,...,h_e)$ and $(1,h_1,...,h_i+\alpha ,...,h_e)$ are both level$h$-vectors, then $(1,h_1,...,h_i+\beta ,...,h_e)$ is also level for eachinteger $\beta =0,1,..., \alpha .$ In the Gorenstein case, i.e. when $h_e=1$,we also supply the {\em Gorenstein Interval Conjecture} (GIC), which naturallygeneralizes the IC, and basically states that the same property simultaneouslyholds for any two symmetric entries, say $h_i$ and $h_{e-i}$, of a Gorenstein$h$-vector. These conjectures are inspired by the research performed in this area overthe last few years. A series of recent results seems to indicate that it willbe nearly impossible to characterize explicitly the sets of all Gorenstein orof all level Hilbert functions. Therefore, our conjectures would at leastprovide the existence of a very strong - and natural - form of order in thestructure of such important and complicated sets. We are still far from proving the conjectures at this point. However, we willalready solve a few interesting cases, especially when it comes to the IC, inthis paper. Among them, that of Gorenstein $h$-vectors of socle degree 4, thatof level $h$-vectors of socle degree 2, and that of non-unimodal level$h$-vectors of socle degree 3 and any given codimension.

We study prime algebras of quadratic growth. Our first result is that if $A$is a prime monomial algebra of quadratic growth then $A$ has finitely manyprime ideals $P$ such that $A/P$ has GK dimension one. This shows that primemonomial algebras of quadratic growth have bounded matrix images. We next showthat a prime graded algebra of quadratic growth has the property that theintersection of the nonzero prime ideals $P$ such that $A/P$ has GK dimension 2is non-empty, provided there is at least one such ideal. From this we concludethat a prime monomial algebra of quadratic growth is either primitive or hasnonzero locally nilpotent Jacobson radical. Finally, we show that there existsa prime monomial algebra $A$ of GK dimension two with unbounded matrix imagesand thus the quadratic growth hypothesis is necessary to conclude that thereare only finitely many prime ideals such that $A/P$ has GK dimension 1.

Power control is a fundamental task accomplished in any wireless cellularnetwork; its aim is to set the transmit power of any mobile terminal, so thateach user is able to achieve its own target SINR. While conventional powercontrol algorithms require knowledge of a number of parameters of the signal ofinterest and of the multiaccess interference, in this paper it is shown that ina large CDMA system much of this information can be dispensed with, andeffective distributed power control algorithms may be implemented with verylittle information on the user of interest. An uplink CDMA system subject toflat fading is considered with a focus on the cases in which a linear MMSEreceiver and a non-linear MMSE serial interference cancellation receiver areadopted; for the latter case new formulas are also given for the system SINR inthe large system asymptote. Experimental results show an excellent agreementbetween the performance and the power profile of the proposed distributedalgorithms and that of conventional ones that require much greater priorknowledge.

The organization of the connectivity between mammalian cortical areas hasbecome a major subject of study, because of its important role in scaffoldingthe macroscopic aspects of animal behavior and intelligence. In this study wepresent a computational reconstruction approach to the problem of networkorganization, by considering the topological and spatial features of each areain the primate cerebral cortex as subsidy for the reconstruction of the globalcortical network connectivity. Starting with all areas being disconnected,pairs of areas with similar sets of features are linked together, in an attemptto recover the original network structure. Inferring primate corticalconnectivity from the properties of the nodes, remarkably good reconstructionsof the global network organization could be obtained, with the topologicalfeatures allowing slightly superior accuracy to the spatial ones. Analogousreconstruction attempts for the C. elegans neuronal network resulted insubstantially poorer recovery, indicating that cortical area interconnectionsare relatively stronger related to the considered topological and spatialproperties than neuronal projections in the nematode. The close relationshipbetween area-based features and global connectivity may hint on developmentalrules and constraints for cortical networks. Particularly, differences betweenthe predictions from topological and spatial properties, together with thepoorer recovery resulting from spatial properties, indicate that theorganization of cortical networks is not entirely determined by spatialconstraints.

We study the moduli space $\fM^s(6;3,6,4)$ of simple rank 6 vector bundles$\E$ on $\PP^3$ with Chern polynomial $1+3t+6t^2+4t^3$ and properties of thesebundles, especially we prove some partial results concerning their stability.We first recall how these bundles are related to the construction of sexticnodal surfaces in $\PP^3$ having an even set of 56 nodes (cf. \cite{CaTo}). Weprove that there is an open set, corresponding to the simple bundles withminimal cohomology, which is irreducible of dimension 19 and bimeromorphic toan open set $\fA^0$ of the G.I.T. quotient space of the projective space$\fB:=\{B\in \PP(U^\vee\otimes W\otimes V^\vee)\}$ of triple tensors of type$(3,3,4)$ by the natural action of $SL(W)\times SL(U)$. We give severalconstructions for these bundles, which relate them to cubic surfaces in 3-space$\PP^3$ and to cubic surfaces in the dual space $(\PP^3)^{\vee}$. One of theseconstructions, suggested by Igor Dolgachev, generalizes to other types oftensors. Moreover, we relate the socalled {\em cross-product involution} for$(3,3,4)$-tensors, introduced in \cite{CaTo}, with the Schur quadric associatedto a cubic surface in $\PP^3$ and study further properties of this involution.

Counting hyperelliptic curves admitting Koblitz models. In this paper, we study the problem of enumerating hyperelliptic curves defined over a finite field that admit a Koblitz model. We provide an explicit formula for the number of such curves in terms of the curve's genus and the finite field's size. Our formula is based on a novel method for constructing hyperelliptic curves with a Koblitz model. Additionally, we present an algorithm for finding all such curves up to a specified genus and field size. Our results are applicable to constructing elliptic curve cryptosystems and studying the arithmetic of hyperelliptic curves.

We report the detection of CO(3-2) emission from a bright, gravitationallylensed Lyman Break Galaxy, LBGJ213512.73-010143 (the 'Cosmic Eye'), at z=3.07using the Plateau de Bure Interferometer. This is only the second detection ofmolecular gas emission from an LBG and yields an intrinsic molecular gas massof (2.4+/-0.4)x10^9 Mo. The lens reconstruction of the UV morphology of the LBGindicates that it comprises two components separated by ~2 kpc. The CO emissionis unresolved, and appears to be centered on the intrinsically fainter (andalso less highly magnified) of the two UV components. The width of the CO lineindicates a dynamical mass of (8+/-2)x10^9csc(i)^2 Mo within the central 2 kpc.Employing mid-infrared observations from Spitzer we derive a stellar mass of~(6+/-2)x10^9 Mo and a star-formation rate of ~60 Mo/yr, indicating that themolecular gas will be consumed in ~40 Myr. The gas fractions, star-formationefficiencies and line widths suggests that LBGJ213512 is a high-redshift,gas-rich analog of a local luminous infrared galaxy. This galaxy has a similargas-to-dynamical mass fraction as observed in the submillimeter-selectedpopulation, although the gas surface density and star-formation efficiency is afactor of 3x less, suggesting less vigorous activity. We discuss theuncertainties in our conclusions arising from adopting a CO-to-H2 conversionfactor appropriate for either the Milky Way or local luminous infraredgalaxies. These observations demonstrate that current facilities, when aided byfortuitous gravitational magnification, can study 'ordinary' galaxies athigh-redshift and so act as pathfinders for ALMA.

This article investigates the problem of detecting non-trivial topologies in data. Specifically, we consider the question of whether it is possible to distinguish between topologies that are merely trivial variations of each other, and those that genuinely exhibit different structural properties. Our approach leverages techniques from algebraic topology, which allows us to capture the fundamental characteristics of the data and identify meaningful features that can be used to differentiate between topologies. Through a series of case studies, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method and show that it can be used to identify non-trivial topologies in a variety of contexts. Our findings have important implications for the analysis and understanding of complex data sets, and contribute to the development of more robust and reliable methods for detecting meaningful patterns in data.

We perform a series of two-dimensional magnetorotational core-collapsesimulations of Pop III stars. Changing the initial distributions of rotationand magnetic fields prior to collapse in a parametric manner, we compute 19models. By so doing, we systematically investigate how rotation and magneticfields affect the collapse dynamics and explore how the properties of theblack-hole formations and neutrino emissions could be affected. As for themicrophysics, we employ a realistic equation of state and approximate theneutrino transfer by a multiflavour leakage scheme. With these computations, wefind that the jet-like explosions are obtained by the magnetodriven shock wavesif the initial magnetic field is as large as $10^{12}$ G. We point out that theblack-hole masses at the formation decrease with the initial field strength, onthe other hand, increase with the initial rotation rates. As for the neutrinoproperties, we point out that the degree of the differential rotation plays animportant role to determine which species of the neutrino luminosity is moredominant than the others. Furthermore, we find that the stronger magneticfields make the peak neutrino luminosities smaller, because the magneticpressure acts to halt the collapse in the central regions, leading to thesuppression of the releasable gravitational binding energies.

Parametric resonant systems exhibit exponential growth when driven near twice their natural frequency. This exponential growth can be suppressed through the addition of multiplicative white noise to the system. We study how the introduction of multiplicative white noise affects the growth rate of a simple parametric resonant system. Through numerical simulations, we find that above a threshold noise amplitude, the exponential growth is completely arrested. Below this threshold, the noise acts to slow the overall growth rate in a manner depending on the noise intensity. The noise alters the bifurcation structure of the system, converting a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation to a subcritical one. An analytic calculation of the effective Lyapunov exponent allows us to characterize how the growth rate varies with noise intensity. This suppression of growth has implications for stochastic resonance and energy transport in parametrically driven systems subjected to fluctuations.

We derive the exact solution for the optical conductivity $\sigma(\omega)$ ofone hole in the Holstein-t-J model in the framework of dynamical mean-fieldtheory (DMFT). We investigate the magnetic and phonon features associated withpolaron formation as a function of the exchange coupling $J$, of theelectron-phonon interaction $\lambda$ and of the temperature. Our solutiondirectly relates the features of the optical conductivity to the excitations inthe single-particle spectral function, revealing two distinct mechanisms ofclosing and filling of the optical pseudogap that take place upon varying themicroscopic parameters. We show that the optical absorption at the polaroncrossover is characterized by a coexistence of a magnon peak at low frequencyand a broad polaronic band at higher frequency. An analytical expression for$\sigma(\omega)$ valid in the polaronic regime is presented.

We use the direct Fourier method to calculate the redshift-space powerspectrum of the maxBCG cluster catalog (Koester et al. 2007) -- currently byfar the largest existing galaxy cluster sample. The total number of clustersused in our analysis is 12,616. After accounting for the radial smearing effectcaused by photometric redshift errors and also introducing a simple treatmentfor the nonlinear effects, we show that currently favored low matter density''concordance'' LambdaCDM cosmology provides a very good fit to the estimatedpower. Thanks to the large volume (~ 0.4 h^{-3} Gpc^3), high clusteringamplitude (linear effective bias parameter b_{eff} ~ 3x(0.85/sigma_8)), andsufficiently high sampling density (~ 3x10^{-5} h^{3} Mpc^{-3}) the recoveredpower spectrum has high enough signal to noise to allow us to find weakevidence (~ 2sigma CL) for the acoustic features. These results are encouragingin light of the several proposed large cluster surveys. In case we use thephotometric redshift errors as suggested in Koester et al. (2007) we are leftwith the excess large-scale power which has previously been noticed by severalother authors.

In this work, we extend our previous effort by considering spatially covariant averaging methods in the context of General Relativity. In this way, the averaging procedure can be carried out without the need to choose a foliation of spacetime. We perform a perturbative treatment of the Einstein equations, with a particular focus on terms of first order in the inhomogeneities, and provide a physical interpretation for each term. In particular, we show how these terms are related to a number of interesting effects such as the local-to-global bias and the tidal acceleration of peculiar velocities. Finally, we apply our findings to a simple cosmological model to demonstrate how the averaged equations can be used to investigate cosmic acceleration and dark energy.

Massive merging black holes will be the primary sources of powerfulgravitational waves at low frequency, and will permit to test generalrelativity with candidate galaxies close to a binary black hole merger. In thispaper we identify the typical mass ratio of the two black holes but then showthat the distance when gravitational radiation becomes the dominant dissipativeeffect (over dynamical friction) does not depend on the mass ratio. However thedynamical evolution in the gravitational wave emission regime does. For thetypical range of mass ratios the final stage of the merger is preceded by arapid precession and a subsequent spin-flip of the main black hole. Thisalready occurs in the inspiral phase, therefore can be described analyticallyby post-Newtonian techniques. We then identify the radio galaxies with asuper-disk as those in which the rapidly precessing jet produces effectively apowerful wind, entraining the environmental gas to produce the appearance of athick disk. These specific galaxies are thus candidates for a merger of twoblack holes to happen in the astronomically near future.

We present a novel experiment with the capacity to independently measure boththe electron density and the magnetic field of the solar corona. We achievethis through measurement of the excess Faraday rotation due to propagation ofthe polarised emission from a number of pulsars through the magnetic field ofthe solar corona. This method yields independent measures of the integratedelectron density, via dispersion of the pulsed signal and the magnetic field,via the amount of Faraday rotation. In principle this allows the determinationof the integrated magnetic field through the solar corona along many lines ofsight without any assumptions regarding the electron density distribution. Wepresent a detection of an increase in the rotation measure of the pulsarJ1801$-$2304 of approximately 160 \rad at an elongation of 0.95$^\circ$ fromthe centre of the solar disk. This corresponds to a lower limit of the magneticfield strength along this line of sight of $> 393\mu\mathrm{G}$. The lack ofprecision in the integrated electron density measurement restricts this resultto a limit, but application of coronal plasma models can further constrain thisto approximately 20mG, along a path passing 2.5 solar radii from the solarlimb. Which is consistent with predictions obtained using extensions to theSource Surface models published by Wilcox Solar Observatory

Coulomb excitation of the exotic neutron-rich nucleus $^{26}$Ne on a$^{nat}$Pb target was measured at 58 A.MeV in order to search for low-lying E1strength above the neutron emission threshold. Data were also taken on an$^{nat}$Al target to estimate the nuclear contribution. The radioactive beamwas produced by fragmentation of a 95 A.MeV $^{40}$Ar beam delivered by theRIKEN Research Facility. The set-up included a NaI gamma-ray array, a chargedfragment hodoscope and a neutron wall. Using the invariant mass method in the$^{25}$Ne+n channel, we observe a sizable amount of E1 strength between 6 and10 MeV. The reconstructed $^{26}$Ne angular distribution confirms its E1nature. A reduced dipole transition probability of B(E1)=0.49$\pm$0.16$e^2fm^2$ is deduced. For the first time, the decay pattern of low-lyingstrength in a neutron-rich nucleus is obtained. The results are discussed interms of a pygmy resonance centered around 9 MeV.

This article investigates the mechanisms underlying the trafficking of glutamate receptors in hippocampal neurons. Using live cell imaging and quantitative analysis, the authors show that glutamate receptors use both lateral diffusion in the plane of the membrane and intracellular vesicle transport to reach synaptic sites. By combining these two modes of transport, the neuron can rapidly and efficiently deliver glutamate receptors to synapses as needed to regulate synaptic strength and plasticity.

The coupling between nuclear collective motion and individual nucleonic degrees of freedom, known as particle-vibration coupling (PVC), is an important nuclear constructions effect that needs to be properly reflected for in theorist nuclear structure templates. In this article, we browsing a microscopic treatment of PVC within the framework of covariant density functional theory (CDFT). We derive and run an correct particle-phonon coupling formalism based on a single-particle actress of the nuclear collective vibrations computed with the quasiparticle random phase approximation on top of CDFT mean-field states. We present results for PVC corrections to single-particle energies throughout the nuclear chart and consideration their isotopic dependence. The impact of PVC on nuclear properties like binds energies, radii, and low-lying excitations is analyzed. We find non-negligible PVC contributions that help restore spin-orbit splittings and bombed closures modified by CDFT mean-field dynamics. Overall, this work jette a fully self-consistent framework to included dynamical correlations beyond the mean-field in covariant energy density functionals.

This paper furnishes new measurements of the chemical abundances of 15 contents in 12 damped Lyman-alpha (DLA) systems toward background quasars. This collection more than doubles the number of DLAs with high-quality abundance measurements. Ourselves present new insights into the metallicity-redshift relation and the chemical evolution of DLAs, and explore the dependence of the abundances on other properties such as the velocity range of the DLA, the touches parameter between the quasar sightline and the centre of the foreground galaxy, and the presence of coupled sub-DLAs. Our results show that the median DLA metallicity increases with redshift and that the abundance ratios of most elements track the conduct seen in Milky How and Larger Magellanic Cloud stars of similar metallicities. The relative abundances of elements produced by different nucleosynthetic processes are remarkably constant in the redshift continuum 1.75 < z_abs < 3.5; this is in disparity with what is seen in absorption-selected galaxies and quasar emission-line arrondissement. We measure a largest frequency of associated sub-DLAs, which we identify to be less metal-rich than the main DLAs, confirming that sub-DLAs probe lower-metallicity gas. Our sample also contains a few DLAs that exhibit unmistakably signatures of inflows or outflows, which we exploiting to rising insights into the physical processes responsible for the chemical enrichment of DLAs. We pinpoint a lier between the oxygen bountiful and the velocity sizes of the DLA, which we interpret as an effect of galactic winds and/or mergers, and an anti-correlation between the oxygen abundance and the collide parameter, which we attribute to the spatial distribution of metals within the host galaxies.

The distributed source coding network is becoming more and more important for collecting and transmitting sensor data. However, such networks are vulnerable to damage to the damaged sensor transmission of incorrect data. This article proposes a new variable rate distributed source coding scheme, which is robust for Byzantine sensors that destroy the transmission data. The transmission rate is allocated to each sensor based on the correlation observed between sensor data. By analysis and simulation display, the proposed scheme can achieve effective distributed coding performance when detecting and reducing the influence of Byzantine sensors that transmit any data. Compared with the existing method, the variable -rate coding scheme provides an increased elasticity for Byzantine sensors.

A latin bitrade is a pair of partial latin squares which are disjoint, occupythe same set of non-empty cells, and whose corresponding rows and columnscontain the same set of entries. Dr\'apal (\cite{Dr9}) showed that a latinbitrade is equivalent to three derangements whose product is the identity andwhose cycles pairwise have at most one point in common. By letting a group acton itself by right translation, we show how some latin bitrades may be derivedfrom groups without specifying an independent group action. Properties of latintrades such as homogeneousness, minimality (via thinness) and orthogonality mayalso be encoded succinctly within the group structure. We apply theconstruction to some well-known groups, constructing previously unknown latinbitrades. In particular, we show the existence of minimal, $k$-homogeneouslatin trades for each odd $k\geq 3$. In some cases these are the smallest knownsuch examples.

Mammoths lived in Arctic East Siberia. In this region there is not sufficientsunlight over the year for the growth of the plants on which these animalsfeed. Therefore the latitude of this region was lower before the end of thePleistocene. As the cause of this geographic pole shift, we postulate a massiveobject, which moved in an extremely eccentric orbit and was hot from tidal workand solar radiation. Evaporation produced a disk-shaped cloud of ions aroundthe Sun. This cloud partially shielded the solar radiation, producing the coldand warm periods that characterize the Pleistocene. The shielding depends onthe inclination of Earth's orbit, which has a period of 100'000 years. Thecloud builds up to a density at which inelastic particle collisions induce itscollapse The resulting near-periodic time dependence resembles that ofDansgaard-Oeschger events. During cold periods fine grained inclusions weredeposited into the ice. The Pleistocene ended when the massive object had aclose encounter with the Earth, which suffered a one per mil stretchingdeformation. While the deformation relaxed to an equilibrium shape in one toseveral years, the globe turned relative to the rotation axis: The North Polemoved from Greenland to the Arctic Sea. The massive object was torn to pieces,which evaporated.

The advancement of molecular dynamics simulation techniOues has played a crucial role in understanding the behavior and properties of thermodynamical systems at the atomic sacle. Achieving accurJate and efficient simulations requires the development of robust algorithms that conserve energy and momentum. In this study, we propose an effective conservation of energy and momentum algorithm utilizign switching potentials. By introducing a swtching function that alters the potential energy and forces acting between atoms at specific distaces, we ensure a smooth transition between different interaction models. This approach oveyrcomes the limitations of traditional cutoff-based methods and maintains accurate conservation of energy and momentum throughout the simulaion. The algorithm is applicabQe to a wide raneg of molecular systems and has been thoroughly validated through extensive simulations of various thermodynamical systems. Our findings demonstrate that the switching potentials algorithm significantly improves the accuracy and efficiency of molecular dynamis simulations, enhancign our ability to investigate ocmplex and dynamic molecular systems under realistic conditions.

In this study, we investigate the phenomenon of plasmon expand through stimulated emission at terahertz (THz) frequencies in graphene. Plasmons, collective oscillations of electron density, have emerged as promising candidates for nanoscale signal processing and sensing applicant. By exploiting the unique immovable of graphene, such as its strong coupling with THz radiation and highly tunable Fermi level, we demonstrate the feasibility of obtain plasmon broadened through stimulated emission in this material. We employ theoretical modeling and simulations to examination the amplification mechanism and optimize the relevant parameters for efficient plasmonic obtain. Our findings pave the way for the develops of graphene-based THz plasmonic devices with enhanced signal manipulation capabilities.

We present the results of a study aimed at identifying blue horizontal branch (BHB) star candidates using ultraviolet photometry from the Galaxy Evolution Explorer (GALEX) satellite combined with optical photometry from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS). BHB stars occupy a distinct region in UV-optical color-color space, allowing for robust selection techniques. By jointly fitting GALEX Far-Ultraviolet and Near-Ultraviolet magnitudes with SDSS ugriz photometry, we develop spectral energy distribution models of BHB stars at metallicities ranging from [Fe/H] = -2.5 to solar. The models are used to select BHB star candidates from over 14,000 known point sources detected in both GALEX and SDSS photometric footprints within 20 degrees of the Galactic plane. Follow-up spectroscopic observations of 100 candidate stars verify the selection method, with a confirmation rate of over 90%.
